fix: Remove '.py' from one of the two lists to make the intent unambiguous — either drop it from allowed_extensions if executable/script uploads should never be permitted, or drop it from dangerous_extensions if .py uploads are an intentional supported use case (and instead rely on content-based scanning/sandboxing for that case).

title: CORS allowed_origins defaults to wildcard '*'
detail: `SecurityConfig.allowed_origins` (line 100) defaults to `["*"]`. If this default is consumed directly by CORS middleware elsewhere without being overridden via `SECURITY_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` in production, any origin can make cross-origin requests to the API, which is risky if credentials/cookies are also allowed.
fix: Default to a restrictive value (e.g. empty list or an explicit local dev origin) and require SECURITY_ALLOWED_ORIGINS to be set explicitly for any non-dev deployment, or add a startup check in validate_config() that warns/fails if allowed_origins is still '*' when debug=False.

title: Synchronous SQLAlchemy DB calls executed directly inside async def token-storage methods, blocking the event loop
detail: get_tokens/set_tokens/get_client_info/set_client_info (lines 119-133) are `async def` but call the plain synchronous helpers `_load()`/`_update()` (lines 92-117), which open a SQLAlchemy Session and run `db.query(...).first()` / `db.commit()` synchronously on the calling coroutine — no `run_in_executor`/`asyncio.to_thread`. The `mcp` SDK's OAuthClientProvider awaits these on every token refresh and on every outgoing MCP request that needs a bearer token, so every such call blocks the single-threaded asyncio event loop for the duration of a SQLite/DB round trip. Under concurrent MCP tool calls from multiple users/sessions, one slow disk write (`_update`) stalls all other coroutines scheduled on that loop (chat streaming, other MCP calls, HTTP request handling) for the DB latency.
fix: Wrap the blocking calls: `return await asyncio.to_thread(self._load)` / `await asyncio.to_thread(self._update, key, value)` (or use an async SQLAlchemy session) so the event loop isn't blocked by DB I/O.

title: Concurrent OAuth flows for the same server_id clobber shared module state, misrouting the callback
detail: `_auth_urls` (line 36) is keyed only by `server_id`, not by flow/state. If two OAuth attempts for the same server run concurrently (e.g. user double-clicks 'connect' or opens two tabs, or a retry races with the original), `redirect_handler` (line 165) unconditionally overwrites `_auth_urls[server_id]` with the second flow's URL. The first flow's `callback_handler` (lines 173-184) subsequently reads `_auth_urls.get(server_id)` and derives the *second* flow's `state`, then waits on the *second* flow's pending Future — while the second flow's own callback_handler, running concurrently, does the same lookup and also grabs that same state/Future. The result is a race where one flow's authorization code can resolve the wrong caller's future, or one flow hangs for the full 300s and then raises a misleading 'No pending OAuth flow' error after the other consumed the shared entry, and `_auth_urls.pop(server_id, None)` (line 184) from either coroutine can delete the URL out from under the other.
fix: Scope `_auth_urls` (and the callback lookup) by a per-flow key (e.g. the `state` value generated at redirect time) instead of `server_id`, or serialize OAuth flow initiation per server_id with a lock so only one flow can be pending at a time.

title: Synchronous httpx calls block the event loop inside async route handlers
detail:
`_start_device_flow` (line 101, calling `copilot.request_device_code` at line 107), `_poll_device_flow` (line 138, calling `copilot.poll_access_token` at line 140), and `_provision_endpoint` (line 44, calling `copilot.fetch_models` at line 47) are all plain synchronous functions that make blocking `httpx.post`/`httpx.get` calls (see src/clients/copilot.py:153-211, which uses the module-level sync `httpx.post`/`httpx.get`, not `httpx.AsyncClient`). They are invoked from `device_start`/`device_poll` in routes/device_flow.py via `_maybe_await(start_flow(...))` and `_maybe_await(poll_flow(...))`. Since `_start_device_flow`/`_poll_device_flow` are ordinary functions (not coroutines) and are called directly rather than via `run_in_threadpool`/`anyio.to_thread.run_sync`, `_maybe_await` sees a non-awaitable and the blocking HTTP call executes synchronously on the single asyncio event-loop thread that FastAPI/uvicorn uses to serve all requests.

Concrete failure scenario: a user starts the Copilot login flow; the frontend polls `/api/copilot/device/poll` every few seconds for up to `expires_in` (default 900s / 15 minutes, line 134). Each poll call blocks the event loop for up to the 10s `poll_access_token` timeout (src/clients/copilot.py:163, default timeout=10.0), and on the authorizing poll it additionally blocks for up to 15s more on `fetch_models` (timeout=15.0). During each of these blocking windows, every other concurrent request the server is handling — chat completions for other users, unrelated API calls, health checks — stalls because the single-threaded async event loop cannot process anything else while waiting on the synchronous socket read. If GitHub's device-code/token/models endpoints are slow or the enterprise host is unreachable, the block can last the full timeout on every single poll cycle for the whole 15-minute window, effectively causing repeated multi-second outages for the entire application.
fix: Either (a) convert `src/clients/copilot.py`'s `request_device_code`, `poll_access_token`, and `fetch_models` to use `httpx.AsyncClient` and make `_start_device_flow`/`_poll_device_flow`/`_provision_endpoint` `async def` functions that `await` them (device_flow.py's `_maybe_await` already supports this — it will properly `await` a coroutine instead of blocking), or (b) if keeping them synchronous, wrap the calls with `starlette.concurrency.run_in_threadpool` (or `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`) so the blocking I/O runs off the event-loop thread.

title: add_directory allows indexing/exposing arbitrary filesystem paths (path traversal / arbitrary file disclosure)
detail: In `add_directory` (lines 103-116), `directory` is taken verbatim from the tool call arguments, only `os.path.expanduser`+`os.path.abspath`-normalized, and checked merely for `os.path.isdir`. There is no allowlist restricting it to a safe root (e.g. PERSONAL_DIR). A caller can pass `/etc`, `/root/.ssh`, `/home/<user>/.aws`, or any other directory readable by the server process; `_rag_manager.index_personal_documents(directory)` will read and chunk every file under it into the RAG index. The subsequent `list` action (lines 76-99) then echoes indexed filenames, and RAG retrieval elsewhere in the app will happily return the contents of those files (e.g. SSH private keys, credentials, `.env` files) to any user/agent that queries the RAG index. This is a straightforward arbitrary-file-read primitive with no owner/permission check.
fix: Restrict `directory` to be inside an allowed root (e.g. require `os.path.commonpath([abs_directory, PERSONAL_DIR]) == PERSONAL_DIR`, or otherwise validate against a per-user allowed base directory) before calling `index_personal_documents`, and reject/step out on any path outside that root.

title: Blocking, potentially long-running indexing call executed synchronously inside the async event loop
detail: `call_tool` is `async def`, but `_rag_manager.index_personal_documents(directory)` (line 116) is invoked directly with no `await`/executor offload. This method walks a directory tree, reads files, and computes embeddings — CPU- and I/O-bound work that can take many seconds to minutes for a large directory. Because this MCP server is single-threaded asyncio (see `run()`/`stdio_server`), this call blocks the entire event loop, stalling `list_tools`, other concurrent `manage_rag` calls, and any keep-alive/stdio traffic for the whole duration.
fix: Offload the blocking call via `await asyncio.to_thread(_rag_manager.index_personal_documents, directory)` (same for the synchronous `add_directory`/`remove_directory` calls on the personal docs manager) so the event loop stays responsive.

title: _ensure_init swallows all initialization errors and latches _initialized=True permanently
detail: `_initialized = True` is set unconditionally at line 30, before the fallible imports/construction in the `try/except Exception: pass` blocks (lines 32-43) run. If `get_rag_manager()` or `PersonalDocsManager(...)` raises for a transient reason (e.g. DB briefly locked, missing optional dependency at that moment, misconfigured env var during startup), the exception is silently discarded, both managers stay `None` forever, and every subsequent call for the life of the process just returns the generic 'not available' message — with no log line indicating why RAG stopped working and no way to recover without restarting the process.
fix: Log the caught exception (e.g. `logger.exception(...)`) instead of bare `pass`, and consider not latching `_initialized = True` on failure so a later call can retry initialization.

title: remove_directory path normalization mismatch silently fails to match stored (abspath) directories, but always reports success
detail: `add_directory` stores directories normalized with `os.path.abspath(os.path.expanduser(...))` (line 110, per the comment referencing #1660). `remove_directory` only applies `os.path.expanduser` (line 138), not `abspath`. If the caller supplies a relative path or a path with `.`/`..` segments (e.g. `docs` while the stored entry is `/home/user/docs`), the underlying `remove_directory` calls (lines 142-145) will not find a match, yet the handler unconditionally returns `"Directory '...' removed from RAG index"` (line 146) regardless of whether anything was actually removed, misleading the caller into believing the directory was deleted from the index when it was not.
fix: Normalize with `os.path.abspath(os.path.expanduser(directory))` to match `add_directory`, and have `remove_directory`/`_rag_manager.remove_directory` return a success indicator that is checked before reporting removal success to the caller.

title: Gallery DB insert failures are silently swallowed
detail: `_store_gallery_image` catches all exceptions from `db.add`/`db.commit` and just returns None (line 95-96), with no logging. If the DB write fails (constraint violation, disk full, locked SQLite file), the caller gets `image_id=None` in the response and the generated PNG on disk becomes orphaned from the gallery with zero diagnostic trail — the failure is invisible in logs.
fix: Log the exception (e.g. `logger.error("Failed to store gallery image: %s", e, exc_info=True)`) before returning None so failures are observable, and consider rolling back explicitly (`db.rollback()`) before returning.

title: Synchronous file write and DB commit block the event loop inside an async handler
detail: `generate_image` is `async def`, but `_save_generated_png` (line 71-77, decodes base64 and does a blocking `Path.write_bytes`) and `_store_gallery_image` (line 80-98, uses the synchronous SQLAlchemy `SessionLocal`) are called directly (not via `run_in_threadpool`/`asyncio.to_thread`) at lines 130 and 132. For large generated images this blocks the single-threaded event loop, stalling all other concurrent requests being served by the same worker for the duration of the disk write and DB commit.
fix: Wrap the blocking calls with `await run_in_threadpool(_save_generated_png, raw_b64)` and `await run_in_threadpool(_store_gallery_image, ...)` (FastAPI/Starlette's `starlette.concurrency.run_in_threadpool`), or move them off the request-handling coroutine.

title: Synchronous SQLAlchemy DB calls block the asyncio event loop inside async def handlers
detail: Every route in this file is declared `async def` but does its DB work with the synchronous `SessionLocal()`/`db.query()` API (e.g. lines 78-116, 165-211, 230-262, 295-317, 350-368, 431-457, 604-645). FastAPI runs `async def` endpoints directly on the single asyncio event loop thread (it does NOT dispatch them to a worker thread the way it does for plain `def` handlers), so any blocking syscall performed by SQLAlchemy against SQLite (opening the file, reading/writing pages, disk fsync on commit) stalls the entire event loop. `compact_session` (lines 604-645) is the worst offender: it runs a SELECT of the whole session's messages, N individual `db.delete()` calls, two `db.add()` calls and a `db.commit()`/fsync — all synchronously — after already having awaited an LLM call. While this runs, every other concurrent request to the app (any user, any session) is frozen because the loop cannot service other coroutines. Under load (e.g. two users hitting the API while one triggers /compact on a long session) this causes app-wide latency spikes/timeouts, not just for the caller.
fix: Either wrap the DB blocks in `await run_in_threadpool(...)` (or `asyncio.to_thread`) so the blocking calls run off the event loop, or switch to SQLAlchemy's async engine/session (`AsyncSession` with `aiosqlite`) and `await` the queries/commits directly.

title: compact_session snapshots session.history before an await and unconditionally overwrites it after, losing concurrent edits and desyncing the DB
detail: `older`/`recent` are sliced from `session.history` at lines 556-557, then the code `await`s `llm_call_async` (line 575), which can take up to the 30s timeout. During that await, the event loop can service other requests against the same session_id (e.g. `/message`, `/delete-messages`, `/mark-stopped` in this same file), which mutate `session.history` in place. When the await returns, line 599 does `session.history = new_history`, unconditionally discarding whatever `session.history` looked like at that moment — any message added or edited by a concurrent request during the compaction window is silently lost from memory. The DB side then re-queries `db_msgs` fresh (line 606-608) and deletes `db_msgs[:-keep_count]`, i.e. it keeps whatever the last 4 DB rows are *at that later time* (which may now include a message the summarization never saw and that was just wiped from `session.history`), so the DB and in-memory history end up holding different, uncoordinated sets of 'recent' messages.
fix: Take an optimistic-concurrency guard: capture `len(session.history)`/a version marker before the await, and after the await re-check that nothing changed (or merge any messages appended after the snapshot into `new_history` before assigning) instead of blindly overwriting; alternatively hold a per-session asyncio.Lock across the compact operation so other mutating routes for the same session_id are serialized against it.

title: Raw exception text is returned to API clients in 500 responses
detail: Nearly every handler's generic `except Exception as e` re-raises `HTTPException(500, str(e))` (lines 137, 216, 269-... via edit_message's own catch is fine but see 375, 464, 517, 661). `str(e)` on a SQLAlchemy error can include SQL fragments, file paths (e.g. the sqlite db path), or other internals of the exception; on other library exceptions it can leak implementation details. This is returned verbatim in the JSON error body to any authenticated caller, and could aid an attacker probing the API for internal information.
fix: Log `str(e)` server-side (already done via `logger.error`) but return a generic client-facing message, e.g. `raise HTTPException(500, "Internal error")`, keeping the detailed message only in the log.

title: DDGS client instantiated without context manager — never explicitly closed
detail: `ddgs = DDGS()` (line 428) creates the duckduckgo-search client and calls `.text(...)` on it, but the object is never used as `with DDGS() as ddgs:` nor explicitly `.close()`d. The library's DDGS class opens an underlying httpx.Client (holding a connection pool/sockets) in `__init__`; the documented/recommended usage is the context-manager form specifically so the client's connections are closed deterministically. Under CPython's refcounting the client is *usually* collected promptly when `ddgs` goes out of scope, but that guarantee breaks the moment a reference to the client escapes the function (e.g. via an exception traceback held elsewhere, a caching layer, or if the library changes to hold background threads/executors) — at that point sockets accumulate across searches. Concrete failure scenario: high query volume against a deployment where the DDGS backend spawns worker threads or is kept alive by an exception frame (common when `error_logger`/tracebacks retain references) will slowly leak open connections and file descriptors until the process hits `ulimit -n` and search requests start failing.
fix: Use `with DDGS() as ddgs: raw = ddgs.text(...)` (lines 428-434) so the client's connections are closed deterministically on every call, success or exception, instead of relying on GC timing.

title: searxng_search_api can issue up to 4 sequential, connection-per-request HTTP calls with no client reuse
detail: `_run()` (line 186) calls the module-level `httpx.get(...)` which opens a brand-new TCP+TLS connection, sends one request, and tears the connection down again. `searxng_search_api` (lines 197-234) can invoke `_run` up to four times in sequence for a single logical search (initial attempt, news-category fallback, no-language fallback, no-engines fallback), each paying a fresh connect+TLS-handshake cost to the *same* SearXNG host instead of reusing a pooled connection. Concrete scenario: a 'news'-style query that returns zero results on the first two attempts pays 3-4x the connection-setup latency (each handshake commonly 50-300ms depending on network/TLS) on top of the actual search latency, directly increasing user-facing response time for exactly the queries (freshness/news) this fallback logic targets.
fix: Create one `httpx.Client(timeout=15)` per `searxng_search_api` call (or a module-level/shared client) and reuse it across the retry/fallback `_run()` invocations instead of calling the stateless `httpx.get()` each time.

title: index_personal_documents has no root confinement, letting arbitrary readable files be indexed and later leaked via unscoped search
detail: index_personal_documents(directory, ...) (lines 404-458) walks `directory` with os.walk and reads/embeds the content of every file matching DEFAULT_FILE_EXTENSIONS, with zero validation that `directory` is confined to an allowed personal-docs root. The only caller-side check upstream (src/agent/ai_interaction.py do_manage_rag, action=add_directory, line 1225-1244) is `os.path.isdir(directory)` on an LLM/tool-content-controlled path string, and it calls `_rag_manager.index_personal_documents(directory)` with owner left as the default None. Concretely: an agent turn that gets the model to emit a manage_rag tool call with content 'add_directory\n/etc' (or '~/.ssh', or another tenant's personal_dir) will cause this file to chunk and embed every readable text/pdf/etc. file under that path into the shared 'atenea_rag' collection with metadata owner unset. Because search() (line 266) only applies an owner where-filter when `owner` is truthy, and _keyword_search_fallback (line 314) iterates every doc in every active collection when `owner` is falsy, any later call to search()/retrieve() without an owner (or the keyword fallback path) will return these indexed secrets to whichever user's query happens to match, i.e. cross-tenant/arbitrary-file disclosure with no confinement enforced anywhere in this file.
fix: In index_personal_documents, normalize and validate `directory` against an explicit allow-list of roots (e.g. the caller's personal_dir / a configured base docs directory) using os.path.realpath + os.path.commonpath, and reject/raise on paths outside it before calling os.walk; do not rely on callers to pre-validate the path.

title: remove_directory and the keyword-search fallback load an entire Chroma collection into memory instead of filtering or paginating
detail: remove_directory (line 480: `results = collection.get(include=["metadatas"])`) and _keyword_search_fallback (line 324: `all_docs = collection.get(include=["documents", "metadatas"])`) both fetch every id/document/metadata row of an entire lane's collection into a Python list with no limit/offset, then filter client-side. remove_directory does this on every single directory removal/reindex call (reindex_directory calls it before every reindex), and the keyword fallback does it on every search() exception. As the corpus grows across all owners (this is a shared collection per lane, not per-tenant), each call becomes an O(n) full materialization of the whole vector store in process memory and an O(n) Python-side scan, which will degrade latency and memory usage significantly and can turn a single reindex or a single failed vector search into a multi-second/very-high-memory operation.
fix: Use Chroma's server-side `where` filtering with a stored normalized parent-directory (or owner) metadata field instead of pulling everything and filtering in Python, or page through collection.get(limit=..., offset=...) in bounded batches rather than a single unbounded get().

title: O(n^2) token-budget trimming loops in trim_for_context
detail: The while loops at lines 284 (`while old_msgs and estimate_tokens(...) > budget: old_msgs.pop(0)`) and 289 (`while prior_convo and estimate_tokens(...) > budget: prior_convo.pop(0)`) pop one message at a time and recompute estimate_tokens() over the entire remaining message list (which itself scans every message's content) on every iteration. For a long conversation history that needs heavy trimming (e.g. hundreds/thousands of stale messages accumulated because compaction was skipped, disabled, or failed via the except-path at line 382-387), this is O(n^2) — each pop re-serializes/measures the whole remaining list. This runs synchronously inside an async request path (trim_for_context is called from request handling), so a large-enough history will visibly stall a request.
fix: Track a running token total and subtract the popped message's own estimate_tokens([msg]) each iteration instead of recomputing over the whole list, or binary-search for the cut point using cumulative token sums computed once.

title: compaction_count computation assumes system message content is always a string
detail: `"[Conversation summary" in m.get("content", "")` at line 353 only falls back to "" when the `content` key is missing; if a system message is present with `content: None` (content is stored as None elsewhere in this file for tool-only turns, e.g. line 193's `out.get("content", "")` pattern shows the codebase is aware content can be None), this raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` and the whole compaction attempt crashes instead of degrading gracefully, since this line runs before the try/except at line 372 that guards only the LLM call.
fix: Use `m.get("content") or ""` instead of `m.get("content", "")` to normalize None to an empty string before the `in` check.

title: Synchronous, potentially long-running calls block the event loop in async handlers
detail: `add_directory_to_rag` (line 98) is declared `async def` but calls `rag.index_personal_documents(directory, owner=owner)` synchronously at line 128. This performs disk-walking, file reads and embedding calls for an entire directory tree — potentially seconds to minutes of blocking work. Because it runs directly on the event loop thread (no `run_in_threadpool`/`asyncio.to_thread`), every other coroutine on that worker (including unrelated users' requests) is frozen for the whole duration. Same pattern in `/upload` (lines 215-216 `open(...).write(content_bytes)`, line 221 `extract_pdf_text(file_path)`, and the RAG chunk/index loop at 230-245) and in `/file` delete (`os.remove` at line 290). A single admin indexing a large personal-docs folder, or a user uploading a big PDF, will stall the whole FastAPI worker for all concurrent requests.
fix: Wrap the blocking calls with `await run_in_threadpool(...)` (Starlette) or `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`, e.g. `result = await run_in_threadpool(rag.index_personal_documents, directory, owner=owner)`, and similarly for the file write, `extract_pdf_text`, the chunk/index loop, and `os.remove`.

title: remove_directory endpoint skips the path-containment check used by add_directory
detail: `add_directory_to_rag` funnels its `directory` argument through `_resolve_allowed_personal_dir` (line 114) specifically to stop `..`/symlink traversal outside `PERSONAL_DIR` (the function's own comment at lines 71-73 explains why `realpath` must be used). `remove_directory_from_rag` (lines 152-191) takes the same kind of user-supplied `directory` query parameter but passes it straight to `personal_docs_manager.remove_directory(directory)` and `rag.remove_directory(directory)` with no containment check at all. If either downstream call uses the path for filesystem operations (e.g. deleting on-disk index artifacts, matching by directory prefix), a caller can pass an arbitrary path (e.g. `/etc` or a path outside PERSONAL_DIR) and have it processed as if it were a valid indexed directory.
fix: Route `directory` through the same `_resolve_allowed_personal_dir(directory)` validation used in `add_directory_to_rag` before calling `personal_docs_manager.remove_directory` / `rag.remove_directory`.

title: File-delete containment check uses abspath instead of realpath, allowing symlink escape
detail: `delete_file_from_rag` computes `abs_target = os.path.abspath(filepath)` and checks it against `UPLOADS_DIR` with `os.path.commonpath` (lines 279-284) before calling `os.remove(abs_target)` at line 290. Unlike `_resolve_allowed_personal_dir`, which deliberately uses `os.path.realpath` because `abspath` does not resolve symlinks (see the comment at lines 71-73), this check only normalizes `..` segments. If a symlink were ever present inside `UPLOADS_DIR` pointing outside of it (e.g. planted by another process, a prior bug, or a race), `abs_target` would still report as 'inside' the uploads dir while `os.remove` follows the symlink and deletes the external target.
fix: Use `os.path.realpath(filepath)` (and `os.path.realpath(UPLOADS_DIR)`) for the containment check, matching the pattern already used in `_resolve_allowed_personal_dir`.

title: Unclosed file handle when reading persisted endpoint config
detail: `open(endpoint_file, encoding="utf-8").read()` opens the file but never closes it (no `with` block, no explicit `.close()`). `_load_persisted_endpoint()` is called on every invocation of `get_embedding_client()` (e.g. on every RAG/memory/tool probe when `_http_embed_down` is already True, since the persisted-endpoint check runs before that latch check), so under CPython the fd is only closed incidentally by refcounting; on alternative interpreters (PyPy) or if an exception occurs mid-read, the descriptor can linger, and it's a landmine for anyone refactoring this into a loop or long-lived process that opens many fds.
fix: Use `with open(endpoint_file, encoding="utf-8") as f: data = json.load(f)` instead of the open().read() chain.

title: httpx.Client connection pool never closed on failed HTTP-embedding probe
detail: `EmbeddingClient.__init__` opens an `httpx.Client` (a live connection pool) with no corresponding `close()`/`__del__`/context-manager anywhere in the class. In `get_embedding_client()` (lines 233-240), when the health-check probe at line 235 raises (endpoint down), the `client` object — including its already-opened socket/pool — is dropped on the floor and only reclaimed whenever the garbage collector eventually runs, rather than being closed immediately.
fix: Wrap the probe in try/except and call `client._client.close()` (or add a `close()` method to `EmbeddingClient` and call it) before falling back to FastEmbed, e.g. `except Exception as e: client._client.close(); _http_embed_down = True; ...`.

title: Corrupted/unreadable endpoint config file is silently swallowed with no logging
detail: `_load_persisted_endpoint()` catches `except Exception: pass` with zero logging around the file read + `json.loads`. If the admin panel's endpoint file is partially written, corrupted, or has bad permissions, every subsequent call to `get_embedding_client()` silently reverts to env-var defaults with no trace in the logs, making it very hard for an operator to figure out why their saved custom endpoint stopped being used.
fix: Log at debug/warning level in the except clause, e.g. `logger.warning("Failed to load persisted embedding endpoint %s: %s", endpoint_file, e)`, instead of a bare `pass`.

title: Decrypted embedding API key is written into the process environment in plaintext
detail: `os.environ["EMBEDDING_API_KEY"] = decrypt(api_key)` stores the decrypted secret in the whole process's environment (not just this client instance). Any code path that dumps env vars for debugging, any child process spawned later that inherits the environment, or a crash report that includes environment variables would expose the plaintext key, even though it was stored encrypted at rest specifically to avoid that.
fix: Pass the decrypted key directly into `EmbeddingClient(api_key=...)` instead of round-tripping it through `os.environ`, so the plaintext secret only lives on the client instance.

title: async update_token performs blocking DB I/O directly on the event loop
detail: update_token (line 152) is declared `async def`, unlike list_tokens/create_token/delete_token which are plain `def` and therefore get dispatched to FastAPI's worker threadpool automatically. Because update_token is a coroutine, its body — including `with get_db_session() as db: ...` (line 158) which opens a synchronous SQLAlchemy Session (SessionLocal from core/database.py) and issues blocking `db.query(...).first()` / `db.add(...)` calls with a real network/disk round trip to SQLite — runs directly on the asyncio event loop thread. Any concurrent request (chat streaming, other API calls) served by the same event loop stalls for the duration of that DB call. Under load (e.g. an admin bulk-editing many tokens, or a slow disk/lock contention on the sqlite file), this can freeze the entire server for all users, not just the caller.
fix: Either make update_token a plain `def` (so FastAPI runs it in the threadpool like the sibling routes), or if async is required for `await request.json()`, wrap the DB block in `await run_in_threadpool(...)` (starlette.concurrency) or use an async SQLAlchemy session/engine.

title: Malformed JSON body in update_token is silently swallowed and treated as an empty update
detail: Lines 154-157 catch any exception from `await request.json()` (e.g. invalid/truncated JSON, wrong content-type) and silently fall back to `payload = {}`. Since `payload` is then empty, none of the `if` branches at lines 162/168 fire, and the handler proceeds to return a 200 response with the token's current (unchanged) name/scopes — as if the update succeeded. A caller who sent a malformed request body gets a misleading success response instead of a 400, masking the real failure (e.g. a client-side bug serializing JSON) and making it look like their update was applied when nothing changed.
fix: Raise HTTPException(400, "Invalid JSON body") when request.json() fails, or at least log the parse failure, instead of silently defaulting to an empty payload that produces a false-success response.

title: Unsanitized UID/session-id path segments defeat the /api/codex/ scope guard (path traversal / query injection)
detail: The script enforces `path.startswith("/api/codex/")` (line 148-150) as its only authorization boundary, meant to restrict the scoped Codex Agent token to Atenea's codex API surface. But several code paths splice raw argv values into the path via f-strings WITHOUT urllib.parse.quote(), even though the author clearly knows to do this elsewhere (quote() is used for `cookbook cached HOST` at line 106 and `cookbook preset NAME` at line 117). The unsanitized cases are: line 80 `path = f"/api/codex/emails/{sys.argv[3]}"` (emails read UID), line 100 `path = f"/api/codex/cookbook/output/{sid}?tail={tail}"` (cookbook output SESSION_ID), and line 135 `path = f"/api/codex/cookbook/stop/{sys.argv[3]}"` (cookbook stop SESSION_ID). Because the startswith() check only inspects the raw concatenated string (not a normalized path), an argument containing `../` sequences still satisfies the check trivially (the string still literally starts with "/api/codex/") while the actual HTTP request sent via urllib (line 171, `base_url + path`) contains a traversal path that the receiving web server/router/any intermediate proxy will normalize, potentially routing the request to an endpoint entirely outside `/api/codex/` -- defeating the scoping the script exists to enforce. Concrete failure: `atenea_api.py emails read '../../../admin/users'` builds `path = "/api/codex/emails/../../../admin/users"`, passes the prefix check, and is sent to the Atenea server, which (depending on its router's path normalization) may resolve it to `/admin/users`, letting a Codex-scoped token reach unscoped/admin endpoints it should never be able to touch. Similarly an argument containing `?` or `&` (e.g. a UID of `123?limit=99999`) injects extra query parameters into the request. This is a real break in defense-in-depth for a script whose entire purpose is to restrict a scoped token to a safe endpoint prefix.
fix: URL-encode every user-supplied path segment with urllib.parse.quote(value, safe='') before interpolating it into `path`, consistently with what's already done for `cached HOST` and `preset NAME` -- i.e. wrap sys.argv[3] at line 80, `sid` at line 98-100, and sys.argv[3] at line 135. Additionally, perform the `/api/codex/` scope check against the normalized path (e.g. via urllib.parse.urlsplit(path).path with os.path.normpath or a manual '..' rejection) rather than a raw string prefix, so traversal sequences can't slip past the guard even if a future call site forgets to quote().

title: Unescaped user-controlled path segments allow bypassing the /api/codex/ scope restriction (path traversal / SSRF against internal endpoints)
detail:
The script explicitly tries to restrict all outbound requests to the `/api/codex/` prefix (line 148-150: "refusing non-/api/codex path; use scoped Atenea integration endpoints only") as its security boundary. But several code paths interpolate raw CLI arguments straight into the URL path without percent-encoding, unlike the 'cached' (line 106) and 'preset' (line 117) branches which correctly use `urllib.parse.quote`: 
- line 80: `path = f"/api/codex/emails/{sys.argv[3]}"` (emails read UID)
- line 100: `path = f"/api/codex/cookbook/output/{sid}?tail={tail}"` (sid = sys.argv[3])
- line 135: `path = f"/api/codex/cookbook/stop/{sys.argv[3]}"`

Because the value is not encoded, an attacker-influenced argument such as `../../../admin/users` still satisfies the `.startswith('/api/codex/')` check (the literal string starts with that prefix) while producing a request path like `/api/codex/emails/../../../admin/users`. Since this tool is invoked by an LLM agent (Codex) whose arguments can be derived from untrusted content it is processing (e.g. an email body or task output containing a crafted UID/session id via prompt injection), a malicious upstream document can steer the agent into calling this script with a traversal payload, causing it to send an authenticated Bearer-token request to an endpoint outside the intended `/api/codex/` scope once the URL is normalized by the HTTP stack/ASGI server, defeating the very check meant to keep this token scoped to the Codex integration surface. It also lets these same arguments inject stray query parameters or break request framing (e.g. `1?x=y`).
fix: Percent-encode every path segment built from user-supplied arguments with `urllib.parse.quote(value, safe='')` (as already done for the 'cached' and 'preset' branches) before interpolating into the path for the 'emails read', 'cookbook output', and 'cookbook stop' branches (lines 80, 98-100, 135), and additionally reject/normalize any decoded '..' segments after building the final path so the `/api/codex/` prefix check cannot be bypassed by traversal sequences.

title: Subprocess leaked when caller cancels execute()/stream() (only internal TimeoutError is handled)
detail: Both `execute()` (lines 54-86) and `stream()` (lines 101-163) only special-case the internal timeout path (`except TimeoutError`, raised by their own `asyncio.wait_for`) to kill/wait the child process. If the coroutine/async-generator is instead cancelled from the *outside* — e.g. the HTTP request handling this call is aborted, an upstream `asyncio.wait_for`/`asyncio.gather` around the agent turn times out, or (for `stream`) the async-for consumer stops early and triggers `GeneratorExit` at the `yield` on line 144/147 — the raised exception is `asyncio.CancelledError`/`GeneratorExit`, both `BaseException` subclasses that are NOT caught by `except TimeoutError` or `except Exception`. Execution unwinds straight to (or past) `finally`, which in `stream()` only does `t.cancel()` on the reader tasks (line 162-163) and never touches `proc`, and in `execute()` there is no `finally` at all touching `proc`. The spawned child process (and, for `stream`, its pipes) is left running detached from the event loop, never reaped with `proc.wait()`/`proc.kill()`. Concrete scenario: an LLM agent tool call runs `service.stream('sleep 999 && curl ...')`, the request is cancelled by client disconnect, and the shell command keeps running as an orphaned process consuming CPU/network indefinitely, invisible to the app.
fix: Kill the process on any exit path, not just the internal timeout: wrap the body in `try/finally` (or add `except BaseException:` reraise-after-cleanup) that does `if proc and proc.returncode is None: proc.kill(); await proc.wait()`, so cancellation/GeneratorExit still reaps the child before propagating.

title: execute() buffers entire process output before enforcing max_output, allowing unbounded memory growth
detail: `proc.communicate()` (line 62-64) reads stdout/stderr to completion and accumulates all bytes in memory; truncation to `self.max_output` only happens afterward on line 65-66. A command that produces very large output (e.g. `yes`, `find /`, `cat bigfile`) is buffered in full before the size cap is applied, so `max_output` does not bound memory usage — it only bounds the returned string. A long-running/large-output command executed via this 'safe' shell service can exhaust process memory well before the truncation ever takes effect.
fix: Stream-read stdout/stderr with a running byte counter and stop reading once max_output is exceeded (similar to how `stream()` already reads incrementally), or pass `limit=` to `create_subprocess_shell` and read in chunks via `proc.stdout.read(n)`/`proc.stderr.read(n)` instead of `communicate()`, discarding further output once the cap is hit.

title: Token ID truncated to 8 hex chars (32 bits) invites primary-key collisions
detail: `token_id = str(uuid.uuid4())[:8]` keeps only the first 8 hex characters of a UUID4 (32 bits of entropy) and uses it as the primary key `id` for the new ApiToken row. Once a companion/instance has minted on the order of tens of thousands of tokens, the birthday bound (~2^16 for 50% collision odds at 32 bits) makes a duplicate id a realistic occurrence, not a theoretical one. When it happens, `db.add(ApiToken(id=token_id, ...))` inside `with get_db_session() as db:` will raise an IntegrityError on commit; the exception is not caught anywhere in this function, so `mint_token` (and any pairing route calling it) blows up with an unhandled 500 instead of retrying or generating a fresh id. Fix: use the full uuid4 hex (or at least 16 hex chars) for token_id, e.g. `token_id = uuid.uuid4().hex`, or loop/retry on IntegrityError with a fresh id.

title: Overly broad except in QR rendering hides real bugs, not just the optional-dependency case
detail: The docstring says this should return None only 'if the optional qrcode dep is unavailable' (i.e. ImportError), but `except Exception` also swallows any error from `json.dumps(payload, ...)`, `qrcode.make(...)`, or `img.save(buf, format="PNG")` -- e.g. a future change that puts a non-JSON-serializable value into the pairing payload, or a qrcode/Pillow internal error -- and silently returns None. Callers then just see 'no QR available' with no log line, making real regressions invisible in production. Fix: catch `ImportError` specifically for the missing-dependency case and let other exceptions propagate (or log them) so genuine bugs surface.

title: Synchronous fsync'ing file write blocks the event loop on every preset save
detail: update_custom_preset (line 35), save_user_template (line 60), delete_user_template (line 67), and save_group_presets (line 122) are all `async def` handlers, but they call straight through to PresetManager.update_custom/save_user_template/delete_user_template/save_group_presets (src/preset_manager.py lines 134-190), which end in self.save(self.presets) -> core.atomic_io.atomic_write_json. That helper does a synchronous `open()`, `json.dump()`, `f.flush()`, and critically `os.fsync(f.fileno())` before `os.replace()` -- all blocking syscalls with no `await`, `run_in_executor`, or `asyncio.to_thread` wrapper anywhere in the call chain. Since FastAPI/uvicorn runs all `async def` handlers on the single event loop thread, any concurrent request in flight (chat streaming responses, other API calls, SSE) stalls for the full duration of the write+fsync (can be tens of milliseconds or more on slower disks, network filesystems, or under I/O contention/fsync journal flushes) every time an admin edits a preset, saves a template, or saves group chat presets. Under concurrent load (e.g. an admin repeatedly tweaking presets while other users are mid-stream on chat completions) this directly causes visible latency spikes/stalls for unrelated requests app-wide.
fix: Wrap the PresetManager save calls in `await asyncio.to_thread(preset_manager.update_custom, ...)` (and similarly for save_user_template/delete_user_template/save_group_presets), or make PresetManager.save use `asyncio.to_thread`/an executor internally so the fsync'ing write never runs on the event loop thread.

title: Fire-and-forget task created without keeping a reference — can be garbage-collected mid-execution
detail: Line 40: `loop.create_task(_handle_event(event_name, owner))` discards the returned Task object immediately. Per the asyncio docs, the event loop only keeps a weak reference to tasks created with create_task; if no strong reference is retained anywhere, the task can be garbage-collected before it finishes running (typically observed as 'Task was destroyed but it is pending!' warnings and the event silently never being processed). Because fire_event() is called from many places (session creation, message sends, etc.) as pure fire-and-forget with no caller-side storage, any event whose _handle_event coroutine gets scheduled but not yet started before the next GC cycle runs is at risk of being dropped — meaning a scheduled task's trigger counter never increments and the automation silently never fires, with no error surfaced anywhere.
fix: Keep a strong reference to background tasks, e.g. maintain a module-level `set` of pending tasks: `t = loop.create_task(...); _background_tasks.add(t); t.add_done_callback(_background_tasks.discard)`.

title: Blocking synchronous file I/O executed on the event loop thread for every event
detail: `_resolve_event_owner` (lines 58-61) synchronously opens AUTH_FILE and does `json.load` on it. This function is invoked from `_handle_event` (line 76), an `async def` coroutine that normally runs on the running event loop (via `loop.create_task` at line 40). Every ownerless event (which per the docstring at lines 48-50 is the common case for internal/localhost event sources) therefore performs blocking disk I/O and JSON parsing directly on the event loop thread, stalling all other coroutines (HTTP request handling, other scheduled tasks, etc.) for the duration of the file read on every single fire_event() call with no owner.
fix: Move the auth-file read off the event loop, e.g. wrap it with `await asyncio.to_thread(_resolve_event_owner, owner)`, or cache the resolved admin/default owner in memory and invalidate only when the auth file changes.

title: Per-task db.commit() inside the event-handling loop (N+1 commits)
detail: Lines 105 and 113: for every ScheduledTask matched by the query, the loop performs a separate `db.commit()` (once when a threshold is hit, once otherwise). With many active tasks subscribed to the same trigger_event, this issues one DB round-trip/transaction per task instead of batching, adding latency proportional to the number of matched tasks on every event fire.
fix: Accumulate counter/next_run updates across the loop and issue a single db.commit() after the loop (or use bulk update expressions), reserving commits inside the loop only where you specifically need the trigger's next_run persisted before awaiting run_task_now.

title: Hardcoded plaintext credential committed to source control
detail: IMAP_PASSWORD = "demodemo" (line 28) is a real credential literal checked into git history, then encrypt()-ed and written to the DB for both IMAP (line 50) and SMTP (line 57) auth. The comments make clear this is meant to be a throwaway/local-only demo mailbox with a dead SMTP port, which mitigates real-world impact, but the password is nonetheless a static secret in source rather than sourced from an env var or generated randomly, so it is permanently visible in the repo/history and reused across accounts if the script is ever copied to point at a non-dead host/port.
fix: Read the demo password from an environment variable (e.g. os.environ.get("DEMO_IMAP_PASSWORD", <fallback>)) or generate a random per-install secret instead of hardcoding it in source.

title: PID-based tmp filename collides across concurrent writers in the same process
detail: The docstring claims the PID suffix prevents collisions between processes, but within a single process (this is an async FastAPI app) multiple asyncio tasks or threads can call atomic_write_json(same_path, ...) concurrently — e.g. two request handlers both saving `sessions.json` or `settings.json` at nearly the same time. Both share the same os.getpid(), so both compute the identical tmp path `path.tmp.<pid>`. One writer's open('w') truncates the file the other is still writing/fsyncing, and whichever os.replace() runs last wins while the other silently succeeds too — producing a truncated or corrupted JSON file, or a lost update (one caller's data silently disappears), defeating the entire purpose of this module (atomic, non-corrupting writes for auth.json / live state files).
fix: Make the tmp filename unique per call, not just per process, e.g. `tmp = f"{path}.tmp.{os.getpid()}.{uuid.uuid4().hex}"` or use `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=os.path.dirname(path), prefix=os.path.basename(path)+'.tmp.')`, and additionally serialize concurrent writers to the same logical path with an asyncio.Lock keyed by path if last-writer-wins ordering matters.

title: Orphaned tmp files leak on write failure
detail: If json.dump(data, f, ...) raises (e.g. data contains a non-serializable object, or the disk fills up / os.fsync fails with OSError) after the file has been opened, the `with open(tmp, ...)` block closes the fd, but the `path.tmp.<pid>` file itself is never removed — there is no try/except/finally that unlinks it. For long-running services this leaves stray tmp files accumulating in every directory that stores JSON state (auth.json, sessions.json, settings.json, integrations.json, cookbook_state.json) each time a serialization error occurs, and since the name is PID-based (not per-call unique, see next finding) a crash mid-write can also leave a half-written tmp file sitting next to the real file indefinitely.
fix:
Wrap the write in try/except, and on exception call os.remove(tmp) (guarded by another try/except / os.path.exists) before re-raising, e.g.:
 try:
     with open(tmp, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
         json.dump(data, f, indent=indent)
         f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())
     os.replace(tmp, path)
 except Exception:
     with contextlib.suppress(OSError):
         os.remove(tmp)
     raise

title: Sensitive files (auth.json) written with default umask permissions
detail: The module is explicitly documented as being used for `auth.json` (a password DB). `open(tmp, 'w')` creates the tmp file with mode 0o666 minus the process umask (commonly 0o644, world-readable) before os.replace() moves it into place. If the process umask is permissive (e.g. default 022 on many deployment images/containers) the password DB ends up group/world-readable on disk, and since os.replace preserves the tmp file's permissions rather than the original file's, an initially-locked-down auth.json can have its permissions silently loosened on the very first atomic rewrite.
fix: For secret-bearing paths, explicitly set restrictive permissions before replace, e.g. `os.chmod(tmp, 0o600)` prior to `os.replace(tmp, path)`, or accept a `mode` parameter defaulting to 0o600 for atomic_write_json/atomic_write_text and have auth.json's caller pass it explicitly.

title: Unbounded per-page synchronous VL/OCR calls in PDF processing — attacker-controlled DoS via a single upload
detail: `_process_pdf` (lines 119-146) iterates every page of the uploaded PDF with no cap on page count, and for any page with images and <50 chars of extracted text it makes up to 3 *synchronous* network calls to `analyze_image_with_vl` (line 136), each of which can block for up to 120s (see `llm_call(..., timeout=120)` at line 326). A user attaching a scanned/image-heavy PDF with, say, 200 low-text pages can trigger up to 600 sequential blocking HTTP calls in a single request — worst case multiple hours of wall-clock time — before any truncation (`pdf_text[:15000]`, line 150) is applied. `_process_pdf` is reachable from `build_user_content` (line 520) and from the PDF auto-doc-creation path (line 437), which is called from `src.chat.handler.preprocess_message`, an `async def` chat entrypoint — so this isn't just slow for the uploader, it stalls the whole async worker/event loop for all concurrent users for that duration. There is no limit on total pages scanned or total images OCR'd per document.
fix: Cap the total number of pages/images processed per PDF (e.g. stop OCR after N images or M seconds total), and/or run the VL calls concurrently with `asyncio.gather` + a bounded semaphore using the async LLM client (`llm_call_async` already exists in src/llm_core.py) instead of sequential synchronous calls with a 120s timeout each.

title: Synchronous blocking I/O and network calls invoked directly from an async request handler
detail: `analyze_image_with_vl_result` performs a synchronous file read (`open(image_path, 'rb').read()`, line 298) and a synchronous network call via `llm_call(...)` (line 326, no `await`), and `build_user_content` performs synchronous disk reads for every attachment (e.g. lines 392, 408, 449-524) including PDF text extraction and Office-document conversion. Both functions are called directly — not via `run_in_executor`/`asyncio.to_thread` — from `src/chat/handler.py:232` and `:251` inside `async def preprocess_message`. Any one of these calls (large file read, or a slow/unresponsive LLM vision endpoint) blocks the single-threaded asyncio event loop, freezing every other in-flight request (SSE streams, other users' chats) for the duration.
fix: Either wrap the calls in `await asyncio.to_thread(build_user_content, ...)` / `await asyncio.to_thread(analyze_image_with_vl_result, ...)` at the call sites, or convert `analyze_image_with_vl_result` to use the already-present `llm_call_async`/`llm_call_async_with_fallback` (src/llm_core.py) and make file reads use `aiofiles` or offload to a thread pool.

title: Synchronous blocking calls executed inside async route handlers block the event loop
detail: TTSService.synthesize()/synthesize_to_base64() are plain sync methods, and routes/tts_routes.py's `async def synthesize_speech` calls them directly (tts_service.synthesize_to_base64(...) / tts_service.synthesize(...)) without run_in_threadpool or asyncio.to_thread. Inside this file: line 136 does `r = httpx.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=60)` — a synchronous network call that can block for up to 60s — and lines 269-272 run Kokoro GPU inference (`for _, _, audio in self.pipeline(text, voice=voice)`) synchronously. Because the caller awaits nothing before invoking these, the entire asyncio event loop (and therefore every other concurrent request the server is handling — chat, other API calls, health checks) is frozen for the duration of the HTTP call or GPU synthesis. A single slow/unreachable TTS endpoint (e.g. a misconfigured or hanging ModelEndpoint) stalls the whole app for up to 60 seconds per request, and concurrent TTS requests serialize entirely.
fix: Make synthesize/_synthesize_api async and use `await httpx.AsyncClient().post(...)` instead of the sync `httpx.post`, or wrap the sync call sites in `await asyncio.to_thread(tts_service.synthesize, text)` at the route layer so the event loop stays free. Kokoro's GPU inference should also be dispatched via to_thread/a threadpool executor.

title: TTS disk cache grows unbounded with no eviction or size cap
detail: _put_cache() (line 88-90) writes a new file to self.cache_dir for every distinct (provider, model, voice, speed, text) combination and there is no TTL, LRU eviction, or max-size enforcement anywhere in the class — the only way to reclaim space is the manually-invoked clear_cache() (line 92). In production, any variation in prompt text (which is common for TTS of dynamic agent output) produces a permanent new cache file, so disk usage grows without bound over the service's lifetime and can eventually exhaust disk space, causing write failures elsewhere in the app.
fix: Add a cache size/age cap: on write, check total cache_dir size (or file count) and evict oldest files (by mtime) once a configured threshold is exceeded, or add a periodic cleanup task / TTL-based expiry instead of relying solely on manual clear_cache().

title: Synchronous blocking httpx calls invoked unthreaded from async route handler
detail: parse_skill_source (lines 80-84), _fetch_bytes (lines 169-176), and _list_github_dir (lines 194-199, recursing up to depth 4 / MAX_FILES=64) all use synchronous httpx.Client(...).get(...); none of these functions, nor the public fetch_skill_bundle (line 228), are async. routes/skills_routes.py:1251 calls `files, _src = fetch_skill_bundle(body.url.strip())` directly inside `async def import_skill_from_url`, with no run_in_threadpool/asyncio.to_thread wrapper. Every blocking HTTP call therefore runs on the asyncio event-loop thread itself. Fetching a nested skill bundle can trigger dozens of sequential round trips (each with a 20-30s timeout), during which the entire single-threaded event loop is frozen and cannot serve any other request in the process -- a self-inflicted DoS from one skill import.
fix: Convert skill_importer.py to use httpx.AsyncClient throughout (async def fetch_skill_bundle/_fetch_bytes/_list_github_dir/parse_skill_source), or at minimum wrap the call site in routes/skills_routes.py with `await run_in_threadpool(fetch_skill_bundle, url)` / `asyncio.to_thread(...)` so the blocking work runs off the event loop.

title: New httpx.Client (fresh TCP+TLS handshake) created per HTTP call instead of reusing/pooling one client
detail: _fetch_bytes (line 169) and _list_github_dir (line 194) each open a brand-new httpx.Client context manager per call. Because _list_github_dir recurses per subdirectory and calls _fetch_text/_fetch_bytes once per file, importing a bundle with e.g. 40 files across a few folders performs 40+ separate TCP+TLS handshakes to GitHub sequentially instead of reusing one pooled connection, multiplying the latency of the already-blocking fetch described above.
fix: Create a single httpx.Client once in fetch_skill_bundle and thread it through _fetch_bytes/_fetch_text/_list_github_dir calls instead of instantiating a fresh client per HTTP request.

title: Broad except Exception: pass hides unexpected errors during URL-shape probing
detail: fetch_skill_bundle's fallback probing (lines 249-250 and 256-257) uses bare `except Exception: pass` to try folder-vs-blob-vs-flat-repo URL shapes. This intentionally swallows 'not found' cases but also silently swallows unrelated bugs (e.g. a TypeError from a malformed GitHub API response), making such failures indistinguishable from a simple 404.
fix: Narrow the except clauses to (SkillImportError, httpx.HTTPError) so unexpected exceptions propagate instead of being discarded.

title: Silent exception swallowing hides catalog load failures
detail: get_models() (lines 255-264) catches FileNotFoundError and json.JSONDecodeError and silently sets _models_cache = [] with no logging. If hf_models.json becomes corrupted or is deleted/moved, every caller silently receives an empty model catalog instead of an error, making hardware-fit recommendations silently return 'no compatible models' with no diagnostic trail pointing to the root cause (bad JSON, wrong path, etc.).
fix: Log the exception (e.g. logging.exception("failed to load model catalog from %s", data_path)) before falling back to an empty list, so operators can distinguish 'no matching model' from 'catalog failed to load'.

title: Background registration tasks swallow BaseException (including SystemExit/KeyboardInterrupt)
detail: `_connect_python_server` (lines 112-116) and the npx registration loop (lines 170-173) catch `asyncio.CancelledError` and re-raise, but then catch bare `BaseException` and only log a warning. `BaseException` also covers `SystemExit` and `KeyboardInterrupt`; if either is ever raised through this coroutine (e.g. via `sys.exit()` called from deep inside a connect path, or a Ctrl-C landing while inside `await mcp_manager.connect_server(...)`), it gets swallowed and downgraded to a warning log instead of propagating, which can mask an intended process shutdown signal.
fix: Catch `Exception` instead of `BaseException` (CancelledError is already handled separately above it and doesn't derive from Exception in a way that matters here since it's already re-raised); let SystemExit/KeyboardInterrupt propagate normally.

title: N+1 blocking synchronous DB queries inside async def, one full pass per session
detail: run_auto_sort is `async def`, but `db` is a plain synchronous SQLAlchemy Session (core.database.SessionLocal, built on create_engine/sessionmaker — see core/database.py:37-43), so every db.query(...) call in the Phase 1 loop (lines 68-70, 80-83, 84-86, 100-102) executes synchronously on the event-loop thread with no await point in between. For a user with N non-empty sessions, the loop issues up to 4 additional round-trip queries per session (msg_count, first_msg, assistant_count, and — worst case — a full db.query(DbMsg.content)....all() fetch of every message body just to sum len()). With a few hundred sessions this becomes hundreds to low-thousands of blocking SQLite round trips executed back-to-back inside the coroutine, stalling the single asyncio event loop for the whole span and freezing every other concurrent request (chat streaming, other API routes) the FastAPI process is serving. This function is also invoked daily by the background sweep (src/actions/builtin.py action_tidy_sessions), so the stall is triggered automatically, not just on manual admin action.
failure_scenario: A user (or, since owner filtering is a no-op when owner is falsy per this codebase's single-user-mode convention, potentially every user's sessions in one pass) has several hundred short/empty chat sessions. The nightly action_tidy_sessions sweep calls run_auto_sort, which walks every row and fires multiple synchronous SQLite queries per row with no yielding; concurrent chat requests hitting the same process hang for the whole duration of the sweep because the event loop is blocked executing DB I/O synchronously.
fix: Either offload the blocking DB work with `await asyncio.to_thread(_phase1_sync, ...)` / run it in a threadpool executor, or eliminate the N+1 pattern by computing msg_count, first-user-message, assistant_count and total content length in one batched query (e.g. GROUP BY session_id with func.count/func.min/func.sum(func.length(...))) across all candidate sessions up front instead of per-row round trips.

title: Redundant per-item DB round trip in folder-assignment loop despite already having the rows
detail: `remaining = db.query(DbSession)...all()` (line 116-119) already loaded every candidate DbSession row into `db`'s identity map, but `session_list` only keeps a plain dict (id/name/folder) and discards the ORM objects. The Phase 2 loop then re-issues `db.query(DbSession).filter(DbSession.id == full_id).first()` (line 211) for every id the LLM returned across every folder — another synchronous, blocking round trip per assignment, on top of the Phase 1 N+1 pattern.
failure_scenario: An LLM response groups 300 sessions into folders; the loop performs 300 additional synchronous SELECT queries (one per id) purely to re-fetch objects that were already in memory moments earlier, further extending the event-loop-blocking window described above.
fix: Build a dict `{row.id: row for row in remaining}` (or use `db.get(DbSession, full_id)` which consults the session identity map before hitting the DB) instead of re-querying by primary key inside the loop.

title: Synchronous, potentially long-running I/O called directly from an async FastAPI handler blocks the event loop
detail: STTService.transcribe() (called synchronously from `async def transcribe_audio` in routes/stt_routes.py:41, with no `await`, `run_in_executor`, or `asyncio.to_thread`) dispatches to either `_transcribe_local` or `_transcribe_api`, both of which perform blocking work directly on the asyncio event loop thread: `model.transcribe(tmp_path, ...)` at line 105 runs CPU-bound faster-whisper inference (can take many seconds for a large/long audio clip), and `httpx.post(url, ..., timeout=60)` at line 144 is a blocking synchronous network call that can hold the thread for up to 60 seconds while waiting on a remote/possibly slow provider. Because FastAPI runs `async def` route bodies on the single event-loop thread unless work is explicitly offloaded, every other concurrent request to the server (chat completions, health checks, other API routes) stalls for the full duration of a single transcription call. A user uploading a 20-minute audio file, or a slow/unresponsive STT endpoint, freezes the entire app for all other users simultaneously.
fix: Wrap the blocking transcription call in a thread offload, e.g. in routes/stt_routes.py use `text = await asyncio.to_thread(stt_service.transcribe, audio_bytes)` instead of calling it synchronously, or make `_transcribe_api` use `httpx.AsyncClient` with `await client.post(...)` and run `_transcribe_local`'s CPU-bound whisper call via `asyncio.to_thread`/a dedicated executor so the event loop is never blocked.

title: Blocking synchronous file I/O executed directly inside async tool handler, stalling the whole MCP event loop
detail: `call_tool` is declared `async def` (line 76) but every action performs synchronous, unbuffered file I/O on the calling coroutine: `_memory_manager.load()`/`load_all()` do blocking `open()`+`json.load()` (src/memory/store.py:118-121) and `save()` does blocking `open()`+`json.dump()`+`os.replace()` (store.py:210-212), with no `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` or executor offload anywhere in memory_server.py. As memory.json grows (list/search load the *entire* file into memory every call, lines 88/181, with no pagination or size cap), each blocking read+parse+write stalls the single asyncio event loop of the MCP stdio server for the duration of the disk I/O, delaying every other concurrent tool call being served by the same shared server process (per the singleton architecture noted above).
fix: Wrap the MemoryManager calls in `await asyncio.to_thread(_memory_manager.load)` / `await asyncio.to_thread(_memory_manager.save, memories)` (and similarly for load_all) so file I/O runs off the event loop thread.

title: Failure to persist partial response on cancellation is silently swallowed
detail: When a run is stopped/replaced, `_drain`'s CancelledError handler calls `await agen.aclose()` inside a bare `try/except Exception: pass` (lines 115-118). The module docstring states the wrapped generator's own CancelledError/cleanup path is what persists the partial assistant message to the session on stop. If that persistence logic raises (DB error, serialization error, etc.), the exception is discarded with no log line at all -- unlike the sibling error path at lines 119-127 which does `logger.error(...)`. Concrete scenario: user hits 'stop' mid-stream, the underlying generator's cleanup fails to write the partial message to the session store (e.g. a transient DB error), and the failure vanishes silently -- the user sees the run reported as 'stopped' with no error, but their partial conversation state was never saved and there is no log trace to diagnose why.
fix: Log the exception before discarding it, e.g. `except Exception as e: logger.error("[agent-run] %s: aclose() failed while persisting partial response: %s", session_id, e, exc_info=True)` so silent data loss on cancellation is at least observable.

title: Run entries and their replay buffers grow unbounded if the wrapped generator never terminates or is never cancelled
detail: `_RUNS[session_id]` and `run.buffer` are only ever cleared via `_schedule_evict`, which is armed exclusively in the `finally` block of `_drain` (line 138) after `run.status` has become a terminal value (done/error/stopped) -- i.e. only after the wrapped async generator actually stops iterating or is cancelled via `stop()`. There is no maximum run duration and no cap on `run.buffer` length anywhere in this file. If the wrapped generator hangs (e.g. an upstream LLM call that never returns and nobody calls `stop()`), the `_Run` object, its `buffer` list, and any accumulated events remain in memory for the lifetime of the process -- unbounded if the hung generator keeps yielding events, and permanent even if it merely stalls. Since `_RUNS` is a plain module-level dict with no size limit, many such stuck sessions accumulate without any backstop.
fix: Add a hard wall-clock timeout around the `async for ev in agen` loop in `_drain` (e.g. `asyncio.wait_for` or a watchdog task that calls `stop(session_id)` after N minutes) so a hung upstream call cannot pin memory indefinitely, and optionally cap `run.buffer` size/event count as a defense-in-depth bound.

title: Blocking, fsync'd disk I/O runs synchronously inside async request handlers
detail: PresetManager.save() (lines 115-128) opens a file, calls json.dump, f.flush(), os.fsync(f.fileno()) and os.replace() — all blocking syscalls — and load() (71-113) does a blocking open()+json.load(). These methods are invoked directly (no thread offload) from async FastAPI route handlers in routes/preset_routes.py: update_custom_preset -> preset_manager.update_custom() -> save() (line 155), save_user_template -> save() (line 175), delete_user_template -> save() (line 181), save_group_presets -> save() (line 190). Since the routes are `async def` and call these sync methods directly without `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` / `run_in_executor`, every fsync'd write blocks the single asyncio event loop thread for its full duration. Concrete failure: while one user calls POST /api/presets/templates (which fsyncs to disk), every other in-flight request on the same worker — chat streaming, health checks, other API calls — stalls until the write (including fsync, which can take tens of ms on spinning disks/network filesystems or under I/O contention) completes. Under load this serializes otherwise-concurrent traffic and adds latency spikes app-wide.
fix: Offload the file I/O to a worker thread instead of calling it inline on the event loop, e.g. change the route handlers to `await run_in_executor(None, preset_manager.save_user_template, template)` (or wrap PresetManager.save/load with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`), so fsync/replace happen off the event-loop thread.

title: owner_is_admin_or_single_user fails open on exception, contradicting the module's fail-closed policy
detail: Lines 163-174: if AuthManager() construction or auth.is_admin(owner) raises for any reason (bad config, DB error, malformed owner string), the except block logs a warning and returns False from this function's caller path is fine, but examine the actual behavior: owner_is_admin_or_single_user itself returns False on exception (line 174), which then makes blocked_tools_for_owner (line 177-181) return the full NON_ADMIN_BLOCKED_TOOLS set — that part is fail-closed and correct. However, the earlier branch at line 169-170 ('if not auth.is_configured: return True') means ANY owner is treated as admin whenever auth is reported as not configured, with no distinction between 'genuinely single-user deployment' and 'auth subsystem transiently misconfigured/erroring during is_configured check'. If auth.is_configured itself can be true after a partial/failed init (or defaults to a value that doesn't reflect real deployment state), every non-admin user is granted access to all NON_ADMIN_BLOCKED_TOOLS (bash, python, manage_tokens, vault_get, etc.) with no owner check at all.
fix: Distinguish 'single-user mode intentionally enabled by config' from 'auth manager errored or is in an indeterminate state'. Ensure is_configured cannot be true due to an error path, or add an explicit deployment-mode flag rather than inferring open-admin-access from is_configured alone.

title: Memory wipe reports success even when memory.json fails to reset
detail: In `_wipe_memory_files()` (lines 39-53), any `OSError` while truncating memory.json (e.g. disk full, permission denied, file locked by another process) is caught, logged as a warning, and swallowed — the function returns normally. The caller (`kind == "memory"` branch, lines 89-104) has already committed the DB deletion of `Memory` rows and unconditionally returns `{"status": "deleted", ...}` regardless of whether `_wipe_memory_files` actually succeeded. Since `src/memory/store.py` (`MemoryStore.load_all`) reads directly from memory.json as the real persistence store, a failed write here means old memory entries are still loaded on the next request even though the admin API told the caller the wipe succeeded. For a data-deletion/privacy endpoint, silently reporting success on partial failure is a meaningful correctness/security gap.
fix: Track whether every file operation in `_wipe_memory_files` succeeded (return a bool or raise) and propagate the failure to the endpoint so it can return a non-200 status or a partial-success flag instead of unconditionally reporting `status: deleted`.

title: Directory wipes (skills/gallery) report success even when rmtree fails
detail: `_rmtree_quiet()` (lines 56-62) catches `OSError` from `shutil.rmtree` and only logs a warning, never signaling failure. It's used for the skills directory (line 116) and gallery/upload directories (lines 154-155). If rmtree fails partway (e.g. a file is open/locked, or a permission-restricted subfile exists), the DB rows are already deleted and committed, but the endpoint still returns `{"status": "deleted", ...}` even though skill files or uploaded gallery images remain on disk — leaving orphaned, potentially sensitive files (gallery images) accessible via any endpoint that serves from `GALLERY_DIR`/`GALLERY_UPLOADS_DIR` by filename, while the UI believes the wipe succeeded.
fix: Have `_rmtree_quiet` return a success boolean (or re-raise) and include a `partial` / `warnings` field in the response when directory removal fails, rather than unconditionally reporting full success.

title: In-memory session cache clear failure is silently discarded
detail: Lines 83-86: `session_manager.sessions.clear()` is wrapped in a bare `try/except Exception: pass` with no logging at all. If clearing the in-process cache fails (e.g. `sessions` isn't a dict-like object, or a concurrent iterator is active), the DB is emptied but the cache keeps stale session entries, so `/api/sessions` can keep returning already-deleted chats — and there is no log trace to diagnose it.
fix: Log the exception (e.g. `logger.warning(...)`) instead of silently passing, so a failed cache clear is at least observable in logs even if it shouldn't fail the whole wipe request.

title: Synchronous network + DB calls block the asyncio event loop on every device-flow request
detail: device_start and device_poll in routes/device_flow.py are `async def` handlers that call `_start_device_flow` (line 108) and `_poll_device_flow` (line 134) directly (not via run_in_threadpool/asyncio.to_thread). Those functions call `chatgpt_subscription.request_device_code()` (line 110), `chatgpt_subscription.poll_device_auth()` (line 136), `chatgpt_subscription.exchange_authorization_code()` (line 145) and, inside `_provision_endpoint`, `chatgpt_subscription.fetch_available_models()` (line 31) — all of which use synchronous `httpx.get/post` with timeouts up to 15-20s. `_provision_endpoint` also does synchronous SQLAlchemy `SessionLocal()` work (lines 34-97) in the same call path. Because these run inline inside an `async def` FastAPI route, each one blocks the single asyncio event loop thread for the full duration of the outbound HTTP call. Since the UI polls `/device/poll` every few seconds while a user completes the ChatGPT login, and the poll can itself trigger a token exchange + model-list fetch (potentially 25-30s of blocking network I/O), the entire server becomes unresponsive to all other concurrent requests (chat completions, other users' API calls) for that duration.
fix: Wrap the blocking provider calls with `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...)` / `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` in `_start_device_flow`/`_poll_device_flow` (or make them `async def` and swap `httpx` sync client calls in chatgpt_subscription.py for `httpx.AsyncClient`), so device-flow polling never stalls the shared event loop.

title: Synchronous file I/O (refresh/prune/glob/unlink) runs unshielded inside the async poll loop, blocking the event loop
detail: `bg_jobs.pending_followups()` (called from the `async def _loop`) calls `refresh()`, which does `_load()` (blocking `Path.read_text` + `json.loads`), potentially `_kill()`/`_save()` (blocking `atomic_write_json`), and `_prune()` (a `Path.glob` scan plus `p.unlink()` for every stale job's `.sh`/`.cmd.sh`/`.log`/`.exit` files). None of this is offloaded to a thread. Because `_loop` runs directly on the asyncio event loop and awaits nothing during this call, every one of these synchronous filesystem operations blocks ALL other coroutines on the same loop — including in-flight chat SSE streams (`stream_agent_loop`) and any other request being served by the same process. With many stale/finished jobs accumulating (`_prune` walks `_JOBS_DIR.glob` per stale job) or a slow/contended disk, this tick can take from tens of ms up into the hundreds of ms, every 5 seconds, causing visible latency/stalls in concurrent live chat responses.
fix: Wrap the blocking call in `asyncio.to_thread`, e.g. `pending = await asyncio.to_thread(bg_jobs.pending_followups)` in `_loop`, and similarly offload `bg_jobs.mark_followed_up` and the two `bg_jobs.result_text(rec)` calls inside `_run_followup` (lines 104 and 124), which also do blocking `Path.read_text` via `_read_output`.

title: No timeout around the agent drain — a single hung follow-up stalls the entire monitor loop indefinitely
detail: `_loop` (line 136-139) processes `pending_followups()` sequentially with a plain `for` loop, `await`-ing `_run_followup` → `_drain_agent` for each job one at a time, with no `asyncio.wait_for`/timeout. `_drain_agent` just consumes `stream_agent_loop(...)` until it stops yielding, with `max_rounds` bounding round count but not wall-clock time per round (a network hang, a stuck tool call, or an unresponsive LLM endpoint can block a single chunk indefinitely). If one session's follow-up wedges, the monitor never reaches `asyncio.sleep(POLL_INTERVAL_S)` on line 145, so no other pending job's follow-up runs and no timed-out jobs get their completion message — directly contradicting the module's stated reliability goal that 'completion → agent re-invocation must never silently no-op.'
fix: Bound each follow-up with a timeout, e.g. `await asyncio.wait_for(_run_followup(rec), timeout=SOME_BUDGET)` inside the try/except at line 138, treating `asyncio.TimeoutError` like any other retryable failure (log + leave `followed_up=False`), so one stuck session can't block the others.

title: TOCTOU race between the 'session busy' check and the history append/save
detail: `_run_followup` checks `agent_runs.is_active(sess.id)` once at line 96 to avoid interleaving with a live turn, then — with no lock held — proceeds through `await _drain_agent(...)` (a multi-round, potentially long-running network call) before appending to history and calling `sm.save_sessions()` at lines 118-127. If a live turn starts anywhere in that window (which can be seconds to minutes long), both paths call `sm.add_message` / `sm.save_sessions()` concurrently with no per-session lock, exactly the reordered/clobbered-message scenario the surrounding comment (lines 90-93) says this check exists to prevent — the check only prevents starting when *already* busy, not becoming busy mid-flight.
fix: Re-check `agent_runs.is_active(sess.id)` immediately before the `sm.add_message`/`sm.save_sessions()` calls (or acquire a real per-session lock spanning drain+persist) so a live turn that started during `_drain_agent` still causes a deferred retry instead of a racy write.

title: Synchronous filesystem I/O blocks the asyncio event loop on every request
detail: emoji_svg is declared `async def` but every disk operation on the hot path is a blocking syscall: `_CACHE_DIR.mkdir(...)` (line 81), `fp.exists()` (line 83), `fp.read_bytes()` (line 85), `fp.unlink(...)` (line 88), and `fp.write_bytes(r.content)` (line 100). Under concurrent load (many chat messages rendering many distinct emoji, or a slow/loaded disk, e.g. network filesystem for EMOJI_CACHE_DIR), each of these calls stalls the single-threaded asyncio event loop, so every other in-flight request/coroutine in the process (including unrelated API routes) stops making progress for the duration of the syscall. This defeats the purpose of using async FastAPI handlers and can turn brief disk latency into app-wide request stalls.
fix: Move the filesystem calls off the event loop, e.g. wrap the cache-read and cache-write logic in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` calls, or use an async file library (aiofiles) for read_bytes/write_bytes/exists/mkdir/unlink.

title: Unbounded codepoint length/segment count enables oversized paths and unlimited outbound CDN requests
detail: `_CODE_RE = re.compile(r"^[0-9a-f]{2,6}(?:-[0-9a-f]{2,6})*$")` has no cap on the number of `-xx` repetitions or total string length, and `code` comes directly from the URL path.
