A client can request e.g. `/api/emoji/<10000 hex groups>.svg`; this string is used to build both a cache file path (`fp = _CACHE_DIR / f"{code}.svg"`, line 82) and, on a cache miss, an outbound GET to the OpenMoji CDN (line 97). Extremely long filenames can raise OSError (ENAMETOOLONG) from `fp.exists()` at line 83, which is not wrapped in a try/except, causing an unhandled exception (500) for that request. More importantly, because negative results (CDN 404/unreachable) are never cached, an attacker can repeatedly request large volumes of distinct never-cacheable bogus codepoints to force the server to issue an unbounded number of outbound HTTP requests to a third-party CDN with no rate limiting, tying up httpx client/socket resources per request.
fix: Bound the regex to a realistic maximum, e.g. limit segment count (`(?:-[0-9a-f]{2,6}){0,7}`) and/or add an explicit `if len(code) > N: return _blank()` guard before any filesystem/network work; also wrap the `fp.exists()`/cache-read block in the existing try/except (currently only read/unlink are covered, not the `exists()` call itself) so a filesystem error still falls back to `_blank()` instead of propagating as a 500.

title: Fernet master key file written world/group-readable
detail: get_or_create_key() (lines 20-22) creates the Fernet secret with open(self.key_file, 'wb') using the process's default umask (typically 0644, i.e. world-readable) instead of restricting permissions. This .key file is the single symmetric key that decrypts every stored provider API key and every webhook secret (see routes/webhook_routes.py:120 which reuses this manager to encrypt webhook secrets). Any other local user/process on the host (or a container image layer, or a backup that preserves permissions) can read src/clients/api_key_manager.py's .key file and decrypt all API keys and webhook secrets ever stored in api_keys.json. Fix: create the file with os.open(self.key_file, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL, 0o600) (or os.open with 0o600 then os.fdopen) instead of the bare open('wb'), and chmod 0o600 on an already-existing file defensively.

title: Non-atomic read-modify-write in save() loses concurrent provider-key updates
detail: save() (lines 61-72) does load-raw-dict -> mutate -> write-whole-file with no locking and no read of the file's state at write time. FastAPI runs sync def routes (e.g. any settings/API-key route in this multi-provider app) in a thread pool, so two concurrent save() calls for different providers (e.g. saving an OpenAI key and an Anthropic key in two near-simultaneous requests) can both call _load_raw() before either writes: thread A loads {}, thread B loads {}, A writes {openai: ...}, then B overwrites the file with {anthropic: ...}, silently discarding A's just-saved key with no error surfaced to either caller. Fix: serialize save() with a threading.Lock (module- or instance-level) around the load+mutate+write, or use an OS-level advisory file lock (fcntl.flock) while reading and writing api_keys.json.

title: TOCTOU race can generate two different encryption keys on first use
detail: get_or_create_key() (lines 16-23) checks os.path.exists(self.key_file) then, if absent, generates and writes a new key with no lock. If two threads call this concurrently before the key file exists (e.g. two simultaneous first-time API-key saves), both see the file missing, both generate different Fernet keys, and both write — the second write wins on disk while the first thread's already-returned key object differs from what's now stored. Any value encrypted in-memory with the first thread's stale key becomes permanently undecryptable once persisted keys elsewhere rely on the second key. Fix: guard key creation with a lock, or create the file exclusively via os.open(..., os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL, 0o600) and fall back to reading it on EEXIST.

title: Blocking synchronous DB calls executed inside async route handlers
detail: get_session() (line 407) calls sync_session_metadata() (line 430) and _touch_session() (line 489), each opening its own SessionLocal(), running a query, and (for _touch_session) committing — all synchronous SQLAlchemy/SQLite calls. add_message() (line 242) then also calls _persist_message() (line 256), a third blocking SessionLocal()+insert+commit. routes/history_routes.py:150 invokes `session_manager.add_message(session_id, msg)` directly inside `async def add_message(...)` with no run_in_threadpool/asyncio.to_thread wrapper, so three sequential blocking SQLite round-trips run on the event loop thread for every single chat message persisted, stalling all other concurrent requests/websockets for that duration.
fix: Offload these calls at the route layer with `await run_in_threadpool(session_manager.add_message, ...)`, or migrate to an async SQLAlchemy engine/session. Also collapse sync_session_metadata + _touch_session (called back-to-back on every get_session) into a single query to cut redundant round-trips.

title: Persistence failures in _persist_message are silently swallowed
detail: add_message() (line 251) appends the message to session.history in memory before calling _persist_message(). Inside _persist_message, any exception from the DB insert/commit (e.g. 'database is locked' under concurrent SQLite writers, disk full) is caught, logged, and rolled back at lines 305-309, but never re-raised. add_message() then returns normally, so the caller (e.g. routes/history_routes.py:150) responds success to the client even though the message was never written to the database. If the session is later evicted and rehydrated via _load_session_from_db (line 462), which rebuilds history purely from DB rows, the message silently vanishes with no error ever surfaced.
fix: Re-raise the exception (or return a bool that add_message checks and propagates) instead of swallowing it, so callers can detect and surface the persistence failure rather than silently losing user data.

title: self.sessions cache grows unbounded for the process lifetime
detail: load_sessions()'s docstring (lines 117-123) explains it stopped loading every message at boot to avoid holding tens of thousands of rows in RAM forever, but that only fixes the initial bulk load. Every session subsequently opened is fully hydrated via _load_session_from_db (line 462) and stored permanently in self.sessions (lines 472/479) with its complete message history, and is never evicted except by delete_session or the empty-session branch of cleanup_empty_sessions (message_count==0, line 690). An archived-but-nonempty old session stays resident with full history indefinitely. On a long-running personal server where a user revisits many old sessions over time, self.sessions accumulates full message histories without bound.
fix: Add an LRU-style cap/eviction: for sessions not accessed within N minutes, drop `history` back to [] (keeping metadata), relying on the existing lazy-hydrate path in get_session (lines 417-419) to reload on next access.

title: get_sessions_for_user(None) returns a live reference to internal state
detail: When username is None, get_sessions_for_user returns `self.sessions` itself rather than a copy (the filtered branch at lines 665-668 returns a fresh dict). Any caller that mutates the returned dict (pop/del/reassignment) directly corrupts the manager's authoritative session table, and concurrent iteration elsewhere while another thread inserts/removes a key can raise RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration.
fix: Return `dict(self.sessions)` for the None case to match the filtered branch's copy semantics.

title: SSRF protection is defeated by DNS-rebinding TOCTOU
detail: _public_http_url() (lines 68-88) resolves the hostname via socket.getaddrinfo/ipaddress checks to decide if a URL is 'public', but the actual request is then made by httpx.get() at line 96, which performs its own independent DNS resolution at connect time. An attacker who controls the DNS for the target hostname (e.g. serves a low/zero TTL A record) can return a public IP for the validation lookup and then return a private/internal IP (e.g. 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata, or an internal service) for the connection httpx actually makes moments later. Because the two resolutions are decoupled, the check in _public_http_url provides no real guarantee about what IP is actually contacted, allowing SSRF into internal services/cloud metadata despite the allowlist logic. This also applies on every redirect hop inside _get_public_url (lines 91-103): each hop is 'validated' then independently re-resolved by httpx.
fix: Resolve the hostname once, select a validated public IP, and force the HTTP client to connect to that exact IP (e.g. build the request against the literal IP with the Host header set to the original hostname, or supply a custom httpx transport/resolver that pins the already-validated address) instead of letting httpx re-resolve DNS after the check passes.

title: Unbounded response body read allows memory-exhaustion DoS
detail: _get_public_url uses httpx.get(...) (non-streaming), which buffers the entire response body in memory regardless of size; response.text (line 303) and response.content (line 279, fed into pdfminer) then hold the full payload again. A malicious or compromised remote server can return an arbitrarily large body (e.g. multi-GB) for any URL fetched by this function, causing the process to exhaust memory. There is no Content-Length check and no streaming cap anywhere in the fetch path.
fix: Stream the response (client.stream / response.iter_bytes) and enforce a hard byte cap (e.g. 10-20 MB), aborting the download once exceeded; also reject up front based on a Content-Length header that exceeds the cap when present.

title: Shared module-level cache index mutated without synchronization
detail: content_cache_index (imported from .cache) is a plain dict mutated here via pop() at lines 240/244 and assignment at line 370, plus iterated/mutated inside cleanup_cache() at line 371. fetch_webpage_content is a synchronous function that will typically be invoked from multiple worker threads concurrently (FastAPI thread pool) for different requests hitting the same or different cache keys. Concurrent pop/assignment plus a concurrent cleanup pass iterating the same dict can race (e.g. 'dictionary changed size during iteration' or lost cache-index updates that cause cleanup_cache to miss/duplicate entries), since nothing in this file (nor evidently the imported helpers, based on usage here) takes a lock around these operations.
fix: Guard reads/writes to content_cache_index with a threading.Lock (or use a thread-safe structure) shared across all callers, or restrict cache-index mutation to a single-threaded path (e.g. an async lock/queue) since it is process-wide shared state accessed from concurrent request-handling threads.

title: Permanent data loss if collection rewrite AND restore both fail
detail: In _get_or_reset_collection, line 184 unconditionally deletes the original collection (`chroma_client.delete_collection(name)`) before the new/re-embedded data has been durably written. The re-embedded rows are then written in a try block (lines 187-194); if that write fails, the code tries to restore the *original* preserved rows into a freshly recreated collection (lines 197-214). But if this restore attempt also fails (e.g. same transient Chroma/disk error that caused the first failure, such as disk-full or a Chroma server restart mid-operation), the exception is only logged at line 216 (`logger.warning(...)`) and swallowed — the function then raises a RuntimeError describing only the *first* failure. The original collection was already deleted at line 184 and the in-memory `preserved` data (ids/documents/metadatas/embeddings) is never persisted anywhere, so all vectors for that collection are permanently lost with only a warning log line as evidence.
failure_scenario: An operator changes the custom embedding endpoint config, triggering a fingerprint mismatch and collection reset for a memory/RAG collection with thousands of stored vectors. Chroma's disk briefly fills up or the Chroma server restarts during the reset. Both the rewrite (line 189) and the restore fallback (line 209) fail because of the same underlying disk/connection issue. All previously stored embeddings for that collection are irrecoverably gone; the caller only sees a RuntimeError and a log line, with no backup of the data that existed seconds earlier.

title: Entire collection (docs + embeddings) loaded into memory with no pagination
detail: _get_or_reset_collection calls `collection.get(include=["documents", "metadatas", "embeddings"])` (line 159) with no limit/offset, pulling every document, metadata dict, and embedding vector for the whole collection into a single Python list in memory. migrate_legacy_collection does the same at line 277 (`legacy.get(include=["documents", "metadatas"])`). Both then also re-embed the whole preserved document set synchronously (line 179) before any of it is written back.
failure_scenario: A collection with e.g. 200k stored chunks (RAG collections can easily reach this for a large document corpus) triggers a lane fingerprint change (model/endpoint swap). `_get_or_reset_collection` loads all 200k documents + embeddings into memory at once and then synchronously re-embeds all 200k documents via the new client before writing anything back, causing large memory spikes and a multi-minute blocking call on whatever thread triggered the config change (e.g. an HTTP request handler), with no batching/streaming of the read or progress feedback.

title: No locking around delete+recreate of shared Chroma collections
detail: build_embedding_lanes/_create_lane/_get_or_reset_collection perform a read-then-delete-then-recreate sequence (get_collection at 139, delete_collection at 184, get_or_create_collection at 185) against a Chroma collection identified only by name, with no lock or transaction guarding the sequence. `chroma_client` is a shared, process-wide client (via get_chroma_client()).
failure_scenario: Two concurrent requests both cause an embedding-lane rebuild for the same base_name (e.g. two admins update embedding config back-to-back, or MemoryVectorStore._initialize and an explicit rebuild race). Thread A deletes and recreates collection X and begins writing re-embedded batches into it; thread B's delete_collection(name) at line 184 fires while thread A is still writing, wiping out the rows thread A just wrote, or thread B's get_or_create_collection returns thread A's freshly-created (metadata-updated) collection and both threads write duplicate/conflicting batches into it.

title: Blanket except-Exception-pass hides real config/reset failures
detail: reset_embedding_lane_state (lines 62-68) and _load_custom_endpoint's persisted-config load (lines 92-96) catch bare `Exception` and silently continue (`pass` / `persisted = {}`), with no logging in the reset_embedding_lane_state case. Any bug in reset_http_embed_state (e.g. an AttributeError from a refactor) or a corrupted persisted-endpoint file is invisible to operators.
failure_scenario: reset_http_embed_state raises due to an unrelated import-time error; reset_embedding_lane_state swallows it entirely with no log line, so after an admin updates the embedding endpoint, stale HTTP embedding client state silently persists and subsequent embedding calls keep using the old endpoint/model with no error surfaced anywhere.

title: TOCTOU race in _get_or_create can seed duplicate personal-assistant CrewMembers
detail: In `_get_or_create` (lines 147-172), the function queries for an existing default-assistant CrewMember, and if none exists, calls `await task_scheduler.ensure_assistant_defaults(owner)` (an async DB write) then re-queries. There is no DB-level unique constraint on (owner, is_default_assistant) in core/database.py's CrewMember model, and `ensure_assistant_defaults` (src/scheduling/task_scheduler.py:2172-2179) performs the identical unlocked check-then-insert pattern in its own separate session. If a user's browser fires two concurrent requests to any /api/assistant/* endpoint before the assistant has been seeded (e.g. loading /session and /settings in parallel on first visit), both requests can see `existing is None` and both proceed to create a full CrewMember + pinned Session + three daily ScheduledTasks, producing duplicate 'Morning/Midday/Evening check-in' rows that double-fire — the exact bug the code comments (lines 141-144, task_scheduler.py:2160-2165) say was already hit and manually cleaned up once, but nothing was added to actually prevent recurrence (only synthetic-owner rejection was added).
fix: Add a unique index/constraint on (owner, is_default_assistant) where true (or a simpler unique (owner) partial index) in the CrewMember table, and catch the IntegrityError in ensure_assistant_defaults to fall back to re-querying the existing row; alternatively take a per-owner asyncio.Lock (or DB row lock via SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, if the DB supports it) around the check-and-create sequence in _get_or_create.

title: Synchronous SQLAlchemy Session used directly inside async route handlers
detail: core/database.py wires SessionLocal to a synchronous create_engine/sessionmaker (blocking sqlite3 driver under the hood). Every route in this file (get_assistant_session, get_assistant_settings, update_assistant_settings, run_check_in_now, run_status — lines 174-334) calls `db.query(...)`/`db.commit()` synchronously from inside `async def` handlers with no `run_in_executor`/threadpool offload. Each blocking DB call therefore blocks the single asyncio event loop thread, so a slow/locked write (SQLite serializes writers) in update_assistant_settings stalls every other concurrent request the process is serving until it returns.
fix: Either move the DB work to a worker thread with `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...)` / `fastapi.concurrency.run_in_threadpool(...)`, or switch to an async SQLAlchemy engine/session (aiosqlite) for these routes.

title: Non-atomic read-modify-write on the memory store causes lost updates under concurrency
detail: NativeMemoryProvider.remember() (lines 161-163) does memories = self.memory_manager.load_all(); memories.append(entry); self.memory_manager.save(memories) — a classic read-modify-write with no lock. delete() (lines 227-243) does the same pattern: load_all(), filter, save(remaining). In an async FastAPI app, concurrent requests (e.g. two users calling remember() at nearly the same time, or a remember() racing a delete()) will interleave at the await points inside load_all()/save() (file or DB I/O). Whichever save() completes last wins and silently overwrites the other coroutine's change: a concurrent remember() can be lost entirely (never persisted, though remember() still returns a MemoryRecord as if it succeeded), or a concurrent delete() can be undone (the deleted entry reappears because it was still present in the other coroutine's stale snapshot). There is no lock, no transaction, and no optimistic-concurrency check (e.g. version/etag) guarding the load->mutate->save sequence.
fix: Guard the read-modify-write sequence with an asyncio.Lock (or, better, push add/delete semantics down into memory_manager as atomic operations backed by a DB transaction / row-level SQL UPDATE-DELETE rather than load-entire-list-then-save-entire-list). At minimum, serialize remember()/delete() calls per memory store with an asyncio.Lock held across the load/mutate/save section so concurrent calls cannot interleave.

title: Reachability check re-runs blocking socket connects for every endpoint on every unreachable session (O(sessions*endpoints) network I/O)
detail: `_best_replacement` (lines 68-73) loops over the full `endpoints` list and calls `_host_port_reachable` (a blocking TCP connect with up to 0.8s timeout, line 21-31) for each endpoint. This function is invoked once per session that has an unreachable `current_url` (line 146), and `endpoints` is the same list every time — none of the reachability results are cached across the session loop. With N sessions whose endpoint is down and M configured endpoints, the script performs up to N*M blocking socket connection attempts. Concrete scenario: 200 stale sessions (common after decommissioning a model host) and 10 configured endpoints, several of which are also down, means up to 2000 connection attempts at ~0.8s timeout each — over 26 minutes of wall time for what should be at most 10 checks total. This also repeats the exact same check redundantly for sessions sharing the same unreachable endpoint.
fix: Compute the reachable-endpoints list once before the `for sess in sessions:` loop (e.g. `reachable_eps = [(ep, build_chat_url(normalize_base(ep.base_url or ''))) for ep in endpoints if _host_port_reachable(...)]`) and pass that precomputed list into `_best_replacement` instead of recomputing it per session. Optionally also cache reachability of `current_url` by URL string across sessions to dedupe repeated checks at line 143.

title: MemoryService has no owner/tenant scoping — cross-user memory read, search, and delete
detail: MemoryManager.load(owner=...) and NativeMemoryProvider.remember/recall/delete all accept an `owner` kwarg specifically to isolate one user's memories from another's (see src/memory/store.py load()/claim_ownerless and src/memory/provider.py NativeMemoryProvider.delete, which explicitly checks `entry.get('owner') != owner`). MemoryService never accepts or passes an owner anywhere: remember() (line 87) calls `self.provider.remember(text, session_id=session_id)` with no owner, so stored memories are ownerless; recall() (line 102) calls `self.provider.recall(query, top_k=top_k)` with no owner, so search hits span every user's memories; get_all() (line 113) calls `self.manager.load_all()` directly — the explicitly 'unfiltered' method — returning every tenant's memories; delete() (lines 118-125) also calls `self.manager.load_all()` and removes any entry whose id matches, with zero ownership check, so any caller who knows/guesses a memory id can delete another user's memory. Concrete scenario: two users share this Atenea deployment; user B calls service.recall('salary') and receives user A's private memory about their salary, or calls service.delete(<user A's memory id>) and it succeeds silently (returns True), permanently destroying user A's data with no authorization check at all. Contrast with routes/memory_routes.py in the same codebase, which carefully calls memory_manager.load(owner=user) and _verify_memory_owner() before every read/update/delete — this class bypasses all of that.
fix: Add an `owner: str | None = None` parameter to __init__ or to each of remember/recall/get_all/delete, and thread it through: `self.provider.remember(text, session_id=session_id, owner=owner)`, `self.provider.recall(query, top_k=top_k, owner=owner)`, `self.manager.load(owner=owner)[:limit]` instead of load_all() in get_all(), and in delete() either use `self.provider.delete(memory_id, owner=owner)` (which already enforces ownership) or replicate the same `entry.get('owner') != owner` guard before removing the entry.

title: Blocking synchronous file I/O executed inside async methods
detail: remember() (line 87) and recall() (line 102) are `async def` but await calls into NativeMemoryProvider, which synchronously opens, reads (json.load) and rewrites (json.dump + os.replace) memory.json on every single call via MemoryManager.load_all()/save() (src/memory/store.py) — plain blocking file I/O with no executor/offload. Because this runs directly on the asyncio event loop, every remember()/recall() call blocks all other concurrent coroutines (other requests, other sessions) for the duration of the disk read/write. Concrete scenario: under moderate concurrent chat load, many sessions calling `await service.remember(...)` back-to-back will serialize on disk I/O on the single event loop thread, causing latency spikes/timeouts for unrelated concurrent requests even though the API is nominally async.
fix: Offload the underlying synchronous manager/provider calls with `await asyncio.to_thread(self.manager.load_all)` / `await asyncio.to_thread(self.manager.save, entries)` (or move the sync I/O in MemoryManager behind a thread-pool executor) so remember()/recall() no longer block the event loop.

title: self.fetch_content attribute shadows the fetch_content method, breaking it
detail: In __init__ (line 45), `self.fetch_content = fetch_content` assigns a bool instance attribute named `fetch_content`. The class also defines a method `async def fetch_content(self, url)` at line 96. Since instance attributes take precedence over class methods in Python's attribute lookup, after any SearchService is constructed, `self.fetch_content` is permanently rebound to the bool passed to __init__ (default True), completely shadowing the method. Any call to `service.fetch_content(url)` raises `TypeError: 'bool' object is not callable` (or, if constructed with fetch_content=False, `'bool' object is not callable` still, just False instead of True — either way it's never callable). This means the fetch_content() method documented as part of the service's public API (see class docstring usage example implying full interface) is dead code that will crash any caller.
fix: Rename the constructor parameter/instance attribute to something like `self.fetch_content_enabled` (and update its use as the default in `search()`), or rename the method to `fetch_page_content`/`fetch_url_content`, so the flag and the method don't collide on the same name.

title: DB failure is swallowed and reported as success
detail: In main(), the try/except around the DB updates (lines 65-93) catches any Exception, rolls back, and prints an ERROR line, but the function does not sys.exit() or re-raise. Execution falls through to lines 95-96, which unconditionally print 'Done! All ownerless data now belongs to <owner>' and instruct the operator to restart the service. If the DB update fails (e.g. locked SQLite file, schema mismatch, constraint error), the script still exits with status 0 and tells the admin the claim succeeded, so they restart the server believing ownership was fixed when it was not — silently leaving data ownerless/invisible.
fix: After catching the exception, either `sys.exit(1)` inside the except block (skipping the trailing success message) or track a failure flag and guard the final print/exit code on it, e.g. `except Exception as e: db.rollback(); print(f'  ERROR: {e}'); sys.exit(1)`.

title: Non-atomic JSON rewrite can corrupt memory/skills files
detail: claim_json_entries writes the updated entries straight back to the original path with `open(path, 'w')` (lines 50-51). If the process is killed or crashes mid-write (e.g. disk full, SIGKILL, power loss) after truncating but before the new JSON is fully flushed, MEMORY_FILE/SKILLS_FILE is left truncated/corrupted, and since these are the app's live data files, the running app would then fail to parse them on next load.
fix: Write to a temp file in the same directory and os.replace() it into place, e.g. write to f'{path}.tmp', then `os.replace(f'{path}.tmp', path)` for an atomic swap.

title: Blocking DNS resolution (socket.getaddrinfo) runs synchronously inside an async request handler
detail: `_resolve_hostname_ips` calls `socket.getaddrinfo(hostname, None)` (line 41), a blocking, synchronous syscall that can take seconds if the DNS server is slow or the query times out (glibc default resolver timeouts can be 5-30s per nameserver). `validate_public_http_url` (called via `is_public_http_url` -> `_host_resolves_publicly` -> `_resolve_hostname_ips`) is invoked directly, with no thread-pool offload, from `routes/webhook_routes.py:285` inside `async def sync_chat(...)` (line 234 in that file). Because this runs on the asyncio event loop thread, any request that supplies a `base_url` whose hostname resolves slowly (or an attacker-controlled domain configured to stall/blackhole DNS responses) blocks the entire event loop for the duration of the DNS lookup, stalling all other concurrent requests being served by that worker -- a low-cost DoS vector as well as a general latency/availability bug.
fix: Run the DNS lookup off the event loop, e.g. `await asyncio.get_running_loop().run_in_executor(None, socket.getaddrinfo, hostname, None)` in an async variant of `_resolve_hostname_ips`/`is_public_http_url`, and have `sync_chat` `await` the async validator instead of calling `validate_public_http_url` synchronously. Also consider passing an explicit resolver timeout so a stalling DNS server can't hang the lookup indefinitely.

title: DNS-rebinding TOCTOU: the IP validated here is not guaranteed to be the IP actually connected to
detail: `validate_public_http_url` only checks that the hostname *currently* resolves to a public IP (lines 63-71); it returns the original URL string, and the caller (`routes/webhook_routes.py`) later passes that same hostname to the actual HTTP client, which re-resolves DNS itself. An attacker who controls the DNS for their supplied `base_url` domain can return a public IP for the validation lookup and then, once validated, return `127.0.0.1`/`169.254.169.254`/an internal RFC1918 address for the follow-up connection performed by the HTTP client (classic DNS-rebinding SSRF), reaching internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint despite passing this check. The docstring at lines 86-87 acknowledges this is not eliminated, but the caller in webhook_routes.py has no additional mitigation (no IP pinning, no re-validation at connect time), so the gap is live and exploitable end-to-end.
fix: Resolve the hostname once, validate the resolved IP(s), and force the outbound HTTP client to connect to that pinned IP (e.g. via a custom DNS resolver/transport, or by connecting to the IP directly and setting the Host header/SNI), so the IP that is validated is the IP that is actually connected to. Alternatively, re-validate immediately before each connection and reject on redirect to a non-public host.

title: Synchronous blocking file I/O inside async route handlers
detail: All three route handlers (get_all_prefs line 72-74, get_pref line 77-80, set_pref line 83-88) are declared `async def` but call _load/_save, which perform synchronous open()/json.load, and for writes also os.makedirs, open()/json.dump, f.flush, os.fsync, and os.replace (lines 14-28) directly on the event loop thread. os.fsync in particular forces a synchronous disk flush. Under load (many simultaneous prefs requests, or a slow/contended disk), each of these calls blocks the single asyncio event loop, stalling every other concurrent request being served by the same worker (including unrelated endpoints), not just prefs traffic.
fix: Offload the blocking calls to a thread, e.g. `prefs = await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(_load_for_user, user)` and `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(_save_for_user, user, prefs)`, or make _load/_save async using aiofiles, so the event loop is never blocked on disk I/O.

title: Key file created world/group-readable before permissions are locked down
detail: In `_load_or_create_key` (lines 39-44), `_KEY_PATH.write_bytes(key)` creates the file using the process umask (commonly 0o644 or 0o664) and `safe_chmod(_KEY_PATH, 0o600)` is only applied afterward. Between those two calls there is a window where the Fernet master key is readable by other local users/processes (e.g. other tenants on a shared host, a sibling container mount, or a backup job that snapshots the directory mid-write). Anyone who reads the key file during that window can decrypt every IMAP/SMTP secret ever stored, defeating the exact threat model described in the module docstring ("stolen backup, leaked container layer, sibling-tenant read"). Fix: create the file with restrictive permissions atomically, e.g. open with `os.open(path, os.O_CREAT|os.O_WRONLY|os.O_EXCL, 0o600)` and write through that fd (or write to a temp file created with mode 0o600 in the same directory, then `os.rename` it into place), so the file never exists on disk with default permissions.
fix: Use os.open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL and mode=0o600 (or write to a 0o600 temp file and os.rename into place) instead of write_bytes()+chmod(), so the restrictive mode is applied atomically at creation time.

title: Unsynchronized first-run key creation can race across threads/processes
detail: `_load_or_create_key` (lines 36-46) does a plain `exists()` check then generates and writes a new key with no locking. If two threads (FastAPI's sync-endpoint thread pool) or two worker processes hit an empty `data/` directory concurrently on first run, both can see `exists() == False`, both generate a *different* key, and both write it — the second write wins on disk. Whichever request cached the first Fernet instance in its own `_fernet` global (or in another worker process) will keep encrypting/decrypting with a key that no longer matches the file, so secrets it encrypts become permanently undecryptable by the rest of the app once they read the second key. Fix: guard key creation with a file lock (e.g. `fcntl.flock` on POSIX, or a lockfile) or do the create-if-absent step during single-process app startup only, before workers are forked.
fix: Serialize first-run key generation with a file lock or perform it once during app bootstrap before any worker/thread can call encrypt()/decrypt().

title: Unbounded in-memory cache regions (no size cap, only lazy TTL eviction)
detail: All four regions (db_region, llm_region, settings_region, context_region; lines 35-57) use dogpile.cache.memory, a plain dict-backed store whose expiration_time only causes lazy eviction on access to that specific key -- keys that are set but never re-requested after expiry are never purged, and there is no maximum entry count / LRU eviction at all. If any region's cache key includes high-cardinality or externally influenced data (e.g. llm_region keyed by prompt/response content per the module docstring, or context_region keyed by (endpoint_url, model)), the underlying dict can grow without bound as distinct keys accumulate, since nothing enforces the '~128 entries' assumption noted only in a comment on line 41. Concrete scenario: a client that varies prompts or hits many endpoint_url/model combinations within the TTL window causes steady, unbounded process memory growth with no cap or alarm, eventually leading to OOM.
fix: Use a bounded backend (e.g. a size-capped LRU wrapper around dogpile.cache.memory, or an external backend like Redis configured with maxmemory-policy) instead of relying on TTL comments; alternatively cap max entries explicitly in a custom backend/wrapper around region.set().

title: Synchronous, blocking SQLAlchemy calls run directly inside async def request handlers, stalling the event loop
detail: SessionLocal (core/database.py:43) is a plain synchronous sessionmaker bound to a sync engine. Every public function here (archive_inactive_sessions L54-77, cleanup_old_sessions L96-157, get_cleanup_preview L179-259) is declared `async def` but does its DB work with plain blocking calls: db.query(...).all(), db.commit(), db.query(...).delete(...), db.query(DbChatMessage)...count() in a loop, etc. None of this is offloaded via run_in_executor/asyncio.to_thread. These functions are invoked directly from FastAPI async route handlers (routes/cleanup_routes.py: `await get_cleanup_preview(...)`, `await cleanup_sessions(...)`), which run on the single-threaded asyncio event loop. Any authenticated user hitting GET /api/cleanup/preview or POST /api/cleanup will block that event loop for the full duration of the SELECT/COUNT/DELETE queries -- freezing every other concurrent request (chat streaming, other users' API calls) on the server for that window. This gets worse as the sessions/messages tables grow, and is compounded by the N+1 counting loop noted separately.
fix: Either wrap the synchronous DB work in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` (or run via a thread-pool executor) so it doesn't block the loop, or migrate this module to an async SQLAlchemy session (AsyncSession/async engine) and await the queries properly.

title: N+1 query when estimating space freed per session to delete
detail: In cleanup_old_sessions, for every session slated for deletion the code issues a separate `db.query(DbChatMessage).filter(DbChatMessage.session_id == session.id).count()` (L133-135). For N candidate sessions this is N separate round-trips to the database instead of one aggregate query, and combined with the blocking-I/O issue above it multiplies the amount of time the event loop is stalled proportional to the number of sessions being cleaned up.
fix: Replace the per-session count loop with a single grouped query, e.g. `db.query(DbChatMessage.session_id, func.count()).filter(DbChatMessage.session_id.in_(session_ids)).group_by(DbChatMessage.session_id).all()`, then look up counts from the resulting dict.

title: Cleanup failures are swallowed and reported to callers as a successful, empty result
detail: archive_inactive_sessions (L73-77), cleanup_old_sessions (L153-157), and get_cleanup_preview (L256-259) each catch bare `Exception`, log it, and return their default/zeroed values (0 archived, (0, 0.0) deleted, or partially-filled preview dict) without re-raising. cleanup_sessions (L283-291) then wraps calls to the first two in additional try/except blocks that also just log and continue. The route layer (routes/cleanup_routes.py) awaits these functions inside its own try/except, so from the HTTP caller's perspective a transient DB error (e.g. connection drop, lock timeout) during cleanup produces a 200 OK with `{"archived_count": 0, "deleted_count": 0, "space_freed_mb": 0.0}` -- indistinguishable from 'nothing needed cleaning up.' No error surfaces to the client or triggers alerting, so a persistently broken cleanup job (e.g. sessions never archived/deleted) can go unnoticed indefinitely.
fix: Re-raise (or return a distinct error indicator) from the inner functions so the route can return a 5xx / include an `errors` field, instead of silently coalescing failures into a zero-count success response.

title: Profiles silently dropped (function can return []) for models with context_length < 8192
detail: In compute_serve_profiles, for each spec: `cur_ctx = min(ctx, model_ctx_max)` (line 190) then `while cur_ctx >= 8192: ... break` (line 191). If model_ctx_max (derived from the model's context_length/n_ctx_train/etc., or the model's catalog metadata) is below 8192 — e.g. a small/older GGUF model reporting context_length=4096 or 2048 — cur_ctx starts below 8192 and the while loop body never executes, so no profile dict is appended for that spec at all. Since all three specs (quality/balanced/speed) compute ctx as min(target, model_ctx_max), the same failure applies to every spec, so compute_serve_profiles returns an empty list even though the model fits in VRAM and is perfectly servable at its native (small) context. The caller's contract per the docstring is that an empty list means 'no GGUF path makes sense, fall back to manual flags' — but here the real cause is an off-by-threshold gap in the context-shrinking loop, not any actual lack of viable serving options. Concrete scenario: request a profile for a small dense model whose catalog entry has context_length=4096 and vram fits comfortably; compute_serve_profiles returns [], and the caller falls back to manual flags for a model that should have gotten clean Quality/Balanced/Speed presets at ctx=4096.
fix: Don't hardcode the loop's lower bound at 8192; instead floor the shrink loop at the model's own limit, e.g. `floor_ctx = min(model_ctx_max, 8192)` and use `while cur_ctx >= floor_ctx` with `cur_ctx = max(cur_ctx // 2, floor_ctx)`, or simply special-case: if model_ctx_max < 8192, always append a single profile at ctx=model_ctx_max without ever entering the shrink loop.

title: Non-atomic read-modify-write on shared JSON stores lets concurrent writers clobber each other's data
detail: import_data does load_all()/get_all()/load_settings() etc, mutates an in-memory copy, then calls save()/save_settings() with the whole snapshot (lines 79-98 for memories, 170-176 for presets, 181-183 for settings, 188-190 for features, 196-198 for preferences). There is no lock and no optimistic-concurrency check. If any other request (another admin's concurrent import, or an ordinary memory/preset/settings-write endpoint elsewhere in the app) reads and saves in between this read and this save, its update is silently overwritten by the stale snapshot this handler saves back. Concrete scenario: admin A starts a large import (server reads existing memories at t0, is still processing 5000 rows), while at t1 a normal user creates a new memory via the standard memory-add endpoint (read+write completes at t1). At t2 admin A's import calls memory_manager.save(existing) with the t0 snapshot plus imported rows, wiping out the memory the user created at t1. The same pattern applies to settings/features/presets/preferences.
fix: Take a per-resource lock (e.g. asyncio.Lock or a file lock via core.atomic_io) around the read-modify-write sequence for each store during import, or switch these managers to support atomic merge/upsert operations instead of full load+save-the-whole-collection semantics.

title: Synchronous disk I/O executed directly inside async route handlers blocks the event loop
detail: export_data and import_data are 'async def' handlers but call memory_manager.load/load_all/save, skills_manager.load/add_skill, preset_manager.get_all/save, load_settings/save_settings, and load_features/save_features — all confirmed to do blocking file I/O (open()/json.load()/atomic_write_json in src/settings.py:205-219 and src/memory/store.py:109-210) — with no await/executor offload (the only 'await' in the whole file is request.json() at line 68). For a large backup (many thousands of memories/skills) or a slow disk, each of these calls stalls the single asyncio event loop, blocking every other concurrent request the FastAPI process is serving (health checks, chat completions, etc.) until the export/import finishes.
fix: Wrap the manager calls in `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...)` (or `run_in_executor`) so the blocking file I/O runs off the event loop, e.g. `memories = await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(memory_manager.load, user)`, and similarly for the save calls and the skills_manager.add_skill loop.

title: Synchronous SQLAlchemy session used inside async route handlers blocks the event loop
detail: All five handlers (list_drafts, get_draft, create_draft, update_draft, delete_draft) are declared `async def` but call the synchronous `SessionLocal()`/`db.query(...).all()`/`db.commit()` directly (lines 84-92, 97-109, 114-135, 140-167, 172-186). These synchronous DB calls run on the event-loop thread rather than being offloaded, so under load (many concurrent requests, or a slow disk/SQLite lock contention) each blocking call stalls the entire event loop for every other in-flight coroutine in the process, not just this request.
fix: Either make the handlers plain `def` (FastAPI will run them in a threadpool automatically) or move the DB session/session.commit() into `await run_in_threadpool(...)`, or migrate to an async SQLAlchemy engine/session.

title: Synchronous SQLAlchemy session used directly inside an async function blocks the event loop
detail: `run_document_tidy` is `async def`, but `db = SessionLocal()` (core/database.py uses a plain synchronous `sessionmaker` over a sync `create_engine`) and every DB call in this function — `db.query(...).all()` (lines 72/74), the per-doc `db.delete(doc)` calls (lines 125, 165), and `db.commit()` (line 169) — are blocking synchronous calls executed directly on the asyncio event loop thread. This function is awaited from an async request-handling path (`do_manage_documents` in src/tools/implementations.py, itself invoked from a FastAPI route) as well as from the task scheduler. For an owner with a large document set, the full table scan plus row-by-row delete plus commit can take a non-trivial amount of wall-clock time, during which the entire single-threaded event loop is stalled — freezing all other concurrent requests/websocket traffic being served by the same process, not just the caller's own request.
fix: Offload the synchronous DB work to a thread, e.g. wrap the body in `await asyncio.to_thread(_run_document_tidy_sync, owner)` (or use `run_in_executor`), or migrate to an async SQLAlchemy session/engine (`AsyncSession` + `create_async_engine`) so the awaits actually yield control back to the event loop.

title: Synchronous DB I/O executed directly in async route handlers
detail: list_signatures, create_signature, and delete_signature (lines 87-99, 102-128, 131-149) are declared `async def` but call the synchronous SQLAlchemy Session (SessionLocal()) directly — db.query(...).all(), db.commit(), db.delete() — with no run_in_executor/to_thread wrapping. Each of these calls is a blocking syscall (SQLite file I/O) executed on the single asyncio event loop thread. Under concurrent load (e.g. several signature list/create/delete requests overlapping with other async handlers such as chat streaming), each blocking DB call stalls the entire event loop for its duration, delaying unrelated requests app-wide. The codebase itself demonstrates the correct pattern elsewhere (app.py's _touch_last_used wraps its sync DB write in `await asyncio.to_thread(_do)`), showing this file diverges from that convention.
failure_scenario: A user triggers create_signature with a large (near 2MB) PNG while another user's request is mid-stream on an async chat/LLM endpoint sharing the same event loop; the synchronous db.commit() for the signature insert blocks the loop for the duration of the SQLite write, adding latency/stalls to the unrelated concurrent request.
fix: Wrap the DB read/write portions in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`, or switch to an async SQLAlchemy session/engine (aiosqlite) for these routes, consistent with the to_thread pattern already used in app.py.

title: Raw exception text returned to API caller in 500 responses
detail: Lines 126 and 147 build the HTTPException detail as an f-string embedding the raw exception object (`f"Failed to save signature: {e}"` / `f"Failed to delete signature: {e}"`). Depending on the underlying SQLAlchemy/SQLite error, this can leak internal details (file paths, column/constraint names, driver internals) to the HTTP client instead of a generic message, aiding an attacker's reconnaissance of the backend.
failure_scenario: A malformed or constraint-violating write (e.g. a DB-level integrity error, disk-full error revealing the SQLite file path) surfaces the raw driver exception string directly in the JSON error response sent to the client.
fix: Log the full exception server-side (already done via logger.error at line 125 for create) and return a generic client-facing message, e.g. `raise HTTPException(500, "Failed to save signature")`, without interpolating `e` into the response body.

title: Upload size limit enforced only after buffering entire file into memory
detail: Line 79: `content = await file.read()` reads the whole multipart body into a single in-memory bytes object with no size cap, and only afterward (line 80) is `len(content) > MAX_FILE_SIZE` checked. Since there is no auth (see separate finding) and no reverse-proxy body-size limit implied by this file, any caller can POST a multi-GB body to `/api/backgrounds/upload`; the process will attempt to buffer it entirely in RAM before rejecting it, and concurrent large uploads can exhaust memory and crash/OOM-kill the worker. Fix: stream the upload in bounded chunks (e.g. `while chunk := await file.read(1<<20): total += len(chunk); if total > MAX_FILE_SIZE: raise HTTPException(400, ...)`), writing each chunk to disk as you go, or configure a request body size limit ahead of this handler (e.g. via ASGI middleware / ASGI server config) so oversized bodies are rejected before reaching this code.
fix: Read/write the upload in bounded chunks and abort as soon as MAX_FILE_SIZE is exceeded instead of buffering the whole file before checking its length.

title: Upload/delete endpoints have no authentication or ownership check
detail: Lines 66 and 87: both `upload_background` and `delete_background` accept a `Request` parameter but never use it to check identity/authorization. Any client that can reach `/api/backgrounds/upload` or `DELETE /api/backgrounds/{name}` can overwrite or permanently delete another user's background image just by knowing (or guessing/listing via `/api/backgrounds/list`) its filename — there is no per-user directory or ownership metadata, so this is a shared global namespace with no access control. Concrete scenario: user A uploads `vacation.png`; user B calls `DELETE /api/backgrounds/vacation.png` (discovered via the public `/list` endpoint) and deletes it with no ownership verification, or re-uploads a file with the same name to silently replace A's image (upload dedups by appending `_1`, but an attacker can still enumerate and delete first). Fix: require an authenticated user identity (e.g. from `request.state.user` / session) and either scope files under a per-user subdirectory or store/check an owner record before permitting delete/overwrite.
fix: Add authentication/authorization checks using the (currently unused) Request object, and scope background files per-user or verify ownership before delete/overwrite.

title: Blocking synchronous filesystem calls inside async route handlers
detail: Lines 51-63 (`os.makedirs`, `os.listdir`, `os.path.isfile`, `os.path.getsize` in a loop), lines 70-83 (`os.makedirs`, `os.path.exists` loop, synchronous `open(...).write(...)`), and lines 92/99 (`os.remove`, `os.path.isfile`) all perform blocking disk I/O directly inside `async def` handlers. Under FastAPI/uvicorn these run on the single event-loop thread, so a slow/large directory listing or disk write stalls every other concurrent request being served by that worker. With many uploaded backgrounds or a slow disk (e.g. network-mounted storage), `list_backgrounds` in particular does an `os.listdir` + `os.path.getsize` per file on every call, blocking the loop each time. Fix: offload these calls via `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...)` / `run_in_executor`, or use an async file library, especially for `upload_background`'s file write and `list_backgrounds`'s directory scan.
fix: Move blocking os.* / open() calls off the event loop using run_in_executor/anyio.to_thread.run_sync, or an async file I/O library.

title: Dedup key ignores endpoint owner, allowing cross-tenant disabling
detail: `model_endpoints` is a multi-tenant table (has an `owner` column, per core/database.py:821-823, backfilled per-user). `_canon()` (line 33-43) computes a grouping key purely from the URL (host:port+path), and `main()` groups all enabled endpoints across all users by that key alone (line 54-57), with no owner filter. If two different users each configure an endpoint pointing at the same base_url (e.g. both point at the same shared local vLLM/Ollama server, or the same public API base_url like https://api.openai.com/v1), they land in the same group and are treated as duplicates of each other. The scoring/sort at lines 63-74 then keeps only one (e.g. whichever is reachable / has cached models / was updated more recently) and disables the other via `ep.is_enabled = False` at lines 92-96 — even though it belongs to a completely different user who never asked for it to be touched. Running `--apply` in a multi-user deployment can silently disable another user's working, correctly-configured endpoint.
fix: Include the endpoint owner in the grouping key, e.g. `key = (ep.owner or "", _canon(ep.base_url or ""))`, so only endpoints belonging to the same owner (or all sharing NULL/no-owner) are ever compared/disabled against each other.

title: N+1 DB/session hydration inside the per-session loop
detail: For every owned, non-archived session, `session_manager.get_session(session_id)` is called individually inside the loop (lines 53-55) instead of batch-loading histories once. If `get_session` performs a DB lookup (as its docstring purpose — 'load history from DB if needed' — implies), a user with N sessions triggers N sequential round trips per call to `analyze_topics`, and this is invoked synchronously from the `/api/conversations/topics` request handler, blocking on each round trip in turn. A user with a few hundred sessions turns one API request into a few hundred sequential DB queries.
fix: Add/use a batch API on session_manager (e.g. `get_sessions_bulk(ids)` or a single query with `WHERE owner = ? AND archived = 0`) that returns all needed histories in one round trip, then iterate the in-memory result instead of calling get_session per id.

title: Regex patterns recompiled on every message/keyword instead of precompiled once
detail: `re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(kw)}\b", content)` (line 71) and the identical pattern again at line 75 rebuild and recompile a fresh regex string for every (message, topic, keyword) combination — up to 8 topics * ~8 keywords = ~64 regex compiles per message, times every message in every session the owner has. Python's internal regex cache (default size 512) gets thrashed once total distinct compiled patterns from concurrent requests/topics exceed it, defeating even that caching. For a session history of a few thousand messages this becomes a measurable CPU hot path executed synchronously inside the request handler.
fix: Precompile all keyword patterns once at module load time, e.g. `TOPIC_PATTERNS = {t: [(kw, re.compile(rf'\b{re.escape(kw)}\b')) for kw in kws] for t, kws in TOPIC_KEYWORDS.items()}`, and reuse `pattern.search(content)` in the loop instead of rebuilding the pattern string every time.

title: Unbounded per-topic match accumulation before truncation, run synchronously in an async handler
detail: `topic_matches[topic]` (lines 39, 76-82) accumulates every matching sentence across every message in every owned session before any capping happens; only at the very end (line 99, `unique[:5]`) is the list truncated to 5 examples. For a heavy user (many long-lived sessions with e.g. thousands of messages containing common words like 'work' or 'plan'), this list can grow to tens of thousands of dict entries held in memory for the duration of the request, all of it CPU-bound synchronous work executed inline in what is presumably an `async def` route handler (blocking the event loop for other concurrent requests during that time).
fix: Track only a bounded number of examples per topic while scanning (e.g. stop appending to topic_matches[topic] once len() reaches a small cap like 20, since only 5 are ever used) and/or move analyze_topics execution off the event loop via `run_in_threadpool`/`asyncio.to_thread` if the FastAPI route awaits it directly.

title: DNS rebinding / TOCTOU bypasses the SSRF guard entirely
detail: check_outbound_url() resolves the hostname (lines 74-80), validates the returned IPs, and returns ok/reason — but it never pins or returns the validated IP for the caller to actually connect to. Per the module docstring, the caller (the /api/embeddings/endpoint flow) then makes a *separate* httpx call using the same hostname, which triggers its own independent DNS resolution. An attacker who controls the DNS record for the supplied hostname (e.g. a domain they own, or via a short-TTL rebinding setup) can serve a safe public IP at check time and then flip the record to 169.254.169.254 or a private/loopback address by the time httpx connects milliseconds later, completely bypassing the link-local/private-IP block this module exists to enforce. Because the guard checks a hostname rather than a pinned connection, it provides no real protection against this classic SSRF bypass technique.
fix: Have check_outbound_url() (or a wrapper) return the validated IP address(es) alongside ok/reason, and require callers to connect using the pinned IP (e.g. via httpx's transport-level IP override / Host header trick, or resolving once and passing the resolved address into the connection) rather than re-resolving the hostname at request time.

title: Blocking DNS resolution called synchronously from async request handlers
detail: _default_resolver() calls socket.getaddrinfo() synchronously (line 31), and check_outbound_url() calls it directly with no async wrapper. Per the module docstring this function is meant to run 'before the server makes a request to a user-supplied URL' triggered by an API endpoint (POST /api/embeddings/endpoint), which in a FastAPI app is normally an `async def` handler. A synchronous getaddrinfo() call can block for seconds on a slow/unresponsive DNS server, and since it runs directly on the event loop thread (not offloaded to a thread pool), it will stall all other concurrent requests being served by that worker for the duration of the DNS lookup.
fix: Run the resolution via `await loop.run_in_executor(None, resolve, host)` in the async caller, or provide an async variant of check_outbound_url that offloads socket.getaddrinfo to a thread pool before calling from request handlers.

title: Unbounded growth of _log dict — no cap on number of distinct keys
detail: self._log (line 20) is a plain dict with no maximum size and no per-request eviction; growth is only trimmed periodically by _maybe_cleanup (line 40), which runs at most once every _cleanup_interval (>=120s, line 23) and only when check() happens to be called after that interval has elapsed. Between cleanups, every distinct key passed to check() gets its own list entry that is never removed while it keeps being 'refreshed' (any key hit again before it goes stale survives the sweep at line 46). If the key is derived from attacker-controllable data (e.g. client IP, or worse X-Forwarded-For/X-Real-IP as is common for rate limiters behind a proxy), an attacker can send a burst of requests each with a distinct/spoofed key, causing _log to accumulate one list per key with no bound, consuming memory that is only reclaimed on the next scheduled cleanup pass — and even then only for keys that go fully idle. A sustained low-rate flood of unique keys (below max_requests each, so never rejected) keeps every key 'fresh' forever and the dict never shrinks, giving an unbounded memory-growth DoS.
fix: Bound the number of tracked keys (e.g. LRU eviction with a max size, or a TTL cache such as cachetools.TTLCache) instead of an unbounded dict, and/or run cleanup based on dict size (e.g. trigger a sweep once len(self._log) exceeds a threshold) rather than purely on elapsed time.

title: file_to_data_url reads entire file into memory with no size bound
detail: open(path, 'rb').read() loads the whole file into memory, then base64-encodes it (roughly 1.33x the size again) before returning a single string. If this is ever called on a large or attacker-influenced file (e.g. an uploaded attachment), it can spike memory usage significantly with no cap or streaming. Not currently exploitable from any caller found in the repo (function appears unused outside this module), but it is a latent DoS vector if wired up to user-controlled paths.
fix: Add an explicit size check (os.path.getsize) before reading, or stream/chunk the base64 encoding, and reject files above a configured limit.

title: read_if_exists swallows all exceptions, not just 'file not found'
detail: The bare `except Exception` catches everything, not just FileNotFoundError: permission errors (PermissionError), the path being a directory (IsADirectoryError), or a UnicodeDecodeError from unexpected binary content all silently return ''. A caller relying on this for a config/prompt file would treat a permission-misconfiguration or encoding corruption identically to 'file legitimately absent', hiding a real operational bug.
fix: Catch FileNotFoundError specifically (and optionally IsADirectoryError) and let other exceptions propagate or be logged.

title: Dead 'skip page with no widgets' check causes unconditional get_text() on every page
detail: In extract_fields (lines 160-163), `widgets = page.widgets() or []` never falls back to `[]` because fitz.Page.widgets() is a generator function — the returned generator object is always truthy even when it will yield zero items (confirmed against installed pymupdf 1.28.0 source: `def widgets(self, types=None): ... for xref in widget_xrefs: yield widget`). This makes `if not widgets: continue` dead code, so `words = page.get_text("words")` (a full text/word extraction pass) runs on every page of every processed PDF, including pages with no form widgets at all. For multi-page content PDFs with only a handful of widget-bearing pages (the exact case the module's own docstrings describe — Excel-exported invoices with stray widgets, long contracts with one signature page), this wastes a full-page text extraction on every non-form page each time extract_fields is invoked.
fix: Materialize the generator before testing truthiness: `widgets = list(page.widgets() or [])` so pages with zero widgets are correctly skipped and get_text("words") is only called when needed.

title: Blocking Docker SDK calls executed directly inside async route handlers
detail: All three routes (`status`, `start`, `stop`) are declared `async def` but call the synchronous `docker` SDK (`docker.from_env()`, `client.containers.list()`, `container.start()`, `client.images.pull()`, `client.containers.run()`, `container.stop()`) directly on the event loop with no `run_in_threadpool`/`asyncio.to_thread`. `client.images.pull(...)` at line 133 in particular can block for tens of seconds to minutes while downloading a multi-GB image over the network. Because FastAPI runs all `async def` handlers on the single event loop, this call (and the others) stalls every other concurrent request being served by that worker for the full duration — a single `/api/docker/ollama/start` call while an image pull is needed effectively DoSes the whole app for that worker.
fix: Either declare these route functions as plain `def` (FastAPI will run them in a worker thread pool automatically) or wrap the blocking docker-SDK calls with `await run_in_threadpool(...)` / `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`.

title: New Docker client created and never closed on every request
detail: `_docker_client()` calls `docker.from_env()` on every invocation of `/status`, `/start`, and `/stop` (lines 106, 116, 153) and the resulting `DockerClient` (which owns a urllib3 connection pool / unix-socket transport) is never closed — there is no `client.close()` and no context-manager usage anywhere in the file. Under sustained polling of `/status` (a natural pattern for a UI that shows container state), this steadily leaks open sockets/file descriptors until the process hits its FD limit and subsequent Docker calls (or any other socket use in the process) start failing.
fix: Wrap the docker calls in a `try/finally: client.close()` block, or cache a single module-level `docker.DockerClient` instance and reuse it across requests instead of constructing/discarding one per call.

title: No authorization check on container start/stop/status endpoints
detail: `/api/docker/ollama/start` and `/stop` let any caller who can reach this router start or stop a Docker container, and `start` will additionally pull an arbitrary-sized image from docker.io and bind it to `0.0.0.0:{_OLLAMA_PORT}` (line 142) exposing it on all interfaces. There is no `Depends(current_user)`/permission check visible in this file gating these state-changing operations, so if the router is mounted without an upstream auth dependency, any unauthenticated user can trigger image pulls (bandwidth/disk exhaustion) or repeatedly start/stop the container (denial of service against legitimate users of the Ollama service).
fix: Add an explicit auth/permission dependency (e.g. `Depends(require_admin)` or similar) to the `start` and `stop` routes so only authorized users can change container state.

title: Container lookup silently swallows all exceptions
detail: `_find_ollama_container` catches `Exception` and does `pass`, returning `None` regardless of the failure cause (e.g. Docker daemon permission error, malformed filter, socket timeout). Callers treat a `None` return as "container does not exist" — e.g. in `start()` (line 120-121) this leads the code down the 'create new container' path even when the real problem was a transient Docker API error, potentially attempting `client.containers.run(...)` and hitting a confusing 'container name already in use' error instead of surfacing the actual underlying failure to the caller/logs.
fix: Log the exception (`logger.warning("Failed to look up ollama container: %s", exc)`) before returning `None`, and consider re-raising for error classes that are not simple 'not found' cases so `start`/`stop` can report the real cause.

title: Unbounded growth of query_patterns dict / analytics file
detail: `_record_query` (lines 97-120) inserts a new key into `analytics['query_patterns']` for every distinct query string ever seen, with no cap, TTL, or eviction. In a long-running production instance this dict — and the on-disk `search_analytics.json` it is serialized to on every single query (line 120) — grows without bound as users issue novel search queries. Over time this makes `_save_analytics` (a full-file rewrite on every call) increasingly slow and the JSON file increasingly large, degrading `get_search_stats`/`_record_query` latency and disk usage indefinitely. There is no top-N trim or LRU eviction of `query_patterns` anywhere in the module.
fix: Cap the number of tracked patterns (e.g. keep only the top N by count using a bounded structure, or evict least-recently-used entries) before writing back, e.g. after updating: `if len(patterns) > MAX_PATTERNS: keep only the most common N via Counter(patterns_counts).most_common(N)`.

title: Non-atomic read-modify-write race on shared analytics file
detail: `_record_query` does load-JSON -> mutate in-memory dict -> write-JSON with no locking (file lock, threading.Lock, or atomic increment) around the three steps (lines 99-120). Under concurrent requests (multiple threads/workers/async tasks calling `searxng_search_results` simultaneously, which is the normal case for a web service), two callers can both `_load_analytics()` the same counters, increment their own in-memory copies, and then `_save_analytics()` — the second writer's save clobbers the first writer's increments, silently losing counts (total_queries, successful_queries, cache_hits, per-query pattern counts). This makes `get_search_stats()` under-report traffic under load, and the write itself (`open(..., 'w')` at line 91) is not atomic (no temp-file + rename), so a crash or concurrent write mid-`json.dump` can also corrupt/truncate the file, which `_load_analytics` would then silently fall back to `_default_analytics()` for (line 83-85), losing all history.
fix: Serialize access with a module-level `threading.Lock()` around the load+mutate+save sequence in `_record_query`, and make `_save_analytics` atomic by writing to a temp file and `os.replace()`-ing it over `ANALYTICS_FILE`; alternatively move the counters into the existing SQLite/DB layer with a single atomic UPDATE instead of a JSON file.

title: Blocking synchronous HTTP calls executed inside async route handlers
detail: do_web_search (line 60), search_with_provider (line 103), and list_search_providers (lines 76-79 via _get_provider_key/_get_search_instance) call comprehensive_web_search / _call_provider / _get_provider_key / _get_search_instance directly (no await, no run_in_executor/to_thread). These are plain `def` functions in services/search/core.py and services/search/providers.py that perform synchronous outbound HTTP requests to external search providers (searxng, brave, duckduckgo, google_pse, tavily, serper). Since the route handlers are `async def`, calling a blocking network function directly ties up the single asyncio event loop thread for the full duration of the HTTP request (can be seconds, longer on timeouts/retries). Under concurrent load, one slow/stalled search provider request stalls ALL other requests being served by the same worker (including unrelated endpoints like health checks, chat, etc.), causing cascading latency or apparent hangs.
fix: Wrap the blocking calls with `await run_in_threadpool(comprehensive_web_search, ...)` (from starlette.concurrency) or `await asyncio.to_thread(_call_provider, ...)`, e.g. in do_web_search: `context, sources = await run_in_threadpool(comprehensive_web_search, query, return_sources=True, time_filter=time_filter)`; similarly for `_call_provider` in search_with_provider and for `_get_provider_key`/`_get_search_instance` in list_search_providers.

title: Orphaned .cache files never get deleted after process restart, growing disk usage unboundedly
detail: search_cache_index / content_cache_index (lines 27-28) are plain in-memory module-level dicts, not persisted to disk. cleanup_cache() only ever iterates cache_index.items() (line 45) to decide what to delete; it builds files_in_dir (line 42) solely to check whether an *indexed* key is missing its backing file (line 46), but never does the reverse check of removing a file that exists on disk but has no corresponding entry in cache_index. Concrete failure: the process restarts (deploy, crash, worker respawn) — the in-memory index resets to {} while every previously written *.cache file remains in SEARCH_CACHE_DIR/CONTENT_CACHE_DIR. From then on, cleanup_cache(cache_dir, cache_index, max_age) iterates an empty/near-empty cache_index, so to_remove stays empty for those orphans, and neither the age-based expiry nor the CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES cap (lines 55-62, which also only look at cache_index) ever touches them. The cache directory grows without bound across restarts, and CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES is not actually an enforced ceiling on disk usage, only on the (possibly reset) in-memory index.
fix: In cleanup_cache, also delete any file in files_in_dir whose key is not present in cache_index (i.e. compute orphans = set(files_in_dir) - set(cache_index) and unlink them), or persist the index to disk / rebuild it from directory contents (with file mtimes) at startup so restarts don't lose eviction bookkeeping.

title: Unsynchronized read-modify-write on shared module-level cache_index/cache_metrics during blocking file I/O
detail: search_cache_index, content_cache_index and cache_metrics (lines 27-31) are shared mutable module state with no lock anywhere in the file. cleanup_cache mutates cache_index (pop) and increments cache_metrics['evictions'] (lines 51-53, 58-62) while also performing blocking syscalls (Path.glob at line 42, Path.unlink at lines 49 and 61) inside the same function. If cleanup_cache is invoked concurrently for the same cache_index — e.g. two overlapping requests each trigger a cache-write-then-cleanup cycle and this function runs in different threadpool threads (typical for FastAPI when sync code is offloaded via run_in_executor) — the unlink() calls release the GIL, allowing interleaving: both threads independently snapshot cache_index (line 45 and line 56), both compute their own to_remove/excess_count from stale reads, and the cache_metrics['evictions'] += 1 read-modify-write (not a single atomic bytecode) can lose increments. The net effect is inaccurate eviction metrics and cache_index size enforcement (CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES at line 55) that can drift from the true state because two threads race to trim to the same target count using stale length reads.
fix: Add a module-level threading.Lock() and hold it for the full read-decide-mutate critical section in cleanup_cache (snapshot, unlink decisions, and all cache_index/cache_metrics mutations), so concurrent callers serialize instead of racing on the shared dicts.

title: Synchronous, potentially CPU/network-bound transcription call blocks the event loop
detail: Line 41 calls `stt_service.transcribe(audio_bytes)` directly (no `await`, no `run_in_executor`/`asyncio.to_thread`) inside `async def transcribe_audio`. `STTService.transcribe` (services/stt/stt_service.py:156) is a fully synchronous method: for the 'local' provider it runs Whisper inference (CPU-bound, can take seconds to tens of seconds for a 25MB audio file), and for the 'endpoint:' provider it does a blocking `httpx.post(..., timeout=60)` (services/stt/stt_service.py:144). Because FastAPI runs `async def` handlers on the single event-loop thread, this call stalls the entire event loop for the duration of transcription/HTTP call, freezing every other concurrent request (including unrelated endpoints like `/api/stt/stats` or health checks) for up to 60+ seconds per request.
fix: Offload the blocking call: `text = await asyncio.to_thread(stt_service.transcribe, audio_bytes)` (or run it via `loop.run_in_executor`), so the event loop stays free while transcription/HTTP I/O completes.

title: Unhandled ValueError on malformed gpu_count crashes the /models request with a raw 500
detail: At L169, `n = int(gpu_count)` is called with no try/except, unlike the equivalent conversions at L154-157 (gpu_group) and L192-195 (ctx) which both wrap `int(...)` in try/except ValueError. If a caller sends `GET /api/hwfit/models?gpu_count=abc`, this raises an unhandled ValueError inside the route handler, producing an unhandled-exception 500 instead of the graceful fallback used everywhere else in the same function for equivalent malformed input.
fix: Wrap the conversion the same way the other numeric params are handled, e.g. `try: n = int(gpu_count) except ValueError: n = 1` (or return a 400) before using it in the branch starting at L168.

title: rebuild() deletes existing collections before confirming new lanes are usable, causing silent full data loss
detail: rebuild() (lines 187-243) first calls client.delete_collection() on all three lane collection names (lines 201-205), unconditionally destroying all existing memory vectors, and only afterwards calls build_embedding_lanes() (line 208) to recreate lanes. Unlike __init__ (line 40: `if not self._lanes: raise RuntimeError(...)`), rebuild() never checks whether build_embedding_lanes() returned an empty list. If the embedding backend is temporarily unavailable (the exact condition __init__ guards against), self._lanes becomes [], the `for lane in self._lanes:` insert loop at line 229 silently does nothing, and the function returns normally after logging an info message that misleadingly reports success (line 243: 'MemoryVectorStore rebuilt with {len(ids)} entries...' — len(ids) is the count attempted, not the count actually inserted). The caller gets no exception and no signal that all memories were just permanently deleted with none restored. Concrete scenario: a background job calls memory_store.rebuild(all_memories) while the embedding service/chromadb is briefly down; the old collections are dropped, build_embedding_lanes() returns [], and the store ends up empty and healthy (self._healthy stays True since it isn't touched here) with all searches/finds returning [] from then on, with no error raised anywhere.
fix: Guard the rebuild the same way __init__ does: after line 208, `if not self._lanes: raise RuntimeError("rebuild failed: no embedding lanes available")` before deleting anything, or better — build the new lanes and verify they are populated BEFORE calling delete_collection on the old ones, so a failed rebuild leaves the previous data intact instead of destroying it first.

title: Non-atomic check-then-insert in add() can create duplicate vectors under concurrent calls
detail: add() (lines 103-119) does `existing = lane.collection.get(ids=[memory_id])`, checks `if existing["ids"]: continue`, and only then calls `lane.collection.add(...)`. If two requests add the same memory_id concurrently (e.g. two FastAPI worker threads/async tasks processing the same memory-save event, or a retry racing the original), both can pass the existence check before either has inserted, resulting in duplicate/racing writes to the same id in the underlying chroma collection (behavior then depends on chromadb's own dedup semantics, which are not guaranteed here) and inconsistent state across lanes if one lane wins the race and another doesn't.
fix: Rely on chromadb's own upsert semantics instead of check-then-add: call `lane.collection.upsert(ids=[memory_id], ...)` (chromadb supports upsert directly) so the operation is atomic and idempotent, removing the need for the separate get() check entirely.

title: rebuild() mutates self._lanes while concurrent add()/search() hold references to already-deleted chroma collections
detail: rebuild() calls client.delete_collection() on the live collection names (lines 201-205) and only afterward reassigns self._lanes = build_embedding_lanes(...) (line 208). There is no lock around this class, and other threads/async tasks can be concurrently executing add()/search()/remove() using the previous self._lanes list captured at loop-start (e.g. `for lane in self._lanes:` at line 107). During the window between delete_collection() and the reassignment, any concurrent add() call will invoke methods on a lane.collection object whose backing chroma collection was just deleted, raising an exception that add() only logs as a warning (line 119) — the caller believes the memory was added but it silently was not, and there is no retry or surfacing of the failure.
fix: Protect rebuild()'s delete+recreate sequence and the lane list swap with a lock (e.g. `threading.RLock`) also held by add()/remove()/search() around their use of self._lanes, or perform rebuild by building the new lanes into a fresh object first and only doing the atomic swap-and-delete-old at the very end, so in-flight operations never observe a torn state.

title: Module-global _last_print dict keyed by id(self) is never cleaned up and can alias between distinct PipeTqdm instances
detail: `_last_print` (line 17) is a process-global dict that PipeTqdm.update() (lines 61-65) writes into using `id(self)` as the key, but PipeTqdm.close() (lines 111-112) never removes the corresponding entry. huggingface_hub's snapshot_download creates one PipeTqdm instance per downloaded file (and can run several in parallel via max_workers, line 167), so over the course of downloading a repo with many shards/files, `_last_print` accumulates one stale float entry per file for the remainder of the process — never freed until the script exits. Separately, because CPython can reuse the same `id()` for a new PipeTqdm object once an earlier one is garbage-collected, a freshly created instance can inherit a stale timestamp left behind by an unrelated, already-closed instance, causing incorrect throttling (e.g. suppressing that new file's first progress line) — a real correctness bug from using an object's memory address as a durable dict key. Concrete scenario: downloading a repo with hundreds of sharded weight files causes hundreds of leaked entries in `_last_print`, and whenever a GC'd PipeTqdm's id is reused by a new file's progress bar, that new bar's first update is silently throttled based on the dead object's last-print time.
fix: Give each PipeTqdm instance a stable, private last-print timestamp field (e.g. `self._last_print = 0`) instead of a module-global dict keyed by `id(self)`, eliminating both the unbounded accumulation and the id-reuse aliasing. If cross-instance throttling truly is required, at minimum pop the entry in close(): `_last_print.pop(id(self), None)`.

title: index() has no bound on directory size / result list
