detail: index() indexes an entire directory in one synchronous call and index_personal_documents presumably walks the whole tree in memory before returning indexed/failed/errors lists. If a caller points this at a very large directory, this single request call has no pagination/streaming/limit, so it can run for a very long time and build large in-memory error lists, compounding the blocking-event-loop issue above.
fix: Consider streaming/batching the indexing work and/or capping the number of files processed per call, or making this an explicitly background/async-task-queue operation rather than a single request-response call.

title: Synchronous blocking network calls invoked from async request handlers
detail: get_chroma_client() performs a blocking socket.create_connection() probe (line 25) and a blocking chromadb.HttpClient(...).heartbeat() call (lines 59-64). It is a plain 'def', not 'async def', and get_rag_manager()/callers in routes/personal_routes.py invoke it synchronously inside 'async def' route handlers (e.g. personal_routes.py lines 126, 174, 197, 269 call _rag() -> get_rag_manager() -> get_chroma_client()). Under FastAPI/uvicorn's single-threaded event loop, if ChromaDB is slow or the network probe takes close to CHROMADB_CONNECT_TIMEOUT (2s default), the entire event loop stalls for that duration on every concurrent request until the singleton is cached, blocking all other in-flight requests.
fix: Wrap the first-time initialization in fastapi.concurrency.run_in_threadpool (or asyncio.to_thread) at the call sites, or make get_chroma_client async and offload the socket probe / HttpClient creation to a thread.

title: Unsynchronized global singleton write is a benign but real race under concurrent first calls
detail: get_chroma_client() reads/writes the module-global _client without a lock (lines 37-65). If two requests race in before the first caches _client, both will run the connect probe + HttpClient() + heartbeat() concurrently (wasted work, doubled connections at startup), and the last one to finish wins the assignment. Not corruption-level since chromadb.HttpClient is stateless-ish, but it's a non-atomic check-then-act on shared mutable state.
fix: Guard the check-and-set with a threading.Lock (or asyncio.Lock if this becomes async) around the double-checked-locking pattern.

title: Blocking VectorRAG construction invoked synchronously from async route handlers
detail: get_rag_manager() is a plain 'def' that synchronously constructs VectorRAG(persist_directory=persist_dir) (line 46), which internally calls into ChromaDB (get_chroma_client(), collection setup, embedding lane init) — all blocking I/O. routes/personal_routes.py calls this directly inside 'async def' handlers (e.g. lines 126, 174, 197, 269: 'rag = _rag()') without run_in_threadpool/to_thread. On every retry window boundary (every _RETRY_INTERVAL=30s when ChromaDB was previously down, or on cold start), a request thread will block the entire asyncio event loop for however long VectorRAG init/ChromaDB heartbeat takes, stalling all other concurrent requests being served by the same worker.
fix: Offload the VectorRAG(...) construction via 'await run_in_threadpool(VectorRAG, persist_directory=persist_dir)' inside an async wrapper, or convert get_rag_manager to async and have callers await it.

title: Unsynchronized global singleton read-modify-write on rag_instance / _last_attempt
detail: rag_instance and _last_attempt (module globals) are read and written without any lock across concurrent requests (lines 32-58). Two concurrent requests arriving when rag_instance is None and the retry window has just elapsed can both pass the 'now - _last_attempt < _RETRY_INTERVAL' check and both proceed to construct a second VectorRAG instance concurrently, wasting a ChromaDB connection/heartbeat and briefly having two live VectorRAG objects before the second assignment wins.
fix: Guard the check/construct/assign sequence with a threading.Lock so only one caller performs the (re)initialization while others either wait or get the throttled None.
